Social Darwinists to tech bros: tracing the long fight against equality in US
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
16:38:06 UTC
01:38:06 KST

The historian Kim Phillips-Fein’s new book is published amid celebrations of the 250th anniversary of the declaration of independence and its truth “self-evident, that all men are created equal.” Country of Lords, however, is a history of Neo-Aristocrats, Social Darwinists, Tech Utopians and the Long Fight Against Equality in America.
Concise and hard-hitting, the book arrives at a time of glaring social and economic inequality, Phillips-Fein seeing Elon Musk “emerging as a trillionaire very much on people’s minds, with a deep level of discomfort, both fear and anger about what this portends.”
“It’s always hard to know what’s going to be happening when you have written a book,” she said. “But I think those questions about economic equality and the impact of extreme levels of economic hierarchy and concentration, and the questions, ‘Can you still have a democracy any longer? What are the ways that you can counter that? What alternate visions are there if you want to live in a world that’s not characterized that way?’, are present.”
Photo: AP
RIGHTS FOR THE POOR
Phillips-Fein studies conservatism and “questions about capitalism and democracy.” Her first book, Invisible Hands, was a study of businessmen who fought the New Deal of the 1930s. Her second, Fear City, about the New York economic crisis of the 1970s, was a finalist for the Pulitzer prize. Hers is a major voice. It’s also unique. Not many books start with founder John Adams and end with Peter Thiel of Palantir, Musk’s fellow techno-fascist. Might such company seem unfair on Adams, the Boston lawyer who was part of a great revolution but feared what was unleashed?
“I hope this comes through,” Phillips-Fein said. “Adams is very different from [steel magnate] Andrew Carnegie and [Yale professor] William Graham Sumner and the late 19th-century social Darwinists, and the pro-slavery advocates. He’s also definitely very different from people who are saying extreme levels of economic inequality are good.” Adams, however, was “very ambivalent and skeptical of egalitarian claims … during and after the French Revolution: a deep sense of you can have too much egalitarianism.”
Photo: AFP
“In his writing, he does also give a strong kind of conservative temperament and foundational sense of the problems of arguing for greater equality and a deep wariness and sense of pessimism about a politics that claims to do that.”
And so Adams takes his place in Country of Lords. Other subjects include preachers of race-based inequality from George Fitzhugh, a Confederate theorist of slavery as natural good, to Theodore Lothrop Stoddard, a hack journalist who had a huge bestseller in 1920 with The Rising Tide of Color Against White World-Supremacy, “part of a larger intellectual subculture of ‘scientific’ racism … in the aftermath of world war one.”
There is also Carnegie, the Scottish-born tycoon who flourished in the Gilded Age of the late 19th century.
“What makes Carnegie so interesting is that he at least allows himself to have some sense of ambivalence,” Phillips-Fein said. “He says that while the concentration of wealth is absolutely necessary and inevitable, and the people at the top … should have the ultimate say over resources, he is deeply aware that this is politically dangerous, that … it creates an unstable society in which the poor and the working class might actually hate the wealthy, and that’s not in the interest of the wealthy in the long run. Also, he has a sense that human brotherhood is lost, or some kind of community that had existed.”
Carnegie’s father was a Chartist, seeking working-class rights. Carnegie’s major outlet for doubts about his wealth came through philanthropy, prominently the construction of libraries for working people.
“He had a very deep sense of paternalism,” Phillips-Fein said. “He was very invested in the idea of business as a romance and kind of a space of adventure and conquest and feudal benevolence. I think Carnegie’s answer was ultimately that the wealthy should have their money but they shouldn’t bequeath much to their descendants, they should invest it in massive philanthropic projects, and this was better than raising wages or other things like that … It is his level of guilt and ambivalence that I think does make him appealing, if also troubling. I think it raises a set of questions that he certainly was never really able to resolve.”
The 1892 Carnegie Steel strike and its violent suppression devastated Homestead, Pennsylvania, and left Carnegie disillusioned. Now, in Washington, Carnegie Science is the Qatari embassy. At Mount Vernon, the Carnegie library hosts an Apple Store.
INEQUALITY
Country of Lords is also a primer on modern inequality. In the early 1900s, Henry Ford mixed mass auto production with vicious racism. In mid-century, William Shockley was a proto-tech mogul “who went completely off the rails.”
“He was a co-inventor of the transistor and he figures in different histories of Silicon Valley because he ran this company and wanted to maintain a tremendous amount of control, and as a result a bunch of the employees quit and founded their own firm [two eventually founding Intel] … So after Shockley Labs fell apart, Shockley started to become drawn to racist science, pseudoscience and IQ testing in particular. I don’t think anybody really knows exactly what triggered this, but he starts to talk a lot about it publicly in the mid-60s. He was at Stanford at the time. He was supposed to be teaching physics and engineering.”
Shockley, Phillips-Fein says, was really “a uniquely horrible person, and probably quite unhappy as well.”
If that sounds familiar, also like Musk, Shockley wasn’t unique. Linked to the meritocratic movement of the mid-century, he was “not isolated. He is actually part of what is a growing, troubling community of people who coalesce in the late 60s, early 70s, and who are really responding, not always directly, to the context of the civil rights movement.
“It was obviously focused on overturning racist legislation that undergirded segregation, but it also made claims about the distribution of resources, saying the reasons for Black poverty are not innate, they reflect centuries of legal and political structures that have upheld white wealth and laid the foundation for exploitation of Black workers and working-class people, and the political disfranchisement has resulted in this distribution of resources. In other words, that’s nothing to do with merit at all.”
In such soil, Phillips-Fein finds the roots of “the tech titans of today,” rejecting liberal ideals.
“They are very skeptical and hostile towards elite institutions, or at least, have a very broad relationship to them,” she said. “So Peter Thiel embraces this set of ideas about competition drawn from the economist Joseph Schumpeter. He writes about how companies in a normal marketplace are competing at the margins … but every so often someone will come along and create a new invention, usually that winds up dominating the marketplace and changing it, and whoever does that first will completely change the marketplace.
“Thiel has the same idea. He kind of writes about how, ‘I was growing up, I wanted to be the best, I wanted to go to these elite institutions. I went to law school, I had the straight and narrow path, but then I realized that all that was wrong, and actually you had to disrupt everything, create your own monopoly, a monopoly of one: nobody else can ever be you,’ and then the people who are kind of blessed with this genius to recognize how to create something completely new in the world, those are the people who will deserve to win in this race and deserve to command the resources of society.”
The Country of Lords endures.

Instead, major forest fires typically occur during October to April, when the country is drier. The death toll from a magnitude 7.4 earthquake that struck western Colombia has risen to 239, according to a damage assessment released Wednesday by the National Unit for Disaster Risk Management (UNGRD).
The quake, centered in the area of San Jose del Palmar, affected 14 departments and 403 municipalities, said the assessment.

The quake has triggered an emergency response across affected areas, with international assistance also offered to Colombia.

“They laid down their weapons, raised their hands”: Russia has executed at least 345 surrendered Ukrainian soldiers on the ground
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
16:34:12 UTC
01:34:12 KST

Russian forces have executed at least 345 Ukrainian soldiers who surrendered since the start of the full-scale war, Ukrainian Ombudsperson Dmytro Lubinets said at a press conference at Ukrinform.
The figure is the latest point on a documented and rising curve of a systematic war crime. Ukraine's prosecutors and international monitors have tracked these killings from 268 confirmed by July 2025 to over 330 by March 2026. Financial Times investigation found the executions appear to be systematic military policy directed from Russian command, with intercepted orders to "shoot prisoners on the spot."
The victims had surrendered
Lubinets described people killed after they had given up.
"It means that they laid down their weapons, came out with raised hands, lay on the ground, and showed they were no longer fighting," he said, and Russian soldiers examined them and confirmed they were unarmed.
Then the soldiers killed them.
"We have recorded cases where they fully demand that the clothes be removed. And after that, they force them to lie on the ground the same way, and shoot the Ukrainian soldiers at point-blank range," Lubinets added.
Killing a surrendered soldier is a war crime
Lubinets stressed the legal character of the act. The killing of soldiers who have surrendered is a distinct war crime, he said.
The prohibition is absolute. Under the Geneva Conventions, a soldier who lays down arms and surrenders is protected, and killing a prisoner of war is a grave breach of international law. Common Article 3 of the Third Geneva Convention prohibits "violence to life and person, in particular murder of all kinds" against those who have laid down their arms, with no battlefield circumstance that permits it, per the ICRC.
The count keeps rising and accountability lags
Ukraine documents each case for eventual prosecution, but most perpetrators are in Russia, beyond reach, and Russian courts and media have glorified the killings rather than punished them.

Exclusive: Major changes expected within Iraq's Popular Mobilisation Forces
Major changes are expected within Iraq's Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF), influential sources within the group told The New Arab, including the replacement of its chairman, Faleh al-Fayyad, who was formally appointed in 2020, and chief of staff Abdul Aziz al-Mohammadawi, known as Abu Fadak.
Mohammadawi emerged publicly and assumed his post after his predecessor, Jamal Jaafar, known as Abu Mahdi al-Muhandis, was assassinated in a US airstrike in January 2020.
The sources told The New Arab on Wednesday that other changes are also expected, representing the first steps towards further integrating the PMF into Iraq's regular security and military system.
The changes come amid US pressure on Baghdad to regulate the PMF's status and restrict the weapons of Iran-aligned factions incorporated into and funded by the PMF itself.
The sources told The New Arab that "the committee for restricting weapons to state control, which was formed in March, has finally reached several measures concerning the Popular Mobilisation Forces, including changing the PMF uniform and providing it with new clothing, insignia and ranks, under the heading of replacing its visual identity, so that it is closer to the visual identity of the Iraqi army and the rest of the security branches, and preventing the use of religious and sectarian propaganda during tours and security and military operations when the PMF carries them out".
They also spoke of "organising the status of older personnel, as the issue of retirement from the PMF remains complicated and confusing because this matter has not been regulated through clear legal procedures".
The sources added that "the latest directives call for the inclusion of army officers with senior ranks in the PMF ranks to restructure security duties, the deployment map and disciplined compliance with military orders".
"The directives also included redistributing fighters among brigades and provinces after an electronic database was restructured and made subject to military procedures, with no mediation from brigade commanders or factions incorporated into the Popular Mobilisation Forces as part of eliminating intermediary directives and establishing the final relationship of affiliation with the armed forces' leadership, rather than with the leaders and formations that emerged with the establishment of the PMF and which exploited the PMF for political and electoral purposes."
According to political sources who spoke to The New Arab, "Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi, backed by Shia political movements and parties, is seeking to implement these measures after removing Faleh al-Fayyad, who is clinging to the post and unwilling to leave it, despite political efforts on more than one occasion to remove him".
The sources also referred to accusations made by political forces that Fayyad exploited PMF brigades and formed new brigades to support his electoral list and his party, the Ata Movement.
They noted that "the Asaib Ahl al-Haq group, which surrendered its weapons and announced its separation from the Popular Mobilisation Forces and its decision to focus solely on political activity, has renewed its demand for the position of chairman of the Popular Mobilisation Forces and for Fayyad to be removed".
They added that despite the persistent efforts and numerous media campaigns waged by Asaib against Fayyad, Zaidi's view is to replace Fayyad with a military commander from within the "Popular Mobilisation Forces" who believes in the Iraqi state.
Three candidates for the post are not affiliated with a political party or entity.
Regarding Abu Fadak, commander of the PMF's staff, the sources said that "he is among the security changes proposed by the Zaidi government, which are in line with changing plans and bringing in new blood".
"But the real reason behind his replacement is to comply with the US desire not to allow those it has sanctioned over allegations of corruption and terrorism to remain in positions in the Iraqi state," they said.
They expected that "the position of chief of staff of the Popular Mobilisation Forces may pose a difficult situation in the coming period because the post is considered the second most important position within the PMF, in addition to being of great benefit to the factions, particularly Hezbollah Brigades, which is close to Abu Fadak".
Over the past weeks, the Asaib Ahl al-Haq movement, led by Qais al-Khazali, has resumed discussing failures within the PMF as part of a campaign against Faleh al-Fayyad and efforts to push for his dismissal.
The campaign intensified after Saudi-US airstrikes targeted PMF headquarters in more than one Iraqi province at the end of July, killing and wounding about 60 PMF members.
This was followed by leaks claiming that "Zaidi had informed Fayyad to evacuate the headquarters before the bombing, after receiving information about the planned strikes, but Fayyad did not take any precautions to prevent the PMF fighters from being killed".
Asaib Ahl al-Haq used this issue as part of its campaign to remove Fayyad from his post.
Sheikhani: Fayyad should be questioned after PMF headquarters bombed
Commenting on the issue, Hussein al-Sheikhani, a member of the political bureau of the Asaib Ahl al-Haq movement, said Zaidi "had informed the leaders of the Coordination Framework of the details of the strike during a meeting attended by Fayyad, but an unclear matter that we do not know about prevented the latter from taking measures to protect the Popular Mobilisation Forces fighters".
He told The New Arab that "Parliament is required to question Fayyad after the incident in which PMF headquarters were bombed by Saudi Arabia and then move towards dismissing or holding those responsible accountable according to the results of the questioning and the official investigation".
First Deputy Speaker of Parliament Adnan Faihan, a leader in Asaib, had previously called for a committee to investigate whether the government had prior knowledge of the timing of the Saudi-US targeting and failed to take the necessary measures.
The committee was expected to submit its report within a week. However, the results have not yet emerged.
The restructuring of the leadership of the PMF appears to have already begun, particularly after the Interior Ministry announced the closure of 71 headquarters described as "fake" and claiming affiliation with the PMF.
This prompted the PMF to issue a clarification confirming that those headquarters had no connection to it.
This indicates the emergence of a dispute between the prime minister and PMF chairman Faleh al-Fayyad.
In a statement, the PMF said that "the measures to close and monitor those headquarters were carried out by the General Directorate of Security and Discipline at the Popular Mobilisation Forces as part of the work of the Permanent Committee for Restricting Weapons".
The Interior Ministry's statement did not mention the specific body that carried out the closure of the fake headquarters.
Security and political affairs researcher Abdullah al-Rakabi said that "the security changes Zaidi made in the security agencies over the past weeks excluded the Popular Mobilisation Forces, given the sensitivity of the organisation".
"But the coming period may witness major changes within the PMF institution, particularly the position of chairman, as there are political parties that have objected to Fayyad's presence in his post for about 10 years," he said.
"His dismissal may also not cause political problems and is not difficult because Fayyad does not have political backing. It appears that the same applies to PMF chief of staff Abu Fadak."
Speaking to The New Arab, he said that "there are many political disputes over Fayyad. As for Abu Fadak, he is rejected by the US, and the two may be replaced before Sept. 30 as part of the US-Iraqi agreement to end the factions' weapons and the withdrawal of foreign forces from Iraq".
 
How were the Popular Mobilisation Forces established?
The Popular Mobilisation Forces are an umbrella organisation bringing together more than 70 armed formations and factions in Iraq.
The roots of its establishment date back to June 2014, when the Iraqi government decided to organise volunteers to repel Islamic State's invasion of Mosul and its surrounding areas.
This came before religious authority Ali al-Sistani issued a fatwa calling for "defensive jihad", urging those capable of carrying weapons to volunteer in the security forces.
This prompted thousands to join the armed formations later known as the "Popular Mobilisation Forces", which also included factions that were already active.
In February 2016, the Popular Mobilisation Forces were reorganised under a cabinet order.
In November of the same year, the Iraqi parliament passed the Popular Mobilisation Forces Law No. 40, which made it part of the armed forces and placed it under the authority of the commander-in-chief of the armed forces.
The move came amid objections and a boycott by lawmakers from Sunni political forces.

Who will miss the 12 August eclipse: geography, clouds or work
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
16:28:33 UTC
01:28:33 KST

As the country prepares for its first total eclipse over the peninsula since 1912, many will miss it: where they live, the weather, work shifts or simple caution about their eyesight.
Spain is already looking to the sky. Or at least, getting ready to. But not everyone in the country will see the same thing. The total solar eclipse on 12 August is, meteorologists and astronomers agree, a phenomenon that will literally split the country in two: those who will see the Sun disappear completely and those who will be left at the threshold.
Outside the path: Madrid, Barcelona and much of the south
The path of totality, the narrow corridor where the Moon covers the Sun 100%, crosses the peninsula from west to east and takes in capitals such as La Coruña, Oviedo, León, Bilbao, Zaragoza, Valencia and Palma. Outside that track, the rest of the country will see a partial eclipse, deeper or shallower depending on the distance from the central line.
Madrid and Barcelona are the two big absentees. The band passes right between the two cities, so residents will experience an afternoon with the Sun almost completely covered, up to 99% in some places, but without those few seconds of total darkness that turn the event into something unlike anything else.
Huesca and Zamora lie right on the edge of totality, meaning that the uneven lunar profile could make the key moment imperceptible to the naked eye. And the entire southern half of the peninsula will, quite simply, have to settle for a partial eclipse.
The enemy nobody can control: the clouds
Being in the right strip is no guarantee of anything if the sky does not cooperate. The Cantabrian coast, Galicia, Asturias, Cantabria, has a meteorological track record that is not very favourable at this time of year, with clear-sky probabilities that in some analyses do not exceed 50%.
The latest forecasts point to better chances in the west and interior of Galicia, Castile and León and the Balearic Islands, although the models can still shift up to the last minute. For anyone who has travelled hundreds of kilometres chasing totality, a poorly placed cloud on the western horizon can ruin in seconds what geography had granted them.
Those who will keep working as the sky goes dark
There is no special permit in Spain to leave your workplace during the eclipse, and labour legislation does not treat it as a force majeure event. So drivers, hospitality staff or construction workers on shift this afternoon will, in principle, continue their working day while everything around them stops to look up.
At most, the moment of totality, barely a minute or so in the best locations, can be fitted into the 15-minute break laid down in the Workers' Statute for working days of more than six hours, but that requires prior agreement with the employer.
The DGT, in fact, has set up a special operation in anticipation of traffic jams in the busiest areas, so a large part of road personnel will have a much busier afternoon than usual.
For safety, it is better not to look at it directly
Some people could watch it and choose not to, or should not. Ophthalmologists have been insisting for weeks that looking at the Sun without ISO 12312-2 certified glasses, not even for a few seconds, and not with normal sunglasses, X-ray films or homemade filters, can cause solar retinopathy: a burn on the retina that does not hurt, is not noticeable at the time and can take between 4 and 48 hours to appear as a dark spot in the centre of your vision.
The ONCE Social Group has distributed nearly two million certified glasses across the country precisely to avoid accidents, and ophthalmology societies recommend that young children in particular should not watch the event without an adult directly supervising them. Anyone without certified protection to hand really has two safe options: either not to look, or to watch it via a 'streaming'.
ESA will provide two live feeds. The first will be the official broadcast, produced from the Javalambre Astrophysical Observatory in Teruel. It will include live interviews, explanations, images and information about eclipses, as well as live coverage of totality at 20:31. It will be in English and can be followed via ESA Web TV and YouTube.
ESA's second live feed will show images captured by telescopes, without commentary or explanations: just the eclipse live, also available on YouTube.
For its part, NASA will also offer its own streaming, starting at 19:15. The broadcast will show different views of the eclipse as it moves along its path and will include interviews with experts. It can be followed both on NASA's website and on YouTube, with links to different locations where totality can be observed, such as Iceland at 19:45 or Spain at 20:28.
A phenomenon you can listen to as well
For blind and partially sighted people, an eclipse has traditionally been a spectacle from which they were, by definition, excluded. That changes this year with the Inclusive Eclipse project, led by the CSIC research council, which is distributing LightSound devices at different viewing points around the country.
The device converts the intensity of sunlight into sound in real time: a tone that gradually fades and lowers in pitch as the Moon covers the solar disc, almost disappearing during totality. It is not the same as seeing it, but it is a way to follow the same moment that millions of people will be spending this afternoon looking up at the sky to share.
Those who do not want to watch it
Not everyone missing out on the eclipse this afternoon does so because they cannot watch it: some people simply prefer not to go out and look. In recent weeks, several hoaxes have circulated on social media mixing the event with conspiracy theories, from warnings about supposed neurological problems caused by observing it to the claim, without any scientific basis, that the Earth would lose gravity for seven seconds, attributed to a non-existent leaked NASA document.
Fact-checkers have spent days dismantling these messages, but they keep being repeated, and some literally warn people "not to go out" during the eclipse. For part of the population, that constant murmur is enough to make them stay at home with the blinds down.
Then there are those who do not fear the event itself, but what surrounds it. Villages lying in the path of totality have seen an increase of more than 800% in tourism searches compared with a normal year, and many locals in those areas are already saying they will spend the afternoon away from the crowds, leaving the best spots to watch the Sun to the thousands of visitors who have ended up clogging roads and accommodation. For them, the eclipse is less an astronomical spectacle than an annual invasion they prefer to avoid.

Vučić Welcomes Zelensky in Serbia: Turning Point or Tactical Gambit?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
16:28:00 UTC
01:28:00 KST

On Saturday, Volodymyr Zelensky made his first official visit to Serbia, a country long seen as one of Russia’s closest European partners. For some in the West, it was proof that Serbian President Aleksandar Vučić was finally moving toward Europe and away from Moscow.
That celebration is likely premature.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Vučić has long sought to play East and West off each other. Currently facing the biggest protests of his decade-long rule, he craves the appearance of European legitimacy to help shore up his hold on power. For Vučić, hosting Zelensky is a tactical gambit rather than a sign Belgrade has fundamentally changed its geopolitical strategy.
Despite being a nominal candidate for EU accession, since Moscow launched its 2022 invasion of Ukraine, Vučić’s political machinery has cast the conflict in a light favorable to Russia. Pro-government media have repeated Kremlin narratives that Ukraine attacked Russia, promoted Russian propaganda about supposed Ukrainian bioweapons, and amplified fears of that Western aid for Kyiv could lead to World War III.
At the same time, Vučić has turned the war into a lucrative business opportunity. Serbian ammunition has reached Kyiv through third countries, prompting former US Ambassador to Serbia Christopher Hill to describe the arms trade as evidence of a “lasting and sustainable relationship” between Serbia and Ukraine. But Serbia’s weapons trade has never been about choosing geopolitical camps. Its defense industry sells to whoever will pay, from Western partners to Azerbaijan, the Gulf states, and African countries. Reportedly, Serbia’s weapons also reached the authoritarian regime in Myanmar, Sudan and armed groups in the Sahel.
Ukraine to Continue Youth Housing Reform Push
Meanwhile, Belgrade has continued to receive arms from Russia and China. Last year, Serbia conducted its first combined exercise with China and acquired Chinese drones and air defense systems.
While Serbia suspended military exercises with Russia after the invasion, deeper intelligence ties survived. Serbian intelligence has maintained contacts with Russia’s foreign intelligence service, or SVR. Aleksandar Vulin, a close ally of Vučić who is under US sanctions and until recently served as intelligence chief and then deputy prime minister, cultivating a particularly close relationship with SVR head Sergey Naryshkin. In March 2025, as mass protests shook Serbia, Vulin said Russian intelligence had assisted Serbian authorities in confronting what Belgrade portrayed as a potential “color revolution.”
Leaked documents show that Serbian intelligence and Russia’s FSB jointly test anti-protest sound cannons on dogs last year shortly after demonstrators in Belgrade reported being struck by a mysterious sonic blast. Russian intelligence has used Serbia as a permissive hub for operations in Europe, from training paramilitaries to destabilize Moldova to recruiting agents for provocations in France.
Likewise, the Serbian Orthodox Church remains one of Moscow’s key channels of soft power in the Balkans. Serbian Patriarch Porfirije has publicly thanked Vladimir Putin for Russia’s support on Kosovo, while Vučić awarded Russia’s Patriarch Kirill Serbia’s highest state decoration in 2025.
Energy is a perfect example of how Belgrade balances between East and West. Serbia remains heavily dependent on Russian gas even as Vučić promises Western partners that Belgrade will diversify. His latest pitch is a US-Serbia energy partnership centered on the planned Đerdap 3 hydropower project. Yet after the United States sanctioned Serbia’s Russian-owned oil company, NIS, Vučić has sought to buy time by securing sanctions waivers and attempting to restructure the company’s Russian ownership.
Then there is Kosovo, which helps explain why Russia remains so useful to Vučić. Russia rejects Kosovo’s 2008 declaration of independence, and Belgrade depends on Moscow to wield its veto at the UN Security Council to block full international recognition of Kosovar sovereignty. While Vučić insists that he will never recognize Russian control over occupied Ukrainian territory, he does so not out of loyalty to Kyiv but to defend Serbia’s own claim to Kosovo.
Brussels and Washington want Serbia closer to Europe and less dependent on Moscow. The Kremlin wants Serbia as a foothold in the Balkans. Vučić wants all the two sides to keep competing for his attention, and none to demand too high a price for it.
That strategy is particularly valuable now. Serbia’s opposition protests have presented Vučić’s greatest political challenge in years. A high-profile visit by Zelensky allows him to demonstrate relevance to Western governments at precisely the moment his domestic legitimacy is under strain. And it costs him relatively little: welcoming Zelensky does not require him to impose sanctions on Russia, abandon Russian energy or sever intelligence ties.
Washington has tolerated Belgrade’s antics because US officials fear that taking too hard a line would push the country into Moscow’s bear hug. In July, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Foreign Minister Marko Djuric held the inaugural US-Serbia Strategic Dialogue, pledging to deepen relations even as Vučić continues to balance between the two sides.
That approach needs to change. Washington should consider imposing Global Magnitsky sanctions on Serbian officials involved in repression, corruption, and cooperation with Moscow, Beijing and Tehran.
Zelensky’s visit should not be measured by the handshake in Belgrade, but by what comes next. If Vučić wants the legitimacy and benefits of the West, he should be asked to make real choices – not simply promises. Until then, Washington and Brussels should stop mistaking his balancing act for a strategic turn toward the West.

Zelensky's Serbia gamble puts Ukraine's principles to the test
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
16:26:04 UTC
01:26:04 KST

Zelensky's Serbia gamble puts Ukraine's principles to the test
Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic (L) meets with President Volodymyr Zelensky (R) during Zelensky's first visit to Serbia at the Palace of Serbia in Belgrade, Serbia, on Aug. 8, 2026. (Stringer / Anadolu / Getty Images)
Blerim Vela
Non-Residential Fellow at UTSYN
President Volodymyr Zelensky's first official visit to Serbia was a diplomatic gamble.
Ukraine needs partners wherever it can find them, including states that maintain close ties with Moscow. But Serbia is not becoming a conventional Ukrainian ally. Belgrade nominally supports Ukraine's territorial integrity and has provided humanitarian assistance, while Serbian-made ammunition has reached Ukraine through third countries.
At the same time, Serbia has not joined the European Union's sanctions regime against Russia and continues to maintain close political and economic ties with Moscow.
That contradiction is not necessarily a reason for Kyiv to disengage. A country fighting a major war cannot afford to disregard useful diplomatic relationships, economic opportunities, or practical assistance. The challenge is to distinguish between cooperation and alignment, pragmatism and endorsement.
In Belgrade, Zelensky and President Aleksandar Vucic announced deeper cooperation in energy, infrastructure, food security, and trade, with Serbia offering additional humanitarian assistance, support for reconstruction, and a pledge to work toward a free-trade agreement by the end of 2026.
These are useful outcomes. But the optics matter too: in the Western Balkans, as in Brussels and Washington, diplomatic gestures are closely watched.
For a government that has made sovereignty and territorial integrity central to its international appeal, the partners Ukraine chooses, and the language it uses to describe those partnerships, carry strategic weight.
Serbia can be useful, but it is not aligned
There are practical reasons for Kyiv to maintain pragmatic relations with Belgrade: Serbian-made ammunition has reached Ukraine through third countries, and Serbia has provided humanitarian assistance and economic cooperation.
These have real value for a country at war, but should not be mistaken for Serbia's broader geopolitical realignment away from the Russian orbit.
Serbia remains closely connected to Russia politically and economically. Its energy relationship with Moscow remains significant, and Belgrade continues to maintain political channels with the Kremlin. Serbia's domestic political and public environment also remains completely receptive to Russia-sympathetic narratives.
Two days before the full-scale invasion, the pro-government tabloid Informer ran a headline echoing Kremlin claims that Ukraine had attacked Russia. When Serbia's student protests gathered momentum in 2025, Vucic and regime-aligned voices repeatedly cast the demonstrations as a foreign-backed "color revolution," invoking Ukraine and the Maidan as examples of popular uprisings allegedly orchestrated from abroad.
None of this makes Serbia an adversary, and Serbian society should not be equated with the policies of its government. But these episodes show why Kyiv should treat Serbia as a practical partner rather than a strategic or political model for the region.
Territorial integrity cannot be selective
This distinction matters most over Kosovo.
After the Zelensky-Vucic meeting, Vucic reaffirmed Serbia's nominal support for Ukraine's territorial integrity under the UN Charter, and Zelenskyy thanked Serbia for respecting Ukraine's sovereignty, including the status of Crimea. Ukraine's appreciation is understandable. But principles of territorial integrity are strongest when applied consistently.
Zelensky also confirmed that Kyiv's position on Kosovo has not changed: Ukraine still does not recognize its independence. Yet Ukraine has already shown that non-recognition need not mean opposition to Kosovo's membership in European institutions.
In 2023, the Committee of Ministers of the Council of Europe advanced Kosovo's membership application. Ukraine did not vote against the application — instead, it abstained. The decision demonstrated that Kyiv's policy of non-recognition does not include an opposition to Kosovo's membership in European organizations.
Kosovo, for its part, has unequivocally supported Ukraine by aligning with all EU sanctions against Russia, providing humanitarian and military assistance, and hosting a dozen Ukrainian journalists.
Kyiv can keep its formal position while making clear that Serbia's claim on Kosovo gives it no permanent right to political leverage over it. Non-recognition should not justify coercion, destabilization, or indefinite obstruction of Kosovo's international participation; relations between the two should instead rest on mutual recognition and functional coexistence.
This matters beyond Kosovo. In Bosnia and Herzegovina, fragile institutions are still tested by secessionist rhetoric from Republika Srpska, whose leadership is close to both Belgrade and Moscow.
Montenegro, too, has felt significant Serbian political and informational, political and religious influence.
The broader question, whether neighboring states can determine their own political futures free of pressure from a larger state claiming special responsibility for its ethnic kin, is close to the heart of Ukraine's own case against Russia.
Why this matters to Ukraine
Ukraine's diplomatic strength rests on more than military resistance. It also rests on persuading other countries that Russia's conduct violates principles meant to apply universally: sovereignty, territorial integrity, and the right of nations to choose their own futures.
That coalition needs consistency. If these principles hold when Russia invokes history or ethnicity to justify aggression but become negotiable when another state makes a similar argument on a smaller scale, their legitimacy erodes, which is exactly why Kyiv needs to separate cooperation from endorsement.
The EU's own approach offers a template: its 2023 Agreement on the Path to Normalization envisaged Serbia not objecting to Kosovo's membership in international organizations, even without recognition. Ukraine can draw on the same distinction: it can support Kosovo's security and international agency until it changes its position on recognition once the war is over.
What Ukraine could do differently
Kyiv should continue engaging Serbia, but with clearer political boundaries.
It should compartmentalize the relationship by welcoming practical cooperation without assuming that it signals a Serbian realignment away from Russia. It should also clarify its position on Kosovo while explicitly supporting regional normalization and Kosovo's international agency.
Kyiv should also deepen direct engagement with Kosovo, as other EU member states, such as Greece, that do not recognize it, have done.
Finally, Ukraine should apply the principle of sovereignty consistently by challenging any doctrine — Russian, Serbian, or otherwise — that grants a state special rights over its neighbors on ethnic or historical grounds.
A Europe that is whole, free, and at peace cannot be built on selective principles. Ukraine has shown its commitment to resisting hegemonic aggression on the battlefield. Its diplomacy in the Balkans should now demonstrate that the same commitment to sovereignty, self-determination, and the security of smaller states extends beyond Ukraine's borders.
Editor's note: The opinions expressed in the op-ed section are those of the authors and do not purport to reflect the views of the Kyiv Independent.

Trump administration again urges US Supreme Court intervention on mail ballots
Aug 12 - President Donald Trump's administration again asked the U.S. Supreme Court on Wednesday to intervene to fully implement his executive order restricting the use of mail-in ballots ahead of the November midterm elections that will decide control of Congress.
The Justice Department filed a request asking the justices to put on hold a decision made on Tuesday by U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani in Boston that blocks the U.S. Postal Service from nationwide enforcement of the directive's tighter rules for voting by mail.
Trump, a Republican, signed his executive order in March after years of calling for restrictions on voting by mail and pushing the false claim that his 2020 election defeat was the result of widespread voter fraud.
Talwani's decision on Tuesday, in a case brought by several voting rights groups and represented by the American Civil Liberties Union, effectively expands on an earlier order she issued in June preventing the enforcement of Trump's order in 23 mostly Democratic-governed states and Washington, D.C., which had also challenged the action as unconstitutional.
The administration has already asked the Supreme Court to pause the June decision. In its brief filing on Wednesday, the Justice Department urged the Supreme Court to lift that decision and make clear that the ruling applies to the judge's action on Tuesday as well.
The administration contends that the lawsuits are premature as federal agencies have not yet taken any concrete actions that impact the plaintiffs, and so any harm they allege is speculative.
Trump's executive order directed the Department of Homeland Security to compile and transmit to the states a list of U.S. citizens eligible to vote in each state, and the Justice Department to prioritize investigating and prosecuting state and local election officials who issue ballots to people deemed "not eligible" to vote in federal elections.
It also required the Postal Service to deliver ballots only to voters on each state's approved mail-in ballot list. The Postal Service recently moved to implement Trump's directive.
In siding with the voting rights groups on Tuesday, Talwani wrote that the executive branch of the federal government had no authority to regulate elections, a responsibility that the U.S. Constitution assigns to individual states. REUTERS

Mike McCarthy and Eli Heidenreich’s Pittsburgh homecomings get real as preseason begins
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12

Mike McCarthy and Eli Heidenreich’s Pittsburgh homecomings get real as preseason begins
PITTSBURGH (AP) — The vibes for Mike McCarthy and Eli Heidenreich over the last few months have been immaculate. How could they not be?
The chance for McCarthy to lead his hometown team brought the first-year Pittsburgh Steelers coach to tears when he was hired in January. The image last April of Heidenreich walking onto the draft stage in full Naval dress uniform outside Acrisure Stadium — just a few miles from the Mount Lebanon neighborhood where he grew up — felt like something out of a movie.
Their respective homecomings have provided plenty of “fairy tale” narratives during an eventful offseason for the typically low-key Steelers. And while there will be a little bit of “hey, is this really happening?” on Thursday night when they walk onto the field for the first time as the Steelers host Green Bay in the preseason opener, they’re both aware of the reality check that awaits under the lights.
“Naturally, there’s some people that might assume that it was like you said, like a hometown pick or whatever, whatever someone wants to say,” Heidenreich said. “But I’m here to play football, and that’s it.”
Good thing, because evolving from a seventh-round flyer following a record-setting career at Navy — where he set program marks for career receiving yards and receiving touchdowns — into an NFL roster spot will take some doing. Nobody knows that more than the 6-foot, 206-pound Heidenreich, who politely dismissed comparisons between himself and San Francisco 49ers running back and 2023 NFL Offense Player of the Year Christian McCaffrey.
Both are on the smaller side, sure. And yes, both are shifty. But one came to the league as a Heisman Trophy finalist and a first-round pick. And it wasn’t Heidenreich.
“He’s a fantastic player and one of the best to ever do it,” he said. “And he’s just someone that I look up to and really try to do my best to model him in certain ways. But yeah, I do see the (comparisons) and I know people get pretty fired up one way or the other about them.”
Heidenreich wants no part of that discussion. He’s too focused on trying to carve out a niche in Pittsburgh, where his best chance to avoid getting cut for the first time in his life will be as a contributor on special teams.
While the chance for reps at running back might be difficult to come by — though Heidenreich has basically attached himself to backfield coach Ramon Chinyoung since camp started — his elusiveness could make him an intriguing option as a kick returner.
Whether Heidenreich gets any opportunities against the Packers in front of dozens of friends and family members who will make the short drive to Acrisure Stadium is uncertain. He tweaked his hamstring recently, which limited him for a stretch, though his No. 29 was noticeable during a walkthrough on Tuesday.
Either way, it figures to be a “pinch-me” type of moment when he jogs onto the field and looks up, a point of view that will be markedly different from the one he enjoyed as a fan.
“It’s an honor to just get out there and play in that stadium,” he said. “I think that’s the best way for me to put it. It’s something that I have dreamed of for a long time.”
How long the dream lasts now that he’s exchanged his fandom for a uniform with his name across the back is up to him.
“Preseason is really important,” he said. “So I’ve got to put my best foot forward and be locked in when I get there.”
The same goes for McCarthy, though perhaps for different reasons. He’s walked onto the turf a handful of times during his career, but has never stood on the home sideline. He figures the significance will start to hit as he makes the drive in.
The fact that he gets to begin what is likely the final chapter of his head coaching career against the team where it all began makes it just a little sweeter.
“Obviously, having a personal and professional connection to Green Bay, that’s part of my life,” he said.
Of course, all the nostalgia will wear off once the ball is kicked. Then the more pressing needs of the moment — like figuring out how much progress his group has made during his first camp and seeing what he has to work with in young quarterbacks Will Howard and Drew Allar — will take over.
And in a way, it will be a relief. While he has embraced all the trappings of being the hometown boy made good, the Steelers didn’t hire him to curry favor with the fanbase but to win games. The process starts in earnest on Thursday.
“I just want to see these young guys play,” he said. “I want to see how they play connected to each other. The pre-snap of the operation, having an understanding of what’s in front of them ... This is what these games are for.”

Music Review: Carly Simon’s ‘Comes in Waves’ is a journey through love and loss
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
16:23:02 UTC
01:23:02 KST

Music Review: Carly Simon’s ‘Comes in Waves’ is a journey through love and loss
On her first album with original songs in nearly 20 years, Carly Simon is still working on some old demons and still determined to outlast them.
“Maybe I never loved you / But anyway, I thought I did / I married you, we had a kid,” she sings in a ballad you could imagine Simon addressing to her ex-husband, James Taylor. “And maybe you never loved me / Although God knows you said you did.”
Simon announced last month that she had been diagnosed with Parkinson’s disease while recording “Comes in Waves,” and that she also had surgery to remove a cancerous skin growth. But this album feels less like an ending than a continuation of themes and events that have inspired and defined her from early in her career — yearning, discontent, desire, uncertainty, her marriage to Taylor and the loss of her father, the publisher Richard Simon, who died when Carly was in her teens.
“Howl” is the album’s lead track, first single and table setter — a midtempo rocker addressed to a heartbroken friend (or to herself?) whom Simon urges to “Get it out of your system / Bang your fists and beat your brow.”
The other songs unfold as if to dramatize the album’s title, as Simon’s mood shifts from defiance to regret to melancholy to resolve and a willingness to try again, a cycle cushioned (to a fault) by the literal-minded production and arrangements of David Spencer, Frank Filipetti and son Ben Taylor among others.
“Comes in Waves” includes a remaster of Simon’s decades-old political song “Share the End,” and elsewhere echoes moments from her previous records. “Maybe I Never Loved You,” inspired by the late playwright Tim Mayer, feels like Simon’s version of “I Get Along Without You Very Well (Except Sometimes),” the Hoagy Carmichael standard she covered on her 1981 “Torch” album. “The Father-Daughter Dance” suggests the pain of a ballad about her father from the early 1970s, “Embrace Me, You Child.”
Simon also teases courtship (“Peaches”); celebrates parenthood (“Mother of Pearl,” a tribute to daughter and “child of divorce” Sally Taylor); and savors life’s “wild ride” (“Love the Way I Do”).
The catchiest song is by a departed friend, the late Judy Belushi, widow of comedian John Belushi: “Four in the Morning” has a close-up, tiptoeing pace fitting for lyrics about an unhappy wife who slips away from her snoring husband.
Simon, who turned 83 this year, doesn’t hit all the notes of her best known records, but she has lost none of her gifts for taking hold of a melody, and putting her whole self into the words. Her musical journey has always been personal, and longtime Simon fans are the most likely to enjoy catching up with her. Others may feel like they had to be there.
___
“Comes in Waves,” by Carly Simon
Three stars out of five
On repeat: “Love the Way I Do,” “Four in the Morning”
Skip it: “Share the End”
For fans of: Carly Simon, most of all, and of pop torch singers in general.

Moscow says Ukrainian drone strikes threaten global food security
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
16:21:12 UTC
01:21:12 KST

Elena Teslova
12 August 2026•Update: 12 August 2026
Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova accused Ukraine on Wednesday of intensifying attacks on civilian vessels and transport infrastructure in the Azov-Black Sea region.
Zakharova said the strikes were disrupting agricultural exports and threatening global food security.
She pointed out that Ukrainian forces had carried out attacks throughout the summer using drone systems and intelligence provided by NATO and EU countries.
The attacks targeted coastal transport and logistics infrastructure, as well as civilian vessels carrying agricultural products, including grain and sunflower oil, she said.
Zakharova cited several incidents she said had caused casualties.
“These strikes ... have created difficulties with the shipment of prepared cargoes along established export routes,” said Zakharova, arguing that the attacks were contrary to international law protecting the safety of civilian shipping.
Russia recorded at least 100 drone attacks on commercial vessels carrying Russian agricultural products in the Azov and Black seas in July, she noted.
Zakharova said the attacks were causing delays in the export of grain, oilseed and feed products to international markets and creating difficulties for importers that rely on Russian agricultural supplies.
Zakharova emphasized that Kyiv's actions are fraught with instability on global food markets, and that the consequences would be particularly damaging for countries in the Global South and East through higher food and fertilizer costs.
The Russian armed forces are taking measures to protect navigation in the Black Sea, including strikes against facilities it said are used by Ukrainian forces to disrupt maritime traffic, according to Zakharova.
Moscow is also targeting infrastructure and vessels involved in transporting Western weapons and military equipment to Ukraine, she said.
Zakharova urged international organizations and other countries to assess the incidents and take measures to ensure the “unimpeded export of agricultural products.”

Russian Banks, Email and Internal Systems Become “Easy Targets” as Trusted Certificates Disappear
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
16:19:18 UTC
01:19:18 KST

- Category
- World
Russian Banks, Email and Internal Systems Become “Easy Targets” as Trusted Certificates Disappear
Russian companies could be forced to spend heavily rebuilding national web infrastructure to keep state and corporate sites online, after mass revocations of international security certificates began locking Russian domains out of mainstream browsers.
This was reported by Ukraine's Foreign Intelligence Service on its official website on August 12.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The service assessed that Russia's war has hollowed out its economy and is now spreading into its digital sector. State services such as the Federal Tax Service, along with major banks, are increasingly failing to load in mainstream browsers such as Chrome, Firefox and Safari.
More than 20,000 Russian domains have been left without internationally recognized security validation, the agency estimated, among them the state-linked lender Gazprombank and the diamond miner Alrosa. Roughly 90 percent of the Russian market still leans on foreign-issued certificates, it noted.
The disruption traces back to Japanese certificate authority GlobalSign, which began revoking certificates issued to sanctioned Russian companies in June. One documented wave covered about 310 domains across 44 firms, including entities tied to Rosneft, Gazprombank, Alrosa, VEB.RF and the United Aircraft Corporation.
Market sources cited by RBC estimated the initial revocation list touched 15,000 to 20,000 second-level domains. A second-level domain is the core registered name that sits directly before a country suffix, like .ru—for example, gazprombank in gazprombank.ru.
Once the subdomains layered beneath each one are counted, the number of affected certificates could run into the hundreds of thousands. Independent analysis of the affected .ru domains has painted a similar picture of the reach of the revocations.
When a certificate is revoked, a site loses the credential that browsers rely on to verify its authenticity and encrypt traffic. Chrome, Safari, Firefox and Edge can then mark the connection as unsafe or block the page outright.
The revocations followed new rules from the CA/Browser Forum, an industry body of certificate authorities and browser makers, that require issuers to screen clients against US and other sanctions lists. GlobalSign, owned by Japan's GMO Internet Group, had little room to keep serving sanctioned Russian clients.
Moscow's response has been to push homegrown substitutes. Russia's Digital Development Ministry has urged users to install state-issued certificates via the Gosuslugi public services portal, and Yandex Browser already ships with the domestic certificate built in. Those credentials work inside Russia's own systems but carry no automatic trust in Chrome, Safari or Firefox.
Ukraine's Foreign Intelligence Service emphasized that the domestic certificates cost nothing, while the rebuild around them does not. Reconfiguring infrastructure at large corporations could take up to six months and demand a wholesale swap of software and operating systems, the agency indicated, leaving the bill with Russian businesses already squeezed by war and sanctions.
It warned that the loss of trusted certificates turns Russian internal systems, email and banking interfaces into soft targets for hackers. The service also dismissed the recommended switch to Yandex Browser as prone to freezing and cache failures, and as offering no real protection for user data.
The certificate crisis is only the latest step in Russia's drift toward a walled-off internet. In 2025, Russia stripped more applications from Apple's App Store than any other country, 1,213 in total, up from 171 the year before. Much of that purge targeted VPNs and other tools used to evade state blocks, as Roskomnadzor tightened its grip on what Russians can access online.

Ukraine has approved a new domestic interceptor and put it on the shelf for units to buy. Ukraine's Defense Ministry has codified the high-speed TAF Kolibri-i10 interceptor from TAF Industries, the company announced.
The approval adds one more weapon to Ukraine's fast-scaling interceptor arsenal and its state procurement pipeline. Ukraine now fields drone-hunters from dozens of makers to counter Russia's massed drone attacks. Units can order it directly through the state marketplace, the same DOT-Chain and Brave1 Market system that has turned battlefield-proven drones into off-the-shelf purchases.
The interceptor grew out of combat use
The Kolibri-i10 came from an improvised solution that worked. The idea grew from using the FPV drone Kolibri 10 to intercept Russian fixed-wing drones, and combat experience showed the approach was so effective that TAF built a new, specialized interceptor rather than modifying the existing model.

It is built to work under jamming. Manual control gives the operator full command at critical moments; digital day-and-night cameras enable operation in varied conditions. MilELRS firmware ensures stable operation in the presence of active electronic warfare. That jam-resistance is a recurring requirement for Ukrainian interceptors, since signal-dependent ones fail against the electronic warfare saturating the front.
The drone is available to order on Brave1 Market, priced at about $760 with a day camera and $1,550 with a night camera.

Who is Atef Najib, Assad cousin sentenced to death over Daraa?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
16:15:13 UTC
01:15:13 KST

Breadcrumb
Who is Atef Najib, Assad cousin sentenced to death over Daraa crackdown?
A Syrian court has sentenced Atef Najib, the former security chief whose name became synonymous with the crackdown that helped ignite the 2011 uprising, to death for crimes against humanity.
Najib, a cousin of ousted president Bashar al-Assad, was convicted by the Fourth Criminal Court in Damascus on Tuesday over his role in the repression of protesters in the southern province of Daraa.
The court found him guilty of crimes including murder and torture, including the torture of children, and responsibility for killings during the 2011 crackdown.
Unlike Assad and several other former officials sentenced alongside him in absentia, Najib is in Syrian custody and appeared in court during his trial. His prosecution is one of the most significant involving a senior Assad-era security official since the former government was toppled in December 2024.
But who is Najib, and why has his name been associated with the beginning of Syria's uprising for more than 15 years?
Who is Atef Najib?
Najib, 66, is a former brigadier general and cousin of Bashar al-Assad through the former president's mother, Anisa Makhlouf.
He served in several branches of Syria's powerful Political Security Directorate before becoming its chief in Daraa, where he was accused of corruption, extortion and abuse of power. Syrian records show he previously served in Political Security branches in Damascus and Tartous.
But it was his role in the events of March 2011 that made him one of the most notorious figures of Assad's security establishment.
What happened in Daraa?
Najib's grip on Daraa was such that he reportedly used the phrase “I am God in Daraa” to describe his authority over the province.
In March 2011, a group of schoolchildren were detained after anti-government slogans were painted on their school walls in Daraa.
The children were allegedly tortured in detention, including accusations that their fingernails were pulled out. Najib, then head of Political Security in Daraa, became one of the officials blamed for their treatment and for the authorities' response to demands for their release.
When families and local dignitaries appealed for the children to be freed, accounts from Daraa say Najib responded with insults and threats, further inflaming anger.
Protesters soon began chanting against him and demanding his removal.
Demonstrations erupted in Daraa on 18 March 2011, and security forces opened fire on protesters. The unrest quickly spread across Syria, transforming local anger into a nationwide uprising against Assad's rule.
The government's violent suppression of those protests eventually developed into a devastating war that killed hundreds of thousands of people and displaced millions.
Najib was subsequently removed from Daraa and transferred to Idlib. The US sanctioned him in April 2011 over human rights abuses, followed by European sanctions the following month.
How was Najib caught?
Najib largely disappeared from public view during the war, but resurfaced following Assad's overthrow in December 2024.
Syrian security forces arrested him near al-Haffah in Latakia province on 31 January 2025, making him one of the most senior former security officials captured by the new authorities.
His public trial began in Damascus in April 2026.
The court heard evidence linking Najib to the interrogation and torture of detainees, the security campaign against civilians and the storming of Daraa's Omari Mosque, which became an early centre of the uprising.
Najib denied the accusations. The presiding judge said he showed no remorse or offered an apology when confronted by victims during the proceedings.
Why does his conviction matter?
Najib's conviction is one of the first major tests of Syria's attempts to hold senior Assad-era officials accountable for abuses committed under the former government.
Its symbolism is particularly powerful because of his connection to Daraa.
The arrest and alleged torture of the schoolchildren, followed by the government's violent response to demonstrations demanding their release, are widely regarded as among the events that triggered the Syrian uprising.
Najib is also unusual among the senior former officials now facing Syrian justice because he is actually in custody. Assad, his brother Maher and other defendants sentenced on Tuesday were tried in absentia.
For Syria's transitional authorities, the case therefore represents more than the prosecution of one former security chief. It is an early indication of how the country intends to confront the abuses of the Assad era and deliver justice for their victims.

Russia steers its long-range drones from ground towers—Kyiv says it hit one in occupied Crimea
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
16:14:20 UTC
01:14:20 KST

Ukraine struck a Russian drone-control relay station and two other military targets in occupied Crimea and the occupied south overnight on 12 August, its General Staff said. Explosions rolled across the peninsula through the night, Sevastopol declared repeated air-raid alerts, and towns across occupied Crimea lost power, according to Ukrainian monitoring channels and Russian occupation authorities.
Russia launches its attack drones at Ukraine from sites inside Russia and across occupied territory every day, and relay stations let it steer those drones over long distances. Occupied Crimea is the logistical spine of Russia's hold on southern Ukraine, the funnel through which fuel, ammunition, and reinforcements reach the front, and its fixed airfields, power plants, and control stations sit within reach of Ukraine's growing long-range arsenal.
What the General Staff says was hit
Ukraine's Defense Forces struck three targets overnight, the General Staff reported. The first was a ground relay station used to control Geran and Gerbera attack drones near Olenivka in occupied Crimea. The others were a Russian repair unit near Mariupol in Donetsk Oblast and a staging point for an enemy drone unit near Marivka in Luhansk Oblast.
Hitting these sites weakens Russia's ability to command its attack drones, keep its military vehicles running, and sustain its units, the General Staff said.
Euromaidan Press could not independently verify the strikes and damage.
Ukraine’s Crimea campaign could strike seven times more targets with faster funding, Brovdi says
Russia flies these drones through a chain of ground repeaters, often mounted on mobile-operator towers or similar tall structures, boost the control signal so operators inside Russia can steer Geran and Gerbera drones over Ukraine from hundreds of kilometers away. Kyiv has dismantled similar relay networks before, including one Russia had built on towers and rooftops in Belarus.
Explosions and blackouts across occupied Crimea
Sevastopol declared three air-raid alerts, and the Russian-installed governor Mikhail Razvozhaev claimed Russian forces downed more than 30 drones, with the heaviest activity over the Balaklava district and no one hurt.
The Ukrainian monitoring channel Krymsky Veter reported explosions in Feodosia and Kerch, and drones close to the Kacha and Belbek airfields. Residents reported air-defense activity near major cities.
The channel said explosions sounded near the Balaklava thermal power plant, a mobile gas-turbine station, and a substation in Sevastopol. Power cut out across parts of occupied Crimea, leaving Sevastopol, Simferopol, and several more cities and districts without electricity.
After the attack, Krymsky Veter's monitoring group reported two large fires near Sevastopol, citing satellite data. One sat by a road junction near the village of Pervomaiske under Balaklava, where a bridge crosses the railway. The other burned near one of the local beaches. The group also logged an already-extinguished fire in the Inzhyr tract that had been reported the day before.
The same night, Ukraine also struck Russia's naval base at Novorossiysk, the fleet's main Black Sea base since late 2023.
Part of the campaign to isolate Crimea
The overnight strikes fit Ukraine's months-long effort to cut occupied Crimea off from the forces and supplies that sustain it. Ukrainian drones have severed road and rail links to the peninsula, left it rationing fuel under rolling blackouts, and pushed the campaign onto the sea by hunting the tankers that supply it.

Syria: Tartous port berth resumes activity after Russia handover
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
16:13:05 UTC
01:13:05 KST

Breadcrumb
Tartous port berth resumes activity after Russia hand over control to Syria
Activity at Berth Four of the Port of Tartous has resumed following its handover from Russian to Syrian government control, a move that is expected to increase the capacity at the port, but which analysts told The New Arab may not translate into bettering daily life for Syrians.
The berth, which was handed over to the Syrian government following the signing of a memorandum of understanding with Russia on Sunday, received its first commercial ship on Tuesday, according to state news Sana.
The berth, which has a 360-meter waterfront and a draft that ranges between 10 and 13 meters, is expected to add capacity to the port, with head of the Operations and Investment department, Youssef Arnous, saying that its specifications allow three large vessels to dock at the berth simultaneously and accelerate services for users.
Alongside the reopening of the berth, two cranes from the Dubai-based logistics company and port operator DP World also arrived on Tuesday as part of a modernisation of port facilities.
DP World signed a 30-year concession valued at $800 million in July 2025 that would see the company operate the port and invest in its infrastructure.
It is not immediately clear if the company will take control of Berth Four, however, according to Jad Baghdadi, a Nonresident Fellow at TIMEP focusing on political economy issues in both Syria and Lebanon.
Baghdadi told The New Arab that there were several economic benefits of the opening of the new berth at the port, but cautioned it may not see wide-reaching effects for Syria's people, who continue to suffer from high levels of poverty.
"In principle, that can lower the cost of bringing goods into the country, though whether that reaches ordinary people is harder to say."
"Since any saving at the quayside still has to survive exchange-rate swings, fuel, inland transport customs costs, and where a few importers dominate a sector, the lower costs can end up as wider profit margins rather than cheaper prices in the shops," he added.
Syria's civil war, which ravaged the country for close to 15 years, saw widespread destruction across much of the country, with vital infrastructure such as roads, housing, schools and hospitals all being severely affected.
Though the IMF has said that it expects Syria's GDP growth to exceed 10% in 2026 through the recovery of the agricultural sector, oil and gas production, improved electricity and the expansion of trade services, the country still needs significant help, including continued international humanitarian and development support alongside the maintenance of fiscal and monetary policies.
The reintegration of the berth from Russian control "sits alongside a broader choice by the new authorities to hand the country's main ports, and increasingly its energy and other strategic sectors, to foreign operators on long concessions," Baghdadi noted.
Alongside DP World's control of Tartous' port, which has been agreed to alongside the operation of Latakia's port by France's CMA CGM Latakia and is part of a wider effort to integrate Syria into regional supply chains, circumventing the blockaded Strait of Hormuz, other sections of the economy have also been given to foreign operators.
This includes Syria's oil and gas sector, with US gas firm ConocoPhillips signing a deal with the Syrian government to revive the country's gas production.
"That model can pull in investment very quickly, which Syria badly needs given the scale of reconstruction, but the risk is tilting the economy towards becoming more dependent on imports and foreign operators, and less reliant on its productive sectors," Baghdadi said, noting that the agricultural and industrial sectors need serious support, with a 2025 drought impacting production, and cheap industrial imports leading to the closure of factories.
"For most Syrians, whether farms and factories recover and start producing again matters far more."

Zhu Rongji: reformer who led China’s economic transformation through ‘minefield or abyss’

ObituaryZhu Rongji: reformer who led China’s economic transformation through ‘minefield or abyss’
China’s bold economic tsar who drove sweeping SOE reforms and secured WTO entry has died aged 97
“Regardless of what lies ahead – be it a minefield or a deep abyss – I will forge ahead unswervingly, dedicating my entire life and energy to the country until my dying day.”
His remarks at a press conference in 1998 came as China was undertaking sweeping state-owned enterprise (SOE) reforms that caused widespread job losses, even as it reeled from the 1997 Asian financial crisis.
Zhu, dubbed China’s economic tsar by the media, was known for his determination to steer the country through the rough waters of reforms and external shocks during his tenure as vice-premier and premier between 1991 and 2003.
He shook up the centrally planned economy, overhauled the state-owned business sector, fought corruption, revamped the tax system and secured China’s entry to the World Trade Organization – changes that some economists say brought about a historic transformation in China’s economic system, ushering in a modern state and making it an integral part of the world economy.
His straight-talking, no-nonsense style earned him a host of nicknames – including “iron-face Zhu”, “no-nonsense leader”, “problem solver”, “fire-brigade captain”, “crisis manager” and “troubleshooter”.

Mozart tribute ends on sour note after mass figurine theft
August 12, 2026
More than 200 gold-colored Mozart figures have vanished from a public art installation in Salzburg, forcing organizers to end part of the exhibition early.
The theft has disrupted a major public art project marking the 270th anniversary of composer Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart's birth in his home city.
What do we know about the theft of the mini-Mozarts?
The Mozarteum Foundation said 210 of the 320 figures installed in the city's Mirabell Garden had disappeared. The theft forced organizers to end the garden display early.
Organizers had kept some replacements in reserve, but not enough to offset the scale of the theft.
The manufacturer is also on summer holiday, leaving no quick way to replace them.
Several dozen figures remain on display at the Mozarteum and Mozart's birthplace until the end of August.
The figures had been placed in the Mirabell Garden and at several Mozart-related sites around Austria's fourth-largest city.
The polymer figures show Mozart with his dog Pimperl, a nod to the composer's everyday life in Salzburg.
German conceptual artist Ottmar Hörl, who is behind the display, said he wanted to show Mozart not as a monument but "as a normal human being despite his genius."
Who might have taken the mini-Mozarts?
Hörl is known for installations made up of large numbers of identical figures depicting famous personalities.
"The worst thing for an artist is when his work dissolves," Hörl said.
Hörl said he did not believe tourists had simply walked off with the 50-centimeter (20-inch) figures.
"This is organized theft," he said, suggesting they were probably taken at night after the garden had closed. "I find it a bit cheeky."
Hörl had planned to sell the figures after the exhibition for around €90 each, putting the loss at roughly €20,000.
A previous Hörl display in Bayreuth suffered a similar fate when 100 figures of composer Richard Wagner disappeared.
"That's just the nature of public space," Hörl said. "When you work as an artist in a public space, you mustn't complain about what is happening there. It ranges from destruction to theft. That’s just how it is."
