Latin America's rightward turn is reshaping its ties with Israel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
15:31:14 UTC
00:31:14 KST

Breadcrumb
Latin America's rightward turn is reshaping its ties with Israel
The rise of pro-Israel diplomacy in Latin America is staggering. From renewing diplomatic relations to rekindling trade, newly elected right-wing leaders are more interested in forming strategic alliances than upholding international law.
This marks a departure from the political “pink-tide” that guided many Latin American countries in solidarity with Palestine after October 2023.
Nicaragua, Colombia, Mexico, Chile, Bolivia, Cuba and Belize all intervened in support of South Africa’s case against Israel at the International Court of Justice (ICJ), while Colombia went one step further, placing a total ban on coal exports to Israel and terminating its bilateral free trade agreement.
On 31 January 2025, Colombia, Cuba, Bolivia, and Honduras also became founding members of The Hague Group. In response to Israel’s ongoing genocide in Gaza and occupation of the West Bank, they committed to “coordinated legal and diplomatic measures in defence of international law and solidarity with the people of Palestine”.
But in the aftermath of right-wing presidential victories, Bolivia and Honduras have both withdrawn from The Hague Group, and Chile and Honduras have returned their ambassadors to Israel.
The new president of Colombia, Abelardo de la Espriella, is ready to renew ties with Israel by ramping up security coordination, resuming coal exports, and withdrawing from The Hague Group.
This week, the new right-wing government also recognised Israel's claim to the occupied Golan Heights, which it captured from Syria in 1967, becoming only the second country to do so after the Trump administration in 2019.
“To learn about international experiences that have yielded results will be fundamental to strengthen our security policy and our penitentiary system,” De La Espriella posted on 10 August, days after entering office.
“Israel will find in Colombia a friend and a determined ally in the fight against terrorism and organised crime.”
In longtime pro-Palestine Venezuela, meanwhile, Israel and Caracas this week agreed to resume consular relations after diplomatic ties were cut in 2009. This comes in the wake of the US' military capture of Nicolás Maduro in January, marking a striking shift in Caracas' foreign policy.
A new alignment in Latin America
Bolivia and Honduras' withdrawal from The Hague Group on 4 March 2026 revealed the limitations of non-aligned movements in the absence of political will.
“The Hague Group was an important, organised response from states that were tired of waiting for countries in the UN Security Council to act,” María Alejandra Gómez, a legal researcher at Law for Palestine, told The New Arab.
At that time, the US had already utilised its veto power in the UNSC to block four ceasefire resolutions in Gaza.
“Every single state in the world is bound to prevent and punish genocide, regardless of what treaties they have signed,” she explained to The New Arab. “The Hague Group only did what it was obliged to do.”
Nonetheless, “the enforcement of international law is always subject to the political will of states, so if they change governments, they tend to change their stance,” Gómez said. “This is a structural problem with international law; it is not just about The Hague Group.”
In fact, months before their withdrawal, Israel’s Minister of Foreign Affairs Gideon Sa'ar and his Bolivian counterpart Fernando Armayo had already signed an agreement to renew diplomatic relations.
Similarly, on 3 June, Honduras and Israel signed an addendum to their pre-existing cooperation agreement. With a renewed focus on agriculture, water management, health, education and security, Israel’s Ambassador to Honduras Nadav D Goren called it “another milestone in the bilateral relationship between Israel and Honduras”.
Chile's turn towards Israel
On 3 August, the new right-wing governments of Chile and Honduras returned ambassadors to Israel nearly three years after they were recalled by former presidents Gabriel Boric and Xiomara Castro.
The appointment of Chilean Ambassador Gabriel Zaliasnik, a self-proclaimed “proud Zionist”, by President José Antonio Kast, was unequivocally denounced by the Palestinian community of Chile.
In June, they described the decision as “contrary to the national interest, incoherent with Chile's history of defending international law, and deeply offensive to the hundreds of thousands of Chileans of Palestinian origin”.
“Today, relations between Chile and the State of Israel have been normalised across all sectors,” Nelson Hadad, a Chilean lawyer and former ambassador to Iraq, Jordan and Egypt, told The New Arab. “The outlook is very bleak.”
In fact, “during a recent World Health Organisation vote, Chile, for the first time, abstained from supporting measures regarding public health and the delivery of humanitarian aid to Palestinians facing starvation in the Gaza Strip,” said Hadad.
Such pro-Israel foreign policy is particularly daunting in Chile, home to the largest Palestinian community outside of the Middle East and North Africa.
Last week, upon visiting relatives in Beit Jala, a Chilean-Palestinian named José Nicolás Khamis was detained at Ben Gurion Airport in Tel Aviv.
“He was interrogated for 36 hours without the right to a defence or to call a lawyer,” said Hadad. “Ultimately, he was accused of being involved in far-left, communist terrorist activities and was subsequently deported on national security grounds.”
These security concerns were "false and baseless,” said Hadad. As such, “this constitutes a serious violation of diplomatic reciprocity between the two nations and reflects a clear bias against Chileans of Palestinian or Arab origin”.
Enter 'El Tigre'
With even more vigour than his neighbours, Colombia’s President Abelardo De La Espriella, who calls himself ‘El Tigre’, has pledged to nullify his predecessor’s anti-Zionist legacy.
Before winning the elections in June, he proposed an “unprecedented offensive against organised crime in Colombia based on strengthening strategic alliances with the United States and Israel”.
Dubbed “a second Plan Colombia”, an homage to the 1999 US-Colombian military project to combat drug cartels and destroy left-wing guerrilla groups, it emphasises Israel’s value as “a leader in artificial intelligence applied to defence, drone surveillance systems, cybersecurity, and military training”.
After all, the State of Israel “is doing what must be done to defend its people,” declared De La Espriella during an interview in June. “And that is exactly what I am going to do to defend Colombia.”
Since then he has pledged to resume coal exports and leave The Hague Group, to withdraw Colombia’s intervention from South Africa’s case against Israel at the ICJ, to terminate plans to establish a Colombian consulate in Ramallah, and recognise the Israeli-occupied Golan Heights.
He has previously outlined plans to relocate the Colombian embassy to Jerusalem, flagrantly disregarding the city’s divided status under international law.
Unsurprisingly, one day before he entered office on 7 August, Gideon Sa'ar was right by his side.
“I had the privilege of meeting him in his office in Barranquilla,” wrote Sa’ar, describing their discussion about “the immediate establishment of diplomatic, security, and economic relations.”
“The golden age in relations between Colombia and Israel begins today,” he confirmed.
The battle moves beyond governments
Given former President Gustavo Petro's outspoken opposition to Israel, this realignment is momentous.
As co-founder of The Hague Group, Colombia and its keffiyeh-donning leader had highlighted the fundamentality of political will when enforcing international law.
His most brazen act of solidarity occurred at the UN General Assembly (UNGA) in September 2025, when he proposed invoking UN Resolution 377 A, also known as Uniting for Peace, to “establish a peacekeeping force” to defend Palestine.
But “it was not just the will of the president,” pointed out Gómez, describing the impact of public pressure from activists and civil society. In fact, “it is not just about the states of The Hague Group. Activism all over the world will enable states to take more coherent action towards Palestine”.
Latin American domestic courts provide another essential avenue to uphold international law, regardless of a government's political position or a president’s personal interests.
“Their impartiality enables us to force governments to comply with their international obligations,” Gómez told The New Arab.
“For example, when the government of Argentina, under President Javier Milei, invited Benjamin Netanyahu to visit, the Prime Minister of Israel had to cancel his trip because Argentinian courts were [preparing] to issue an arrest warrant.”
Similarly, “in Colombia, we have something called the constitutional bloc which means that many international laws are considered to be incorporated into our constitution,” said Gómez. This gives them the same credence as constitutional laws, she explained.
Meanwhile, despite the difficulties, The Hague Group has continued to gain momentum. With 40 states in attendance at its most recent conference, this was the largest gathering since its founding.
“Participants reaffirmed the paramount importance of the Charter of the United Nations and the international legal order as the foundation of peaceful and just relations among states and peoples,” read the official statement.
With Colombia ready to withdraw, abandoning its role as co-chair, “The Hague Group must find ways to reinvent itself,” said Gómez.
In that process, “the role that activists and citizens will play in order for there to be more accountability in the international arena is going to be transcendental”.
Ana Maria Monjardino is an independent journalist and writer from London

Russian Warships, Submarines and Shadow Fleet Tankers Keep Britain’s Navy Busier Than Ever
British warships and helicopters spent significantly more time tracking Russian naval activity in July as Moscow maintained an elevated presence around UK waters and across the North Atlantic, according to Zona Militar on August 11.
Royal Navy patrol ships and aircraft devoted 21 days to monitoring Russian vessels during the month, up 25% from July 2025, according to figures released by the British Navy.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The increase reflects a broader rise in Russian naval activity involving surface combatants, submarines, and vessels linked to Moscow’s shadow fleet.
According to Zona Militar, the patrol ships HMS Tyne, HMS Mersey, and HMS Severn were all involved in tracking Russian naval units during July.
They were supported by Wildcat helicopters from 815 Naval Air Squadron and Merlin helicopters configured for anti-submarine warfare, allowing the Royal Navy to monitor both surface ships and underwater activity across British areas of responsibility.
The Royal Navy also said the number of deployments triggered by Russian naval movements during the first seven months of 2026 was 25% higher than during the same period in 2025.
Among the vessels repeatedly monitored was the Russian frigate Neustrashimy, which crossed areas under British surveillance several times while escorting oil tankers associated with Russia’s so-called shadow fleet.
The heightened monitoring comes as Britain increasingly targets the maritime network Moscow uses to move Russian energy exports.
In June, the UK intercepted the sanctioned tanker Smyrtos in the English Channel. London has also sanctioned more than 500 vessels linked to Russia’s shadow fleet.
Russian Frigate conducts live-fire under British watch
One of the more notable encounters came on July 20, when Neustrashimy conducted live-fire exercises in international waters.
The Russian frigate notified nearby vessels in advance and asked HMS Tyne to move to a safe distance while the drills were underway.
The British patrol ship positioned itself approximately five nautical miles from the Russian vessel and continued monitoring the exercise.
According to the Royal Navy, Neustrashimy fired around 20 rounds from its main 100mm gun and also used its 30mm weapons.
HMS Tyne remained nearby throughout the exercise, gathering information on the Russian ship’s operations.
“A sustained presence and close cooperation with our allies meant HMS Tyne was perfectly prepared for this task, providing reassurance and surveillance while allowing other Fleet units to continue with their operational commitments,” Lt. Cmdr. Sam Fields, HMS Tyne’s commanding officer, said.
Russian warship escorts shadow fleet tanker
Neustrashimy was again tracked later in July, this time by HMS Severn during a three-day mission from July 23 to July 26.
According to Zona Militar, Severn took over surveillance duties in the North Sea from HMS Mersey while the Russian frigate escorted the tanker MV Vulkan from the Baltic.
The vessels continued through the Dover Strait before heading toward Ushant off the French coast.
The operation highlights the increasingly close connection between conventional Russian naval assets and tankers linked to Moscow’s shadow fleet, which Russia uses to move energy exports despite Western restrictions.
British frigate spends months hunting
At the same time, the Type 23 frigate HMS Somerset completed a four-month North Atlantic deployment focused on monitoring both surface and submarine activity.
The ship operated with advanced underwater sensors and a Merlin anti-submarine warfare helicopter from 814 Naval Air Squadron.
According to Zona Militar, the mission formed part of wider British operations to protect the country’s strategic nuclear deterrent while maintaining awareness of Russian submarine movements.
HMS Somerset returned to the UK on August 7 after traveling more than 26,500 nautical miles during the deployment.
“This deployment demonstrates exactly what the Royal Navy exists for—to protect the United Kingdom and our allies wherever our interests are threatened,” commanding officer Matt Millyard said.
Millyard also highlighted the ship’s submarine-tracking missions and cooperation with NATO allies during the deployment.
The July operations show that Britain is increasingly dedicating both ships and aircraft to tracking Russian military movements across UK waters and the wider North Atlantic.
Earlier, reports emerged that Russia has assembled an unprecedentedly large fleet of tankers, which have either begun or are preparing to transport nearly 8 million barrels of crude oil through the Northern Sea Route (NSR).

Russia’s “Spy Priests”: FSB Allegedly Uses Orthodox Church to Reach US Targets

Russia’s “Spy Priests”: FSB Allegedly Uses Orthodox Church to Reach US Targets
The Russian Orthodox Church (ROC) has systematically coordinated with Russia's FSB security service to identify and punish priests who oppose the war against Ukraine, religious scholar Sergei Chapnin alleges in a newly published book.
The findings were reported by the independent Russian outlet Agentstvo on August 12, drawing on Chapnin's English-language study, "Religious Communities Under Pressure: Documenting Religious Persecution in Russia 2022–2026."
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Chapnin, a former editor of the Journal of the Moscow Patriarchate, wrote that documented cases reveal notable patterns of coordination between state agencies and church authorities.
That coordination, according to Chapnin's account, took several forms. Evidence gathered by state agencies—wiretapped calls and intercepted messages—surfaced verbatim in church court proceedings.
State-controlled media and church information services published nearly identical accounts of targeted clergy, deploying the same arguments to discredit them. In many regions, FSB officers personally visited local bishops to discuss priests who had taken, or might take, an anti-war stance.
After the invasion, the FSB sharply expanded monitoring of parish-level communications, social media groups, and correspondence among believers, Chapnin noted, allowing it to flag dissent early.
He also pointed to a declassified 2009 memorandum, recovered in part from the laptop of a church external-relations official and disclosed by journalists Andrei Soldatov and Irina Borogan.
In Chapnin's telling, the document authorized "coordination with the counterintelligence service of the FSB" and treated church representatives as intermediaries for reaching potential intelligence targets in the US. Enlisting them for operational work, it noted, required only the patriarch's blessing, with a dedicated church body coordinating contact with the security services.
Chapnin traced the arrangement to Patriarch Kirill, writing that one of the ROC leader's first initiatives after taking office was to restore cooperation with Russia's intelligence services.
The book cites the case of Archpriest Sergei Rybakov, former rector of a university church in Samara, who criticized the war online. In March 2023, Rybakov recounted, a local metropolitan warned him he was under FSB surveillance; by September, he had been barred from the ministry.
In another instance, seminary graduates Denis Popovich and Nikita Ivankovich, both ethnic Ukrainians, were accused in 2025 of plotting to kill Metropolitan Tikhon. A campaign to discredit them began in late 2022 via a Telegram channel that Chapnin linked to the Moscow Patriarchate and the FSB.
By Chapnin's count, authorities have secured at least 35 convictions against religious figures and believers since the full-scale invasion, with at least three more criminal cases under investigation as of June 2026.
At least 30 administrative cases were recorded for "discrediting" the army, 13 religious figures and organizations were labeled "foreign agents," five people were placed on "terrorist" lists, and 10 organizations were declared "undesirable."
The church imposed its own penalties on at least 38 priests, defrocking 17, barring 14 from ministry, and pushing seven into retirement. In all, the study documents more than 115 cases involving clergy, believers, and religious activists.
Meanwhile, assessments circulated in mid-2026 described ROC priests posted abroad as recruited by or affiliated with Russian intelligence agencies, including the FSB, casting the church's overseas parishes as instruments for espionage and pro-Kremlin influence across Europe.

Held under the theme "The Rise of Autonomous Systems: Implications for Defence and Security in Africa," the one-day conference gathered policymakers, security leaders, researchers, and development partners to deliberate on emerging threats, security transformation, governance, ethics, legal and policy frameworks, and Africa's technological preparedness.
Rwandan Foreign Minister Olivier Nduhungirehe said that Africa cannot afford to fall behind as military and security technologies continue to evolve.
"We must understand the implications for our security, but also for our sovereignty and strategic autonomy. At the same time, autonomous systems also present opportunities," he noted. "They can help us respond more effectively to some of our most pressing security challenges, including terrorism, armed insurgencies and organized crime."
Nduhungirehe said that autonomous systems and artificial intelligence are increasingly accessible, including to non-state actors, which means that defence and security institutions must continuously adapt and stay ahead.
ISCA Executive Director Frank Mushyo Kamanzi said that AI and autonomous aerial, maritime and ground systems are reshaping warfare, border security, peace support operations and national defence.
"How do we ensure meaningful human oversight and accountability regarding the use of force? These questions demand collective leadership and cooperation," he said.
Mali's Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation Abdoulaye Diop said that autonomous systems are not just a technological issue or a military issue. "They are political. They are geostrategic. They require a political response," he added.
ISCA is an international non-governmental organization dedicated to fostering dialogue, collaboration and actionable solutions to address security challenges across the African continent. ■

====================================================================================================

Summer at USAFA: Academy Aims to Teach Airmanship to All
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
15:29:35 UTC
00:29:35 KST

Editor’s Note: This is the third and final article in a multipart series on military training during the summer at the U.S. Air Force Academy. The first, on Basic Cadet Training, is available here. The second, on Combat Skills, is available here.
AIR FORCE ACADEMY, Colo.—It’s a warm, windy morning at one of the busiest flightlines in the U.S. Air Force, and not a single officer or jet is in sight. Instead, dozens of 18-22-year-old cadets scurry around sleek, engine-less gliders as classic pop tunes blare from a speaker.
Every few moments, a prop plane takes off with a glider careening behind, pulled with battered tow rope, or the planes land, having successfully released a sailplane.
Across the runway, in an ops building, a dozen more cadets are strapped into simulators, soaring over a virtual replica of the Colorado landscape. Nearby, more cadets mill around the step desk, where an old-school “puckboard” displays names on the day’s schedule.
The Air Force Academy operates the largest glider program in the U.S., with more than 15,000 flights every year—almost entirely led and managed by the youngest instructor pilots in the Air Force. The enterprise is poised to get even busier as USAFA leaders drive toward their ambitious objective: to get every cadet serious time in the air.
70-Year Legacy
The USAFA glider program dates to the 1950s. Overseen today by the 94th Flying Training Squadron, participation levels have fluctuated over the years. There was a “Soar-for-All” program in the 1970s to give every cadet at least some time in a glider; today, about 500 to 600 members of every class—about half—take the Academy’s basic soaring class, 94th Commander Lt. Col. Curtis Holtman told Air & Space Forces Magazine during a recent visit. (The school also has a powered flight program, and as of 2018, about 70 percent of cadets participated in one or the other flying program.)
Now, once again, the academy’s is aiming to give every cadet a chance to fly.
Airmanship for All means ensuring all 4,000 or so USAFA cadets “obtain real flight experience,” said C1C Noel Migliaccio, cadet commander of the Operations Group this summer.
Some will do so in an expanded powered flight program, where cadets fly in T-53A Kadett II with a rated officer. But more will get that opportunity in one of USAFA’s 23 gliders, Migliaccio said.
Holtman said the program has evolved over time. “We in the 94th have actually kind of led … this over the last three years,” he said. “Three years ago, we were sitting right around 300ish cadets coming through. We’ve incrementally scaled that over the last two years to we’re heading into fiscal year ’27, we’ll push over 500 to 600 cadets through our basic soaring program.”
Changes to the syllabus helped. And with “access to cadet time, operating hour increases, things of that nature, then we can absolutely get to the 800 to 1,000 cadet throughput mark,” Holtman said. “If we can get to Airmanship for All through the soaring program, that is our end state objective.”
Cadet IPs
Each participating cadet gets eight flights—any less, Holtman said, and study shows cadets don’t get comfortable in the air. But some cadets get much more than those eight sorties.
After going through the basic soaring class, about 70 to 80 percent of participants apply to be instructor pilots. To be selected, they must pass an interview with a board of current cadet IPs, in which the candidate must teach the board members something to demonstrate their teaching style. The teaching topic is wide open—one cadet tought how to change a diaper, while another showed how to use a yo-yo.
Around 60 candidates are selected, after which they go through scores of flights to earn their “G” wings, then scores more as IPs. C1C James Callaghan estimates he has made more than 300 glider flights to date.
Holtman said the ranks of IPs will have to grow to achieve Airmanship for All, perhaps by an additional 10. Beyond teaching other cadets to fly, he says, IPs are also getting their first taste of life in an operational squadron. They rotate through different leadership positions throughout the year, conduct morning safety briefs, and run the step desk.
“Everything you see in this facility is what they are going to go see as soon as they go fly gray tails,” Holtman said.
The simulators cadets train on are the same immersive training devices that Air Education and Training Command uses at undergraduate pilot training, with virtual reality headsets and controls that mimic a real cockpit.
“If we can move the needle left, then we’re only preparing them better to have that high rate of fidelity transfer from what they have here to what they’ll go do in the future,” Holtman said.
Airmanship
Many academy instructor pilots have gone on to become full-fledged Air Force pilots. The halls of the 94th ops building are full of memorabilia from glider fliers who went on to Thunderbird pilots, general officers, astronauts, and more.
The skills developed in soaring build a strong foundation for future pilots—and future officers in any career.
“I think gliders are unique in that they really do build situational awareness and energy management, which are things that we’re gonna use throughout a career, no matter what platform we end up flying on when we graduate,” Callaghan said. “Those are values that take practice to build, and my bubble for both of those have increased exponentially. And then, on top of that, being an instructor pilot and being able to talk through your flying and get someone that has never touched an airplane before to basically learn how to fly has really helped with my communication skills.”
Not that flying a glider is the same as a powered aircraft, C1C Joseph Fitzsimmons said, but flying demands “soft skill and hard skills,” and gliders give cadets a jump start on the soft skills.
“The air awareness, the airmindedness, the task management skills, all of those are baked into us now, and we will be able to carry that into whatever experience we have in the Air Force, whether it’s aviation or just leading Airmen,” Fitzsimmons said.
Indeed, while the Airmanship for All program might inspire more cadets to want to become aviators, there are only so many slots for rated career fields like pilot, air battle manager, or combat systems officer. In USAFA’s class of 2026, almost 47 percent of graduates went into non-rated career fields.
In the Air
Whether they wind up becoming pilots, intelligence analysts, force support officers, or something else, cadets who go through the soaring program get to experience flying differently than most.
“I would argue that it is the most pure form of flying. Truly, you feel every bump of air, every input of the stick, every move of your rudder, you feel everything,” said Callaghan.
With the Academy located right on the windy edge of the Rocky Mountains, handling the glider requires vigilance and many small adjustments, Callaghan said. And because the gliders are so sleek, even flying while attached to the tow plane requires focus and touch.
It’s quiet aboard the glider—no engine roar, no ear-splitting whine. But there is maneuver, and glider fliers learn how to pull Gs and perform aerobatics. Some go on to compete, representing the Air Force Academy in competitions with other schools. USAFA cadets regularly bring home national championships.
The aerobatics come at the tail end of the eight sorties in the basic program—along with sick bags just in case cadets (or visiting reporters) can’t quite stomach 5 Gs.
“You feel everything about flying and build such an intimate connection with aviation,” Gallaghan said. It’s “flying in its purest form.”

Tehran, Iran – Shortly after meeting China’s ambassador, Iran’s new security chief left no room for doubt about Tehran’s position after nearly six months of war with the United States.

“Until all conditions are met, the Strait will remain closed,” added the former wartime commander-in-chief of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).

Abdollahi is tasked with integrating the Khatam headquarters, which was formed during the eight-year war with Iraq in the 1980s to coordinate operations between the then-nascent IRGC and Iran’s regular army, with the general staff overseeing all armed personnel.

“The country’s borders are fully safe and impenetrable through the vigilance of border personnel and the backing of people living in border areas, including the brave people of Kurdistan, Sistan and Baluchistan, and Khuzestan,” he was quoted as saying by state media.
In the meantime, most of Iran’s population of about 90 million people continues to weather the worsening impact of war and uncertainty, as well as a tightening security grip at home.
“I have given up on predicting what’s going to happen,” Jamshid, a 36-year-old resident of central Tehran, told Al Jazeera.

Should You Let Your Dog Lick Your Face? 9 Animal Hygiene Questions, Answered
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
15:28:35 UTC
00:28:35 KST

You might be surprised to learn that Dr. Daniel Griffin, chief of infectious diseases at Island Infectious Disease Medical in Long Island, N.Y., lets his two dogs lick him.
He’s not delusional. “We know how dogs greet each other,” he says. “We know where that tongue has been.” But he lets his expertise take over afterward. Griffin diligently washes his hands after his dogs lick them, especially before picking up a slice of pizza.
That’s more or less the expert consensus: love the pet, wash your hands. Living closely with pets brings you closer to germs, but for most people, ordinary contact is low-risk. There are exceptions, however. Here, experts answer the face-licking question and eight others about hygiene and animals you might encounter.
Should you let your dog lick your face?
First, forget the thing you may have heard your whole life. “I used to hear, ‘Oh, dogs’ mouths are like 10 times cleaner than people’s mouths,’” says Kelley Steury, a veterinarian and clinical associate professor at the University of Nevada, Reno School of Public Health. “I don’t think that’s based in science.”
A dog’s mouth, like a person’s, is full of bacteria. One species commonly found in dogs, Capnocytophaga canimorsus, can occasionally cause serious illness in people. Most of the time, though, nothing happens. “It doesn’t really pose a problem,” Steury says. The trouble starts when saliva gets past the body’s defenses—through a bite or into an open cut, for example. In rare cases, the infection can progress to sepsis and become fatal.
The risk also depends on who’s getting licked. People being treated for cancer or taking immune-suppressing drugs are more vulnerable to severe C. canimorsus infection. So are people without a spleen and those with alcohol-use disorder. But for healthy kids and adults, the occasional lick is fine, experts say.
Official guidance takes the cautious route, though: Keep dogs away from your mouth and face, and don’t let them lick open wounds. Saliva is more of a concern when it reaches broken skin or a mucous membrane, such as the mouth or eyes. If your dog gets you anyway, wash the area afterward. And if you’re immunocompromised or don’t have a spleen, ask your doctor what precautions make sense. But the fact that dogs, like so many of our daily exposures, can carry germs is not “a reason to not own a dog,” she says.
What if your cat licks you?
A cat lick is usually a non-event, too, provided your skin is intact. Cats commonly carry Pasteurella multocida, but on unbroken skin, Steury says, it “pretty much will not be a problem at all.”
Experts are more concerned about bites. A cat’s teeth are narrow and sharp, so they often puncture instead of scraping the surface. “The tooth acts kind of like a needle,” Steury says, “and it’ll inject that bacteria into your deep tissues.” What looks like a pinprick can be a deeper wound than it appears.
If a cat bite breaks the skin, wash it immediately with soap and running water and see a medical provider, Steury says.
What should you do about a cat scratch?
“I definitely respect the claws of cats,” says Dr. Peter Chin-Hong, an infectious disease specialist at the University of California, San Francisco.
If a claw catches you, wash your skin right away with soap and running water. The goal is to rinse the bacteria away before it settles in, not to disinfect. “Disinfectants don’t kill everything,” he says. “Running things are better than stagnant things in general.”
After that, pay attention to the area. Increasing redness, pus, or a fever over the next several days are all reasons to see a medical professional. So is a swollen lymph node on the same side of your body as the scratch, which can signal cat-scratch disease, a bacterial infection most common in kids. Location matters, too. Chin-Hong is extra cautious when a bite or scratch lands directly over a joint, where an infection can be harder to treat.
What if you have a fresh surgical site?
Coming home from surgery might be when you most want your furry friend on your bed. It’s also when experts want you to put a little distance between your pet and whatever is healing.
Dr. Ashley Drews, an infectious disease specialist at Houston Methodist, has seen patients develop infections after a pet licked an incision or surgical drain. “That’s not a good idea,” she says. Keep the site covered and your pet away from it.
Do you need to worry about the litter box?
Yes. Cats can shed Toxoplasma gondii in their poop, and the parasite can travel from the box to your hands to your mouth.
Yet the litter box isn’t the only way to get toxoplasmosis. The parasite can also turn up in soil, unwashed produce, contaminated water, and undercooked meat—especially pork, lamb, and venison.
“I think people are aware of the cat litter thing,” says Jill Roberts, a molecular epidemiologist and professor at the University of South Florida College of Public Health. Meat gets less attention. Roberts is so wary of undercooked pork that she skips thick cuts, which she worries are harder to bring to a safe temperature. “All I can see is Toxoplasma,” she says. You don’t have to give up pork chops, but you should use a food thermometer: Whole cuts of pork should reach 145°F. Once they come off the heat, wait at least three minutes before cutting or eating them; the meat’s temperature holds steady or continues to rise during that time, helping destroy pathogens.
While the pork chop may deserve more attention, the litter-box rule still stands. If you’re pregnant or immunocompromised, hand off the scooping if you can. If you have to do it yourself, wear disposable gloves and wash your hands afterward. Change the litter daily, too: The parasite takes one to five days after being shed to become infectious.
Can you catch your dog’s parasites?
Sometimes, but your dog’s diagnosis doesn’t automatically mean the whole household is next. When Griffin’s dogs had giardia, an intestinal illness caused by a microscopic parasite, he wasn’t panicking about catching it himself. “In general, it’s a different giardia that we get vs. dogs,” he says. The type that usually makes people sick isn’t the same type that usually infects dogs and cats.
Pay special attention during cleanup. Giardia can travel through tiny traces of feces on soil, water, fur, surfaces, and objects. Clean up dog poop promptly; keep up with veterinary care and parasite prevention; and clean the bowls, bedding, crates, and toys of a pet being treated for giardia. Your veterinarian may also recommend a bath to remove contaminated feces from its fur.
Always use actual soap and water after handling a sick pet or cleaning up poop. Sanitizer is helpful when it’s all you have, but it doesn’t remove dirt or every kind of germ.
Are your pets bringing ticks into the house?
Quite possibly. Your dog can come inside alone and still bring company. Dogs and cats can carry ticks indoors, where the ticks may disembark and choose a human for their next meal. Dr. Heidi Torres, an infectious disease physician and assistant hospital epidemiologist at Weill Cornell Medicine in New York, takes the possibility seriously enough to pack fine-tipped tweezers for overnight trips to the country.
Ticks are remarkably good at hiding in plain sight. On people, they tend to hide under arms, behind knees, around the waist, and in the hair. On dogs, check the ears, under the front legs, and between the toes. Torres says many people who develop Lyme disease or another tickborne illness “have no recollection of ever being bitten by a tick or ever seeing a tick.”
After spending time in tall grasses or woods, make sure everyone gets inspected. “Check yourself, check your partner, check your kids, check your dogs,” Torres says. If you find a tick attached to your skin, remove it then and there; waiting for a doctor only gives it more time to feed and potentially transmit disease. Use fine-tipped tweezers to grasp it close to the skin, pull upward with steady pressure, and then clean the bite and your hands. Finding a tick doesn’t automatically necessitate a trip to urgent care, but call your doctor if you develop a rash, fever, or other symptoms over the next several days or weeks.
What about backyard chickens and petting zoos?
Your pets aren’t the only animals capable of handing something off. More than 60% of known infectious diseases in people can spread between animals and humans, Steury says. The list of germs that can make the trip includes E. coli, Campylobacter, Cryptosporidium, and Salmonella—none of which care whether the animal carrying them looks clean.
Backyard chickens deserve special mention, in part because more people are keeping them. A chicken can look perfectly healthy and still carry Salmonella. Steury’s rules for handling them are uncomplicated: Wash your hands afterward, and “don’t kiss them,” she says.
The same logic applies at the petting zoo, with the added complication that children are extraordinarily efficient at putting their hands in their mouths. Steury isn’t telling you to skip it; just wash everyone’s hands with soap and water on the way out, and keep fingers and pacifiers out of mouths until you find a sink. Hand sanitizer is a useful backup, but it isn’t an equal substitute.
When does an animal encounter require a same-day phone call?
If an animal bites you hard enough to break the skin, or if you’ve had a possible encounter with a bat, seek medical care immediately. For animal bites, wash the wound right away with soap and water, then call a health-care provider—especially if the animal was wild, a stray, or behaving strangely, or if you don’t know whether it’s been vaccinated against rabies, a fatal disease that affects mammals.
The reassuring part is that less than 10 people die from rabies each year in the U.S., largely because most pets are vaccinated and people who may have been exposed can get preventive treatment.
The bar for what counts as a bat exposure is even lower because people may not realize they were bitten. “People think, ‘Well, I think I’d know it if a bat bit me,’” Steury says, “but you may not.” Bat teeth are so small that their bites can be painless or barely noticeable. If you wake up with a bat in your bedroom, find one near a sleeping child, or think you might have touched one, don’t open the window and shoo it out before asking what to do, Steury recommends. Call animal control or your health department. If it can be safely contained, health officials can test it for rabies. If it’s already disappeared, call anyway; public-health officials can determine whether you need post-exposure vaccination.
Steury knew a veterinarian in Alabama who had an unnerving encounter. “A bat just fell out of the sky and fell on her neck,” she says. It tested positive for rabies, and the veterinarian needed post-exposure shots even though she’d already been vaccinated in the past.
Of course, none of this means treating every animal like a biohazard. It means knowing what calls for soap, what calls for a phone call or doctor’s visit, and what you can stop worrying about. As Chin-Hong puts it, “The benefits of pets outweigh the disadvantages.”

Police had imposed tighter controls around the site by Wednesday, while volunteers were being directed to specific tasks, helping rescuers work more effectively, he said.
Among those still waiting for news about loved ones was Marcela Perez, who said her partner's 11-year-old daughter was trapped with the girl's grandparents when the building collapsed.

Movie Review: ‘The End of Oak Street’ is a gonzo good time
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
15:23:02 UTC
00:23:02 KST

Movie Review: ‘The End of Oak Street’ is a gonzo good time
At the end of the block in David Robert Mitchell’s “The End of Oak Street,” is a cul-de-sac with a telephone pole in the middle and wires radiating out like the cables of a big top. It’s a fitting touch for a breakneck, carnivalesque movie made with throwback showmanship.
Summer movies, of course, are not known for lacking in circus-like mayhem. But much of the pastiche delight of the 1980s-set “The End of Oak Street,” a mid-August surprise, is how it absorbs an Amblin-style blockbuster spirit and conjures, without winking irony or belabored homage, a summer thrill ride seemingly designed for the drive-in.
Mitchell’s breakthrough was the nifty 2014 horror “It Follows,” which he followed up with an admirably ambitious but shaggily self-indulgent Los Angeles neo noir, “Under the Silver Lake.” But any indulgences in “The End of Oak Street,” about a 1980s suburban family whose neighborhood is transported through time, are for the audience. “The End of Oak Street” is a bonkers blast.
It’s best going in not knowing anything about the movie’s twists, so tread carefully on the rest of this review. That’s not to say that an enormous amount of “The End of Oak Street” isn’t immediately familiar, starting with the central family.
The Platts live in what looks like a San Fernando Valley neighborhood full of split levels and tidy little streets. Denise (Anne Hathaway) and Greg (Ewan McGregor) have two kids and a dog named Starbuck. Audrey (Maisy Stella) is a teenager and Brian (Christian Convery) is her younger brother.
But from the moment we meet them, during a neighborhood fair, there are obvious cracks in their all-American life. Greg is working a side job delivering pizzas while Denise is secretly typing up a maybe-aspirational novel about a woman dreaming of leaving her family. The kids have their own secrets, too. They suspect their parents are on the cusp of divorcing, and so, seemingly, do Greg and Denise.
Such a framework for sci-fi cataclysm is, naturally, Spielberg 101. But while “The End of Oak Street” is sure to test and restore their familial bonds, Mitchell, who also wrote the script, takes a route that leans more into horror, absurdism and outright silliness.
In any case, yes, there are dinosaurs. It’s both skillful and a lot of fun how Mitchell teases them out. The first signs are mysterious. A flash of light. A strange exotic flower in a neighbor’s backyard. A giant mount of feces in another’s. But soon, the Platts find that their neighborhood is overrun with primordial beasts and surrounded by jungle: Oak Street is suddenly a suburban island in a prehistoric world.
It’s a perfectly “Twilight Zone” plot that inadvertently solves the problems that have plagued the “Jurassic Park” movies for 20 years. If those films have struggled to find an off-island setting, “The End of Oak Street” instead brings the dino isle straight into suburbia. Encounters with raptors and worse transpire across front porches and shag carpets.
You could chalk it all up to good dumb fun. And it is mostly that, with set pieces built to make an audience groan in anticipation or cheer for the successful swing of a sledgehammer. But where “The End of Oak Street” succeeds where so many others fail is in the sincerity it has for its characters. Ridiculous and over-the-top as the concept is, the Platts are firmly grounded. (Hathaway, especially, helps in this department.) The combination of an earnest family drama with CGI hijinks, plus increasingly nutty plotting, make “The End of Oak Street” a fairly nonstop hoot.
Composer Michael Giacchino does his best John Williams impression to match. But Mitchell’s film also increasingly detours from the Spielberg playbook. Only Mitchell would take a moment for a freaked-out Audrey to sneak into the car to pop a cassette in and listen to Steve Winwood’s “Valerie.”
And while it would be pushing it to say there’s that much underneath “The End of Oak Street,” its characters are united in keeping certain things secret out of fear that their spouse or kids or parents can’t handle the truth. The swiftness that the dinosaurs invade their neighborhood could be symbolic of any ecological disaster, but the subsequent challenges prove each member of the family can handle quite a bit more than expected — even when the parental assurance that everything’s going to be OK, like when a giant snake is slithering through their home, is laughably disputable.
It adds up to a gonzo good time that gives an old-school family adventure a darker, modern spin. Mitchell has quickly made suburbia his evident domain, where “it,” or something else, is sure to follow.
“The End of Oak Street,” a Warner Bros. release in theaters Thursday, is rated PG-13 by the Motion Picture Association for some strong violent content, bloody images, some strong language and suggestive material. Running time: 99 minutes. Three stars out of four.

Tropical Storm Cristobal forms in the Atlantic and a Pacific system could threaten Hawaii
MIAMI (AP) — Tropical Storm Cristobal formed Wednesday in the Atlantic Ocean well west of the Azores, and a Pacific storm system could threaten Hawaii this weekend, forecasters said.
There were no coastal watches or warnings in effect, the National Hurricane Center in Miami said, and the storm was forecast to dissipate on Thursday.
Cristobal was located about 880 miles (1,416 kilometers) west of the Azores with maximum sustained winds of 45 mph (72 kph). It was moving east.
Meanwhile, in the Pacific Ocean, the NHC initiated advisories on Potential Tropical Cyclone One-C, which was located about 1,000 miles (1,609 kilometers) east-southeast of the Hawaiian Islands and packed winds of 35 mph (56 kph).
The NHC said the system was moving west and was expected to strengthen into a tropical storm before nearing the Hawaiian Islands by late Friday. A hurricane watch or tropical storm watch will likely be needed for the islands by early Thursday, forecasters said.
The system could bring rainfall totals of 5 to 10 inches (13 to 25 centimeters) in the island chain, with up to 20 inches (51 centimeters) possible, forecasters said. That could produce flooding and mudslides, the NHC said.

WHO says Congo’s Ebola outbreak is on track to eclipse the deadliest one in history
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
15:23:02 UTC
00:23:02 KST

WHO says Congo’s Ebola outbreak is on track to surpass the deadliest one in history
The ongoing Ebola outbreak in Congo is on track to surpass the deadliest one in history that killed over 11,000 people, the head of the World Health Organization said Wednesday.
“At its current pace, it’s on track to eclipse the West African Ebola outbreak of 2014 to 2016,” Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus told reporters. That outbreak horrified the world and jolted efforts to develop a vaccine.
The outbreak in eastern Congo, considered the fastest-growing in history, has killed over 2,000 people out of more than 4,300 cases. The outbreak was declared on May 15, but health authorities now say sequencing showed it began months earlier, in February.
It is unlike recent Ebola outbreaks because the rare Bundibugyo virus responsible for it has no approved vaccines or treatments, though efforts to address that are underway.
WHO says this outbreak ‘had a big head start’
Experts say this outbreak is moving faster than efforts to track and manage it in a remote part of eastern Congo facing ongoing conflict, near the borders with South Sudan, Uganda and Rwanda.
Most new cases and deaths are being reported in communities outside the reach of health workers in a region of poor infrastructure and ill-equipped health centers. Some workers have gone on strike over lack of pay. Misinformation about the virus circulates in communities where some are wary of outsiders, keeping some people from clinics.
“The outbreak had a big head start, still way ahead of us. and we’re playing catch-up,” Tedros said.
Dr. Abdirahman Mahamud, WHO’s director for health emergency alert and response operations, said the agency expects the peak of the outbreak to be reached in six months.
“But ... that’s the moderate scenario,” Mahamud said. “There is a one-case scenario where this outbreak may last nine months to 12 months.”
This Ebola outbreak has killed more people at a faster rate than any other, including the 2014-2016 outbreak that had at least 28,000 cases. That one took about eight months to reach 1,000 deaths.
Two vaccines for this type are being tested
Ebola is rare but highly contagious and can be contracted from bodily fluids such as vomit, blood or semen and from contaminated surfaces and materials such as bedding and clothing. The disease it causes is severe and often fatal.
Clinical trials of two possible treatments for this type of Ebola began last month in Ituri, the most affected of the five provinces where cases have been reported.
Two vaccines developed specifically for the Bundibugyo virus are now being tested in people for the first time, Tedros said Wednesday.
WHO also plans to test whether an existing Ebola vaccine could protect people against the virus after studies in animals showed promising results.
The origins of the outbreak are becoming increasingly clear.
A study published in Nature Medicine on Monday added evidence that the outbreak began when the virus jumped from an infected animal to a person, rather than stemming from earlier outbreaks. Researchers found the virus is genetically different from versions seen in Bundibugyo Ebola outbreaks in 2007 and 2012.

A blockbuster $12.5B deal as Josh Kushner and Bob Iger buy the Los Angeles Lakers, AP source says

A blockbuster $12.5B deal as Josh Kushner and Bob Iger agree to buy the Lakers, AP source says
LOS ANGELES (AP) — The Los Angeles Lakers are being sold for the second time in a year, going to businessmen Josh Kushner and Bob Iger for a record-breaking price.
This sale agreement is $12.5 billion, according to a person familiar with the terms who spoke to The Associated Press on condition of anonymity Wednesday because neither side revealed specific details of the latest stunning development with one of North America’s marquee sports teams.
ESPN first reported that Kushner and Iger are buying the NBA’s most valuable franchise. The Lakers were valued last year at $10 billion — a record for a pro sports team — when Mark Walter purchased a controlling stake from the Buss family, which had owned the team since 1979.
Kushner, a venture capitalist, and former Walt Disney Company CEO Iger had been working together on landing a possible NBA expansion team for Las Vegas. By buying the Lakers, they don’t have to wait until the possibility of expansion in the 2028-29 season at the earliest.
The sale still will need approval from the NBA’s board of governors, and that process can take several weeks. The next board meeting is set for September in New York.
The $12.5 billion price tag is not only a record for U.S. pro sports but a new summit in skyrocketing NBA franchise values. Only three years ago, Michael Jordan sold his majority stake in the Charlotte Hornets for a $3 billion valuation, while the Boston Celtics were sold last year to private equity mogul Bill Chisholm at a valuation of just over $6 billion.
Walter’s agreement to purchase a controlling stake in the Lakers at the $10 billion valuation last summer obliterated that mark, and now Iger and Kushner have pushed the bar even higher.
The 66-year-old Walter’s shocking decision to sell the Lakers after just 10 months of official ownership is reverberating throughout the team’s massive fan base, which appeared to be uniformly excited about the purchase last year. Walter has stewarded the Los Angeles Dodgers into the most successful stretch in franchise history, with three World Series championships in the past six seasons as the most aggressive spenders in baseball.
Multiple media outlets last month reported that Walter’s business empire is under scrutiny from both federal prosecutors and the Securities and Exchange Commission in tax fraud investigations.
The 41-year-old Kushner’s capital holding company, Thrive Eternal, was set to be the “anchor investor” in FIFA President Gianni Infantino’s plan to sell stakes in future World Cup profits. Infantino abandoned the idea on July 31. Kushner’s brother is Jared Kushner, son-in-law of U.S. President Donald Trump.
Josh Kushner currently owns a minority stake in the Miami Heat, and he previously owned a stake in the Memphis Grizzlies.
The 75-year-old Iger became one of Hollywood’s most well-known executives while he ran Disney for two lengthy stints between 2005 and last March, when he stepped aside. Iger and his wife, former sports journalist Willow Bay, are the controlling owners of NWSL team Angel City FC.
Walter’s purchase of the Lakers was approved by NBA owners last October. He originally bought a 27% minority stake in the team in 2021 before purchasing control of the team last year.
Walter and his partners also have ownership interests in the WNBA’s Los Angeles Sparks, English Premier League club Chelsea, the Professional Women’s Hockey League and the new Cadillac Formula 1 racing team.
When Walter bought his controlling interest in the Lakers, the deal specified that Jeanie Buss would stay on as the team’s governor. With new ownership, it’s unclear whether Buss will have a continuing role in the team she inherited along with her siblings from her father, Jerry Buss, who died in 2013.
The Lakers have won 17 championships going back to the franchise’s origin in Minneapolis, the second-most in NBA history behind Boston’s 18. It is a global brand, always at or near the top of the league’s merchandise-sales rankings.
This record sale price comes just weeks after LeBron James, the league’s all-time leading scorer, left the Lakers after eight seasons to become a free agent. James ultimately decided to sign with the Philadelphia 76ers.
The Lakers won their most recent title in 2020, and they have made the playoffs in each of the past four seasons. Their current roster is built around NBA scoring champion Luka Doncic, who is signed through the 2028-29 season.

David Crowley’s razor-thin Wisconsin primary win sets up match against Trump pick

David Crowley’s razor-thin Wisconsin primary win sets up a match against a Trump pick
MADISON, Wis. (AP) — David Crowley’s razor-thin primary win over a democratic socialist sets up a Wisconsin governor’s race against a Republican congressman who has voted with President Donald Trump 100% of the time, potentially giving moderate Democrats an ideal matchup as Trump’s approval ratings sag in the swing state.
Crowley overcame Francesca Hong in dramatic fashion in Tuesday’s primary, stunning pundits and pollsters who had long placed Hong as the frontrunner. That means Crowley’s challenger, U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany, must pivot to face a Democrat known for working across the aisle with Republicans as the county executive in Milwaukee, the state’s largest source of Democratic voters.
Crowley immediately leans into Tiffany’s ties with Trump
In his first comments Wednesday after his win, Crowley linked Tiffany to Trump and called him a “MAGA extremist,” referring to the president’s Make America Great Again movement. Crowley promised to build a broad coalition to defeat Tiffany, who he accused of being in “lockstep” with Trump.
“The biggest difference between me and the congressman is I’m loyal to the people of Wisconsin, I’m not loyal to MAGA,” Crowley said.
It will be easier for Tiffany to pivot away from his ties with Trump and unpopular federal policies because he’s running for governor and not Congress, said former Republican Gov. Scott Walker, a Trump supporter.
“He’s got to be on point, on message every time that comes up and say, ‘That’s not what’s on the ballot,’” Walker told The Associated Press. “What’s on the ballot is who’s going to be governor the next four years.”
Tiffany represents a broad swath of Wisconsin’s rural, conservative north woods. Trump won the state in 2024 and 2016, but lost in 2020. All three elections were decided by less than a percentage point. Crowley’s win on Tuesday was even more narrow — less than half a point, further cementing Wisconsin’s well-earned place as one of the most purple states in the country.
Democrats look for a trifecta in Wisconsin
Democrats have been savoring the shift in focus from their chaotic primary to the general election against Tiffany, an opponent they’ve long seen as vulnerable. They hope to capitalize on Trump’s low approval ratings to retain control of the governor’s office and flip both chambers of the Legislature to earn full control of Wisconsin state government for the first time since 2010.
Just as Crowley highlighted his Republican opponent’s ties to Trump, Tiffany began the general election campaign with a message connecting Crowley to Hong.
“I’ve said all along that there’s not a dime’s worth of difference between these Democrat candidates,” Tiffany said in a statement Wednesday. “His record in Milwaukee County shows exactly what Wisconsin would get: mismanage the government, run up the bill, and raise your taxes to pay for it.”
Walker said Tiffany’s messaging was on point. “High taxes, high costs, failing schools — make that the definition of David Crowley,” Walker said.
Crowley’s surprise win came after he had dropped out of the race
Crowley has been the head of Wisconsin’s largest county since 2020. Prior to that, he served just over three years in the state Assembly. In 2023, as county executive, Crowley helped spearhead a bipartisan deal in the Legislature that sent more state aid to Milwaukee and local communities.
Crowley dropped out of the governor’s race on July 8, saying he didn’t see a path to victory. He rejoined it on July 18, less than a month before Tuesday’s primary. With the backing of Democratic Gov. Tony Evers, a fellow moderate who crisscrossed the state with him in the final week, Crowley pulled out the narrow win on the argument that he was the better matchup against Tiffany.
“Obviously Hong was the never-ending gift in terms of one gaffe after another, wasn’t really ready for prime time,” Walker said. “But Crowley didn’t get any real scrutiny either.”
Crowley planned to appear at a unity event later Wednesday with Democratic leaders, including U.S. Sen. Tammy Baldwin, before launching a statewide tour. Evers is not seeking a third term as governor.
Crowley, 40, became the first Black person to win a major party nomination for Wisconsin governor. Now he’s vying to become the first Black governor of the state.
“This historic moment is not lost on me. But I’m not even thinking about that because we’ve still got work to do,” Crowley said. “The job is not done. The job is not finished. My job is not to become the first, and if I do become the first, my job is to make sure I’m not the last.”

WHO chief warns US childhood vaccine policy changes ‘not aligned with best science’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
15:19:35 UTC
00:19:35 KST

Beyza Binnur Donmez
12 August 2026•Update: 12 August 2026
The World Health Organization (WHO) chief expressed concern Wednesday about recent changes to childhood vaccination policy in the US, warning that they are "not aligned" with the best available scientific evidence.
Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus told a media briefing in Geneva that decades of research have established when children are most vulnerable to disease, when vaccines provide the strongest protection, how doses should be administered, and which vaccines can safely be given together.
“WHO is concerned that the changes to immunization policy in the US are not aligned with the best science,” said Tedros.
He stressed that available evidence remains clear on the safety of vaccines, including the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine.
“The current evidence is unequivocal: vaccines – including the MMR vaccine – are safe and do not cause autism,” he said.
Tedros also warned that delaying vaccinations or unnecessarily separating doses does not make immunization safer and can instead leave children unprotected against preventable diseases.
He said vaccination policy should be based on "rigorous, independent and transparent" assessment of scientific evidence as new data emerge, and "not by political influence."
US President Donald Trump issued an order Monday, establishing new “Gold Standard Childhood Vaccine Recommendations,” saying the policy aims to support "maximum parental choice" over childhood vaccines.
The order divides childhood immunizations into three groups: those recommended for all children, those advised for certain high-risk groups, and those based on shared clinical decision-making.
It also calls for the MMR vaccine to be given as three separate shots once single-disease vaccines become available in the US, and says childhood vaccines should, where feasible, be administered at separate medical visits.

Andrew Tate, 39, and Tristan Tate, 38, dual US-British citizens and former professional kickboxers, built a global following promoting views on wealth and masculinity before becoming among the internet's most polarizing figures. The agreement also includes "operator training, as well as the supply of the Ground Control Station and the ATLAS mission system".
The AR5 drone, which has a wingspan of almost 8 m and weighs about 200 kg, is specifically designed for maritime missions. The systems are expected to enable the Portuguese Air Force to "strengthen its operational autonomy on long-range missions".
These include maritime surveillance, security and defence, monitoring of the exclusive economic zone and support for missions in the public interest.
Tekever said that in the first phase it will train Portuguese Air Force personnel by September so that the military could operate the systems immediately after delivery. A second phase of training will then begin in October to consolidate "full operational readiness and the development of new skills within the operating teams".
Tekever did not disclose the value of the contract. However, Portugal's Ministry of Defence issued an order in November authorising the Air Force to purchase an unmanned aerial system for maritime patrols with a maximum total budget of just over €7.79 million.

Astronomers discover a new kind of cosmic object – a black hole ‘star’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
15:17:40 UTC
00:17:40 KST

Astronomers claim to have discovered a new kind of cosmic object, a black hole “star”, which is the size of the entire solar system and glows with a brilliant red light.
The international team made the breakthrough after focusing their attention on a mysterious red spot in images of the early solar system captured by Nasa’s James Webb space telescope.
The object was lurking in the constellation of Cetus, the Whale, billions of light years from Earth. It is thought to have formed 660m years after the big bang, astronomers’ leading theory as to how the universe began.
Measurements of the exotic body found that while it resembles an immense star, it releases 100bn times more energy than any known star can produce. The energy output is far closer to that observed from black holes than stars.
“We have found a new type of astrophysical object, a black hole star,” said Dr Rohan Naidu at the Kavli Institute for Astrophysics and Space Research, part of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. It “shines with the energy typically associated with black holes, but at the same time bears signatures classically associated with stars”, he added.
The scientists were using the James Webb space telescope to find the most distant galaxies in the known universe. After succeeding with a galaxy named Mom-z14, which formed a mere 280m years after the big bang, they turned their attention to other cosmic objects.
Writing in Nature, the astronomers describe how they focused on an extremely bright red spot known as MoM-BH*-1, the reddest object in the telescope’s image archive. “The way its light is almost entirely red, and abruptly disappears below a certain wavelength, is so dramatic that there is no comparison among any known class of objects,” Naidu said.
Computer simulations showed that rather than being an enormous star powered by nuclear fusion, the object is a black hole so swaddled in shrouds of dense gas that it radiates like a star.
If the astronomers are correct, it suggests that scores of other mysterious Little Red Dots, or LRDs, that appear in nearly every deep space image from the James Webb space telescope are also black hole stars.
Naidu suspects that black hole stars play a major role in the evolution of galaxies. They might be the seeds of present-day supermassive black holes, such as the one at the centre of the Milky Way. “For decades we have anticipated something spectacular must be afoot in the very early universe. Black hole stars may be the ‘something spectacular’. They may be the nascent, swaddled phase that marks the beginning of almost every supermassive black hole’s journey,” he said.
Supermassive black holes are found at the centres of almost all galaxies such as the Milky Way and are thought to shape the fate of those galaxies. “They may govern when stars are able to form and when they cease forming, setting the course for everything that follows from star formation: the birth of planets, the rise of life, the emergence of species that may one day piece together this entire history,” Naidu said.
