Iraqi PM seeks parliamentary backing to monopolise weapons
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
13:26:33 UTC
22:26:33 KST

Breadcrumb
Iraq's prime minister seeks parliamentary backing to monopolise weapons under the state
Monopolising weapons by the state in Iraq has entered a more sensitive phase, with Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi preparing a parliamentary bill restricting weapons to official institutions.
The move is an attempt to shift the issue from an executive decision for which the government alone bears responsibility to a legislative process backed and supported by parliament.
It would also give the state broader legal cover in confronting factional weapons. This reflects the complexities facing the issue, as al-Zaidi stressed that uncontrolled weapons pose "the greatest threat" to the state because they undermine the authority of the law and weaken the standing of security institutions.
Al-Zaidi held a meeting with the parliamentary security committee on Tuesday evening, 11 August, attended by its chairman, Khaled Meteb al-Obaidi, and members of the committee, according to a statement issued by al-Zaidi's office.
"The meeting reviewed the situation in the country and the efforts being made by the security services in their various branches and formations to impose security and stability and protect the country's borders and airspace against various threats, particularly in light of the events and repercussions taking place in the region," it said.
It said al-Zaidi "directed the preparation of a bill to restrict weapons to the hands of the state, in accordance with constitutional procedures".
"The greatest threat to the state is uncontrolled weapons, as they undermine the authority of the law and weaken the standing of security institutions," al-Zaidi said at the meeting.
"The importance of strengthening the position of the state through its sovereignty, standing and constitutional institutions and enhancing the capabilities of the military institution to ensure internal stability linked to economic, political and security stability in a way that safeguards the security and safety of Iraq and the resources of its people," he reportedly stressed.
In this context, al-Zaidi called for "integrated work and coordination between the executive and legislative authorities to enhance stability, enact laws and provide legislative cover for government development plans and programmes", stressing "the importance of holding regular meetings with the parliamentary security and defence committee to complete these issues".
Parliamentary backing
An informed government source, who requested anonymity, told The New Arab, "Al-Zaidi's move towards a law to restrict weapons aims to legislate the issue and give it legal and political cover and to secure parliamentary support, preventing the issue from remaining solely in the hands of the government and ensuring it is not left alone to confront factions that reject the decision".
"The government is currently facing major complications over the issue, given the factions' overlap with political systems and external links, as well as the influence and political representation they enjoy," he explained.
"Passing a parliamentary law would make the issue of restricting weapons a legislative obligation binding on state institutions rather than merely a government programme open to political disputes," the government source added. "It would also allow the government to rely on a legal provision when making decisions towards factions that refuse to cooperate on the issue."
This point appears to be particularly important for al-Zaidi, as any confrontation with the factions could entail major security risks.
Meanwhile, the existence of a law enacted by parliament would give al-Zaidi a significant opportunity to move forward with the issue, because the government would be implementing a constitutional and legislative mandate issued by the Iraqi state rather than a personal decision by al-Zaidi.
But, passing the law will not be straightforward.
Parliament itself reflects political balances, while factions and forces linked to them have significant parliamentary influence, making it difficult to pass legislation restricting weapons.
For his part, parliamentary security committee member MP Sherwan al-Doberdani affirmed his committee's support for al-Zaidi's directives to restrict weapons to the hands of the state.
Doberdani, who attended the meeting, said that "the committee expressed its readiness to cooperate on the issue of restricting weapons, as sovereignty and the law must belong to the state".
He warned in a press statement that "after Sept. 30—the deadline set by the government to end the issue of weapons outside the framework of the state—factions have to choose either the state or the non-state” .
The above developments comes at a highly sensitive time, as debate grows inside Iraq over the future of armed factions.
In this context, Ismail Qaani's visit to Baghdad two days ago, as commander of the Quds Force of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, takes on particular significance.
This is especially the case given the series of separate meetings he held with several leaders of the Coordination Framework and Iraqi armed faction commanders during an unannounced visit.
These meetings appear to be influential in the course of the issue, which topped Qaani's discussions, particularly as the end of September approaches.
It is a deadline that has raised growing concerns that the Iraqi government could resort to tougher options, potentially including the use of force to impose its decision on armed factions.

Ukraine's HUR reveals size of Russia's Geran attack drone stockpile
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
13:26:11 UTC
22:26:11 KST

Russian forces have accumulated around 6,200 Geran kamikaze drones of various types as of August, Ukrainian media outlet Militarnyi reported on Aug. 12, citing Ukraine's military intelligence agency (HUR).
The Geran is a Russian-made long-range attack drone based on Iran's Shahed design. Russia initially received a steady supply of Shahed drones from Iran in its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, before establishing domestic production of the drones.
Russia typically builds up large drone stockpiles ahead of major attacks. At the same time, the number of long-range drones launched against Ukraine has declined significantly in recent months.
Russia's largest drone attacks can involve between 600 and 1,000 drones. During periods when Russian forces are replenishing their stockpiles, however, they typically launch around 150–200 drones per attack, with the number occasionally reaching 300, Militarnyi reported.
One of Russia's largest drone attacks against Ukraine in 2026 took place in May. Russian forces launched 1,560 drones at Ukraine over a 24-hour period on May 13 and May 14. Ukrainian forces intercepted 94% of them, according to President Volodymyr Zelensky.
According to daily reports from Ukraine's Air Force, Russian forces significantly increased their use of long-range drones in the spring. While Russia launched around 4,450 drones in January, the figure reached a record 8,150 in May.
At the same time, the number of launches has declined again over the summer, with Russian forces launching nearly 5,000 drones in July.
Since the start of the full-scale invasion, Russia has also significantly upgraded its long-range drones. The latest modification, the Geran-5, which Russia began using against Ukraine in 2026, carries a 90-kilogram warhead, has a range of around 950 kilometers (590 miles), and can reach speeds of up to 600 km/h (370 mph), according to HUR.
By comparison, the Geran-1, which is the Russian equivalent of the Shahed-131, carries a warhead of up to 20 kilograms, can reach speeds of up to 185 km/h (115 mph), and has a range of around 900 kilometers (560 miles).

India: Data centers boom as water supply runs low
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
13:25:00 UTC
22:25:00 KST

India: Data centers boom as water supply runs low
August 12, 2026
Residents of Khora, a densely populated area in the city of Ghaziabad, just outside New Delhi, have long struggled to obtain a reliable water supply.
"We are dependent on groundwater. In some parts, one has to dig 1,000-1,200 feet (305-366 meters) to extract water," said Deepak Joshi, president of the Khora Residents' Association.
"The residents have been trying to get the water issue in Khora resolved for the last 10 years, but nothing has changed," he told DW.
Now, several data centers have been built in the area. Companies around the world are still scrambling to set up new AI infrastructure and India is increasingly positioning itself as a data center hub — but the new sites demand enormous quantities of water to cool the servers.
Many of India's water-stressed regions, including Khora, are feeling the bite.
Paying for well access
Carpenter Naeemuddin Saifi has been living in Khora for the last 35 years, but he still does not own his water connection. Like many in the locality, he relies on a shared borewell connection and pays 1,000-1,200 rupees (about $10.50-$12.50, €9.10-€10.90) every month for it.
"I cannot afford it alone," he said.
Joshi says each borewell costs around half a million rupees, or some $5,250. Many families here simply don't have that kind of money.
"Even a borewell is not a permanent solution. The levels of water could drop anytime. Maybe in two months, or it could take six months; we don't know," Joshi said.
The situation is so dire that many families have moved away, according to Joshi.
Water extraction at more than 270% of recommended level
More than half of India's data centers are located in water-stressed regions, according to a recent report by World Resources Institute (WRI) India.
The city of Ghaziabad is one of the regions where groundwater remains overexploited.
According to the Central Ground Water Board, its annual extractable groundwater resources stood at around 2,714 hectare meters (ham), but the amount of water taken out in 2024-2025 was around 272% of the recommended share.
"When the Ghaziabad and Noida region started urbanizing, the biggest thing that they started marketing… is that there is an abundance of water because of the canal water, the river water and the groundwater," Ranjana Ray Chaudhuri, head of the Department of Natural and Applied Sciences at TERI University, said.
But rapid urbanization has changed the equation, she said.
Now, the region is also required to support data centers, which need substantial cooling, and the heat expunged by cooling systems can affect the local microclimate, Chaudhuri explained. Higher temperatures could in turn increase air-conditioning demand in surrounding buildings.
"Overall, there is an increase in the use of water, and that water use is not just groundwater use," she said. "It is also because of the surrounding areas needing to use more water."
At the same time, Chaudhuri cautioned there is still not enough data to fully assess the local impact of large data centers.
Uttar Pradesh pledges uninterrupted water supply for data centers
In 2025, the authorities officially called off a long-demanded project which would have rerouted some of the Ganges water directly to Khora. An executive officer in Ghaziabad Municipal Council told DW an alternative water project was in the works.
But Joshi says residents received no updates on the alternative solution.
Meanwhile, just a few minutes' drive from Khora, the shiny new AdaniConnex data center stands tall. DW asked the facility, which is a 50:50 joint venture between India's Adani Group and the United States-based global data center operator EdgeConneX, about its water consumption, but received no reply by the time of publication.
AdaniConnex is one of more than 20 such facilities in Noida, an industrial city bordering Ghaziabad on the outskirts of New Delhi. And, as per Uttar Pradesh 2026 Data Center Policy Draft, the state government has promised an "uninterrupted 24x7" water supply to data centers.
"[In Noida] the water stress is particularly high because urban demand has grown quickly and groundwater has remained an important source," said Prateek Aggarwal, a senior representative of the Council on Energy, Environment and Water (CEEW), a well-established non-profit research institution in Asia.
There is no official estimate of how much water data centers currently consume across the National Capital Region, Aggarwal said.
No transparency mandate for data centers
India's total data center capacity has increased by a factor of four since the start of the decade, jumping from about 375 megawatts in 2020 to around 1,500 megawatts in 2025, according to the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology.
As of today, there are 305 data centers across India, according to the Data Center Map. They consumed around 150 million tons of water in 2025, and some estimates say this will double by 2030.
On top of the concerns triggered by the sheer volume of water consumption, there is also the issue of how that consumption is monitored and regulated.
Gayatri Naik, co-director of the Center for Environmental Law, Education, Research and Advocacy at the National Law School of India University, described India's approach as fragmented.
"We don't have a conclusive regulatory aspect with regard to governing any of the water uses by these data centers," she said.
Commercial entities are required to obtain a no-objection certificate to extract groundwater, she said, and the permission specifies how much water can be extracted. But companies are not generally required to publish regular monthly or annual figures showing their actual consumption.
Who gets water when supply runs low?
Comparing India's policy with those in European countries, Naik said the EU requires data centers to disclose their water consumption — a requirement that is absent in India.
Also, under EU rules, data centers with an IT power capacity of at least 500 kW are required to report key sustainability data to a European database.
CEEW activist Aggarwal agrees mandatory disclosure should be the first step.
"Energy, water, and carbon use reported every year, including exactly where the water comes from and how much gets recycled," he said.
He also called for phased efficiency standards for water and power, and for decision makers to also consider water availability alongside land and electricity infrastructure before approving a data center.
"The real strain in a place like National Capital Region comes from many facilities sharing one aquifer, not any single project," Aggarwal said.
Naik said the issue ultimately raises a broader question about who gets priority when water is scarce.
"How will you bring a balance between this water that is required for drinking as well as the water demands by these companies who are extracting the water from a water scarce area?" she asked.
"So this can lead to social and distributive injustice."

Bill proposes banning people convicted of serious crimes from changing their name
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
13:24:00 UTC
22:24:00 KST

Bill proposes banning people convicted of serious crimes from changing their name
The Ministry of the Interior has submitted a draft Personal Names Act to the government for approval that would, among other things, restrict the right of people convicted of serious crimes to obtain a new name.
The Personal Names Act will replace the Names Act, which has been in force for more than 20 years. The bill revises terminology, clarifies what name-related procedures entail and overhauls the process for granting a new name at a person's request, the ministry said.
One of the bill's most significant changes would permanently bar people who have committed particularly serious crimes from obtaining a new name by any means.
Interior Minister Igor Taro (Eesti 200) said the changes must meet society's expectations while helping ensure public safety and maintain trust.
"Particularly serious crimes are not committed by accident, and this is an area where we must put everyone's safety first. We cannot allow a situation in which people convicted of terrorism, war crimes, crimes against the state or serious crimes against the person can use a new name to conceal their past or avoid being linked to their previous actions," Taro said.
Under the bill, the restriction would apply to people who have committed crimes including crimes against humanity, genocide, aggression, war crimes, terrorism, crimes against the state, organizing mass disorder and serious offenses involving explosives or explosive materials.
"The seriousness of these crimes and their impact on society are such that it is in the public interest for the identities of their perpetrators to remain clear and traceable," the interior minister stressed.
The existing Names Act's restriction on name changes for people convicted of sexual offenses against minors, which was recently added at the proposal of the Riigikogu, will be carried over. The new Personal Names Act would likewise impose a lifelong restriction on name-related procedures for those convicted of sexual offenses against minors.
The bill also clarifies the rules for granting a new surname at a person's request.
In the future, people choosing a surname freely will not be able to select one already held by a living person listed in the Population Register. The change is intended to prevent the appearance of a family or kinship relationship and reduce the risk of identity theft.
At the same time, the new rules will allow new Estonian-style surnames to be created, helping develop Estonia's naming tradition.
The options for changing a minor's surname will also be narrowed. In the future, a minor may only be given a surname held by one of their parents. The change is intended to protect the child's interests, ensure continuity of identity and maintain a clear connection with their family.
The new law is expected to enter into force in 2028.

Advertisers are slashing their ad budgets on Wildberries after a series of Ukrainian drone attacks on the company’s warehouses, the Kommersant business newspaper reported Wednesday, citing sources at major ad agencies.
From June to July, ad tracking firm Digital Budget said spending on direct banner ads on Wildberries plummeted 63%.
A source told Kommersant that many advertisers had either frozen their promotional budgets or sharply cut back across major retail categories, including electronics, household appliances and pharmaceuticals.
Meanwhile, average ad prices fell by up to 15% as product availability fell. Analysts explained that advertising becomes ineffective when sellers run out of stock or face delivery delays.
Wildberries acknowledged lower ad activity on its platform but insisted that the extent of the decline was exaggerated.
“Some change in the volume of advertising and promotion tools is understandable,” Wildberries told Kommersant.
“In the current environment, sellers are reevaluating their economic models to assess the impact on their businesses,” it added.
Analysts estimate the ad slump on Wildberries could last two to six months as Russia’s largest e-commerce company rebuilds damaged infrastructure and reroutes supply chains.
Russia’s marketplace ad platforms grew by 58% to 580 billion rubles ($6.9 billion) in 2025, according to the Interactive Advertising Development Association. That accounts for over one-third of Russia’s digital advertising market, which totals 1.57 trillion rubles ($18.9 billion).
Wildberries and its chief competitor Ozon ranked among Russia’s top 10 largest advertisers in 2025, with the former spending 7.8 billion rubles ($94 million) and the latter 9.7 billion rubles ($117 million) on digital ad campaigns.
Ukraine has attacked almost two dozen Wildberries logistics centers since mid-July, accusing the company of supplying the Russian military with drone parts and other equipment.
Both Wildberries and the Kremlin have rejected this characterization. Since the strikes, the company appears to have removed a search tag from its website linked to Ukraine war paraphernalia.
The strikes have wiped out a significant portion of the e-commerce giant's storage capacity and cost third-party merchants hundreds of billions of rubles, according to Forbes Russia.
Denys Shtilerman, head of Ukrainian defense firm Fire Point, said the targeted attacks were partly aimed at harming Russia's economy and hoped it could trigger a financial crisis.
Last month, Wildberries launched a major advertising campaign across Russia with the tagline “support entrepreneurs with an order.”

Six Latvian Artists Explore Background Noise in Helsinki in Exhibition LATVIESHI INTERNATIONAL  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
13:22:48 UTC
22:22:48 KST

From August 21 to 28, 2026, the art space Toinen Kerros (Nokiantie 2-4, 00510, Helsinki, Finland) will host Latvieshi International, a week-long audiovisual art exhibition. It will feature new works by six Latvian artists based in Latvia, Iceland, and Finland.
The central theme of the exhibition is background noise. Six artists (Uģis Albiņš, Aina Bikše, Jurģis Peters, Mārtiņš Ratniks, Sandijs Ruļuks, and Lidija Zaneripa) approach this phenomenon from different perspectives. Their works explore non-human communication, algorithmic systems, industrial sound, mechanisms of perception and attention, as well as the traces and residues left on memory and identity by moving and existing within other cultural spaces.
The conceptual foundation of the exhibition is the question of the boundary itself: what separates signal from noise, and who defines it? In these artworks, noise is perceived as a material that can be organized, listened to, and purposefully manipulated. What is perceived as a disruptive background in one context can become structure, language, or meaning in another, and often becomes noticeable only when it suddenly disappears.
The exhibition is complemented by a public program that is open to everyone and free of charge:
August 21: Exhibition opening night featuring musical performances created by the artists.
August 23: An educational exhibition tour for children and youth, including students from the Helsinki Latvian diaspora school Pikku Putni, using worksheets and tasks specifically developed for this exhibition.
August 26: A moderated public discussion with Latvian and Finnish cultural representatives on the relationship between signal and noise in the cultural environment. The discussion will be followed by a live sound performance led by musician and artist Michael Holland. It will be based on a score created specifically for this exhibition, performed by six musicians using both traditional instruments and homemade musical instruments crafted by artist James Prevett. The sound piece will combine the themes of the exhibition with the archives of Latvian folk music, particularly highlighting its oldest layer—near-speech singing and chanting. Using the exhibition's motifs and contemporary textual material, the performance will interpret and seek musical parallels between Latvian and Finnish historical traditions.
About the Organizers The Latvieshi International project is organized by the association Datu ainavu kartogrāfi (founded by artist-researcher Jurģis Peters and cultural producer, urban researcher Džesika Petere) in collaboration with the Äänen Lumo organization, the Embassy of the Republic of Latvia in Finland, and the Rozentāls Society (Rozentāls-seura).
Supported by: State Culture Capital Foundation (VKKF), Culture Moves Europe, Labietis Brewery, and Valmiermuiža.
The opening of the Latvieshi International exhibition will take place on August 21 at 18:00 at the Toinen Kerros art space, Nokiantie 2-4, 00510 Helsinki.

US inflation eases to 3.4% in July as the Fed's September call stays on a knife edge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
13:21:47 UTC
22:21:47 KST

US inflation eased for a second month in July, with consumer prices rising 3.4% from a year earlier, down from 3.5% in June, exactly as economists had forecast, a reading that hands neither side of a divided Federal Reserve fresh ammunition before next month's rate decision.
Price growth in the world's largest economy slowed again last month, according to the US Bureau of Labor Statistics figures published on Wednesday, but only as much as expected, leaving the Federal Reserve's September rate decision uncertain.
Prices rose 0.1% on the month after falling 0.4% in June, taking the annual rate to 3.4%, well below May's 4.2%. Core prices, stripping out food and energy, rose 0.2% after being flat in June, easing to 2.5% from 2.6% annually.
Every figure matched the Dow Jones consensus, though the annual falls owe much to comparisons with a strong summer in 2025, and monthly momentum picked up from June's soft readings.
US stock futures moved higher immediately after the release, while traders trimmed their bets on tighter policy.
The odds of a September rate hike on CME's FedWatch tool also quickly fell from 48% to 42%, but money markets continue to price in a scenario that is difficult to read with probabilities not far from a coin toss.
A committee at odds with itself
The Fed held its benchmark rate at 3.50% to 3.75% on 29 July, a fifth straight pause, but three regional presidents dissented in favour of a quarter-point rise, the most in one direction in nearly a decade.
Chair Kevin Warsh, who has scrapped forward guidance and declined to publish his own projections, said the Fed would "deliver price stability" and not hesitate to act, having called inflation a choice earlier.
The Fed's other mandate pulls the opposite way.
The economy shed 23,000 jobs in July against forecasts of roughly 83,000 added, while average hourly earnings grew 3.2% over the year, leaving pay behind prices and reviving stagflation talk. Unemployment, at 4.1%, is close to most estimates of full employment.
Cleveland Fed president Beth Hammack, a dissenter, said on Monday a single quarter-point move would achieve little and several may be needed, arguing rates are not meaningfully restraining growth.
Her New York counterpart, John Williams, expects inflation to fall this half. Investors have been similarly split, with hike odds sitting either side of 50% this week, against 67% only a week ago, and now shifting again after the latest figures published by the US Bureau of Labor Statistics.
The oil problem has not gone away
The bigger threat to disinflation lies in the Gulf.
The Strait of Hormuz remains largely closed, with crossings at 6 to 11 vessels a day against 130 to 140 before the war, and talks to reopen it have stalled over reparations demands, with US President Donald Trump saying Iran should also pay for damages it is responsible for in Lebanon, Syria, Yemen and Gaza.
Brent crude has gained about 5% since Friday to its highest since 31 July, some 25% above early July's lows.
Energy drove US inflation to 4.2% in May, and Goldman Sachs estimates airfares rose 2% last month as jet fuel costs fed through.
US President Donald Trump has signalled he will let economic pressure on Tehran build rather than launch a fresh campaign, telling Axios that Washington is "low-keying it," implying a long standoff and a lasting premium on crude.
Wednesday's figures are not the last word on inflation, producer prices follow on Thursday, retail sales and sentiment on Friday, and another jobs report and inflation reading arrive before policymakers meet in September.

Russia’s fuel crisis is back, with queues and gasoline rationing returning across the country
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
13:21:03 UTC
22:21:03 KST

Russia’s fuel crisis is back, with queues and gasoline rationing returning across the country
In early August, judging by reports from the regions, a new wave of the fuel crisis hit Russia following Ukrainian strikes on oil refineries. Residents of various regions, from the south to the Far East, report lines at gas stations. Limits on how much fuel a person can buy at a time have returned in Orenburg Region and Sochi. The Sochi city administration also asked residents and tourists not to use personal vehicles. Meduza looks at which regions are still experiencing fuel supply problems.
Gas stations in at least 12 Russian regions are once again reporting hours-long lines for fuel, according to a count by the news outlet 7×7. The regions include Krasnodar Krai, the Voronezh, Kaluga, Rostov, Ryazan, Tambov, Tula, Saratov, Smolensk, Penza, and Ulyanovsk regions, as well as Primorsky Krai.
Purchase limits have also returned. The Sochi city administration announced August 11 that gas stations in the region had imposed limits “due to logistical disruptions in fuel supply,” and it asked local residents and tourists to “refrain from using personal vehicles whenever possible” to ease the strain on gas stations.
In the Orenburg region, Governor Yevgeny Solntsev reported a “difficult situation with fuel.” Starting August 12, gas stations there capped purchases at 30 liters (about 8 gallons) of gasoline and 60 liters (about 16 gallons) of diesel and adopted an “odd-even” system: drivers with license plates ending in an even digit can fill up on even-numbered days, while everyone else fills up on odd-numbered days. Solntsev also promised to bring in police officers “to coordinate the situation at gas stations.”
Authorities have also reinstated odd-even refueling in the Lipetsk region. The system will take effect on August 13, Governor Igor Artamonov announced. At the same time, the region introduced a 30-liter fuel limit at Gazprom, Lukoil, Teboil, and Rosneft gas stations.
Residents of Krasnoyarsk Krai and Bashkortostan also report gasoline shortages and the closure of some gas stations. There are indirect signs of rising prices as well, particularly in the regions Vladimir Putin has visited in recent days.
In Krasnoyarsk, gasoline prices at some stations in a regional chain dropped sharply — by 24 rubles per liter — a day before Putin’s visit. The chain attributed the drop to “a temporary improvement in logistics” and “additional fuel supplies coming directly from refineries.” Prices returned to their previous level as soon as the president left.
In Novosibirsk, where Putin traveled next, his motorcade stopped near an empty gas station — it’s unclear whether by chance or intentionally — where children were waiting for the president, and he spoke with them. Kremlin pool reporter Pavel Zarubin filmed the moment, and the footage, widely circulated by media outlets, shows that the station’s price board was turned off.
Few reports have surfaced so far from Moscow and St. Petersburg, though a Business FM follower said she encountered a shortage of AI-95 gasoline at several Rosneft stations while driving to her dacha along the Dmitrovskoye Highway.
Authorities have not officially acknowledged a new wave of the crisis. Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak, who oversees the fuel sector, held a meeting August 11 on the situation in the domestic market. Afterward, relevant agencies, regional authorities, and oil companies were instructed to “continue coordinated efforts to supply the domestic market with fuel,” monitor price trends, and ensure “uninterrupted delivery” of gasoline to consumers.

Household solar plants to receive "green" tariff only during set generation hours - NEURC
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
16:20:52 EEST
22:20:52 KST

Ukraine’s National Energy and Utilities Regulatory Commission (NEURC) has set the summer and winter time periods during which electricity from household solar power plants must be paid for at the "green" tariff.
Under the commission’s decision, the applicable hours are 4:00 a.m. to 11:00 p.m. from April 1 to October 31, and 6:00 a.m. to 9:00 p.m. from November 1 to March 31.
The decision is set out in amendments to the Retail Electricity Market Rules and the Procedure for the Sale and Metering of Electricity, approved by resolution No. 1360 of August 11, 2026.
The energy regulator explained on its website on Wednesday that electricity not eligible for payment at the "green" tariff will be purchased by universal service providers at hourly day-ahead market prices, as set out in law.
NEURC also established that the volume of electricity counted for settlement purposes cannot exceed the contracted capacity of the generating unit for each hour it operates. The commission said this would ensure more accurate metering of output and unify the application of the rules for household solar plant owners.
"The updated provisions create clearer and more predictable conditions for the operation of household solar power plants, and ensure uniform approaches to metering generated electricity and settling payments under the ‘green’ tariff," the commission said.
As previously reported, National Power Company Ukrenergo, which funds payment of the "green" tariff, had earlier raised concerns about distribution system operators’ metering of electricity generated by household solar plants during nighttime hours and in excess of the capacity established under contracts.

CoreWeave surges 20% in premarket after a 'cleaner quarter.' Here's what's happening
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
13:19:43 UTC
22:19:43 KST

Artificial intelligence neocloud CoreWeave saw shares pop 18% on Wednesday after reporting that its second-quarter revenue doubled, driven by surging demand from hyperscalers for AI compute capacity.
The company, which rents out high-powered computing capacity needed to run and build AI, reported after the bell Tuesday that its second-quarter revenue came in at $2.6 billion, up 112% from $1.2 billion in the second quarter of 2025. It's guiding for third-quarter revenue of between $3.4 billion and $3.6 billion.
But the company is still not profitable. Operating expenses for the quarter also more than doubled year-on-year and marginally exceeded revenue, per the results. CoreWeave was last seen up 19.9% in premarket trading. At Tuesday's close, it was up 26% since the start of the year.
Its revenue backlog for the quarter stands at $104 billion as of June 30, which doesn't include $25 billion in new customer commitments for the third quarter.
"To put that in perspective, like $25 billion is virtually the size of our backlog a year ago, and so it gives you an idea of how much demand there is for our product and how much it's growing," CEO Michael Intrator told CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" on Wednesday.
In the earnings release, Intrator said the company had reached "an important inflection point" during the quarter.
But CoreWeave has taken on significant debt as it races to build AI infrastructure.
Operating expenses rose to $2.6 billion from $1.2 billion a year earlier. That left CoreWeave with an operating loss of $49 million, compared with operating income of $19 million a year earlier.
For the full year, the company forecasts revenue of $12.4 billion to $13.2 billion and adjusted operating income of $960 million to $1.15 billion.
Some of its second-quarter highlights include winning customers such as Bentley Systems, Grammarly, Isomorphic Labs, and Sunday Robotics.
It also deepened major commercial partnerships with Jane Street, committing $1 billion in strategic investments, while Meta said it would spend an additional $21 billion with CoreWeave during the quarter.
A 'cleaner quarter' for CoreWeave
Citi analysts said in a note Wednesday that CoreWeave "delivered a confident message" in the second quarter, demonstrating that AI demand was robust, it had stronger pricing power, saw growing demand for its software and tokens business, and posted better-than-expected margins.
They added it was "one of the cleaner quarters" for CoreWeave since it went public last year. "We think shares should move meaningfully higher on increased investor confidence in the execution and improving profitability," the analysts continued.
They pointed to upward revisions to profitability guidance and positive updates on execution and customer and revenue diversification.
The analysts said those developments were positive signs for demand across the hyperscaler and neo-cloud space.
Neocloud boom
Neoclouds — providers specializing in GPU infrastructure — like CoreWeave have seen big gains as a result of the AI boom.
Amsterdam-headquartered, Nasdaq-listed Nebius ripped 20% higher on Wednesday after announcing a strong commercial quarter. Revenue grew 514% to $575 million, and the total value of contracts won quadrupled, the company said. The stock has risen more than 150% in the past 12 months.
U.K.-based Nscale, which is targeting an IPO this year, has drawn large sums in private capital, raising billions of dollars in equity, debt and project financing in 2026.
AI stocks were also buoyed by Taiwan's Foxconn, also known as Hon Hai — the world's largest contract electronics manufacturer which assembles Apple's iPhone and makes servers that hold chips in data centers — reporting a better-than-expected increase in profit on Wednesday.
Supermicro, which makes data center hardware, saw its shares surge about 14% on Wednesday after it reported more than $60 billion in new orders over the past year in its fourth-quarter earnings.

Yabloko receives Supreme Court’s reasoned decision for removal from elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
13:19:03 UTC
22:19:03 KST

MOSCOW, August 12. /TASS/. The Yabloko party has received a reasoned decision of the Supreme Court to withdraw from the elections to the State Duma on the claim of the Rodina party, a participant in the process told TASS.
"The representatives of the party received a reasoned decision of the Supreme Court of the Russian Federation," the participant said. He added that lawyers are now reviewing the documents and will file an appeal in the coming days.
The Supreme Court removed Yabloko from the polls on August 10.
The court session lasted more than nine hours. If the decision comes into force, Yabloko will not be able to participate in the elections to the State Duma. The party will also be deprived of the right to free and paid airtime on federal state TV channels and radio stations, including participation in TV debates. In addition, the party will lose the right to campaign in support of the cancelled list, to produce and distribute campaign materials.
Financial transactions on the special election account of the party will also be terminated, with the exception of settlements on previous obligations and the return of unspent funds. Yabloko will also lose the right to have proxies and authorized representatives on financial matters acting in the interests of the federal list.
At the same time, such restrictions will apply only to Yabloko as a participant in the elections in the federal electoral district and will not affect the party's candidates registered in single-mandate districts. Single-mandate candidates will be able to continue campaigning, manage their own election funds, use free airtime and print space, as well as participate in debates in regional state media in their districts.
About the Rodina party claim
On August 7, Rodina Party Chairman, State Duma deputy Alexey Zhuravlyov told TASS that he had filed a lawsuit with the Supreme Court to remove Yabloko from the elections.
As TASS found out from the materials of the lawsuit, Rodina pointed out that Yabloko exceeded the limits of election campaign financing established by law, made violations during election campaigning, including those related to copyrights, as well as circumstances that the plaintiff attributed to extremist activities.

Russia hit by new wave of fuel crisis
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
16:19:00 EEST
22:19:00 KST

Russia hit by new wave of fuel crisis
A new wave of the fuel crisis appears to have hit Russia at the beginning of August, judging by reports from the regions, amid Ukrainian strikes on oil refineries.
Source: Meduza, a Latvia-based Russian media outlet
Quote: "Residents of various regions – from the south to Primorye – are reporting queues at petrol stations. Restrictions on fuel sales per customer have once again been introduced in Orenburg Oblast and Sochi."
Details: In addition, the Sochi administration has asked residents and tourists to avoid using private vehicles. Other regions are also experiencing problems with petrol supplies.
According to the 7×7 media project, at least 12 regions are once again seeing hours-long queues for fuel at petrol stations. Journalists name Krasnodar Krai, Voronezh, Kaluga, Rostov, Ryazan, Tambov, Tula, Saratov, Smolensk, Penza and Ulyanovsk oblasts, as well as Primorye.
Restrictions on the amount of petrol sold to each customer have also returned, Meduza reports.
On 11 August, the Sochi administration said that limits had been introduced at petrol stations in the region "due to logistical disruptions in supplies". In addition, local residents and tourists were asked to "refrain from travelling by private vehicle where possible" in order to reduce pressure on petrol stations.
In Orenburg Oblast, Governor Yevgeny Solntsev reported a "difficult situation with fuel". From 12 August, limits have also been introduced at all petrol stations in the oblast – up to 30 litres of petrol and up to 60 litres of diesel – along with an odd-even number plate system.
Under the system, vehicles with number plates ending in an even digit can refuel on even-numbered days, while the others can do so on odd-numbered days. Solntsev also promised to deploy police officers "to coordinate the situation at petrol stations".
"In addition, regions are reporting shortages of petrol and the closure of some petrol stations – residents of Krasnoyarsk Krai and Bashkortostan have reported this. There has also been an increase in prices, as indicated by some indirect signs – particularly in regions recently visited by Vladimir Putin," the report says.
In Krasnoyarsk, petrol prices at some stations in the regional network fell sharply – by 24 roubles per litre – the day before Putin's visit.
The petrol station network itself attributed the price reduction to a "temporary improvement in logistics" and the "supply of an additional volume of fuel directly from the refinery". However, immediately after Putin's departure, prices returned to their previous level, the publication reports.
The authorities have not officially reported a new wave of the crisis. Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak, who oversees the fuel industry, held a meeting on the domestic market situation on 11 August.
Following the meeting, relevant government agencies, regional authorities and oil companies were instructed to "continue coordinated efforts to supply the domestic market with fuel".
Background:
- Earlier, it was reported that a fuel crisis was spreading across Russia and the occupied territories amid continued Ukrainian strikes on oil refineries: the shortage of motor fuel, which had previously affected occupied Sevastopol and Crimea, had spread to Moscow Oblast.
- In temporarily occupied Sevastopol, fuel will once again be sold using QR codes – the system will remain in place "until supplies allow fuel to be sold without restrictions".
- At the beginning of June, Novak admitted for the first time that Russian oil processing had fallen since the beginning of 2026 due to "unplanned maintenance" at refineries.
- Later, the Russian government claimed that the fuel market had "partially stabilised" thanks to a ban on petroleum product exports and a shift towards fuel imports, but the situation remains tense in a number of regions.

Expert: Presidential election looks set to head to electoral college
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
13:18:00 UTC
22:18:00 KST

Expert: Presidential election looks set to head to electoral college
The political situation being as it is means the presidential election process due to start next month will likely head to the electoral college, politics expert Annika Arras said.
This is despite an apparent desire to get the next head of state voted in at the Riigikogu in early September, Arras told "Aktuaalne kaamera."
Is Ülle Madise now that person the Riigikogu can find consensus on?
One might hope; the reality is different. The numbers indicate it will not be so easy. As the decision has been made, [nomination] signatures [from MPs] will start to get collected on Wednesday, but no one has expressed outright opposition, so there is a chance.
How should we look at Urmas Reinsalu's desire, and that of other politicians, to get acquainted with Ülle Madise and her views? Is Madise an unknown quantity to politicians?
She is likely not entirely unknown to them, and I believe they will all have encountered her in the course of their political careers, both directly and thanks to her public appearances. That said, there is nothing strange about wanting to meet, to hear Ülle Madise's views in more detail, for example on foreign policy and security issues, as well as on domestic matters, family policy and so on. That should certainly go ahead.
It is clear that there is currently some disagreement over the correct timing, but from a citizen's perspective I would certainly like to hear Madise's views as a potential presidential candidate, at the earliest available opportunity.
How should Tiit Land's candidacy be seen? Has he been put forward to guarantee that the election moves from the Riigikogu to the electoral college, as the opposition would like to happen?
This is always a possibility. During the presidential election process, it should also be borne in mind that we have Riigikogu elections in six months' time, and the opposition's task is to establish a narrative that will help it, heading into those elections. With that in mind, they are not going to immediately rally behind the coalition's candidate, which Ülle Madise is nevertheless now emerging as, even as she herself does not want to be that. She wants to be a candidate for all, and has expressed clearly her desire to remain impartial. Come what may, having alternative candidates serves the opposition's aims. There is right now a willingness to reach consensus at the Riigikogu, but it still seems more likely that the matter will ultimately head to the electoral college.
How likely is it that the electoral college will consider the candidates who have already been put forward? Or is there still a "dark horse" candidate yet to emerge?
An increasing number of candidates have emerged in recent weeks, so nothing should be ruled out. Since the window for nominating candidates is still pretty short, more new names may emerge only once it becomes clear that the Riigikogu is unable to elect a president.
Everyone is saying there needs to be a presidential debate. Could you imagine all these respected people arguing with each other and angrily throwing arguments to and fro? What would a debate like that look like?
If a debate were to take place, it could be a substantive one. ERR has every opportunity to organize a substantive discussion of that kind. When I look at the presidential elections our northern neighbor Finland has, though the electoral system is different, presidential candidates there discuss foreign policy and economic policy, as well as other issues. All the candidates are given equal air time, and the discussion is not adversarial, but substantive. I believe Estonia needs the same thing.
Background:
The presidential candidate nomination window runs Aug. 21-24, with the three Riigikogu ballots to follow Sept. 2-3, with at least 68 votes required. If these draw a blank, the process heads to a 208-member-strong regional electoral college, which convenes in Tallinn. If this, too, fails to get a president elected, the matter returns to the Riigikogu, with parliament's Council of Elders – the speaker, their two deputies, and the heads of the six elected party factions – having the final say on a candidate to be voted on. This last happened in October 2016 when Kersti Kaljulaid was elected president. You can read more about the potential candidates so far, here.

Seven OPEC+ nations boost July oil output by 1.424 mln bpd
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
13:17:33 UTC
22:17:33 KST

MOSCOW, August 12. /TASS/. The seven OPEC+ countries implementing voluntary oil output cuts produced 24.296 million barrels per day (bpd) in July 2026, marking an increase of 1.424 million bpd compared to June, according to the OPEC monthly report.
Under the current agreement, the seven was scheduled to increase production in July by 188,000 bpd month-on-month due to higher quotas. OPEC+ countries had also previously extended the deadline to compensate for past overproduction until the end of 2026, though the updated schedule has not yet been published. The previous timeline slated the end of the compensation period for June 2026. The group's July quota, excluding compensations, stood at 30.633 million bpd.
Among the seven nations, Algeria increased oil production by 8,000 bpd in July, Iraq ramped up by 665,000 bpd, Kuwait boosted output by 393,000 bpd, and Saudi Arabia expanded production by 590,000 bpd. At the same time, Oman reduced its oil output by 3,000 bpd, Kazakhstan cut production by 223,000 bpd, and Russia trimmed output by 6,000 bpd.

Russian Man Taken From Street, Pressured to Sign Army Contract, Relatives Say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
13:17:26 UTC
22:17:26 KST

Russian security personnel detained a 31-year-old man on a street in the Siberian city of Omsk and took him to a military recruitment center, where his relatives say he was pressured into signing a contract with Russia’s defense ministry.
The incident occurred Aug. 8 after the man, identified only as Dmitry S., was seen drinking beer on a public bench, according to the independent Omsk Civil Association, which cited his relatives.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Several men in civilian clothing allegedly restrained Dmitry and drove him away. His passport and military identification documents were at home, according to accounts provided by his family.
He was taken to the Sirius 55 military selection center and subjected to psychological pressure before signing a contract, the relatives said. The man’s relatives appealed to prosecutors, but were asked to provide additional documents and submit another complaint.
The reported incident comes amid mounting evidence that Russian military recruiters are using increasingly coercive methods as Moscow struggles to attract enough volunteers for its war against Ukraine.
Russian police and military officials can formally conduct raids to identify people accused of violating military registration requirements. However, rights advocates say detainees are also being encouraged or pressured to sign military contracts.
The Russian anti-war organization Get Lost, which assists soldiers and deserters, says authorities are finding it increasingly difficult to recruit volunteers despite offering large signing bonuses.
Vance Asked Zelensky to Avoid Key Oil Route as Ukraine Targets Russia’s Black Sea Fleet
Recruitment methods have included street detentions, visits to homes and workplaces and pressure on debtors, people serving suspended sentences and recently discharged conscripts.
Similar allegations have emerged in other Russian regions, including Penza and Ulyanovsk. Russian authorities have denied some previous reports that men were forced to sign contracts.
Russia’s contract recruitment has slowed, according to Ukrainian intelligence and researchers tracking regional spending. Economist Janis Kluge estimated that Russia signed about 93,000 new military contracts in the second quarter of 2026.
Although overall recruitment this year remains only slightly below last year’s level, average regional spending on enlistment bonuses has risen by about 30%, according to Kluge’s calculations.
The combination of higher payments and reports of coercion suggests that finding volunteers is becoming increasingly difficult as Russia attempts to replace continued battlefield losses without announcing another nationwide mobilization.
After four years of full-scale war with Russia, Ukraine’s armed forces are also facing persistent manpower shortages and growing reliance on newly mobilized conscripts. While volunteer enlistment surged after Russia’s 2022 invasion, recruitment has since shifted overwhelmingly to compulsory mobilization.

Farage has turned Clacton into a human zoo. Here’s the truth about what’s happening here | Sarah Elizabeth Cox
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
13:16:21 UTC
22:16:21 KST

Clacton town centre is bustling, the beaches are packed and the pier’s raking in cash. We can credit the weather, but no doubt press coverage and Count Binface’s promotional videos have got us on radars too. The tourists look like they’re having a lovely time.
I moved to Clacton in 2022 and the first year was brilliant. It started with beach walks, cheap drinks and decorating a flat with panoramic sea views, and ended fat and happy from chips and ice-cream, a newborn baby in tow. Privileged with my health and stable income, albeit strained by a Truss-era mortgage, it was a place I loved, and was proud of.
Then Nigel Farage targeted us, and shit hit the fan.
With the general election in 2024, the world’s press descended, and then came thousands of social media comments that left me embarrassed, sad and fuming. You’re all thick, racist, gullible, hateful, toothless, jobless old fools, we were told. You deserve him. The worst of the snobbery was, sadly, on my lefty social media platform of choice, Bluesky.
Farage was elected with 46% of a 58% turnout. Fine, some people actually are gullible fools. But the other parties rolled over and failed to bother, treating us with contempt. I didn’t support, but I understood, why 46% voted as they did. I still loved Clacton, but it got harder to defend. Then things died down and we were forgotten again by everyone, including our new MP.
The gag about Farage not knowing where we are isn’t exactly true – he pops by for photo opportunities like a ceremonial mayor – but he seems less keen on surgeries, or representing Clacton in the Commons. Snaps for the local newspaper’s Facebook make fans think he’s doing great things for businesses and charities. It’s smoke and mirrors. Check Hansard for “Clacton” and see how many times he’s raised a Clacton issue in parliament (six times). Then do “Colchester” for Pam Cox and “Ipswich” for Jack Abbott. Compare and contrast.
We wanted him to actually be an MP. To notice the homeless people, freezing all winter in closed bank doorways, and now lining the coastal paths in tents. To notice how we’ve been priced off the railways – the commuter trains are empty. The worsening health, declining life expectancy. The low employment rates and lack of affordable homes. We don’t have an A&E. We don’t have maternity care after 5pm. It would have been nice too, if he’d spent more time doing what he said he would, and what Binface has achieved instead – promoting our towns and villages’ positives. There are many, I promise.
Nobody wanted a byelection. For the many people struggling here, there is little energy for another awful circus. Clacton didn’t need yet more focus on Farage, Farage, Farage, while the area’s entrenched and complex problems continue to be ignored by him and by the government.
This summer, the media presence has been even bigger than in 2024. Content creators and reporters continually vox pop outside Wetherspoons, cherrypicking quotes about how great Nigel is, how persecuted Nigel is. Well, we’re being swarmed with migrants, aren’t we? Getting put up in hotels while we struggle. It’s not like it used to be round here. The Turks, they’re taking over with the barber shops. Or, I don’t really do politics. They’re all the same as each other. A welcome few, it has been pleasing to see, have started to notice the slipperiness, the back of fag packet policies and his absence.
The “Migrants Out” leaflets were pushed into our homes, a turquoise Reform bus did the rounds and sad men with silly hats and placards yelled things in the town square. I’ve seen anti-racism campaigners told to F off, and can’t leave my flat without the smug face of a British Democratic party candidate leering down at me from giant poster boards. It has all felt surreal, hostile, dividing. Generally bad vibes.
The nasty, stereotyping, hurtful comments about us continue. With some exceptions – like Tim Burrows’ thoughtful portrait of Clacton – we’re a human zoo, and the butt of a joke. Farage used us as a pawn, and the media treats us as clickbait.
Yet in shops, the gym, pubs, on the beach, in the street, at the park, at nursery drop off, I’ve not overheard a single conversation about any of it, unless it was between a reporter and a local. Not one. The leaflets started getting left in the hallway, unread. Few of my family or neighbours plan to vote. We’re angry at him, but we are also bored, and exhausted.
My prediction: It’ll be a low turnout, Farage way ahead, with Binface second but the only real winner. I’ll read about how we wasted the chance for a hilarious outcome, you idiots. You gullible, racist fools. You deserve him. And so on. Limburg wildfire wiped out rare juniper shrubland
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
13:12:10 UTC
22:12:10 KST

Limburg wildfire wiped out rare juniper shrubland
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Fewer than 100 of the roughly 4,000 juniper bushes that grew in the Boschhuizerbergen nature reserve near Venray have survived this month’s wildfire in northern Limburg, the foundation that manages the site says.
The reserve held the largest juniper shrubland in the southern Netherlands, according to Het Limburgs Landschap, with some bushes more than 130 years old. Junipers grow slowly and thrive in the reserve’s nutrient-poor, drifting-sand soil – conditions that have become rare in the region.
The fire, which broke out on August 3, destroyed around 100 hectares, including 20 to 30 hectares of protected Natura 2000 land where the junipers stood. More than a week on, crews were still pouring water on smouldering hotspots to stop them reigniting.
The shrubland might not be able to be re-established, as the soil has changed over the decades and young plants may struggle to take root. “It is questionable whether we will ever get such a beautiful shrubland here again. I am afraid I will not live to see it,” the foundation’s Loek Hendrikx told broadcaster NOS.
Het Limburgs Landschap, set up in 1931 to stop the reserve being cleared for farmland, has appealed for donations towards a recovery it says will take years.

Fragrant fortunes: Doha's Teeb Al Hazm plans London debut as Gulf perfumes gain wider appeal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
13:11:58 UTC
22:11:58 KST

From oud and bukhoor to niche fragrance houses, the Teeb Al Hazm perfume exhibition reflects the Gulf's enduring love of scent as organisers prepare to take the concept to Europe.
Across the Gulf, perfume is more than a luxury. Fragrance has long been part of everyday life, hospitality and religious traditions, with oud, bukhoor, musk, rose and amber remaining among the region's most recognisable scents.
That culture is showcased twice a year at Teeb Al Hazm in Doha, where perfume houses present everything from traditional oud blends to contemporary fragrances inspired by regional ingredients.
Now, organisers say the festival is preparing to take that experience beyond the region with its first European edition in London.
Gulf traditions
Unlike many perfume exhibitions centred on individual brands, Teeb Al Hazm brings together fragrance houses from around the Middle East, allowing visitors to compare a wide range of styles in one place. While traditional oud remains at the heart of many collections, newer perfume houses are blending regional ingredients with more contemporary fragrance trends.
Oud, derived from resin formed naturally in agarwood trees, has been prized throughout the Middle East for centuries. It is often paired with bukhoor – scented woodchips burned in homes and during gatherings – as part of Gulf hospitality and everyday customs.
Speaking to Euronews, Al Hazm Mall CEO Mohamed Al-Emady said the growing reputation of Gulf fragrances had encouraged organisers to expand the festival abroad.
"The next step is London. It's the first time Teeb Al Hazm will be in Europe. It will be the first edition in London, but we are already in the Gulf. We did in Abu Dhabi, we are going to Riyadh, and the third one will be London."
Looking beyond the Gulf
The latest edition marked the festival's 13th outing and drew exhibitors and visitors from across the Gulf despite taking place at the beginning of the summer, when many residents traditionally travel abroad.
"We never expect to have this number of the traffic, this number of the people. Usually the exhibition will be busy from five, but this one from 10 o'clock morning is busy," Al-Emady said.
Among the returning exhibitors was Kuwaiti fragrance house Czar Perfumes, which has become a regular participant at the event.
Sales representative Ehab Fouad said Qatar's appreciation for perfume continued to attract brands from across the region.
"We come from Kuwait. It's our fourth time to share in this festival. It's a very big event. Qatari people like perfumes. So we have good customers here."
Global appeal
The Gulf's long-standing perfume traditions are increasingly influencing the wider fragrance industry, according to Al-Emady.
"The culture of the GCC with the oud and bukhour. This type of perfumes now become international. Even the international brands, they try to have the fragrance of the Arabian oud and bukhour."
That growing international interest is reflected in the increasing visibility of Gulf perfume houses beyond the region, with Arabian fragrance notes now appearing in collections from international brands.
If the planned London edition goes ahead, it would introduce a wider audience to a fragrance tradition that has long been part of everyday life across the Gulf.

Jack Lowden for James Bond: Did British TV presenter and author Richard Osman leak identity of the new 007?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
13:10:42 UTC
22:10:42 KST

Speaking on his podcast, Richard Osman claimed to have insider knowledge that suggests a certain Scottish actor could be next in line to play James Bond...
It's the casting news that continues to drive cinema fans and the internet into a frenzy: Who will be the next 007?
Names like Aaron Taylor-Johnson, Callum Turner, Jacob Elordi, Louis Partridgeand Tom Francis have been circulating as frontrunners for the role of James Bond, and now, there seems to have been a leak.
Speaking on his The Rest Is Entertainment podcast, Richard Osman, the beloved British TV presenter and author of the best-selling Thursday Murder Club mystery novels, has revealed the name of the actor who is reportedly being "strongly considered" for the role.
Osman claimed to have insider knowledge that suggests 36-year-old Scottish actor Jack Lowden could be the next James Bond.
"Someone told me for definite who the new Bond is the other day, but I mean that’s happened before," said Osman. "The name I’ve heard is Jack Lowden."
He added: ‘It is definitively not a “he’s definitely got it” thing. He is definitely being strongly considered. I think he’d be amazing. Lowden would be an incredible Bond. He’s got real Daniel Craig energy.”
In case you didn't know, Lowden is best known for playing River Cartwright in the hit TV show Slow Horses and has been seen on the big screen in Christopher Nolan's Dunkirk, Mary Queen of Scots (2018) and Benediction (2021).
He will appear later this year as Mr Darcy in Netflix's new adaptation of "Pride and Prejudice".
This is not the first time that Lowden's name has come up in conversation regarding Bond. Earlier this year, Euronews Culture reported that the official casting for Bond was underway and that Lowden would be an ideal candidate for the 007 mantle.
We wrote regarding Lowden: " Spy credentials? Check. Charisma levels? Suit him up. Pre-existing rapport with the casting director? Done. Married to Saoirse Ronan who has previously expressed an interest in being cast as a Bond villain? Make this happen."
Indeed, the casting director for Bond 26 is Nina Gold, who cast Lowden in Slow Horses – a detail which gives some extra weight to this recent "leak".
In 2022, while promoting Slow Horses, Lowden addressed speculation about him taking on the role of Bond, telling AP that the rumours are “lovely”, but casting doubt on their validity.
Taking a cue from Lowden, it is worth taking all rumoured contenders with a pinch of salt, as the audition process is ongoing - and traditionally, once a name is out there, the chances are it’ll be another actor who gets the role.
The role of Bond usually makes the star, and rising performers are usually favoured. Sean Connery was a relative unknown before Bond; George Lazenby had never acted outside of a few ads; Roger Moore was a household name thanks to The Saint but hadn’t had a huge break on the big screen; Timothy Dalton had a great stage career but was not an established movie star; Pierce Brosnan was a Bond hopeful for years but remained best known for his role as Remington Steele in the TV show of the same name... Only Daniel Craig had some major big screen credentials with memorable roles in Road To Perdition, Layer Cake and Munich... However, it was Casino Royale that made him a bona fide leading man.
With this in mind, and the fact that already established stars command higher salaries, the odds are that Amazon will bank on a relatively unknown actor in his late 20s rather than someone who is already in demand.
The counter argument could be that Amazon, who took creative control of the Bond franchise last year from long-serving producers Barbara Broccoli and Michael G. Wilson, will buck the trend and cast a more known actor. In which case, we stand by our prior assessment and join Osman in thinking that Jack Lowden would be a terrific shout.
One quibble: get ready for British tabloids to have a field day if Lowden is announced as the seventh actor to play Bond.
Daniel Craig's announcement as Bond in 2005 was met with controversy and a tiresome barrage of headlines / insults regarding his hair colour, with article headers including "Blond Bond". All this despite the fact that Roger Moore had blond hair...
Lowden, who has strawberry blond hair and a distinctly reddish beard, would doubtlessly be met with tediously predictable "Ginger Bond" or "First Ginger To Play Bond" headers - especially since England has a unique cultural fixation on people with red hair, leading to bullying known as "gingerism".
Richard Osman's claims come after Bond 26 producer Amy Pascal recently shared that "the end of the year is a good bet" when it comes to the timing of the new actor's announcement.
“I would say the end of the year is a good bet,” said Pascal. “We are being really, really methodical. Having worked with Barbara Broccoli at the studio, I mean, Daniel Craig is a hard act to follow. And it’s got to be something really different that is stirring and exciting and different.”
Until then, the rumour mill will keep on working overtime...
Bond 26 will be directed by Canadian filmmaker and four-time Oscar nominee Denis Villeneuve and is being written by Peaky Blinders creator Steven Knight. Production is expected to kick off in 2027, with a release planned for 2028.

Why has North Korea fired a missile ahead of US-South Korea drills?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
13:10:14 UTC
22:10:14 KST

Why has North Korea fired a missile ahead of US-South Korea drills?
Pyongyang has repeatedly condemned US–South Korea military drills, claiming they are a ‘rehearsal for invasion’.
North Korea has fired a ballistic missile into waters off its east coast, just days before the United States and South Korea begin annual military drills known as the Ulchi Freedom Shield exercises in the region.
The launch at 6am on Wednesday (21:00 GMT) was the second reported North Korean missile test in less than a week amid tensions over Pyongyang’s growing military ties with Russia and concerns about its expanding weapons programme.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Senior Chinese delegation visits North Korea for talks
- list 2 of 3Western allies warn North Korean IT workers funding nuclear arsenal
- list 3 of 3New York Times reveals Trump administration subpoena over North Korea story
North Korea has not immediately commented on the latest launch but has repeatedly condemned annual US-South Korea drills in its neighbourhood.
Washington and Seoul say the exercises are defensive and designed to prepare their forces for potential North Korean attacks.
Here is what you need to know:
What has happened?
South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff said a ballistic missile was launched from the Wonsan area, where a port city and naval base are located in Kangwon Province, North Korea, at about 6am local time (21:00 GMT). It flew for more than 700km (435 miles) before landing in waters between the Korean Peninsula and Japan.
The launch was also detected by Japanese authorities, which reported that the missile had fallen outside Japan’s exclusive economic zone.
South Korea’s Office of National Security convened an emergency meeting and expressed concern over North Korea’s continued ballistic missile launches. It urged Pyongyang to halt provocations which violate UN Security Council resolutions.
The launch came six days after North Korea fired another ballistic missile from the same area. Pyongyang did not confirm that earlier launch either, which Seoul, Washington and Tokyo all said they detected on August 6.
Why did North Korea fire a missile into the sea?
North Korea has provided no explanation for the missile launch. However, the timing strongly suggests it was partly intended as a warning ahead of the US-South Korea military exercises, analysts say.
North Korea has previously condemned annual joint drills by Washington and Seoul, which it regards as rehearsals for an invasion. The US and South Korea say these are defensive exercises only, designed to prepare for potential attacks by Pyongyang.
North Korea has also previously responded to major US-South Korea exercises with missile tests and threatening rhetoric.
Lim Eul-chul, a North Korea expert at Kyungnam University in South Korea’s South Gyeongsang Province, told AFP that Pyongyang has “never simply let” a South Korea-US joint military exercise pass without a response.
He added that the latest launch can be seen as a message that North Korea is closely watching the upcoming drills and could take further action if it considers it necessary.
Where are the US and South Korea holding joint military drills?
The Ulchi Freedom Shield exercises will take place in South Korea from August 17-27 on and around the Korean Peninsula.
Drills will involve about 18,000 South Korean troops and personnel from the US contingent of roughly 28,500 troops stationed in South Korea.
Why are these drills taking place?
The US and South Korea say their military training is for defensive purposes and is necessary because North Korea possesses nuclear weapons and continues to develop missiles and other military capabilities.
The drills are specifically aimed at countering Pyongyang’s evolving nuclear and weapons capabilities.
This year’s exercises also take into account North Korea’s growing military cooperation with Russia. North Korea has also reportedly sent thousands of soldiers to assist Russia in the war against Ukraine.
North Korean soldiers have “taken those lessons they learned there and brought them back to North Korea”, Colonel Ryan Donald, spokesman for the US and South Korean Combined Forces Command, said on Monday.
How regular are North Korea’s missile tests?
South Korea says this launch is the North’s 11th suspected ballistic missile test this year.
Hong Min, a senior researcher at the Korea Institute for National Unification, told Reuters that the missile test was likely to be part of North Korea’s existing weapons-development programme.
However, Min added that choosing when to conduct such a test was itself a political decision, suggesting the timing may have been selected to send a message ahead of the exercises.
Multiple UN Security Council resolutions ban North Korea from launching ballistic missiles.
What is the context behind all this?
The latest missile launch is part of a broader increase in North Korea’s weapons testing.
Pyongyang has expanded its ballistic missile and other weapons programmes since diplomacy between North Korean leader Kim Jong Un and US President Donald Trump broke down during Trump’s first term in the White House in 2019.
The tests also come amid worsening regional tensions. South Korea and Japan condemned Wednesday’s missile launch, while Seoul said it remained ready to respond to any provocation alongside the United States.
Pyongyang has also criticised South Korea’s plans for nuclear-powered submarines and accused Japan of moving towards greater militarisation.
Earlier this month, Kim Yo Jong, sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, warned that Pyongyang would adopt “additional military options” after Japan test-fired a United States-made Tomahawk cruise missile.
In turn, South Korea and the US have accused North Korea of playing a more active role in the Russian invasion of Ukraine.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy claimed on Tuesday that Moscow had used a North Korean ballistic missile during an attack that killed 12 workers at a Ukrainian steel plant in the southeastern city of Zaporizhzhia.

Tunisia: Fury in Gabes at Saied over environmental issues
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12

Breadcrumb
'Leave': Tunisia's Gabes residents angry at Saied over environmental, health issues
Tunisian President Kais Saied is facing renewed public discontent and protests over the lack of action to close industrial units in the southern coastal Tunisian city of Gabes, which has led to widespread environmental and health issues.
Saied was met with angry protesters during a visit to Chatt Essalam earlier this week, an area located in the northern part of Gabes, near the Tunisian Chemical Group chemical complex. The complex processes phosphate, the main cause of the city’s environmental woes, where residents have been suffering from higher rates of cancer and respiratory illnesses.
Saied made an unannounced visit to the Gabes Governorate to inspect the environmental concerns there, where he stressed that the environmental crisis is a "national cause".
He said that Gabes has paid a heavy price due to the chemical complex—an entity that previous governments had planned to dismantle and sell off at cheap prices, a practice pursued since 2011 and even earlier.
But, Kais stated that Tunisia’s public institutions and facilities were "not for sale or disposal".
The president was met with angry chants from dozens of locals, most vocally: "Leave, leave, leave," and "The people want the units dismantled," in reference to the chemical complex units.
Police forces were seen trying to control the crowd as Saied met with local officials.
He was also confronted by several residents who voiced fury over the issue, with one man going up to Saied and saying, "We have the highest rate of illnesses here, Mr. President. We can’t have children anymore."
Visibly under pressure, Saied responded to protesters, assuring them that the units will be dismantled, and also called for urgent, effective measures alongside the development of long-term solutions for the structural problems.
He could then be seen discussing this with one of the local officials, stressing the need for "clean and pure air" in the region, where phosphate production has caused alarming rates of pollution, and for the city to return to how it was before the environmental crisis.
In January this year, Saied had emphasised the need to begin implementing the required measures—covering technical, financial, and structural aspects— to address the sources of pollution and halt its consequences—though very little progress has been made, given the residents' anger.
The city of Gabes and its surroundings have been plagued by an environmental and health crisis since the 1970s due to the chemical complexes processing phosphate into agricultural fertilizer.
The state-owned phosphate complex has provoked frustration among the local population over what they have described as a failure to protect public health.
Phosphate production and the subsequent toxic fumes is know to have led to higher rates of respiratory illnesses such as asthma, as well as osteoporosis and cancer. Marine life and livelihoods in the coastal town have also been damaged as industrial waste continues to be discharged into the sea.
Protests against the state-owned phosphate company in Gabes over economic grievances and unemployment in the sector have been occurring since the mid-2000s, but those related to the environment and public health intensified in October 2025 after a gas leak sent dozens of residents, including children, to hospitals.
The leak reignited long-standing concern in Gabes over the rising cancer rates in the coastal town, which was once home to a thriving and unique ecosystem.
The last major wave of protest took place in December 2025, which saw dozens of activists arrested.

Australian researchers grow human heart valve tissue from stem cells
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
13:07:29 UTC
22:07:29 KST

Saadet Gokce
12 August 2026•Update: 12 August 2026
Australian researchers have created human heart valve tissues from stem cells that could help advance treatments for childhood heart disease, the Murdoch Children's Research Institute (MCRI) said Wednesday.
The Melbourne-based institute said the three-dimensional tissues mimic key molecular features of human heart valves, providing researchers with a new platform to study how valves form, grow and become damaged.
The research, led by MCRI, was published in the journal Cell Stem Cell.
Heart valve disease affects around 28 million people worldwide and occurs when one or more of the heart's four valves fail to open or close properly. It can result from developmental problems, infections or aging.
There are currently no treatments that can repair damaged heart valves, leaving many patients reliant on surgery to replace them.
For children, existing replacement valves do not grow with the body, meaning they may require multiple open-heart surgeries as they develop.
"By creating heart valve tissues that mimic the molecular features of a human version we can now test and advance new treatments at scale in the lab," lead author Dr. Holly Voges of MCRI said in the institute's statement.
The researchers also demonstrated that the lab-grown tissues could be used to model inflammatory valve disease, which can lead to rheumatic heart disease.
Australia has some of the world's highest recorded rates of rheumatic heart disease, a largely preventable condition that disproportionately affects Indigenous Australians.
Enzo Porrello, director of stem cell medicine at MCRI, said engineered stem cells allowed researchers to recreate the complex structure of heart valves.
"In the future, this technology could be used to more accurately model valve disease and support the development of stem cell-derived replacement valves that grow and adapt with a patient," he said.

“These tragedies show how far our society has deteriorated and how deeply troubled it has become,” Efremova said.
