41 nations call for advance warning on ballistic missile tests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
12:32:09 UTC
21:32:09 KST

A 41-nation coalition has called on nuclear-armed states to provide advance notice of long-range ballistic missile tests, warning that unannounced launches could threaten regional peace and global security.
In a joint statement delivered at the Conference on Disarmament in Geneva on Wednesday, the countries urged states to follow transparency measures under the Hague Code of Conduct Against Ballistic Missile Proliferation (HCOC).
The coalition said nuclear-capable missile tests conducted without sufficient warning and information can increase the risk of miscalculation, particularly for countries located near launch areas.
Coalition calls for 24-hour notice
The signatories urged countries testing intercontinental ballistic missiles, submarine-launched ballistic missiles and space launch vehicles to issue notifications at least 24 hours before launches.
They said advance notices should identify the missile class, launch window, launch area and planned trajectory, along with clear warnings for ships and aircraft operating nearby.
The appeal follows recent missile tests in the Pacific, including China's reported launch of a strategic missile from a nuclear submarine after notifying several Pacific nations.
The coalition said standardised notification procedures would not restrict countries' military development or operational requirements but would instead improve confidence and reduce the possibility of dangerous misunderstandings.
China rejects criticism
China's Ambassador for Disarmament Affairs Li Chijiang rejected the statement, saying Beijing's legitimate defence modernisation should not be questioned.
He also defended China's advance notification of missile launches, arguing that its efforts should not be subjected to geopolitical calculations.
The 41 signatories include the United States, Türkiye, the United Kingdom, France, Germany, Japan, South Korea, Australia, Canada and Ukraine, among others.

A new data center in west London has been approved despite concerns over its demands on electricity and water supplies.
According to a report by the BBC, Hounslow Council’s Planning Committee voted in favor of plans for the facility on a 12.2-acre brownfield site at the Haslemere Heathrow Estate earlier this month.
The scheme requires an 80MVA high-capacity power connection, equivalent to the electricity needs of tens of thousands of homes.
The Greater London Authority (GLA) has warned that around 10 times the electricity capacity currently used by London’s existing data centres has already been requested in the grid connection queue.
Data centers house IT infrastructure, including servers, and are described by the government as underpinning much of the UK’s economic activity and innovation.
London is already home to the vast majority of the UK’s data center capacity, with 99 operational sites and 26 in the planning pipeline as of November last year, according to the GLA.
Ofgem has also identified data centers as a major driver of demand on the UK’s electricity grid.
Hounslow councillors were told that the new center would receive electricity from the National Energy System Operator via the Laleham Grid Supply Point, outside the borough. Planning officers said it would not use capacity earmarked for other developments, including housing.
However, questions remain over its impact on local water supplies.
Affinity Water told MPs in May that some data centers were seeking up to three million liters of water a day—equivalent to the peak demand of around 3,500 homes.
The GLA had previously warned that the scheme did not fully comply with the London Plan, citing concerns over transport and its high water and energy intensity.
Under the approval, the developer must submit a strategy to minimize operational water consumption.
The decision comes after Ealing Council approved a 52,000-square-meter data center at the former Honey Monster factory in Southall last month.
Both schemes remain subject to a Stage 2 referral to the Mayor of London.

British driver sets speed record in hydrogen-powered car
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
12:30:36 UTC
21:30:36 KST

Retired RAF pilot Andy Green has set a world land speed record for a hydrogen-powered car, reaching 406.320 mph (653.908 km/h) at the Bonneville Salt Flats in Utah.
The 64-year-old drove the JCB Hydromax, a 9.75-metre car built by British construction equipment manufacturer JCB. The record, ratified by motorsport's governing body the FIA, was measured as the average of two runs and more than doubled the previous hydrogen combustion mark of 185.5 mph, set in 2004.
Green already held the diesel land speed record, set at Bonneville in 2006, and remains the only person to have broken the sound barrier in a car — a feat he achieved in the jet-powered ThrustSSC in 1997, at 763 mph.
The Hydromax runs on two hydrogen internal combustion engines producing a combined 1,600 horsepower, adapted from those used in JCB's construction machinery. They mix pressurised hydrogen gas with air and ignite it to create power. "You burn hydrogen, water comes out of the exhaust. It doesn't get any cleaner than that," Green said after the run.
JCB hopes the project will strengthen the case for hydrogen in heavy industry. But hydrogen is only as clean as its source: the vast majority is currently produced from fossil fuels, and the green hydrogen the company has contracted to buy makes up a tiny fraction of global production.

Little surprise Beijing doesn’t want Western advice for its economy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
12:30:10 UTC
21:30:10 KST

Little surprise Beijing doesn’t want Western advice for its economy
The lack of forceful stimulus is not policy paralysis, as foreigners assume – China simply operates on a different set of priorities
When a patient repeatedly refuses the same medicine, there are usually three possibilities: he does not understand the diagnosis, cannot afford the treatment, or does not trust the doctor. The same logic applies to economic prescriptions.
In the case of China, the first possibility is unlikely because Beijing understands what ails its economy. The reason it is not acting as expected is probably a combination of the other two scenarios, compounded by a more fundamental difference: China believes it is treating a different disease.
Western economists see weak consumption, a prolonged property downturn, deflationary pressure, a massive trade surplus and indebted local governments. Their standard prescription is to transfer more income to households, strengthen the social safety net and reduce reliance on investment, exports and manufacturing.
Beijing has moved in some of these directions, but not at the scale or decisiveness outsiders expect. This is wrongly interpreted as policy paralysis. A more useful explanation is that China is no longer optimising simply for short-term gross domestic product growth.
Beijing is preparing for prolonged strategic rivalry with the United States, as economist Tan Kong Yam and others have pointed out. Seen through this lens, China’s choices become less puzzling. Beijing is trying to reduce technological dependence, preserve industrial capacity and withstand a longer period of Western pressure. GDP still matters, but it is no longer the be-all and end-all of Beijing’s calculations.

ICJP letter to UK minister calls for sanctions on settlements

2026-08-12
12:28:51 UTC
21:28:51 KST

Breadcrumb
ICJP letter to UK's MENA minister calls for immediate sanctions on illegal Israeli settlements in occupied West Bank
The International Centre of Justice for Palestinians (ICJP) on Wednesday called for the UK to extend sanctions against all trade with illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.
In a letter written to the UK's Middle East Minister, Labour MP Stephen Doughty, and seen by The New Arab, the ICJP welcomed his condemnation of settlement expansion and their illegality under international law.
The letter called on the UK government to "move beyond statements of concern and non-binding warnings directed at a limited number of organisations and address the settlement enterprise, and the economic relationships that sustain it, as a whole."
"We therefore urge you to use your position as Minister of the Middle East and secure targeted measures, without further delay, prohibiting trade with and economic support for illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied Palestinian territory," it continued.
"Such measures should address not merely particular actors or transactions, but the broader commercial and financial relationship that contribute to the maintenance and expansion of the illegal settlement enterprise," the letter added.
"Sanctions are not a radical step–they are the bare minimum required to uphold international law, and the legal position on Israeli settlements is clear," Órlaith Roe, ICJP's Public Affairs and Communication Officer, explained.
"The question for the UK government is no longer whether it condemns settlement expansion, but what concrete measures it is prepared to take in response," she added.
The UK has frequently condemned the existence of illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, alongside the accompanying rise of settler violence that is ongoing in the area.
On Monday, UK foreign secretary Ed Miliband held separate calls with both Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar and Palestinian Prime Minister Mohammad Moustafa.
In a statement released regarding his call with Sa'ar, Miliband said that he "raised the sharp escalation of settler violence and settlement expansion," adding that "Israel must crack down on violence in the West Bank."
Despite the words of condemnation and sanctions on individual settlers, Israeli settler violence has continued to grow, alongside Israeli government decisions to expand Israeli settlements, most notably the E1 settlement that threatens to split the occupied West Bank into two.
The expansion of Israeli state and settler violence, which has seen the forced displacement of tens of thousands of Palestinians in the occupied West Bank, has been described by rights groups as a policy of state-sanctioned "ethnic cleansing".
ICJP noted in its letter to Doughty that the Israeli government approved 13 new settlements on 3 July, and £300 in funding for settlement expansion on 18 July, measures that "form part of an escalating effort to entrench Israel's unlawful settlement enterprise and create further irreversible changes on the ground."
It added that there was an expectation for the government to take further action, following a letter written by 140 Labour MPs to former Foreign Secretary Yvette Cooper on 7 June which called for a ban on trade with settlements, and the announcement by the Charity Commission of an investigation into funding links between UK-based charities and settlements.
Roe told The New Arab that the ongoing changes on the ground in the occupied West Bank require immediate action from the British government.
"Sanctions have to be an immediate priority. With the E1 settlement tenders due to go live imminently, the window to prevent irreversible changes on the ground is rapidly closing," she said.
"This is also an important early test for Minister Doughty: how he responds now will set the tone for his tenure and show how seriously he intends to approach the UK's responsibility to uphold international law and prevent settlement expansion," she added.
Alongside pressure in the UK, the EU is also actively deliberating issuing of trade sanctions against illegal Israeli settlements, though efforts to push through bloc-wide sanctions have so far failed.
ICJP's own letter ended by saying that the implementation of sanctions on Israeli settlements would "demonstrate that the United Kingdom's stated commitment to international law carries real and measurable consequences."

Lebanese parliament passes sweeping amnesty law to reduce overcrowding in prisons
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
12:28:44 UTC
21:28:44 KST

Lebanese parliament passes sweeping amnesty law to reduce overcrowding in prisons
Lebanon's parliament on Wednesday passed a general amnesty law reducing sentences for inmates and people detained for more than 12 years without charges in a bid to reduce prison overcrowding. The legislation was passed a day after Lebanon became the first Middle Eastern country to abolish the death penalty.
Lebanon's parliament on Wednesday passed a sweeping and long-awaited amnesty law that should benefit thousands of prisoners and wanted people, in the first legislation of its kind since 1991.
The law, which had been a demand of various political factions and a topic of debate for years, aims to reduce prison overcrowding with many inmates awaiting trial for years.
The office of the country's parliament speaker announced the "approval of a draft law aimed at granting a general amnesty and exceptionally reducing the terms of certain sentences".
Authorities did not immediately announce the number of people that would benefit from the law.
According to Imad al-Hout, one of the lawmakers in favour of the bill, the law reduced the sentences of those facing death and life imprisonment to 17 prison years.
That is equivalent to 12 years and nine months of actual imprisonment in Lebanon, where a prison year is calculated as nine months.
The new law was passed a day after the Lebanese parliament abolished the death penalty, making the country the first in the Middle East to formally end the practice.
Read moreLebanon becomes first Middle Eastern country to abolish the death penalty
The amnesty law passed Wednesday also calls for the release of inmates detained for more than 12 prison years without charges as their trial continues.
In its 2025 report, the country's National Human Rights Commission said that prisons had an overcrowding rate of 300 percent, with prison authorities reporting at least 6,268 inmates by the end of March.
But general amnesty was brought back into the limelight after the 2024 fall of longtime Syrian president Bashar al-Assad, as many Islamist prisoners in Lebanon were jailed over events linked to the Syrian civil war.
Most of them hail from northern Lebanon's Sunni-majority city Tripoli and are accused of crimes that include attacking the Lebanese army, participating in clashes and planning bombings.
Other political forces, including Iran-backed Shia movement Hezbollah, have been demanding amnesty for their communities.
Thousands of families from the eastern Baalbek and Hermel regions, bastions of Hezbollah and its ally Amal where illicit cannabis cultivation is widespread, have been demanding amnesty for drug-related offences and car theft for years.
Christian parties meanwhile have pushed for the law to include the families of those who joined an Israeli-backed proxy and fled to Israel after its withdrawal from southern Lebanon in 2000, fearing reprisals, particularly from Hezbollah and its supporters.
Lebanon previously passed a general amnesty law in the wake of its 1975-90 civil war, allowing former warlords to transition into politics without facing trial for crimes committed during the conflict.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

According to the WHO, Bangladesh historically possessed herd immunity against measles but lost it in recent years due to decreased vaccination coverage.
Since April 5, the Health Ministry has immunized almost 19.25 million youngsters through a special program in addition to routine vaccinations. Both vaccination programs are continuing as the infection remains unabated across the country.

Southern African bloc raises alarm over severe El Nino
A severe El Nino could deepen the humanitarian crisis across Southern Africa by worsening drought, hunger, water shortages, and disease outbreaks, the Southern African Development Community (SADC) has warned.
SADC Executive Secretary Elias Magosi said seasonal forecasts pointed to a high likelihood of an El Nino event that could surpass the intensity and impact of the 2023/24 phenomenon.
Addressing the opening of the SADC Council of Ministers meeting in Durban on Wednesday, Magosi said the region needed to strengthen its preparedness as climate-related disasters continued to threaten communities and infrastructure.
”Earlier this year, devastating floods claimed lives, damaged critical infrastructure, displaced communities, and disrupted trade across parts of our region.”
Magosi said the expected El Nino could further worsen food and nutrition insecurity while increasing fertilizer and energy costs, putting pressure on government finances and increasing humanitarian needs.
“These interconnected shocks threaten to undermine hard-won development gains and hinder our aspirations for regional integration, industrialization, and inclusive economic growth.”
Magosi said the region could no longer rely solely on responding to disasters once they had occurred and needed to invest more in measures that would allow it to anticipate and withstand climate-related shocks.
”We must therefore move from reacting to disasters to investing in resilience through strengthened early warning systems, anticipatory planning and action, climate-resilient infrastructure, disaster risk financing and resilient recovery efforts,” he said.
Stronger early warning systems and anticipatory planning would allow governments and regional structures to prepare for potential emergencies before they escalated.
Magosi also highlighted the need for infrastructure capable of withstanding climate-related shocks, as well as financing mechanisms that could support countries during disasters and the recovery period that followed.
The SADC Humanitarian Emergency Operations Centre in Nacala, Mozambique, was identified as an important part of the region’s response capacity, he said.
”Adequate financial and human resources must be provided to enable the Centre to co-ordinate contingency planning, emergency response and recovery efforts effectively and swiftly,” Magosi stressed.

Panama canal fees soar due to Iran war and El Niño as ship ‘pays $4m to jump queue’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
12:26:48 UTC
21:26:48 KST

Commercial ships travelling through the Panama canal are facing a rise in costs amid disruption triggered by the Iran war and falling water levels linked to this year’s intense El Niño weather system.
Highlighting the fragility of global trade, a container ship reportedly paid about $4m (£3m) to jump a queue of vessels waiting to pass through the vital maritime choke point.
Ships are now waiting about 10 days for their turn to pass through the trade route linking the Pacific and Atlantic oceans, the largest backlog since May, according to Argus Media. The route is favoured by shippers as it usually reduces cost and transit times, especially for large retailers and energy companies that trade between Asia and the US.
While shipping companies usually pay a flat fee to reserve a slot to transit the canal, the Panama Canal Authority (ACP), which manages the waterway, also runs daily auctions that allow shipowners to place bids to skip the queue. Starting bids open at about $15,000 for smaller cargo vessels and $55,000 for the largest ships, but these prices can shoot up during times of heavy congestion or high demand.
The buyer of the $4m transit slot was reported to be the Seaspan Benefactor, a 10,100 TEU (20-foot equivalent unit) vessel, according to Bloomberg. The payment was reportedly more than double the average bid placed during the previous seven days.
Shipowners are willing to pay significantly higher prices at auction to avoid queues, as more vessels stay away from the Gulf and the Red Sea as fighting in the Middle East has effectively closed the strait of Hormuz and the Bab al-Mandab, the narrow waterway between the Arabian peninsula and the Horn of Africa.
Prices to travel in the Panama canal’s busiest shipping lanes have hit record highs, according to the Financial Times, at a time when water levels are falling amid the rapidly developing El Niño weather system.
Earlier this month the ACP said it would impose limits in late August and early September on how low vessels can travel through the water, known as a ship’s draft, in an effort to keep traffic flowing.
The authority had also cut the maximum authorised draft in July, in a measure forcing ships transiting its Neopanamax locks – the canal’s wider and deeper lane – to carry lighter cargoes.
The decision was based on water levels and projected conditions for Gatun Lake, an artificial reservoir that feeds the canal, the ACP said, adding it was “ready to implement preventive measures” during El Niño based on lessons learned during the event in 2023-4 and as it monitors weather conditions.
Some shipowners are concerned the ACP could introduce restrictions on the number of vessels allowed to transit the waterway, as in 2023 when a lengthy drought in the central American country led to a logjam.
It comes after the ACP recorded a 5% increase in the number of transits between October and June, representing an average of 35 a day. A higher tonnage was carried through the canal during this period, with the increase driven by container ships and liquefied petroleum gas carriers, the ACP said.
The Panama canal is not the only crucial trade route affected by low water levels, amid growing international concern over the economic consequences of the climate emergency.
A prolonged period of dry weather across Europe has led to record low water levels on the Rhine, with traders warning that it was not possible to book some cargo shipments on the river, forcing them to pay higher costs to transport goods by road and rail instead.
The Rhine is one of Europe’s main arteries for transporting grain, fuel, minerals and goods, but manufacturers have had to reduce the amount of cargo transported on ships as a result of the low water levels.

An endangered eagle in Russia survived a gunshot. It didn’t survive the 50 days officials took to authorize its treatment.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
12:25:54 UTC
21:25:54 KST

An endangered eagle in Russia survived a gunshot. It didn’t survive the 50 days officials took to authorize its treatment.
At the Karelia Zoo, a white-tailed eagle listed in Russia’s Red Book of endangered species has died, months after it was found in June with a gunshot wound near Smolensk. Wildlife rescuers said obtaining the documents needed from authorities to treat the bird took 50 days. A post on the zoo’s social media on August 9 said:
For 50 days (!) the wounded bird waited for medical help. During that time, the wound began to fester, and irreversible processes set in. Every day of delay took away a chance at survival. By the time the necessary documents were finally obtained, there was essentially no time left.
Rosprirodnadzor’s rules require anyone who finds a Red Book-listed animal in need of treatment to first “take urgent measures to help it,” then report the find to the agency and ask its central office for permission to temporarily keep the animal for treatment. Point 34 of Rosprirodnadzor’s regulations says such requests must be forwarded “urgently” to the agency’s director or a deputy, who must sign and deliver a telegram granting permission to the applicant the same day. The regulations also state that the central office is to communicate its decision “promptly.”
The eagle, which had gunshot wounds to its wings, was picked up in the Vyazma district of the Smolensk region in mid-June. A segment on the program Vesti-Smolensk reported that the bird “came to the houses on its own” in one of the local settlements, prompting residents to contact AistYasha, a wild bird rescue foundation opened in 2025 by Andrey and Elena Davydenko in a village near Smolensk.
Wildlife rescuers named the eagle Prince Vyazemsky and took it to veterinarians. The fund’s social media posts said one of the bird’s wings had a through-and-through wound while a bullet was lodged in the other; a local clinic removed the bullet and prescribed treatment for lead poisoning. In one of its first posts, on June 13, AistYasha said it “reported the situation to the police, notified Rosprirodnadzor, and informed the forestry ministry.”
AistYasha staff said from the very start that the bird needed to go somewhere with highly qualified medical care and suitable conditions, naming the Moscow Zoo. “We’re now preparing the paperwork to transport it to the Moscow Zoo, because we, of course… can’t provide it the conditions it needs, the conditions it deserves. Because this is simply a huge eagle with a wingspan of 2.5 meters (8.2 feet),” Andrey Davydenko said on June 15. Judging by his remarks, he had already reached an agreement with the Moscow Zoo.
On June 19, Davydenko said the bird’s condition had “stabilized, more or less,” but that it “urgently needs to be taken to specialists” so its wounded wing could be treated. State television covered Prince Vyazemsky on the program Vesti-Smolensk on June 24, noting that “putting together the necessary package of documents is the hardest part” and that “without a referral from Rosprirodnadzor, the Prince’s move is impossible.” “Prince Vyazemsky will never fly again, but if his wing can be saved, the eagle will be able to live safely and for a long time in Moscow, under the care of zoo specialists,” the reporters concluded.
AistYasha said on June 30 that “there’s been complete silence from Rosprirodnadzor”:
We don’t know what to think anymore; it’s been more than two weeks of unclear limbo. The bird needs urgent help that most likely won’t do any good now: if the documents had been processed promptly, or if someone had at least called the director of MosZoo and had the eagle operated on, the wing could have been straightened and saved; now, at best, it will remain permanently bent or will have to be amputated.
Rosprirodnadzor finally responded in early July, the foundation said, after State Duma deputy Vladimir Burmatov, whom the fund had written to “in desperation” back in June, contacted the agency. Burmatov’s letter, according to the published documents, is dated June 24. On July 1, Stanislav Stefanenko, head of Rosprirodnadzor’s interregional department for the Moscow and Smolensk regions, sent Deputy Agency Head Tatyana Kuznetsova a request to authorize helping the eagle. More than two weeks later, on July 17, AistYasha published Rosprirodnadzor’s response authorizing the transport of the Red Book-listed eagle to the Moscow Zoo.
The very next day, though, the foundation asked its followers to help transport Prince Vyazemsky and two storks in an entirely different direction — to St. Petersburg, home to the Chizhik-Pyzhik veterinary clinic, which treats birds. Responding to followers’ questions on VK, Davydenko said the Moscow Zoo was “taking a very long time to think it over” and that the bird would instead go to the Karelia Zoo, whose management he had reached an agreement with. He said he had also resubmitted documents to Rosprirodnadzor seeking permission to transport the rare bird to Karelia.
As of publication, the Moscow Zoo had not commented on the situation with the wounded eagle or on any possible arrangements with the AistYasha foundation.
As of August 2, the foundation was still waiting for Rosprirodnadzor to make “minor corrections to the paperwork in order to officially register the eagle at its new location.” Those corrections appear to have come through soon after: roughly 50 days after the bird came into the rescuers’ care, the foundation reported on August 5 that the eagle and the storks had arrived at the clinic in St. Petersburg and would head to the zoo after an examination. In a new segment on the regional state broadcaster GTRK Smolensk, Andrey Davydenko complained about “bureaucratic delays with the permit, the seizure act, and referrals” that had kept the eagle from getting help in time. “From the moment the bird arrived to the moment we got the paperwork, 50 days passed,” he said.
The foundation shared news on August 6 that, according to the clinic’s examination, Prince Vyazemsky the eagle “turned out to be a lovely lady,” and that the bird was already on its way to the zoo, where “fairy-tale conditions” awaited it.
The Karelia Zoo reported on August 8, however, that the bird had died, linking the death to the excessively long wait for the necessary documents. The published video includes remarks from a veterinarian at the St. Petersburg clinic, who says the eagle underwent surgery and was prescribed treatment after muscle necrosis had already begun. A voiceover then says that “the aftermath of the overly long wait turned out to be irreversible” and that “the staff of the Karelia Zoo and veterinary specialists did everything possible to ease her suffering and give her care in her final days.”
As of publication, Rosprirodnadzor had not commented on the situation with the eagle.

Several European airlines and charter operators are running dedicated flights Wednesday so passengers and researchers can watch the total solar eclipse from high altitude, turning the rare astronomical event into a premium aerial experience.
Spanish carrier Iberia scheduled a dedicated observational flight, operating as IB1473, departing from and returning to Madrid-Barajas Airport.
Utilizing an Airbus A321XLR, the flight was routed over the province of Palencia at an altitude of approximately 10,000 meters (33,000 feet) to allow researchers from the Shelios project and passengers to observe the eclipse above potential low-level cloud cover. In Belgium, Brussels Airlines has chartered an Airbus A320 in partnership with the Urania public observatory and local universities. The short flight heads toward western France so passengers can observe a deep partial eclipse.
UK-based Air Charter Service is operating a same-day return flight from London Stansted, with the destination to be selected from Valladolid, the Balearic Islands or Keflavik based on weather forecasts. The company is charging £899 per seat and says the fare includes baggage for telescopic equipment, meals and transfers to an approved viewing area.
Seats on several of these flights were sold out.
Wednesday's total solar eclipse will sweep across the Arctic, Greenland, Iceland, the Atlantic Ocean, northern Spain and a small corner of northeastern Portugal, marking the first total eclipse visible from mainland Europe since 1999. A wider partial eclipse will be visible across the northern United States, most of Canada, much of Europe and northwestern Africa.
NASA plans to livestream the event starting at 1.15 pm EDT, featuring views of totality from cameras along the eclipse path and commentary from scientists. The European Space Agency has also been tracking the eclipse's path across the continent, noting Spain will have the largest area of totality in Europe.

Iran has not discussed extending its cease-fire with the U.S. because Tehran considers the deal to have no official start date, a senior Iranian source said Wednesday.

The deal declared an "immediate and permanent termination of military operations on all fronts," but quickly unraveled, with U.S. President Donald Trump saying it was "over" on July 7 and Iran's Foreign Ministry declaring it "suspended" a week later.
"There is no talk of an extension because, from Iran’s perspective, there is no period that began and therefore nothing to extend. The United States violated the interim agreement 48 hours after it was reached and withdrew from it a few days later," the source told Reuters.
In the agreement, the 60-day period refers to an extendable timeframe within which Iran and the U.S. were expected to reach a final deal limiting Tehran's nuclear program and lifting U.S. sanctions.
A series of requirements, such as a ceasefire in Lebanon, free navigation in the Gulf and waivers for Iran to sell its oil, were viewed as necessary before entering the further negotiation period.
"One of the issues that is being discussed via mediators is the U.S. returning to the interim agreement and defining a timeframe for implementing the commitments. There has been absolutely no progress on this issue," the source added.
Earlier Tuesday, U.S. and Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis reported separate attacks on shipping as prospects for ending the war dimmed further, with Tehran saying the Strait of Hormuz would remain closed unless Washington accepts its conditions.
The attacks, in the Gulf of Oman leading to the strait and at the entrance to the Red Sea – both vital chokepoints for global oil supplies – come as the war shows no signs of ending despite repeated assertions from U.S. President Donald Trump of a deal being imminent.
Oil prices gained and global shares retreated amid renewed pessimism about a quick end to the conflict. Brent crude futures climbed 1.4% to settle at $88.91 per barrel and U.S. crude rose 1.3% to $83.20.

Two Yemeni rescuers from an anti-Houthi military group were also killed, Yemen's Coast Guard said.

The Houthi-run news agency Saba reported that the group, which said last month it would impose a naval blockade on Saudi Arabia in the Red Sea, attacked a Saudi ship they said was carrying military equipment in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.

The ship ignored repeated warnings to stop violating a naval blockade on Iranian ports, the U.S. Central Command said. Maritime sources told Reuters the ship was hit off Pakistan while sailing into the Gulf of Oman.
Both Iran and the United States have stepped up rhetoric in the past two days. Iran's top security official, Mohsen Rezaei, said Tuesday that the vital Strait of Hormuz shipping route will remain closed unless the U.S. accepts Iran's conditions to end the war – the release of Iran's frozen assets and an end to conflicts throughout the region, including in Lebanon and Gaza.
That followed a new demand from Trump Monday that Iran should pay compensation for people killed in 50 years of wars, attacks and protests.
Throughout the conflict, Trump has alternated between threats of escalation and claims that a peace deal is imminent.

"We totally control the Strait of Hormuz ... Nobody else, only us," he said.

There was no immediate comment from Washington on Iran's latest comments.
Thousands of people have been killed in the conflict since the U.S. and Israel launched attacks on Iran on Feb. 28.
Iran has struck U.S. assets and infrastructure in countries including Oman, Jordan, Kuwait, Israel, the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia.
Raising the prospect of further escalation, Mohammad Reza Naqdi, an adviser to the commander of Iran's Revolutionary Guards, said on Iranian state TV on Tuesday that the corps was developing the ability to carry out operations "on enemy soil."
"We need to be able to move the operations to the enemy's soil, whenever this is needed and ordered," he said. "This is the characteristic of the offensive doctrine that has to be attained."

MOSCOW, August 12. /TASS/. OPEC+ nations participating in the oil output supply-cut deal increased production by 1.15 million barrels per day (bpd) in July 2026, but still fell significantly short of their targets, the International Energy Agency (IEA) said in its report.
According to IEA data, the combined target for the OPEC+ countries implementing voluntary output limits was set at 34.08 million bpd in July, whereas actual production reached 28.06 million bpd. Thus, the production shortfall against the planned quota amounted to approximately 6.02 million bpd.
The IEA report noted that among the seven key OPEC+ producers in July, Algeria cut output by 10,000 bpd, while Kuwait increased production by 290,000 bpd, Iraq ramped up by 470,000 bpd, and Saudi Arabia boosted output by 900,000 bpd. Meanwhile, Oman reduced its output by 20,000 bpd, and Russia cut production by 100,000 bpd. Additionally, Kazakhstan slashed its oil production by 330,000 bpd in June.
Total production for all OPEC+ member states grew by 1.52 million bpd in July, reaching 34.53 million bpd.

Deaths, damage reported as severe weather spawns tornadoes, flash flooding in the Midwest
CHICAGO (AP) — First responders and utility crews worked overnight into Wednesday clearing roads from trees and wires that were downed during severe storms in the Midwest that unleashed tornadoes, heavy rains and flash flooding while knocking out power to hundreds of thousands of customers.
A 4-year-old boy was killed when a tree fell on a home in Geneva, Indiana, during Tuesday’s storms, the Jennings County Sheriff’s Office said. In Ohio, Gov. Mike DeWine said a resident of Roseville died during a health emergency when first responders, faced with flooded roads, couldn’t reach them. Officials in Portage, Indiana, were investigating whether the severe weather played a role in a reported house explosion that killed a person.
Lightning struck a prison complex southwest of Cleveland on Tuesday, injuring 16 incarcerated people who were hospitalized, according to the Ohio Department of Corrections. Their conditions weren’t immediately known.
The storms inflicted a wide swath of damage from the Chicago area to western Pennsylvania, and the National Weather Service said threats of severe thunderstorms and heavy rainfall will continue over the next few days in the Midwest, Ohio Valley and central Appalachians.
More than 700,000 customers were without power Wednesday morning in Illinois, Indiana, Ohio, Kentucky and West Virginia, according to poweroutage.us.
The National Weather Service said it confirmed three tornadoes in counties south of Chicago. Water rescues were reported during heavy rains in several states including Ohio, where DeWine sent 40 Ohio Army National Guard members to help in two counties east of Columbus.
Tornado warning sirens howled Tuesday as the skies darkened in the Chicago area. All flights were temporarily stopped at Chicago’s two major airports, and officials warned of delays as the backlog was cleared.
Photos posted on social media from the Chicago area and across the state line in Indiana showed flooded roads, trees tangled in power lines and homes with gashes in their roofs.
“No power. It was very scary. We were down in the basement,” said Javid Jenkins of Homewood, a Chicago suburb. “We’re built for snow. We’re built for cold. We’re not built for this.”
Jenkins, 54, said he was driving around for gas to fire up a generator to preserve food in his refrigerator.
Forecasters said a wind gust of 99 mph (159 kph) was recorded in Gary, Indiana. Elsewhere there were numerous reports of gusts of 80 mph (128 kph) or more at personal weather stations.
Preliminary information indicated that the intense system that swept from Iowa into Indiana over several hours qualified as a derecho, the weather service’s Storm Prediction Center said Tuesday evening. Derechos are prolonged straight-line wind events that unleash heavy rainfall and travel far distances. The damage they cause is sometimes comparable to the destructive forces of tornadoes or hurricanes.
“Total devastation. No roof,” said Kerry Hourigan, standing outside her home of 25 years in Tinley Park, another Chicago suburb. “Stupid thing, but my focus was I just bought a new barbecue grill, and I have no idea where that is. It’s disappeared.”
Meteorologist Scott Baker said the Midwest was on the outer edge of a “ring of fire,” bringing waves of excessive moisture, instability and storms.
Dayton, Ohio, set a daily rainfall record with 2.07 inches (5.25 cm), shattering a mark set in 1915, the weather service said. Forecasters said multiple rounds of rain would cause flood hazards in the Ohio Valley through early Friday.
___
White reported from Detroit. Associated Press writers Dave Collins in Hartford, Connecticut, Jennifer Garske in Washington, Sudhin Thanawala in Atlanta, and Christopher Weber in Los Angeles contributed.

Survivors describe pleading to turn back before ferry capsized on Zimbabwe lake and killed 44
HARARE, Zimbabwe (AP) — Survivors on Wednesday described frantic passengers pleading with the captain of an overloaded ferry to turn back from strong waves shortly before it capsized and killed at least 44 people on Lake Kariba in Zimbabwe.
The number of people on board Tuesday was unclear as estimates reached as high as 153 people on a government agency-operated ferry whose capacity, authorities said, was just 90.
“Some of us survived by standing on top of the capsized hull,” one of the two crew members who survived, Anyway Chambati, told state broadcaster ZBC News. “Before it went down, passengers were screaming at us that the boat was flooding, water was pouring into the engine room and goods were spilling out.”
Chambati said he was in charge of ticketing and that he counted 153 people on board, including crew and infants, before the disaster.
Multiple witnesses told ZBC that passengers urged the captain to turn back as waves grew perilous, only to be dismissed. When water surged into the vessel, chaos erupted as frantic travelers scrambled for life jackets beneath their seats.
“We argued with him right at the harbor. We told him the waves were too dangerous,” one woman said. “A bag fell overboard before we had even left, and we pointed it out, but he refused to listen.”
Passengers told the broadcaster that bags, dishes and beer bottles began toppling overboard within minutes of setting off.
“About 30 minutes in, we begged again to abort and return, more goods were falling, the wave was getting worse and water was gushing into one side of the boat, but (the captain) just said, ‘My boat has never sunk anyone.’ He even refused to call for help,” another survivor told the broadcaster.
The woman described some people floating in the water and clutching sacks of goods while help did not arrive for nearly an hour.
The captain was among the dead, the state-run Herald newspaper reported.
President Emmerson Mnangagwa declared the incident a state of disaster to enable the government to mobilize “extraordinary measures and resources” to assist victims.
Police on X said bodies had been retrieved from the lake that forms part of the border between Zimbabwe and Zambia, but they did not update how many people were injured or missing.
Zimbabwe’s disaster management agency has said the ferry was carrying at least 114 adult passengers and five crew members, and that 77 people had been rescued.
But the real number was not clear because the figures only included those who bought tickets, and children below ticketing age could have been on board. The state broadcaster reported that children were among the dead.
The ferry is used to take people from rural communities around the lake to the town of Kariba on the shore.
Mutsa Murombedzi, a local member of Parliament, posted a video Tuesday of what she said were people on shore waving at the ferry when it set off. Some of the people expressed concern whether the aging ferry could handle strong waves, according to the video.
Kariba is the largest man-made lake in the world by volume and was created in the late 1950s and early 1960s by building a dam on the Zambezi River. The huge lake is now more than 200 kilometers (124 miles) long and up to 40 kilometers (25 miles) wide in places.

A 3-story Hoosier cabinet in Indiana celebrates an American kitchen icon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
12:23:02 UTC

A 3-story Hoosier cabinet in Indiana celebrates an American kitchen icon
NAPPANEE, Ind. (AP) — Hoosier cabinets — the original all-in-one kitchen — were once a mainstay in early 20th-century American homes. Though they have long since fallen out of fashion, a giant, climbable replica has been unveiled outdoors in a northern Indiana town to celebrate the cabinet’s place in kitchen history.
The 30-foot (9-meter) model of a Dutch Kitchenette opened to the public last month as part of the 150th anniversary celebration of Coppes Napanee, one of two companies still in existence that manufactured the popular Hoosier cabinets more than a century ago. The cabinet name was coined after its largest producer, the Hoosier Manufacturing Co.
Dubbed the world’s largest Hoosier cabinet, the replica built against a brick background is equipped with stairs leading to a loft that visitors to the town of Nappanee can look out from. It overlooks Coppes Commons, the site of the original Coppes Napanee factory that has been converted to an indoor marketplace, artisan hub and museum. The company still produces custom cabinets next door.
Wesley Mast, owner and president of Coppes Napanee, said he typically hears two types of responses when visitors first see the giant cabinet.
“There’s the one extreme where people are like, ‘Why? Why such a big cabinet?’” Mast said. “And my response is always like, ‘Why not?’
“The other response we get is like, ‘That’s so cool. Where did you get this idea? I love it.’”
Mast said the cabinet “brings us another level of attention and branding and makes this place more of a destination than just a pass-through.”
The Hoosier cabinet is a freestanding kitchen workstation and storage area that centralized and sped up food preparation. The cabinets were popular from the 1890s through the 1930s but waned after World War II as built-in, wall-to-wall cabinetry became the norm in new home construction.
A century ago, “this was the kitchen,” Mast said. “This was kind of the first piece of furniture that went into the house as a kitchen and was considered all-in-one, the kitchen itself in just one piece.”
There were 5,000 dealers of Hoosier cabinets across the country, said Mary Figueroa, curator of History at the Indiana State Museum and Historic Sites, which has four Hoosier cabinets in its collection.
Prior to the Hoosier cabinet, a kitchen area would have some shelves, a separate work table and a corner cupboard. “But this was a piece of furniture that kind of consolidated all of that, allowed women to save their steps and have everything that they could possibly need to make a meal right at their fingertips,” Figueroa said.
The Hoosier cabinet had space for storing items such as flour, sugar, spices, loaves of bread and other pantry supplies. They were nicknamed “kitchen pianos” because everything that was needed was within close range. They had built-in flour sifters and came with small cookbooks with recipes involving meats, soups, breads or desserts, among other things. Advertising for the cabinets even made the promise to “strengthen your marriage” and “make you more beautiful” because of the time and steps that it saved for women, Figueroa said.
Nappanee is located in Elkhart County, a region known as a top U.S. hub for recreational vehicle manufacturing, wood products production and home to the third-largest Amish settlement in the nation. It is about 150 miles (241 kilometers) north of Indianapolis.
And now, add Nappanee as a potential tourist attraction for the colossal cabinet.
“It’s bringing awareness,” Figueroa said. “I mean, you can’t miss it.”
___
Raby reported from Charleston, West Virginia.

Germany beefs up its intelligence services as threat from ‘foreign powers’ rises
Unknown

2026-08-12

Germany beefs up its intelligence services as threat from ‘foreign powers’ rises
BERLIN (AP) — Germany’s government plans to give its intelligence services broader powers for actions such as disabling sabotage and hacking attempts in response to a rising threat from powers such as Russia and extremists.
The Cabinet on Wednesday approved draft legislation meant to strengthen Germany’s Federal Intelligence Service, the BND, and its domestic intelligence service, the BfV, and reduce the reliance of the European Union’s most populous nation on tips from its allies.
The powers of Germany’s intelligence services have long lagged behind those of major European counterparts. Modern Germany has traditionally been sensitive to data protection concerns, not least because of memories of repression under the Nazis and later by communist East Germany’s secret police.
“Nowadays, Germany is constantly a target of hybrid attacks by foreign powers and that is a real, very acute danger,” said Nina Warken, Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s chief of staff. “We are simply too dependent on the intelligence services of other countries supporting us, and at the moment this help is a one-way street in too many areas.”
Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said “we are developing our intelligence services into real intelligence services.”
The threats Germany now faces require intelligence services that are “competitive with our partner services in the European Union, but also with friendly services beyond that,” Dobrindt added.
“We are a daily target of espionage, sabotage, cyberattacks and hidden actions by foreign powers with the aim of destabilizing our country, damaging our country, and bringing about political and social changes in our country,” Dobrindt said.
Under the planned reform, which still requires parliamentary approval, the intelligence services will get more powers to access laptops, cellphones and other devices and store the data.
Warken, whose job involves overseeing the intelligence services, said they also will be able to take “active measures.”
The BND could, for example, swap out components in deliveries for faulty ones, access the IT systems of drone factories or chemical weapons laboratories to sabotage them, or disable or switch off the servers of hackers or disinformation agents linked to foreign states, Warken said.
Dobrindt also pointed to the possibility of exchanging explosives for harmless substances.
The reform has been planned for months. The risks Germany faces were underlined last week by the discovery of a drone carrying explosives at Leipzig/Halle airport, a major hub for international freight and for providing support to Ukraine.
That incident is under investigation and authorities haven’t said who might have been responsible.
While Dobrindt and Warken didn’t name the foreign powers they are worried about, Russia’s activities in particular have been a constant concern for authorities across much of Europe in recent years.

Allies still have Patriot missile stocks that could be supplied to Ukraine – German expert
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
12:23:00 UTC

Allies still have Patriot missile stocks that could be supplied to Ukraine – German expert
Klaus Wittmann, a retired Bundeswehr brigadier general and lecturer in contemporary history at the University of Potsdam, said this in an interview with Ukrinform.
"Several European countries, including Spain and Greece, still have stocks of Patriot missiles," Wittmann said.
According to him, Germany has previously tried to persuade allies to transfer their existing stocks to Ukraine.
"Last year or the year before, Germany tried – and this must be acknowledged – through [Defense Minister Boris] Pistorius and the foreign minister, in particular, to persuade countries that still have these stocks that Ukraine is now the front line," Wittmann said.
He cited Denmark as an example, saying the country had transferred a significant portion of its military resources to Ukraine.
"Denmark, for example, transferred a large part of its military assets to Ukraine because the prime minister said: if the front in Ukraine does not hold, we will be next," Wittmann said.
In his opinion, countries that still have stocks of Patriot missiles should be guided by the same logic.
"Ukraine is the front line, and it is buying us time. I always put it somewhat dramatically: Ukraine is fighting a war that we – for now! – do not have to fight ourselves," he said.
The general added that "a short-term option would be for these countries to transfer Patriot missiles."
At the same time, Wittmann pointed out that new air and missile defense systems cannot deliver immediate results.
"There are also new Ukrainian developments and the FREYJA program to counter ballistic missiles, which Ukraine is advancing jointly with European partners. But all of this takes time and is not a solution for today or tomorrow," he added.
According to him, U.S. stocks of interceptors have also likely been significantly depleted.
"U.S. Patriot stocks are also apparently seriously depleted. A lot of missiles were expended during the war with Iran, and producing new ones takes time," Wittmann said.
Against this backdrop, he once again stressed the need not only to intercept Russian missiles but also to prevent the launches themselves.
"That is why I return to the point that everything possible must be done to prevent the launches themselves, rather than simply reacting once the missiles are already in the air," the general said.
He also called for greater international pressure on Russia.
"In addition, the aggressor must be exposed and condemned much more actively, and public pressure on Russia over this criminal way of waging war must be significantly increased," Wittmann said.
He also commented separately on the role of the U.S. president.
"If Trump believes and keeps saying that he has influence over Putin, then let him finally demonstrate it and say: Stop! He has already said that, but then immediately took his words back," the general said.

Live facial recognition cameras to be used on UK’s busiest shopping street
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
12:22:31 UTC
21:22:31 KST

The Metropolitan police are understood to be planning to use live facial recognition (LFR) technology on Britain’s busiest shopping street.
In June, the Met said it would introduce the technology in London’s West End by Christmas and into a further six areas next year. Sadiq Khan, the London mayor, has indicated that the newly pedestrianised Oxford Street will be included.
This would make it among the first areas in the country to have permanent LFR infrastructure scanning the faces of people passing and comparing them with a watchlist of wanted suspects.
The cameras will be fixed and could be attached to street furniture such as lamp-posts, rather than a temporary police van as has been the case in trials.
Human rights groups have widely criticised LFR. One organisation described the proposed introduction on Oxford Street as an escalation in routine public surveillance. There is evidence that the algorithm used to power it can discriminate against black people.
Scotland Yard plans to use static LFR cameras in London’s West End and Soho, which have some of the highest crime rates in the city. The technology has started to be deployed at tube stations this month.
During a city hall session in July, Khan said: “The Met is working really closely with the Oxford Street Development Corporation about how, when we pedestrianise that street, we use LFR in a sensible way, using the opportunity of new CCTV to use LFR.”
Ruth Ehrlich, of the human rights organisation Liberty, said using live facial recognition cameras on Oxford Street would mark “a significant expansion of surveillance in public spaces” and “an escalation”.
“This technology scans the faces of everyone who passes by, regardless of whether they are suspected of any wrongdoing,” she said.
“If live facial recognition is to be deployed in one of the country’s busiest shopping and tourist destinations, there must be full transparency about how it will be used, what safeguards are in place and how its impact on people’s rights will be monitored.”
She urged the Met not to introduce more LFR before the government produces its forthcoming legal framework for the use of facial recognition by law enforcement.
Recent polling commissioned by Liberty suggested 48% of people oppose scanning the faces of those walking on high streets when there is no suspected imminent threat.
Jasleen Chaggar, of the campaign group Big Brother Watch, urged the mayor to abandon the idea. “A face scan is as unique as a fingerprint,” she said. “The police cannot take your fingerprints when you are not suspected of wrongdoing. Taking a faceprint is no less intrusive just because it happens remotely.”
A spokesperson for the mayor said the introduction of LFR was part of the move to make Oxford Street “a world-class, pedestrian-friendly and safe destination”.
He said: “As part of delivering that, the mayor is working with the Met, West End Taskforce and Oxford Street Development Corporation on making best use of technology. Backed by record funding from city hall, the Met are leading the way in using the latest technology, including ebikes, drones and live facial recognition, to arrest dangerous criminals and tackle and prevent violence in the capital.
“In Westminster, neighbourhood crime has fallen, with 14,000 fewer offences in the past year and the Met’s rollout of live facial recognition in the West End and Soho will help drive down crime rates even further.
“The mayor is committed to ensuring the Met is open and transparent around where, when, why and how live facial recognition technology is used. His Office for Policing and Crime will continue to scrutinise and oversee its use to ensure there’s trust and confidence in policing, as we continue to build a safer London for everyone.”

Shifting tides: How the Iran war is reviving Somali piracy
Mogadishu, Somalia - Pirates hijacked MT Asana, a Tanzanian-flagged oil tanker, on 17 July, boarding it about 65 nautical miles off the Yemeni port of Mukalla.
The tanker was moving slowly toward Somalia when a gunman was spotted near the bridge. EU naval officials soon concluded he was not acting alone.
The MT Asana is the fourth ship suspected pirates have hijacked off Somalia since April, in a crisis that has triggered renewed fears about maritime security around the Gulf of Aden and Red Sea region.
Piracy off the Horn of Africa cost more than $400 million in ransom payments between 2005 and 2012, according to a joint study by Interpol, the United Nations, and the World Bank, which recorded 179 ships hijacked over that period before an international coalition brought the crisis under control.
At the height of that earlier crisis, in 2010 alone, pirates hijacked 53 vessels and took 1,090 crew hostage, according to a report by the advocacy group Oceans Beyond Piracy. By June the following year, it counted more than 500 seafarers still being held at once.
The last time there was an uptick in incidents, from 2011 to 2016, it took a large multinational naval coalition to beat it back, made up of NATO’s Operation Ocean Shield, the EU’s Operation Atalanta, and a British-led task force called Combined Task Force 151.
The incidents also reshaped the region, prompting Japan, Italy and eventually China to establish military bases in Djibouti, whose coastline faces Yemen across the mouth of the Red Sea. The US had already maintained a base there, tied to its post-9/11 operations.
Djibouti’s President Ismail Omar Guelleh said at the time that many countries with bases in the country were focused on “protecting their commercial and investment interests”, in a 2024 interview with the Saudi-owned news outlet Asharq Al-Awsat.
Incidents fell from 237 in 2011 to almost none within five years.
In addition to the naval task force, Benoit Lefevre, a French naval intelligence officer, argued that better-guarded ships made it “too risky, too uncertain to stay reliably profitable” for pirates.
The shipping industry was confident enough in that fix after a sustained lull that it formally lifted its “high risk” designation for the Indian Ocean only in 2023.
Since April this year, however, the French navy’s Mica Centre, which monitors the region, has recorded 18 piracy incidents and had three vessels still held for ransom, even before the MT Asana was added to the count.
A new opening at sea
The trigger was the war launched by the United States and Israel against Iran in February. Tehran began restricting passage through the Strait of Hormuz following US-Israeli strikes, later implementing a full blockade of the waterway, which carries 20% of the world’s oil and gas.
Whilst the fighting pulled naval and diplomatic attention to managing and resolving the conflict, merchant ships have been pushed closer to Somali waters, creating a target-rich environment.
Some incidents, however, have occurred far from Somalia, including the MT Asana hijacking near Yemen’s coast, with pirates increasingly relying on GPS and other technologies to track ships and monitor their movements.
“One thing that pirates, the Houthis, the IRGC and others have demonstrated is that chokepoints are highly vulnerable to small-scale attacks capable of crippling global supply chains,” Jatin Dua, a maritime security scholar and author of Captured at Sea: Piracy and Protection in the Indian Ocean, told The New Arab.
“What we’re seeing is low-tech and also ways for non-state actors as well as state actors to make chokepoints bend to their will,” Dua added.
This diversion of focus is felt most acutely in Puntland, the semi-autonomous northern Somali region where most hijackers come from and where they bring their captured ships.
Jethro Norman, a Somalia specialist at the Danish Institute for International Studies, told The New Arab that the revival of hijackings off the Somali coast was being misread as an international maritime security problem, when it should instead be understood as part of the broader challenges facing Puntland.
Norman said three factors, beyond the international naval coalition, had helped suppress the hijackings at their source, though they had done little to address the underlying incentives driving the attacks: the region's coastal police force, the PMPF; local clan elders; and courts in the regional capital, Garowe.
“All these things depend on Puntland’s state capacity,” he said, “and this is what has all fallen apart.”
Since last year, Puntland has deployed a large share of its forces, including members of the PMPF, to a separate offensive against the Somali branch of Islamic State (IS) operating from the region’s mountains.
A rift with Somalia’s federal government has further strained Puntland’s resources, culminating this week in the forcible takeover of three bases in the region housing federal troops.
The economics of piracy
This has dovetailed with broader economic challenges within Somalia related to the Iran war.
Somalia imports around nine-tenths of what it consumes, and the disruption to Hormuz sent fuel and food prices sharply higher within days of the war’s start in February. Inflation has since persisted across the economy, with the Consumer Price Index rising 8.1% in June, according to the national statistics bureau.
Norman told The New Arab that the pirates were deliberately going after fuel tankers rather than selecting ships at random, because the same price rises squeezing Somali households have made fuel cargo unusually valuable. “It is not just opportunism,” he said.
A Puntland security official told the news agency AFP in April that those who seized the cargo ship Sward were mostly poor young men from the coastal town of Garacad, armed and angry over illegal fishing as much as drawn by ransom.
Puntland’s fisheries minister, Mohamed Abdulkadir Salah, said in June that illegal fishing was costing Somalia approximately $300 million a year, with roughly half of those losses occurring in Puntland.
A second official said the group all belonged to the same clan and sub-clan, which is different from that of Puntland’s president, making any crackdown a potentially destabilising move in a region where delicate clan balances need to be maintained.
“That’s why negotiations are best to defuse this kind of situation,” he told AFP. “But it also plays into the hands of the pirates.”
The surge has turned outside attention back toward the Somali coast, from Washington to Brussels to Cairo. Egypt's foreign ministry said in June it was working through its embassies in Mogadishu and Riyadh to secure the release of Egyptian sailors held aboard the tanker Eureka, seized off Somalia in May.
In mid-July, the EU's foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, signed a new Status of Forces Agreement with Djibouti, renewing access for both Atalanta and a second EU mission, Aspides, which patrol the Red Sea and the Horn of Africa.
While Saudi Arabia’s initiative to establish a Red Sea naval task force was likely prompted by Houthi attacks on its ships, a broader group of countries, including Somalia, has since joined the effort.
Abdel Aziz Aluwaisheg, the Gulf Cooperation Council’s assistant secretary-general for political affairs, called for “more support” for the Somali government to help it “contribute effectively to fighting piracy”.
On 2 August, Puntland President Said Abdullahi Deni signed an agreement in the port city of Bosaso with a US delegation led by Major General Claude Tudor of US Africa Command, expanding the US military presence there and pledging closer cooperation on maritime security in the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden.
These measures, however, only address one element of the broader challenge, says Norman.
“Unless the international community directly resources the Puntland institutions that police this coastline,” he said, “neither the immediate threat nor the political economy sustaining it gets resolved.”

Multinational statement on missile launches signals preparations for major war — expert
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
12:21:15 UTC
21:21:15 KST

MOSCOW, August 12. /TASS/. A statement by the United States and 40 other countries calling for 24-hour advance notice before missile launches makes it clear that they are preparing for a potential major war, Alexander Stepanov, military expert with the Institute of Law and National Security at the Russian Presidential Academy of National Economy and Public Administration, said.
Earlier, the United States and 40 other countries issued a joint statement, published on the website of the US mission to the UN Office in Geneva, calling on all relevant countries to provide at least 24 hours’ advance notice of launches of intercontinental ballistic missiles (ICBMs), submarine-launched ballistic missiles (SLBMs) and space launch vehicles (SLVs). "Notifications should include such information as the generic class of the ballistic missile or SLV, the planned launch notification window, the launch area, and the planned direction," the document reads. In addition, "countries should also provide clear notices for airmen and mariners consistent with international standards to reduce risk, including in expected impact or landing areas."
The expert pointed out that, of the 41 countries, only the US, France and Britain possessed ICBM technology. The other countries’ position is not effectively backed by military capabilities that would allow them to set conditions or make demands.
"This is a message to the countries that possess such technologies, primarily Russia and our allies, China and North Korea. This is nothing but the next stage of preparations for a potential large-scale global conflict, creating conditions for our opponents to improve their situational awareness of key directions and the potential deployment of control and interception systems," Stepanov said.
He added that such public calls would lead nowhere unless they were backed by legally binding measures and reciprocal guarantees from "our key opponents.".

12 August 2026•Update: 12 August 2026
Uganda is emerging as a potential migration hub for EU countries, with expectations that it could host the first facility for irregular migrants transferred from Europe in 2027, Greek daily Kathimerini reported Wednesday.
Citing diplomatic sources, the daily said talks with Uganda are at an advanced stage as part of an initiative led by Germany, Austria, the Netherlands, Denmark and Greece.
“The proposal is based on the idea that many migrants would choose to return voluntarily to their countries of origin rather than remain in Uganda,” the daily underlined.
The center in the East African country would initially operate as a pilot program and accommodate up to 10,000 migrants whose asylum applications had already been rejected in the EU countries where they first arrived, according to the daily.
Technical teams are expected to travel to Africa before the end of the month for final discussions, the daily said, adding that Rwanda remains the main alternative option, while Kenya, which had also been considered, appears to have been excluded.
The five countries’ migration ministers are scheduled to meet in Copenhagen on Sept. 4 to review progress in the negotiations.

The 'Musk effect' reaches Lerma: SpaceX books historic Burgos parador to watch eclipse
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
12:20:42 UTC
21:20:42 KST

The aerospace company reserved a 17th-century palace hotel in northern Spain more than a year in advance, fuelling rumours that Musk would attend the eclipse in person.
"Will Elon Musk come?" The question has been echoing through the streets of Lerma, a picturesque town south of Burgos in northern Spain, for days.
The arrival of SpaceX has transformed this community of more than 2,500 residents, where locals, hospitality workers and tourists are looking towards the Parador, one of Spain's state-run heritage hotels, trying to work out what is happening behind its doors.
The company founded by Musk booked it a year and a half ago to watch the total solar eclipse from there this Wednesday.
Musk has ultimately not shown up, but the SpaceX effect is already being felt across the town: fully booked hotels, dozens of coaches and visitors arriving from different countries, shattering Lerma's usual calm, sparking a level of excitement rarely seen here.
The cause of all this commotion is a total solar eclipse that will plunge parts of Spain into darkness for nearly two minutes on Wednesday, an exceptional event that has not been witnessed on the Iberian Peninsula for more than a century.
SpaceX had been planning for the occasion for months. The aerospace company, founded by Musk in 2002, booked Lerma's Parador 18 months in advance to secure a prime vantage point from which to observe the event, right along the path of totality, with clear skies and little light pollution.
The hotel, a 17th-century ducal palace where Napoleon once spent the night, has closed its doors to the public in recent days to host a "private event".
Inside, 140 specialists are staying there, including two professors from Berkeley.
Is Musk in Lerma?
The possibility of Musk turning up in person spread like wildfire across traditional and social media in recent days. The hype grew, fuelled by reports suggesting the billionaire himself might travel to Lerma to witness the eclipse.
Spanish broadcaster COPE has confirmed that Musk is not in the town. Guests at the Parador are technicians and eclipse enthusiasts and, according to the Spanish broadcaster, there are no celebrities among them.
His absence, however, has not stopped the billionaire's name being on the lips of locals and visitors.
The mere presence of SpaceX has been enough to put this small town in Burgos province at the centre of attention for a few days.
