From Promises of Recovery to Death: Three Odrex Patients’ Stories
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
12:41:57 EEST
18:41:57 KST

From Promises of Recovery to Death: Three Odrex Patients’ Stories
Kyiv • UNN
Oncologist Maryna Bielotserkovska appears in all three stories of patients who died after treatment at Odrex. The patients’ families recount details of the course of their\r\nillnesses in the documentary “The Wasp’s Nest.” Meanwhile, the criminal case concerning the death of businessman Adnan Kivan, in which Bielotserkovska is an accused party, has already proceeded to the examination of evidence.
Oncologist Maryna Bielotserkovska figures in three tragic stories involving patients of the private Odrex clinic: businessman Adnan Kivan, Ihor Melai, and Khrystyna Totkailo’s father. UNN examines the treatment methods the oncologist may have preferred and what the three stories have in common.
As the families of the deceased said in the documentary film "The Wasp’s Nest," a similar scenario can be traced in all three stories. At the clinic, they were given hope of recovery and continued treatment even when the patients’ condition had significantly deteriorated. Despite complications and the patients’ general exhaustion, the oncologist, the families claim, continued aggressive chemotherapy.
The Death of Businessman Adnan Kivan
Maryna Bielotserkovska was his oncologist at the Odrex clinic. She is now, together with surgeon Vitalii Rusakov, an accused party in a criminal case under Part 1 of Article 140 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine — improper performance of professional duties by a medical professional.
According to the investigation, after the operation, the doctors may have failed to prescribe Kivan the necessary antibacterial therapy and may have responded improperly to postoperative complications. According to the conclusions of a forensic medical examination, this could have led to the development of sepsis and the patient’s death. The accused do not admit their guilt.
To hold a medical professional criminally liable, the court must establish whether professional standards were violated and whether there was a direct causal link between specific actions or inaction by the doctor and the patient’s death.
That is why the key stage of this case is the examination of medical records, expert assessments, and other evidence. The circumstances of Kivan’s treatment and the actions of his doctors must now be assessed directly in the court proceedings.
The Death of Sailor Ihor Melai
His widow, Olha Melai, said that her husband was one of Bielotserkovska’s last patients before her dismissal from Odrex in May 2025. According to the woman, she initially viewed the oncologist’s willingness to continue treatment as a chance to save her husband. However, after his death, while examining the medical records and procedures performed, she began to question the appropriateness of the aggressive treatment. She believes that, at one stage, her husband’s condition was extremely serious: for about a month, he barely moved and was unable to eat on his own. Nevertheless, Ihor Melai continued to receive chemotherapy. Olha Melai is convinced that the family may have been kept from learning the patient’s true health condition.
She also draws attention to the circumstances of the surgical intervention after which Ihor Melai ended up in intensive care. The man was offered the insertion of a special port for administering medication. According to Olha, the procedure was presented to the family as minimally invasive and not posing significant risks. However, after the operation, the man was transferred to the intensive care unit.
"I ask, ‘Where is my husband?’ ‘In intensive care.’ The duty anesthesiologist tells me that his condition is critical. He won’t make it until morning,’” Olha Melai says in the documentary.
According to her, during the first day after the intervention, about five liters of fluid were drained from her husband’s chest, and for the following three days he was on a ventilator. Chemotherapy treatment was continued.
After her husband’s death, Olha Melai appealed to the Ministry of Health of Ukraine because of discrepancies in the medical records. According to her, the discharge summaries contain virtually no information about the port-insertion surgery itself or its consequences.
She also claims that before the intervention she signed informed consent for surgery under local anesthesia, whereas the copy of the document later provided by the clinic to the court indicated intravenous anesthesia. According to the widow, the description of the nature of the operation itself also differs: the intervention that had been planned in advance was allegedly subsequently recorded in the clinic’s documents as an emergency procedure.
In her complaint, she asks for a clinical and expert assessment of her husband's treatment, verification of the clinic's compliance with licensing requirements, and an examination of the medical documentation and records in the electronic healthcare system eHealth.
A criminal proceeding has also been opened following a complaint by Olha Melai. It concerns, among other things, the circumstances of the operation and medical procedures performed on her husband. In total, the family spent about $50,000 on his treatment.
The death of Khrystyna Totkailo's father
In August 2024, Khrystyna Totkailo's father was diagnosed with cancer. Initially, the family sought help at Kyiv's Feofaniia Hospital. As Khrystyna recounts, after a medical consultation, doctors decided that aggressive chemotherapy could be too dangerous given her father's condition. Surgeon Ihor Bielotserkovskyi attended the consultation. He suggested that the family contact the Odesa clinic Odrex, where his wife, oncologist Maryna Bielotserkovska, worked.
At Odrex, the patient was prescribed a five-day course of chemotherapy. Khrystyna recalls that the family was promised that her father's larynx and voice would be preserved. A feeding gastrostomy was also placed.
According to Khrystyna, she repeatedly asked the medical staff to examine the gastrostomy and change the dressings, but in her view, proper care was not provided. Before discharge, it was discovered that an opening had formed around the gastrostomy site, through which stomach contents were leaking.
After the family returned to Kyiv, the man's condition deteriorated sharply. Khrystyna says that her father's kidneys began to fail and lesions appeared in his oral cavity. When she informed his treating oncologist, Maryna Bielotserkovska, about his deteriorating condition, she was told only that the doctor had a day off.
In addition, Khrystyna points to discrepancies between the records in the medical documentation and the procedures that were actually performed on her father. The total cost of treatment at Odrex exceeded UAH 250,000.
Conclusions
One cannot automatically equate the death of a seriously ill cancer patient with a medical error. Nor can one draw conclusions about a medical professional's responsibility solely from relatives' accounts. However, the same name—the oncologist Maryna Bielotserkovska—recurs in three different stories.
And the families keep asking the same questions: how justified were the decisions regarding aggressive treatment, did the patients and their relatives receive complete information about the risks, what was the response to the sharp deterioration in their condition, and was the medical documentation falsified? At least in one of these cases, the court is already seeking answers to such questions.

C919 jet serves first int'l route to Mongolia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
09:39:48 UTC
18:39:48 KST

China's home-grown C919 narrowbody passenger jet on Wednesday launched its first international commercial route, connecting Beijing with Ulaanbaatar, the capital of Mongolia, according to Air China.
The inaugural flight, CA723, departed from Beijing Capital International Airport at around 3pm, before arriving at Chinggis Khaan International Airport in Ulaanbaatar at around 5.15pm.
Meanwhile, the return flight, CA724, was scheduled to depart from Ulaanbaatar at 7pm and arrive in Beijing at around 9pm.
The route will be operated daily.
Speaking in an interview with RTHK in Beijing, a tourist surnamed Jiang noted that it was his first time to take a flight using the domestically developed C919.
"I feel very excited. Previously I didn't know [that we're taking the C919 passenger jet], but our tour guide just told us about it. 
"I've always wanted to experience the C919 jet, and fortunately, I got the chance to do so today," he said.
Separately, a passenger from Taiwan, surnamed Tang, said he looked forward to visiting Mongolia after travelling in Beijing over the past few days.
"I haven't taken a C919 flight before. I think it'll be very memorable," he told RTHK.
Another visitor, surnamed Peng, believed the new route marked an important step for the C919 as it embarks on routes abroad.
The C919 is the country's first large passenger jetliner, developed in accordance with international standards and with independent intellectual property rights.
It is 38.9 meters long, 3.96 meters wide, and 11.95 meters high, with a capacity to carry 158 passengers.
As of August 10, the C919 passenger jet was serving 57 routes linking 25 cities, including Harbin, Xi'an, Chengdu, Chongqing, Wuhan, Changsha, Guangzhou, Xiamen, Hangzhou, and Shanghai, handling more than 7.5 million passenger trips, according to official data.
The aircraft also completed its first scheduled commercial flight outside the mainland from Shanghai to Hong Kong on January 1, 2025.
It's currently operated by Air China, China Eastern Airlines, and China Southern Airlines, according to its developer, the Commercial Aircraft Corporation of China.

IN BRIEF: Putin’s statements on Western 'piracy, robbery', groundless Japan’s claims
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
09:38:58 UTC
18:38:58 KST

YUZHNO-SAKHALINSK, August 12. /TASS/. Tokyo has territorial claims against Moscow over the Kuril Islands, even though they came into Russia’s possession after World War II, which is enshrined in international documents, President Vladimir Putin said while addressing the Russian Pacific Fleet during military exercises.
He also noted that Western countries’ plans to seize Russian merchant ships constitute "piracy and robbery."
TASS has compiled the Russian leader’s key statements.
Pacific Fleet exercises and operations
Events such as the Pacific Fleet exercises are necessary, among other things, to protect Russia’s interests in the Asia-Pacific region: "Activities such as the exercises we are discussing now are necessary to maintain the fleet’s combat readiness and protect our country’s interests and security in the region. They are also intended to improve Russia’s overall military capabilities in this region."
The Pacific Fleet’s marines carry out missions in the Pacific Operational Area "boldly, professionally, and heroically."
There are no combat missions that are beyond the capabilities of the Pacific Fleet’s marines: "There are no combat missions that the Pacific Fleet’s marines cannot carry out. They are up to any task."
The Pacific Fleet is fully meeting the tasks assigned to it within its area of responsibility: "The fleet is fully meeting the tasks assigned to it within its area of responsibility, and these tasks are becoming increasingly significant, particularly in light of the evolving situation in the region."
Russia will continue to develop its Pacific Fleet and enhance its capabilities: "Appropriate instructions will be given to both the Defense Ministry and the Russian government. We need to identify the responsible parties and sources of funding."
At the same time, Moscow is ready to cooperate with all its neighbors, including Japan and other countries in the region: "I know the Pacific Fleet conducts joint exercises, and it will continue to do so in the future."
Threats in Asia-Pacific and Arctic regions
NATO is infiltrating the Asia-Pacific region: "Unfortunately, we see that the potential for conflict is growing here (in the Asia-Pacific region - TASS). NATO is infiltrating this region. New military-political blocs are being formed. New weapons systems are being deployed here and are planned for deployment, which pose threats to our country as well."
Plans to deploy new weapons in the Asia-Pacific region pose a threat to Russia: "New weapons systems are being deployed here and are planned for deployment, posing threats to our country as well."
Tensions are escalating not only in the Asia-Pacific region but also in the neighboring Arctic region: "Incidentally, tensions are also escalating in the neighboring Arctic region <…> in connection with the Northern Sea Route. Although Russia has always advocated for, and continues to affirm, its readiness to cooperate in the Arctic and to utilize the advantages of the Northern Sea Route. Naturally, this is within the framework of existing international maritime law."
Relations with Japan
Japan has unilaterally imposed sanctions on Russia without delving into the causes of the conflict in Ukraine: "I will only say that we would like to understand the position of Japan, our neighbor, which was mentioned during the reports. Russia has no claims against Japan and does not threaten its security. Under the pretext of events in Ukraine, Japan has imposed unprovoked sanctions on Russia."
Russia has no claims against Japan and does not threaten its security: "We do not threaten Japan. We have absolutely no claims against it."
Nevertheless, Japan's most recent military doctrine documents have classified Russia as a major threat for the first time.
Tokyo has territorial claims against Moscow over the Kuril Islands, which came into Russia’s possession after World War II and are enshrined in international documents: "Japan has territorial claims against our country. I am referring to the issue of the Kuril Islands. However, this is a reality that emerged following the end of World War II and is enshrined in international documents."
Russia had constructive relations with former Prime Minister Shinzo Abe and other Japanese leaders, but now Tokyo has changed its position: "Unfortunately, we are now seeing a shift in their position, one that I emphasize was in no way provoked by us."
Western plans to seize Russian merchant ships
Some Western countries are attempting to restrict the movement of Russian merchant ships, which violates maritime law: "I would like to draw attention to the EU's recent decisions. We see that the authorities of some countries are attempting to restrict the movement of our economic operators’ ships in violation of international maritime law. I want to emphasize that these ships are peaceful. Recently, they’ve even considered seizing our ships and selling property stolen from us."
The West’s plans to seize Russian merchant ships are nothing but "piracy and robbery": "Of course, this is nothing less than piracy and robbery."
Russia will retaliate if Western countries seize its merchant ships: "If this begins to happen in practice, we will be forced to respond in kind."
This will not necessarily take place in the waters where raids on Russian ships are planned: "We will act wherever we deem it necessary and appropriate, including the Pacific Fleet’s area of responsibility."

A boat sank on Lake Kariba in Zimbabwe, killing at least 15 people

A boat sank on Lake Kariba in Zimbabwe, killing at least 15 people
Kyiv • UNN
A boat carrying dozens of people capsized on Lake Kariba in Zimbabwe, killing at least 15 people. Rescuers saved 77 passengers, and the operation is ongoing.
At least 15 people have died after a boat carrying dozens of people sank on Lake Kariba in Zimbabwe. A rescue operation is ongoing. The BBC reports this, citing officials, writes UNN.
Details
Police said that 90 passengers and five crew members were on board the vessel on Tuesday when it capsized, although the boat may have been overloaded. Other reports indicate that more people were on board, based on the number of tickets sold.
According to police, the vessel was hit by a powerful wave and then capsized. Footage published online appears to show the hull of the boat floating in the water.
Lake Kariba, located on the border between Zimbabwe and Zambia, is one of the world's largest artificial reservoirs. It is used for transportation and fishing, and also provides both countries with vital hydroelectric power.
Zimbabwe's Civil Protection Unit (CPU) said that, according to ticket-sale data, 114 adults were on board the vessel. It also said that an unknown number of children below the age at which a ticket is required may have been on board.
The CPU said that 77 passengers had so far been rescued, while the bodies of 15 people who died had been recovered from the water.
Mutsa Murombedzi, a local member of parliament, posted a video on X that she said showed the boat at the beginning of its journey. She added that local residents used it to travel across the lake to the town of Kariba — a trip that took about five hours.
"We have very difficult questions that require honest answers. The authorities must disclose the exact number of people who were on board," she wrote.
Police said that more details would be released later.

2026-08-12

18:37:54 KST

Zelenskyy said the overnight operation hit air defence positions, piers and port infrastructure at a key Black Sea facility of the Russian Navy, as Russian missiles and drones killed two people in Kherson and disrupted port operations in Odesa.
Two people were killed and eight wounded in Russian missile and drone strikes on Kherson overnight on Wednesday, as Ukraine launched what President Volodymyr Zelenskyy described as a major attack on Russia's last significant Black Sea naval base.
One of the victims in the southern Ukrainian city died after their home was struck in the attack, the city's administrator said.
Kherson sits on the western bank of the Dnipro river, directly across from Russian-occupied territory.
The city has been under near-daily fire since Russian forces withdrew from it in November 2022 and entrenched on the river's eastern bank, leaving civilians with no buffer from artillery and drone attacks.
Ukraine's air force said Russia attacked overnight with ballistic missiles and 138 Shahed-type drones, targeting primarily the Odesa region in the south and Sumy in the northeast. Of the 138 drones, 112 were shot down or intercepted, according to officials.
In Odesa, Ukraine's largest port city and primary grain export hub on the Black Sea, which has been repeatedly struck since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, the attack disrupted port operations.
Odesa's port infrastructure has been a recurrent Russian target as Moscow attempts to pressure Ukraine's agricultural export revenues, which fund part of its war effort.
Ukraine strikes Russia's Black Sea 'stronghold'
In the early hours of Wednesday, Ukraine struck the naval base at Novorossiysk on Russia's Black Sea coast.
Zelenskyy said Kyiv had "carried out a unique operation targeting the naval base in Novorossiysk — the last major stronghold of the Russian fleet in the Black Sea, more than 300 kilometres from the front line."
He said hits on air defence positions, piers and seaport infrastructure had been confirmed, and posted footage from Russian social media showing orange flashes of air defence fire and blue counter-drone laser beams against the night sky, followed by a thick grey cloud over the city at dawn.
Novorossiysk is Russia's largest commercial port on the Black Sea and has become the primary base for what remains of the Black Sea Fleet after Ukraine drove the bulk of the fleet from Crimea using naval drones.
The port handles a significant share of Russian oil exports, making it a strategic target beyond its military significance.
Russian authorities said an eight-year-old was killed in Novorossiysk, along with seven other people wounded, including one minor.
A second person was killed when drone debris hit the garden of a private house in the village of Volna, according to regional governor Veniamin Kondratyev.
Two people were wounded in the resort town of Gelendzhik on the Black Sea coast.
Kondratyev said "several hundred" Ukrainian drones had struck the Krasnodar region. Debris damaged 21 buildings in Novorossiysk, with images on social media showing apartment blocks with blown-out windows and burned cars.
Russia's defence ministry said it shot down 502 Ukrainian drones overnight across its territory and over the Black Sea. The ministry's self-reported figures have been unreliable in the past, and Euronews could not verify the claims.
Ukraine has significantly intensified its long-range strikes on Russian territory since mid-2025, following a period in which Western allies lifted restrictions on the use of supplied weapons to strike targets inside Russia.
Kyiv says the campaign is a direct response to Russia's daily strikes on Ukrainian cities and civilian infrastructure.

The same people who systematically destroy monuments and erase the memory of anti-fascism are now shocked by the fascist symbols of the attackers in Plovdiv.”
“There is no place for fascist atrocities in Bulgaria, and we will take the necessary measures”, the prime minister added.

Just 20 of 6,600 Defra staff working on climate adaptation amid drought and wildfires
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
09:36:34 UTC
18:36:34 KST

Just 20 staff are working on climate adaptation within a key government department tasked with protecting the environment and maintaining food security, a freedom of information request has revealed.
The officials make up 0.3% of staff within the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs.
The government has been warned by the climate change adaptation committee that it is lagging far behind in terms of adapting to a new climate as a result of global heating.
The climate crisis is increasing both summer heatwaves and winter rainfall in the UK, with both drought and flooding more likely.
Peak river flows could increase by up to 45%, while water supply shortfalls may surpass 5bn litres daily, the committee has warned. It said the economic cost of failing to adapt could be between 1% and 5% of UK GDP annually by 2050 – £60bn to £260bn a year.
But only 20 staff out of 6,613 in Defra are working on climate adaptation, according to the data.
“England is desperately unprepared for the impacts of the climate crisis, and these shocking figures show how few officials are working on the problem at the top of government,” said environmental writer and campaigner Guy Shrubsole, who obtained the data.
Shrubsole called on the new environment secretary, Angela Eagle, to seize the moment amid heatwaves and wildfires to greatly boost staffing and funds for climate adaptation.
“Andy Burnham has seen the effects of climate change in Makerfield, which flooded in past winters, and as Manchester mayor when wildfire smoke from Peak District grouse moors choked local residents,” he said. “It’s time he levelled with the country about the climate emergency and set out a radical plan to get us off fossil fuels and prepare communities for extreme weather.”
The data is revealed as Burnham is being challenged by the Wildife Trusts and other leading environmental NGOs in his first 100 days in office to reset the government’s approach to the environmental emergencies facing the UK. They want him to recognise that ecological restoration – such as rewetting bogs and managing natural flood defences – is essential to national security and public health.
Since taking office Burnham has not mentioned the climate crisis, the extreme heat the UK is experiencing this summer, the wildfires that have taken hold from the south-west to the north of England, nor the drought covering almost three-quarters of the country. The UK is about to enter its fifth heatwave of the summer, as climate breakdown makes extreme heat, drought and wildfires more likely.
Friends of the Earth’s head of policy, Mike Childs, said: “The UK is in the grip of a growing climate crisis. Across the UK communities are under attack from relentless heatwaves, droughts and wildfires, putting lives, homes, farmers and nature at risk.
“Andy Burnham must end his silence on the climate emergency and pledge to make it a top priority by strengthening plans to protect communities from increasingly frequent and extreme weather – especially those most at risk.
“But we must also tackle the cause, not just the consequences. The government must do more to cut the pollution driving climate change by accelerating the shift to clean energy and ruling out new oil and gas developments like Rosebank and Jackdaw, and a third runway at Heathrow.”
Firefighters across the country are tackling record levels of wildfires – with 966 this year, including 458 in July alone. Steve Wright, the Fire Brigades Union general secretary, is calling for 5,000 more firefighters to be recruited, saying it should be a national priority to have enough properly equipped firefighters to face the threats of climate extremes.
The UK is short of much of the key equipment to tackle wildfires that European fire fighters possess. The country does not have any dedicated fixed-wing water-bombing planes or specialist aerial firefighting aircraft.
On Wednesday, No 10 announced Burnham would chair an emergency Cobra meeting in response to the extreme heat.
The prime minister will meet ministers, officials and agencies as high temperatures continue across the UK, with temperatures of 33C forecast on Wednesday and up to 38C on Thursday.
A Defra spokesperson said: “Climate adaption underlines work throughout the whole department – from nature recovery to flooding response to sustainable farming on top of a direct and dedicated team. It is a key priority for this government.
“We are already strengthening our approach to climate adaptation through our work with the National Drought Group, building nine new reservoirs across the country and investing at least £10.5 billion by March 2036 to construct new flood and coastal erosion schemes, as extreme weather becomes more frequent.”

US Vice President JD Vance asked President Volodymyr Zelensky to avoid attacking a key Kazakh oil export route through Russia’s Black Sea port of Novorossiysk, according to Ukrainian officials and others familiar with the discussions cited by the Financial Times.
Vance made the request during a July 31 phone call with Zelensky as Washington sought to prevent attacks that could disrupt global oil markets and affect US companies involved in transporting Kazakh crude through Russia.

Ukraine agreed not to target infrastructure belonging to the Caspian Pipeline Consortium (CPC) or non-Russian vessels, unless they are under Ukrainian sanctions or carrying Russian oil or other Russian cargo, the FT reported.
Ukraine has not attacked tankers near the CPC terminal since the request was made.
A US administration official confirmed that Washington had warned Kyiv against attacking non-Russian vessels in the Black Sea and CPC infrastructure, describing the pipeline as a vital route for delivering Kazakh energy to European markets as an alternative to Russian supplies.
The CPC pipeline carries oil from Kazakhstan to a terminal near Novorossiysk. It handles about 80% of Kazakhstan’s oil exports and nearly 2% of global crude supplies, according to Reuters. US companies Chevron and ExxonMobil hold stakes in the consortium and in major Kazakh oil fields served by the route.
Ukraine Hits Russian Naval Base
The agreement does not cover Russian military targets at Novorossiysk.

Ukraine struck Russia’s naval base there on Aug. 12, using Neptune missiles, Palyanytsia jet-powered drones and unmanned maritime systems, Zelensky said Wednesday.

FCRA Bill sent to Joint Parliamentary Committee amid opposition ruckus
TOI News Desk / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Updated: Aug 12, 2026, 15:42 IST

FCRA amendment bill sent to JPC (Image: IANS)
NEW DELHI: The Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act (FCRA) Amendment Bill was formally referred to a Joint Parliamentary Committee (JPC) on Wednesday after the Centre moved a motion to this effect in Parliament.Union minister Nityanand Rai moved the motion in the Lok Sabha after the House resumed proceedings following its morning adjournment.
"That the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Amendment Bill, 2026, be referred to a Joint Committee of the Houses consisting of 21 Members of this House to be nominated by the Hon'ble Speaker, Lok Sabha, and 10 members of Rajya Sabha to be nominated by Hon'ble Chairman, Rajya Sabha," the motion moved by the junior home minister stated.According to the Supplementary List of Business for the Lok Sabha, the proposed Joint Committee will comprise 31 members, including 21 from the Lok Sabha and 10 from the Rajya Sabha.The committee will examine the Bill in detail and submit its report to Parliament by the last day of the first week of the Winter Session in 2026.The motion also specified that one-third of the committee’s total membership would constitute the quorum for its meetings.
While the government has moved to refer the Bill to a committee for review, the Congress has maintained its opposition to the legislation and called for its complete withdrawal. The Opposition has previously raised concerns that the proposed amendments could be used to target civil society and minority institutions.Congress MP KC Venugopal sought the withdrawal of the Bill, a demand that also received support from Samajwadi Party MP Akhilesh Yadav.In reply, parliamentary affairs minister Kiren Rijiju said the opposition should welcome the government's decision to refer the Bill to a JPC, adding that it contained no provision targeting minority institutions.The FCRA regulates the receipt and use of foreign contributions by individuals, associations and organisations in India, with the aim of ensuring that such funds are used for the purposes for which they are received.
The Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Amendment Bill, 2026, was introduced in the Lok Sabha on March 25 and is currently under consideration by Parliament.The monsoon session of Parliament began on July 20 and is scheduled to conclude on August 13. Proceedings have been repeatedly disrupted by opposition protests over several issues, including Delhi Police action against protesters on July 20. Several Bills have been passed in the Lok Sabha amid opposition protests and limited debate.

Swiss business backs proposed limit on federal staff costs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
09:32:57 UTC
18:32:57 KST

Swiss business backs proposed limit on federal staff costs
Three major Swiss business organisations are backing a popular initiative to impose limits on federal staffing costs.
The Swiss Business Federation economiesuisse, the Swiss Trade Association and the Swiss Employers’ Association are supporting the initiative, partly due to the shortage of skilled workers.
The Young Liberals political group and the three business associations promoted the initiative against a “bloated federal government”.
Economiesuisse director Monika Rühl described the initiative as necessary for a competitive business location, as “the economy needs relief now”.
Roland Müller, director of the Swiss Employers’ Association, warned that the growth of the civil service was exacerbating the shortage of skilled workers in the private sector. According to a study, the federal government pays a salary premium of around 12% for comparable roles, distorting competition for talent.
Urs Furrer, Director of the Swiss Trade Association, emphasised that the administrative brake was a necessary complement to the debt and regulatory brakes. Small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in particular are unable to compete with the federal government’s pay and employment conditions.
Incentives to reduce bureaucracy
The initiative calls for the federal administration’s personnel expenditure not to grow faster than the median wage in Switzerland in future. This mechanism is intended to prevent excessive growth, in the same way as the debt brake in the financial sector.
According to the initiators, this creates incentives for parliament and the administration to streamline processes and reduce bureaucracy.
Between 2010 and 2024, over 5,600 additional full-time posts were created in the federal administration, representing an increase of 17%, according to Jonas Lüthy, president of the Young Liberals of Switzerland.
Expenditure on staff and external services has risen even more sharply, “namely by 32% to CHF7.1 billion”. This is no longer healthy growth, but rather a structural imbalance.
The committee behind the popular initiative also includes members of parliament from the several parties. The initiative was launched in mid-April. A total of 100,000 valid signatures must be collected by October 14, 2027.

13 suspects in the case of torture at an Odesa district TCR - SBI
Kyiv • UNN
The SBI has identified four more employees of a district TCR in Odesa region involved in unlawful detention and violence. The total number of suspects has risen to 13.
There are already 13 suspects in the case involving torture at a district Territorial Recruitment and Social Support Center in Odesa region. The State Bureau of Investigation has announced new suspicions, the SBI reported on Wednesday, writes UNN.
Details
"SBI employees, with the assistance of the Military Law and Order Service of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, identified four more employees of a district Territorial Recruitment and Social Support Center in Odesa region who were involved in the unlawful detention and violence against citizens," the statement said.
The individuals were notified of suspicion of unlawful deprivation of liberty and abduction of a person, committed by a group of persons acting in prior conspiracy and involving the infliction of physical suffering on the victim (Part 2 of Article 146 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine).
"Thus, the total number of suspects in these proceedings has already risen to 13 people," the SBI noted.
The essence of the case
As reported by the SBI, in June 2026 the bureau exposed a group of nine people — six employees of the same district Territorial Recruitment and Social Support Center and three representatives of a local public organization.
According to the investigation, they organized the unlawful delivery and detention of men in the premises of the recruitment center. Representatives of the public organization helped search for people and collected information about them, the SBI said.
"SBI employees documented numerous instances of cruel treatment. The victims were unlawfully detained, beaten, intimidated and subjected to psychological pressure," the statement said.
As reported, the nine previously exposed members of the group are being held in custody without the right to bail. They are suspected of torture, unlawful deprivation of liberty and robbery committed by an organized group (Part 3 of Article 127, Part 2 of Article 146, Part 4 of Article 186 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine).

Finland sees dramatic drop in student applications from abroad
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
12:30:22 EEST
18:30:22 KST

The number of students applying from abroad to study at Finnish universities of applied sciences has dropped this year to just over 12,000 — a dramatic decrease on the figure of 60,000 two years ago.
Haaga-Helia University of Applied Sciences, for example, received only 1,200 applications from abroad this year — compared to 25,000 in 2023 — while the Kokkola-based Centria University of Applied Sciences has gone from 13,000 to 1,000 during the same time period.
According to Centria rector Tapio Huttula, Finland's dire job situation and, in particular, the low employment prospects faced by foreign students underpin the collapse in application levels.
"They need work to survive," Huttula said. "The whole family may have invested in this student, and therefore the idea is that here too they must be able to earn and support themselves."
Yle reported last year that unscrupulous third-party agents were spreading false and misleading information to prospective fee-paying students about life in Finland. The new arrivals often end up living a life of poverty and marginalisation as a result of the deception, increasingly relying on handouts to survive.
Tighter rules mean fewer applicants
Finland's government has also introduced a series of measures during its term in office that have tightened the rules and criteria for students from outside the EU and EEA areas to study in Finland.
These measures include the revocation of a foreign student’s residence permit if they receive basic social assistance, a higher minimum income requirement, and stricter rules regarding family reunification.
In addition, a 100-euro fee for applications sent from outside the EU and EEA areas came into force in 2025, which was intended to prevent the system from becoming clogged with baseless applications.
Finland's tightening of the rules has coincided with the launching of initiatives in many South Asian countries — such as Bangladesh, India and China — aimed at preventing so-called 'brain drain'.
The loss of fee-paying students from abroad will have a significant financial impact on many Finnish universities of applied sciences, according to Centria rector Tapio Huttula.
"On the other hand, it's good if those who do come are able to complete their degree," he also noted.
Yle News' All Points North video podcast discussed the mismatch between the expectations foreign students have of life in Finland and the reality they face when they arrive in the country.

BEIJING, Aug. 12 (Xinhua) -- China on Wednesday launched the first international route featuring its homegrown C919 aircraft, connecting Beijing with Ulaanbaatar, capital of Mongolia, according to Air China.
Air China flight CA723 took off from Beijing Capital International Airport for Ulaanbaatar at around 3 p.m., marking the latest milestone in the C919's commercial operation since its maiden commercial flight on May 28, 2023.
The C919 is China's first self-developed trunk jetliner in accordance with international airworthiness standards and registered with independent intellectual property rights.
Air China currently operates 12 of these aircraft. The C919 jet is also operated by China Eastern Airlines and China Southern Airlines.
As of Aug. 10, the C919 had served 57 routes linking 25 cities and handled more than 7.5 million passenger trips, said the Commercial Aircraft Corporation of China, Ltd., the jet developer. ■

Explainer: Why a sweet wrapper is sweeping the internet
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
17:30:02 CST
18:30:02 KST

BEIJING, Aug. 12 (Xinhua) -- In 1972, then Chinese Premier Zhou Enlai presented White Rabbit milk candies as a state gift to visiting U.S. President Richard Nixon. More than half a century later, the Shanghai sweet is making another journey abroad -- this time through its wrapper.
Earlier this month, an X user posted two photographs. One featured a White Rabbit candy in its familiar red, blue and white wrapper; the other showed the paper unfolded and laid flat.
"This absolute masterstroke of graphic design..." wrote the user.
Within days, the post had drawn about 6 million views and 265,000 likes. The replies were soon filled with images of White Rabbit tattoos, T-shirts, phone cases and wrappers preserved in notebooks.
The two moments tell different stories about how Chinese culture travels. Once presented as a diplomatic gift, White Rabbit is now being discovered, shared and remade by ordinary people.
A DESIGN REDISCOVERED
For many Chinese, the overseas excitement came as a surprise. What was being celebrated as a design discovery was simply the wrapper of a childhood sweet -- once flattened inside schoolbooks and kept for its faint milky scent, or simply discarded after the candy was eaten.
Now, this object so deeply embedded in Chinese daily life has entered another culture, where people are admiring it, collecting it and making it their own. What a heartening development!
White Rabbit took its present name and image in 1959, replacing an earlier Mickey Mouse design used by a Shanghai candy factory. Its wrapper received a national packaging award in 1983 and remains in use ever since.
Unfolded, it has the coherence of a miniature poster. At the center, a white rabbit sits against a red background. Rows of smaller blue-and-white rabbits run along either side, while Chinese characters share the space with English lettering.
Zhang Di, a professor at Renmin University of China who studies cross-cultural content diffusion, told The Straits Times that the design's visual language requires no specific cultural knowledge for interpretation and is aesthetically accessible across cultures. Viewers can be drawn in before they know its history.
That history, however, gives the image another layer. In China, White Rabbit recalls an era when sweets were scarce, candy bowls were set out during festivals and a milky chew stuck to the teeth. Younger overseas viewers, by contrast, often encounter it without those associations. To them, it looks fresh precisely because its classic design has endured -- a piece of commercial art untouched by the polished uniformity of much contemporary packaging.
Its handmade quality may also hold new appeal. At a time when AI can produce a polished picture in seconds, the hand-drawn rabbit and old-fashioned lettering bear the imprint of a particular designer and era. Wu Weihua, a professor at the Communication University of China, has argued that vintage designs with cultural depth can resonate in an age increasingly filled with AI-generated content.
Yet enduring design alone cannot explain why a wrapper overlooked for decades has suddenly captured so much attention.
WHY NOW?
The rediscovery comes amid growing overseas curiosity about China. Social media users in the West have recently embraced "Chinamaxxing," adopting habits such as drinking hot water and wearing house slippers. Chinese apps, games, food brands and toys have also become more visible abroad.
As Chinese products become more familiar overseas, consumers may begin to look beyond their practical uses. Curiosity about an object can prompt questions about its design, history and origins.
Algorithms accelerate that process. Zhang said recommendation systems have carried content from Chinese diaspora communities to wider audiences, turning a wrapper associated with one community's memories into an image seen on millions of screens.
The result is a broader picture of Chinese culture abroad. Alongside ancient monuments, martial arts and cuisine, ordinary objects are entering the conversation. Reproduced on clothes, phone cases and even skin, the White Rabbit wrapper has shed its original function and become a visual symbol in its own right.
A QUIET INFLUENCE
Formal cultural promotion usually begins by explaining why something matters. Online discovery often works in reverse. Someone first notices the rabbit, saves the photograph or buys the candy. Questions about its origin come later. The encounter feels like a discovery rather than a lesson.
White Rabbit has pursued collaborations and launched new products over the years, yet the element attracting attention today is the very part it chose not to replace. Shi Anbin, a professor at Tsinghua University who studies China's cultural influence, sees the design's longevity as evidence that original Chinese designs can cross generational and cultural boundaries.
Its appeal suggests that going global does not always require a brand to hide where it came from. The wrapper that caught the world's attention was not redesigned for an international audience. It was the same wrapper that generations of Chinese children had peeled from their candy.
This brings the story back to the two photographs. In the first, the wrapper still held the sweet. In the second, it had been unfolded for a closer look.
The sweet would soon disappear. The image has already begun another journey. ■

WELLINGTON, Aug. 12 (Xinhua) -- New Zealand Prime Minister Christopher Luxon has survived a second caucus confidence vote in four months, but the leadership challenge has highlighted growing political pressure on his National Party less than three months before the country's general election on Nov. 7.
Luxon said on Wednesday he had the "full support" of his caucus and would remain leader of the governing National Party following an hours-long meeting at parliament in the capital Wellington.
He called the meeting amid speculation over his leadership after a series of political missteps and clashes, including his "parent-child" comment about businesses, his use of a military plane for travel to Auckland, and his proposal to hold a referendum on the country's mixed-member proportional (MMP) electoral system if re-elected.
The leadership challenge came as National faces a highly competitive election contest. A Taxpayers' Union-Curia poll released on Aug. 7 put National's support rate at 31 percent, up 0.5 percentage points from its previous poll, with the National-led coalition projected to retain a narrow parliamentary majority.
A Radio New Zealand-Reid Research poll in July, however, put National's support rate at 28.7 percent, its lowest level since Luxon became party leader in 2021.
A 1News Verian poll released Wednesday, conducted ahead of the caucus confidence vote, put the opposition Labor Party's support rate at 30 percent, ahead of National at 29 percent, while Luxon's preferred prime minister rating fell one point to 17 percent.
Luxon led National to victory in the 2023 election. But the party now faces pressure over the economy, the cost of living and public services, while Labor is seeking a comeback.
For Labor leader Chris Hipkins, the election represents an opportunity to return to government after the party's defeat in 2023. But Labor must also contend with competition from the Greens and the Maori Party for the wider center-left votes.
New Zealand's annual inflation rose to 4.1 percent in the June quarter, above the Reserve Bank's 1-3 percent target range, while unemployment has remained elevated. The government is also under pressure to control spending and return the budget to surplus.
Cost of living, housing affordability, healthcare and infrastructure are expected to be major issues in the upcoming election. National is likely to campaign on economic recovery, spending restraint, law and order and infrastructure investment, while Labor has focused on household costs, healthcare, jobs and housing.
Maori issues are also expected to feature prominently. The government's approach to the Treaty of Waitangi and proposed changes to Treaty principles have generated strong opposition from Labor, the Greens and the Maori Party.
Other campaign flashpoints are likely to include immigration, climate and energy policy, crime and gang legislation, and the future of the MMP electoral system.
With polls pointing to a tight race and smaller parties potentially holding the balance of power, the upcoming election is shaping up as a major test of New Zealand's economic direction, public services and political future. ■

The first upgraded frigate, the Cheng De, completed all modification tests in early February and held its commissioning ceremony in Kaohsiung. Researchers in Australia create human heart valve tissues from stem cells
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
17:29:42 CST
18:29:42 KST

MELBOURNE, Aug. 12 (Xinhua) -- Researchers in Australia have created human heart valve tissues from stem cells, providing a new platform to advance treatments for childhood heart diseases.
The study, led by Australia's Murdoch Children's Research Institute (MCRI), produced lab-grown heart valve tissues that closely resemble those in the human body, according to an MCRI statement released on Wednesday.
Published in Cell Stem Cell, the findings offer new insights into how human heart valves develop, mature and become damaged.
Holly Voges, a team leader in the MCRI Heart Regeneration group, said the breakthrough could help accelerate regenerative approaches to repairing damaged heart valves in children and adults.
Heart valve disease affects about 28 million people worldwide and can be caused by developmental abnormalities, infection or age-related degeneration. Currently, there are no treatments that can reverse valve damage, with many patients relying on valve replacement surgery, which has significant limitations.
The researchers also showed that the platform could model inflammatory valve disease, an underlying precursor to rheumatic heart disease (RHD), which is largely preventable and disproportionately affects Indigenous populations in Australia.
"When exposed to inflammatory proteins linked to RHD discovered in previous studies, we found the engineered stem cell tissues became stiffer and showed biomarkers consistent with diseased human valves," Voges said.
MCRI Professor Enzo Porrello said the technology could eventually support the development of stem cell-derived replacement valves that grow and adapt with patients. ■

Avraham Hadi, 44, was indicted by prosecutors on Wednesday for allegedly targeting the offices of several news outlets and the Justice Ministry in a series of vandalism and threat incidents.
The indictment comes as Israel heads toward elections following a Knesset term marked by fierce disputes over changes to the media and legal system.
The State Attorney’s Office filed the indictment against the Ramat Gan resident with the Tel Aviv Magistrate’s Court.
According to the indictment, Hadi threw bricks at the entrance doors of the Channel 12 offices on two occasions and at a Justice Ministry building twice, as well as at the entrance to the Haaretz offices. He is also accused of spray-painting a threatening message outside the Channel 13 offices.
The alleged incidents began on November 19, 2025, when Hadi allegedly spray-painted “The traitors’ blood will yet be cleared for publication” on a wall opposite the Channel 13 offices. Prosecutors said the message was intended to frighten or intimidate the outlet’s employees.
Five brick attacks followed during July, all shortly after 3 a.m. or 4 a.m., according to the indictment. Hadi allegedly arrived at each building masked and wearing work gloves.
On July 5, he allegedly threw two bricks at the glass entrance to Channel 12, shattering the door. Three days later, he is accused of carrying out a similar attack at the Haaretz offices.
The Justice Ministry building was then targeted twice. On July 15, Hadi allegedly threw two bricks at its glass entrance, picked them up and threw one of them again, shattering the door before fleeing. On July 22, he allegedly returned and shattered the entrance again with two bricks.
Hadi allegedly demanded apologies for Sde Teiman affair
Prosecutors said Hadi’s choice of targets reflected his own views of the judicial system and of the specific media outlets, and that the attacks were therefore deliberate and planned.
During the second attack on the Channel 12 offices, on July 28, Hadi allegedly left behind a threatening message calling on the outlet to “apologize over the Sde Teiman affair.”
The envelope was addressed to “Keshet 12, the Amalekite mouthpiece,” according to the indictment. It was found by a Channel 12 producer who arrived at the offices at approximately 6:30 a.m.
“Until you apologize over the Sde Teiman affair, I am not stopping,” the note said. It warned that, if no apology were issued, “the next brick will be aimed at one of your heads,” adding that “someone will die.”
The letter also named a series of senior security, legal, political, and protest figures, including former Shin Bet chief Ronen Bar, former IDF chiefs of staff Herzi Halevi and Aharon Haliva, Central Command chief Maj.-Gen. Avi Bluth, protest leader Shikma Bressler, former Supreme Court president Aharon Barak, Democrats chairman Yair Golan, Supreme Court President Isaac Amit, and Attorney-General Gali Baharav-Miara. It concluded by warning that God would punish them.
Hadi then allegedly threw two bricks at the Channel 12 entrance, again shattering the glass door. Prosecutors said the letter and the accompanying attack were intended to force the network’s employees to apologize for the Sde Teiman coverage.
The Sde Teiman affair centered on footage broadcast by Channel 12 in 2024 that appeared to show reservists abusing a Palestinian security detainee at the military detention facility. Five reservists were later indicted, but the military prosecution withdrew the charges in March, citing evidentiary difficulties and concerns over their ability to receive a fair trial.
Hadi was arrested on July 30 following an investigation by the Tel Aviv District Central Unit. Police said clothing and other evidence found during a search of his home linked him to the alleged offenses.
The indictment charges Hadi with extortion by threats, making threats, malicious damage to property, defacing property, and obstruction of justice.
According to the prosecution’s request to keep him detained through the trial, investigators relied on security-camera footage from the targeted buildings and from Hadi’s apartment building.
Prosecutors said the footage showed a masked man wearing work gloves throwing bricks at the buildings. Other footage allegedly showed Hadi leaving for work before the attacks and returning afterward, with clothing matching that worn by the assailant visible beneath and over his reflective Tel Aviv Municipality work vest.
Investigators also found clothing in Hadi’s apartment that allegedly matched the assailant’s clothing. Shoes and trousers said to match those seen in the footage were found in a garbage bin at his apartment building.
The indictment alleges that Hadi discarded the shoes and trousers before his arrest in an attempt to conceal evidence, forming the basis of the obstruction charge.
Hadi is charged with one count of extortion by threats, four counts of making threats, five counts of malicious damage to property, one count of defacing property, and one count of obstruction of justice.
The State Attorney’s Office also asked the court to keep Hadi in custody until the end of the proceedings. Prosecutors argued that the alleged conduct showed a rapid escalation from graffiti to repeated property damage and, ultimately, an explicit threat of physical violence. They also argued that the alleged attempt to discard evidence created a risk that he would obstruct the proceedings if released.
The detention request cited a previous conviction for assault causing bodily harm and defacing property in a case involving graffiti on the Kirya military headquarters. Prosecutors said the alleged Channel 13 offense was committed while a suspended prison sentence from that case remained in force. A separate case over graffiti allegedly sprayed on a courthouse wall is still pending.
Court orders a psychiatric evaluation
At a Sunday remand hearing, the court ordered a psychiatric evaluation of Hadi’s mental condition and his fitness to stand trial.
During an earlier remand hearing, Hadi denied the allegations. The detention request states that he initially admitted during a November 2025 interrogation to spraying the message outside Channel 13. Following his July arrest, however, he denied involvement in the alleged offenses and withdrew that admission, saying it had been made under pressure.
His attorney, Eran Amrani, argued that the alleged acts should be viewed as political protest and noted that they were said to have been carried out at night, when people were unlikely to be present.

Perseid meteor shower peaks over Taiwan Wednesday
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
09:29:10 UTC
18:29:10 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Perseid meteor shower, one of the year's most popular astronomical events, will reach its peak overnight Wednesday under nearly moonless skies, offering skywatchers in Taiwan a good chance to see meteors streak across the sky.
The Taipei Astronomical Museum said the meteor shower will be most active after midnight. The museum will also host a live webcast of the Perseid meteor shower from 10-11 p.m. Wednesday, featuring guests discussing meteors and other astronomical topics, per a press release.
The Perseids are one of three major annual meteor showers. They are known for producing fast, bright meteors and occasional fireballs. Under ideal conditions, the shower can produce as many as 100 meteors per hour.
However, the actual number visible to an individual is usually lower because of light pollution, weather, and the observer's location. The museum estimates that people observing from a dark location under good conditions could see about 70 meteors per hour during this year's peak.
The Perseid radiant, the point in the sky from which the meteors appear to come, will rise at about 8:30 p.m. Wednesday.
The Perseids originate from the famous Comet Swift-Tuttle (109P), which orbits the sun every 133 years. The dust trail it leaves intersects with Earth's orbit, causing tiny fragments to enter the atmosphere at high speed, burn up, and create bright streaks of light.
Despite being called shooting stars, meteors are not stars. Most are tiny pieces of rock or dust, many no larger than a grain of sand, that burn up high above Earth's surface. The shower is named for the constellation Perseus, where its radiant is located.
This year's viewing conditions are especially favorable because the moon will be close to a new-moon phase. This means there will be little moonlight washing out the sky, making it easier to see fainter meteors.
The museum recommends finding a location away from city lights with a wide, unobstructed view of the sky. No telescope or binoculars are needed. In fact, the museum recommends simply watching with the naked eye because meteors can appear anywhere across a large area of the sky.
Skywatchers should also give their eyes time to adjust to the darkness and avoid looking at bright phone screens.
Another celestial attraction comes Saturday, when Venus reaches its only greatest eastern elongation of the year, providing the year's best opportunity to observe the planet, according to the museum.
Weather will ultimately determine how much can be seen of Venus and the Perseid meteor shower, as cloud cover, haze, and city lights can significantly reduce visibility. More information about August's astronomical events is available here.

IAA files indictment against two Fureidis residents caught carrying illegally excavated artifacts
Unknown

2026-08-12
09:29:09 UTC
18:29:09 KST

The Israel Antiquities Authority (IAA) on Wednesday filed an indictment with the Hadera Magistrate's Court against Amir Warkani, 27, and Yosef Warkani, 33, both residents of Fureidis, after they were allegedly caught illegally collecting antiquities at the Horvat Hadarim archaeological site.
Horvat Hadarim, also known as Horvat Haidra, is located west of Moshav Ein Ayala on the Carmel coast in northern Israel. It is considered to be one of the most important archaeological sites in the area between Ein Ayala and Tel Dor.
It was declared an antiquities site in 1964, and over the years, archaeologists have documented remains of an ancient settlement, buildings, graves, quarries, a square structure, and mosaics at the site. Salvage excavations carried out nearby also uncovered the remains of a structure dating to the Roman period.
The incident took place on March 9. According to the indictment, the two arrived at Horvat Hadarim in a private vehicle carrying four metal detectors, two shovels, a pickaxe, a knife, a hammer, three flashlights, chargers, headphones, gloves, and bags intended for carrying their search equipment.
The two men allegedly scanned the area with metal detectors and, whenever they received a signal indicating the presence of metal, dug into the ground in an attempt to locate archaeological finds.
According to the indictment, they succeeded in finding several artifacts.
Shortly before leaving the site, IAA inspector Nir Distelfeld arrived together with an Israel Nature and Parks Authority (INPA) inspector and a police officer.
Distelfeld and the other officials found a total of 13 ancient bronze coins, three ancient bronze items, two ancient lead items, and another 14 unidentified metal objects in the suspects' possession.
Police forced into shelter with two suspects arrested for antiquities theft amid sirens
A week before the Warkanis were arrested, The Jerusalem Post at the time had reported on Distelfeld's arrest of two other antiquities thieves at the Horvat Hermesh site, located near the Elyakim interchange.
The two were in the midst of an illegal excavation of the site when they were discovered by the IAA, an INPA inspector, and a local security guard. Several pieces of ancient pottery had been shattered, and layers of earth had been disturbed during the suspects’ excavation.
While transporting the suspects to the police station, a rocket siren sounded, forcing the police officers and IAA inspectors to stop and take shelter with the apprehended suspects, as well as other civilians, until the Home Front Command issued an all-clear alert.
Approximately 30 people were present in the small, public shelter.
Miriam Sela-Eitam contributed to this report.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) – Importing motorbikes from China is banned, even if the vehicles have been dismantled and are imported as parts, Economics Minister Kung Ming-hsin (龔明鑫) said Wednesday.
The Ministry of Economic Affairs said that after noticing social media posts, it sent investigators to a site in New Taipei on Friday and Tuesday to confiscate motorbikes built with parts imported from China. The bikes had been dismantled in China, sent over separately as parts, and then reassembled in Taiwan, the ministry said.
The import of Chinese motorbikes or their parts is not allowed by existing laws, Kung said Wednesday. He added that any move to open up imports would have to be preceded by trade talks between the two countries, per CNA.
The importer in the New Taipei case may be hit with an import ban from two months to one year, or with the cancellation of his registration as an importer and exporter, the ministry said. A vehicle taking to the road without the necessary permits could also face confiscation.
The ministry called on the public to be careful when buying a motorbike, and to check the origin of the vehicle and the required import documents.

Human Rights Watch urges US not to transfer outdated cluster munitions from Türkiye to Ukraine
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
12:28:15 EEST
18:28:15 KST

The human rights organization Human Rights Watch (HRW) is calling on the US to reject Türkiye’s request to allow the retransfer to Ukraine of tens of thousands of cluster munitions that have been in Türkiye’s stockpiles for decades, according to a report published on the organization’s website on Wednesday.
"Dumping obsolete cluster munitions into a conflict creates a humanitarian liability for civilians that is tragically foreseeable. The impact on civilians of these more than 30-year-old inaccurate and unreliable munitions is what motivated 112 countries to ban the weapon by joining the international Convention on Cluster Munitions," said Nicole Widdersheim, deputy Washington director at Human Rights Watch.
It is noted that these munitions were produced in part by Türkiye under US licenses initiated in 1987.
In addition to selling its entire inventory of 12 M270 multi-barrel rocket launchers, Türkiye’s proposed US$256 million deal includes the transfer of three types of cluster munitions: 70 M39 ATACMS ballistic missiles, each containing 950 M74 antipersonnel/anti-materiel submunitions, totaling 66,500 individual submunitions; 2,524 M26 rockets, each containing 644 M77 dual-purpose improved conventional munitions (DPICM) submunitions, totaling 1,625,456 individual submunitions; and 47,000 M509A1 203mm artillery projectiles, each containing 180 M42 DPICM submunitions, totaling 8,460,000 individual submunitions.
"These types of cluster munitions are notorious for their record of not hitting their targets and hurting civilians.They should never be used. Congress can still act to stop this short-sighted and dangerous transfer," Widdersheim said.
In a letter submitted to Congress on August 6, 2026, notifying it of this deal, an unnamed senior State Department official noted that the US government is prepared to authorize this transfer and that Türkiye "seeks to reduce its inventory of older defense articles to focus its financial resources on modernization and sustaining existing systems". "Ukraine seeks to acquire these systems to bolster its offensive and defense fire support capabilities as it resists the Russian invasion. Ukraine already possesses munitions of the same or essentially similar type," he noted.
HRW notes that cluster munitions are inherently indiscriminate and have a history of creating deadly hazards for civilians whenever they are used, making it difficult to reconcile their use with the prohibition on indiscriminate attacks on civilians, which can be a war crime.
Although the US has not joined the treaty, an export moratorium has been enacted in the annual Defense Department budget since 2009. However, former US President Joseph Biden bypassed the moratorium between July 2023 and October 2024, concluding at least seven transfers of cluster munitions to Ukraine without disclosing the quantities provided. As detailed in Cluster Munition Monitor Report 2025, the US Foreign Assistance Act facilitates this workaround by allowing the president to determine that this type of security assistance is "vital to the security interests of the United States". It is not publicly known whether the administration of current US President Donald Trump has made a similar determination in this case to sidestep the export moratorium.

Germany news: Cabinet approves intelligence service reforms

- Cabinet approved reforms to the foreign and domestic intelligence agencies amid rising hybrid threats
- Transport ministers are set to discuss possible measures as river cargo shipping is hampered by low water levels
