====================================================================================================

Fewer rules: Europe was built on coal and steel, not paperwork
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
08:48:42 UTC
17:48:42 KST

The EU keeps churning out new rules, writes Gitta Connemann, head of Germany's CDU's influential business association, MIT. Small and medium-sized businesses bear the brunt of EU bureaucracy, she argues, calling for a halt to new regulation and for rules that add no value to be scrapped.
Robert Schuman and the founding fathers of the European Community understood: those who cooperate economically do not wage war against one another.
From this conviction emerged our continent's most successful idea of peace and freedom. The single market was therefore never an end in itself; it was a promise of opportunity, competition and economic strength.
'Our mother is Dutch. Our father was German'
For me, this isn't a historical footnote. Our mother is Dutch. Our father was German. In our family, Europe was never theory, but everyday life: reconciliation after war, open borders, shared values, trust instead of mistrust.
My constituency on the Dutch border lives Europe day in, day out. Germany and the Netherlands generate a trade volume of well over 200 billion euros every year.
Commuters, tradespeople, businesses, trainees and students no longer encounter border controls.
This is what Europe looks like when it succeeds.
But is it succeeding everywhere? Is Europe still on the right track? And when did Europe begin to believe that more rules automatically mean more Europe?
The rest of the world builds factories while Europe fills in forms
The world is changing at breathtaking speed. The United States is investing hundreds of billions of dollars in future technologies through the Inflation Reduction Act and the CHIPS Act. China is promoting key industries with a determination that we can and must criticise – but cannot afford to ignore.
And Europe? Europe is still creating rules. Since the start of the last legislative term, well over 10,000 legal acts have been published. At the same time, the European Commission has itself admitted that businesses are suffering from too much bureaucracy. It has therefore promised to cut administrative burdens by 25 percent, and by 35 percent for small and medium-sized enterprises.
The promise was right. But what does reality look like? Yes, there are the omnibus acts. Chapeau! Things are being simplified.
But simplification and deregulation are not the same. In parallel, hundreds of legislative initiatives were launched in the last term – from the Green Deal and digital regulation through to new due diligence, sustainability and reporting obligations. That does not add up.
That cannot be our ambition. Europe does not need less Europe. Europe needs a Europe that once again focuses on its strengths.
Europe's strength is its 'Mittelstand'
The European Mittelstand is not a marginal issue; it is the powerhouse of our continent. The vast majority of companies in the European Union are self-employed, small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). Germany leads the way: more than 99 percent of all companies are Mittelstand businesses.
SMEs in Europe employ around two thirds of all workers in the private sector. They are Europe’s innovation engine – not the administration. The Mittelstand develops ideas. The bureaucracy develops forms.
Yet increasingly, companies are investing not in new machinery or new markets, but in documentation, compliance and reporting obligations. Large corporations can set up their own departments for this. The family firm in a rural area cannot. Nor can the skilled trades. Nor can start-ups.
Many Mittelstand entrepreneurs now tell me: "We are not looking for subsidy programmes. We are looking for freedom to act."
Because every additional rule costs time, money and nerves. Above all, it costs trust. The prevailing assumption now seems to be that every entrepreneur is under general suspicion from the outset.
Yet the real problem is no longer the individual rule; it is the sum total. It is not the famous last drop that makes the barrel overflow. At some point the barrel is simply full.
Europe needs to put the brakes on regulation
That is precisely why Europe now needs a moratorium on new burdens.
No new burdens for businesses until the existing ones have demonstrably been reduced. Not merely announced. Not calculated on paper. But measurable.
From now on, every new law should follow a simple rule: for every new burden, at least one existing one must be removed.
This is not an attack on good rules. On the contrary. Good regulation is measured and proportionate. It sets objectives, but it does not prescribe every single step.
Reporting, documentation and disclosure obligations therefore need to be subjected to systematic scrutiny. Anything that creates no added value has to go.
Today, the courage to cut is more important than the courage to write.
The next wave of regulation is already rolling in
In fact, what should be happening now is a clear-out. Instead, new burdens from Brussels are already being announced.
The planned Digital Fairness Act will bring additional information and transparency obligations. The Green Claims Directive would create new documentation requirements for sustainability claims. The announced Quality Jobs Act threatens a wide range of labour law requirements in a single legislative package.
On top of that comes the national implementation of the Pay Transparency Directive with new reporting obligations – particularly for small and medium-sized enterprises. Or the EUDR (Editor's note: EU Deforestation Regulation, the EU regulation on deforestation-free supply chains).
Each initiative pursues a comprehensible objective in itself. Taken together, however, they produce exactly what Europe’s businesses have long been suffering from: ever more obligations. Ever more evidence. Ever more documentation. Europe will not win any innovation race this way – at best, only the world championship in filling in forms.
Europe needs discontinuity
Europe must have the option of saying goodbye to legislative ideas.
There is an even more fundamental problem. What cannot be adopted in one legislative term often simply moves into the next – as if the world had not changed in five years.
That runs counter to any fresh political start. We therefore finally need a principle that is taken for granted in many parliaments: discontinuity.
Legislative projects that have not been adopted must, as a rule, lapse at the end of a legislative term. Anyone wishing to reintroduce them should have to justify them afresh. With up-to-date figures. With current impact assessments. With renewed democratic legitimacy.
Discontinuity would be far more than a procedural rule. It would be a change of political culture. A genuine new beginning forces politics to set priorities. That is exactly what Europe needs.
Dare to trust
Europe needs high standards. But high standards are not created by ever more micromanagement. They are created by trust.
Entrepreneurs are not adversaries. They are employers. Trainers. Innovators. Taxpayers. They deserve trust. Those who give them freedom to operate create growth.
And Europe must not further weaken itself. When member states then tighten European requirements even more – the so-called gold-plating – new competitive disadvantages arise. That is poison for the single market.
Back to the big idea
Robert Schuman wanted a Europe that brings people together, not one that keeps administrations busy. Europe is an idea of peace. An idea of freedom. An idea of prosperity.
This idea has opened borders. It has brought people together. It has turned neighbours into partners.
Together, both would send a signal: it would be a step back towards Europe’s true strength. Less nit-picking. More trust. More freedom. More Europe.
Gitta Connemann is a member of the Bundestag for the Christian Democratic Union of Germany (CDU). She also serves as Parliamentary State Secretary in the Federal Ministry for Digital Affairs and Administrative Modernisation. Connemann is also the Federal Government Commissioner for the Mittelstand.

UK and Australia boost radar technology and industry cooperation as Defence Minister visits Indo-Pacific partners
The UK and Australia are boosting cooperation on radar technology, as Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry Luke Pollard MP kicks off a visit to Indo-Pacific partners this week.
- New signing will see UK and Australian firms work together on cutting-edge radar systems, boosting growth across both countries’ defence industries.
- Work to build on UK-Australia defence partnership, already supporting tens of thousands of jobs in both countries through AUKUS.
- Comes as Minister Luke Pollard kicks off a visit to Australia and New Zealand to strengthen defence and industrial partnerships.
The statement of intent involving QinetiQ and CEA Technologies, signed today in Canberra, will see both UK and Australian governments and industry work together on advanced radar systems, known as Active Electronically Scanned Array (AESA) technology.
The work builds on the Australia-UK Ministerial Consultations (AUKMIN) agreement reached in June and will strengthen supply chains and open export opportunities for both nations’ defence industries. This advanced technology is supplied to the Australian Armed Forces and allows the UK Armed Forces to keep pace with the evolving operational environment.
At CEA Technologies, Minister Pollard and Australian Defence Industry Minister Pat Conroy welcomed the agreement and met with staff advancing radar technology.
Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry, Luke Pollard MP, said:
  This radar agreement shows what our partnership with Australia delivers in practice: industry stepping up, technology for our Armed Forces, and trust between our nations deepening.
Working in lockstep with Australia we can drive jobs and growth while reinforcing our collective security.
Steve Wadey, Group Chief Executive Officer, QinetiQ, said:
  QinetiQ’s unique expertise positions us as a strategic and trusted partner to the UK MOD and its allies. Current conflicts remind us of the importance of air defences which are increasingly under pressure and QinetiQ is proud to play a key role in bringing this vital technology to the UK.
The signing forms part of a week-long visit by Minister Pollard to Australia and New Zealand, reinforcing the UK’s commitment to two of its closest defence partners in the Indo-Pacific.
In Canberra, the Minister also met the Minister for Resources, Madeleine King, to strengthen UK-Australia cooperation on critical minerals, and the interim National Armaments Director, Nadine Williams, to advance shared defence capability and industrial collaboration.
In Western Australia, Minister Pollard will visit Henderson Shipyard, where investment linked to AUKUS - the trilateral security partnership between Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States - is already supporting skills development and industrial uplift. AUKUS is expected to create more than 10,000 jobs in Western Australia, with a further 10,000 in South Australia.
Recent supply-chain initiatives are also generating work for 39 Australian companies, while Australian personnel are embedded across UK defence and industry organisations, supporting the delivery of the AUKUS partnership.
AUKUS is also delivering for the UK, with more than 3,000 new jobs already created across key UK nuclear sites since July 2024. SSN-AUKUS submarine construction, expected to create more than 7,000 new jobs across the UK supply chain, helping to drive growth in every postcode in the UK.
The Minister will travel to New Zealand later this week, where he will visit Devonport Naval Base in Auckland and meet defence industry leaders to discuss opportunities for closer cooperation on maritime capability. A prospective UK-New Zealand maritime partnership, including Babcock’s Type 31 Frigate offer, could deliver up to 1,000 jobs and NZ£300 million of investment into the New Zealand economy, as well as opportunities for UK industry.
The visit will also include further engagements with Australian and New Zealand government ministers and stops at defence industry sites, including Rocket Lab and SYOS Aerospace.

Kyiv authorities, Teremky residents agree on 2-week moratorium on tree felling for heating pipeline – media
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
11:45:52 EEST
17:45:52 KST

Residents of the Teremky residential area in Holosiivsky district of Kyiv and representatives of the city authorities have agreed to spend two weeks verifying whether a backup heating network can be laid along an alternative route to preserve trees in the green zone, Suspilne reports.
"The city authorities do not yet confirm that the alternative route can be implemented. Currently, the previous heating network project remains valid," the report says.
The meeting was attended by about a hundred residents and activists, as well as Deputy Head of Kyiv City State Administration (KCSA) Petro Panteleyev, representatives of Holosiivsky District State Administration, engineers, and designers.
Residents demanded to be shown design and permit documents and to have it explained why it was decided to lay the heating network through the green zone. They support the construction of the network, but want to preserve the trees, and state that they have still not been provided with documents explaining the choice of route and the tree felling.
Panteleyev explained that the backup heating network is needed to prepare Kyiv for potential accidents in the heat supply system; the current route was chosen due to existing underground utilities, and laying pipes along Teremkivska Street is technically impossible due to sewer, water supply networks, and power cables, and there is currently no other approved project.
At the same time, during the meeting, an engineer representing the community presented a possible alternative option for laying the network. Specialists are to additionally review it and other possibilities within two weeks. Whether the alternative route can be implemented remains unknown.
The conflict at Teremky arose around the construction of a backup heating network intended to provide backup heat supply to 183 residential buildings, three medical institutions, and 18 schools and kindergartens in the event of an emergency shutdown of CHPP-5. Within the construction corridor, the city plans to remove 662 trees, 56 of which are to be transplanted, as well as 70 bushes, 16 of them to be transplanted.
Construction is being carried out through a protective shelterbelt that existed long before the construction of the residential area and was specially preserved during its construction as a recreational zone. Among the trees planned for removal are dozens of oaks aged 60-120 years, over a hundred ash trees, as well as dozens of pear, apple, acacia, maple, linden, hornbeam, poplar, willow, chestnut, and other species. Currently, some of the trees have already been destroyed. The KCSA asserts that the work is being carried out after an inspection of the plantings and necessary approvals, and that after construction is completed, the area will be landscaped and new trees and bushes will be planted.
At the same time, local residents demand documents justifying the felling, oppose the destruction of trees in the green zone, and claim that during 2020-2025 project documentation for laying the heating network along another route, in particular under Teremkivska Street, was funded for over UAH 8 million and developed in several revisions. Municipal Enterprise Kyivteploenergo acted as its client.
Residents also claim that laying the heating network on the site of the shelterbelt may be linked to meeting the needs of the Ozernyi Hai residential complex in the neighboring village of Hatne and the Abrykosovyi residential complex near Teremky.

His appointment is particularly important given the Basij's extensive role in Iran. The organization functions as a vast paramilitary and mobilization network that provides the state with a nationwide workforce. Its responsibilities extend beyond conventional military operations and include internal security, political mobilization, logistical support, local organization and assistance to state institutions.
The Basij demonstrated the breadth of this capacity during recent periods of instability. They have No Money - Their country is 'shot.'"
"Praise be to Allah!" the president concluded.
Who is Ahmed Vahidi, the new commander of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps?
This week has seen some significant appointments from Iran's new — and still unseen — Supreme Leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, as he continues to reshape the country's military and national security leadership.
Six senior military leaders have been appointed in total.
Among the most consequential was the appointment of previous interior and defense minister Brig. Gen. Ahmad Vahidi as commander of the paramilitary Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). Vahidi, a secretive figure accused of involvement in the 1994 bombing of a Jewish community center in Argentina, is seen as one of the most powerful figures in Iran, following the death of former Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei in February.
The IRGC remains one of the most influential institutions in the Islamic Republic, exercising extensive military, political, economic and security influence.
Despite his growing authority, Vahidi has maintained a relatively low public profile since the beginning of the war. Civilian political figures, particularly Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, have been considerably more visible.
Vahidi, an IRGC veteran and former Quds force commander, had already been serving in the role following the February killing of Iranian military officer Mohammad Pakpour.
Oil from tanker grounded off Oman has started reaching mainland, Reuters reports
Oil from a spill off Oman has started to reach the country's mainland, the U.N.'s shipping body said on Wednesday, according to the Reuters news agency.
"Oil is drifting offshore to the northeast of [Oman's] Al-Qibliyyah Island, with some oil reported to be reaching the mainland. Oil spill contingency planning is in place," a spokesperson at the International Maritime Organization (IMO) said.
The oil is believed to be leaking from the grounded tanker Caroline Bezengi, with the slick now covering almost 155 square miles, according to the Omani government.
The IMO said the tanker was carrying approximately 800,000 barrels of oil from Russia to Asia, but grounded off the coast of Oman on June 30, Reuters reported.
"Oil has been leaking from the vessel for some time. The seasonal monsoon has limited access to the vessel and delayed salvage operations," the IMO said.

Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan said Wednesday he hoped more countries would join a defense agreement signed last week between Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan.
"Our vision for it is not limited to the three countries," the Turkish leader told the London-based Asharq Al-Awsat daily, which is owned by the Saudi royal family. It contains a clause saying any attack on one would be seen as an attack on all.

International Energy Agency cuts 2026 oil demand forecast again as traffic on Strait of Hormuz remains low
The International Energy Agency (IEA) on Wednesday sharply reduced its forecast for global oil demand this year, with supplies still crimped by the disruption of shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and high prices deterring buyers.
Demand is expected to slump by 1.6 million barrels per day, compared with its forecast slump of one million barrels in its previous monthly report in July.
Crude prices have remained well above levels seen before the U.S. and Israeli attacks on Iran in late February, sparking a war that has seen oil infrastructure damaged in several Gulf countries and some supply routes for oil severely disrupted.
Tehran also responded by effectively shutting down tanker and cargo traffic in the Strait of Hormuz, through which around one-fifth of global oil supplies usually transit.
"The ongoing closure of the Strait of Hormuz and elevated fuel prices continue to weigh on oil consumption," the Paris-based IEA said.
Despite a purported ceasefire and repeated claims that a deal to open the strait was imminent – which the IEA referred to as "sudden diplomatic pivots" – only a handful of ships are being let through, leading to volatile pricing on global oil markets.
The IEA said global supplies rose by 2.4 million barrels per day in July, to reach 101.5 million barrels per day, but that was still 6.3 million per day lower than a year ago.
But "renewed hostilities and maritime disruptions in July and early August undermined the recovery efforts," the agency said.
It now expects global supply to fall by 4.3 million barrels per day on average this year, before recovering next year.
On the demand side, the IEA is projecting a return to growth in the fourth quarter of this year.

Wisconsin race upset: Key takeaways from US primary election results
Trump-backed candidates both win and lose: Results from Wisconsin, Minnesota, South Carolina and Alabama.
David Crowley has defeated Democratic socialist Francesca Hong in Wisconsin’s Democratic gubernatorial primary election held on Tuesday, in a major upset for the progressive hopeful.
The Democratic race in Wisconsin reflected a wider, ongoing battle inside the Democratic primaries between mainstream, “establishment” candidates, referred to as “moderates” by Democrats, and more left-wing, “progressive” democratic socialists like Hong. In the end, Hong, who had led in the polls ahead of election day, lost by just 0.4 percent to Crowley.
Recommended Stories
list of 2 items
- list 1 of 2Democrats gain momentum in pivotal US Senate and governor’s races in Texas
- list 2 of 2US Senate passes sweeping Russian energy sanctions bill amid Ukraine war
Besides Wisconsin, Alabama, Connecticut, Minnesota, South Carolina and Vermont also conducted primary elections on Tuesday.
In Vermont’s Democratic gubernatorial race, Amanda Janoo won with 49.1 percent of the vote, while Aly Richards trailed behind with 46.5 percent of the vote, with about 98 percent of votes counted, according to The Associated Press. Republican incumbent Phil Scott ran unopposed and won, while Trump-favoured Rhett Marques won in Alabama.
Here are some of the key takeaways from Tuesday’s primary races.
Wisconsin shows how divided Democrats are
Milwaukee County Executive Crowley, endorsed by current governor Tony Evers, took victory with 39.8 percent of the vote in a crowded Democratic gubernatorial primary in Wisconsin. He will face the Republican’s pick, US Representative Tom Tiffany, who won his Republican nomination by 95.3 percent, in the November general election.
The race underscored a split vision of the future of the Democratic Party, with Hong carrying 39.4 percent of the Democratic primary vote.
Her left-leaning policy goals, including abolishing the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agency, a one-year moratorium on new data centres and increased taxation of billionaires and corporations, had proved popular with a sizeable number of Democratic voters.
That supported the findings of a recent Reuters/Ipsos poll which indicates a growing number of Democratic voters want their party’s candidates to track further to the left.
More than seven in 10 Democrats who identify as liberal said they consider it “essential” that their party’s candidates support raising taxes on corporations and billionaires (76 percent), expanding access to abortion (72 percent) and universal government-provided healthcare (71 percent).
But unlike Abdul El-Sayed, a progressive candidate who won the Michigan Democratic Senate primary earlier this month, Hong ran without endorsements from US Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont or US Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York.
She has faced criticism for past posts on social media, including a November 2020 X post, at the height of a COVID-19 wave, in which she wrote, “Please DON’T gather for the colonizer holiday,” and another when she said, “Cancel Thanksgiving. Should have done this in 1621”.
In recent interviews, Hong has walked back those statements, saying that as a chef, she had fond memories of the Thanksgiving holiday, but that Thanksgiving is a time that is painful for many people. In another interview, she said that she did not want to cancel Thanksgiving.
Crowley’s campaign manager, Garren Randolph, said the candidate is “focused on bringing people together, earning the support of Democrats, Republicans, Independents, and anyone who believes Wisconsin is at its best when we work together and deliver results”.
Hong, meanwhile, addressed supporters before the race had been called.
“We have built something that will change politics forever,” she said. “The work we have done will be remembered forever. I know we don’t have the final results right now, but what I do know is we are ready to keep fighting.”
Minnesota: Progressives score a win; Trump ally loses governor nomination
Minnesota’s Democratic Senate primary also showed there is momentum behind left-leaning candidates, with progressive Lieutenant Governor Peggy Flanagan, who was elected on a ticket with Governor Tim Walz in 2018, beating more moderate Representative Angie Craig.
With 99 percent of the votes counted, Flanagan had won 59 percent of the votes while Craig trailed with 39.4 percent.
Tuesday’s primary results in the Upper Midwest also raised questions about the power of an endorsement by United States President Donald Trump.
In Minnesota, former MyPillow CEO Mike Lindell lost the Republican nomination for governor to Speaker of the Minnesota House of Representatives Lisa Demuth, despite the vocal backing of Trump.
With about 99 percent of votes counted, Demuth had 43.4 percent of the votes, while Lindell trailed with 32.5 percent.
Lindell is an enduring Trump ally and proponent of the debunked claim that the 2020 presidential election was “stolen” from the Republicans.
Lindell received Trump’s endorsement in May, when the president wrote on Truth Social, “Mike will be SPECTACULAR!!! He truly loves Minnesota, as do I, and wants to bring it back from oblivion and embarrassment. He can do it!”
Demuth is expected to face a tough battle against Democratic nominee Senator Amy Klobuchar, who won her party’s nomination in the aftermath of “Operation Metro Surge“, the Trump administration’s immigration deportation campaign in Minneapolis that resulted in the killing of two protesters by officers earlier this year.
Trump’s endorsement wins in Alabama
A Trump-backed candidate did win the Republican primary in Alabama’s newly redrawn 2nd Congressional District.
Rhett Marques won the race in the district with 50 percent of the vote while Hampton Harris trailed behind with 21.6 percent of the vote, according to AP.
In April, the Supreme Court ruled that Louisiana Republicans could redraw the electoral map. The redrawn map now favours Republicans by eliminating one of two districts in which Black voters make up a majority or near-majority, raising hopes in the party that they can flip it from the Democrats.
The Republican nominee will face Democrat Shomari Figures, who is hoping for a second term in the seat but now faces a tougher challenge.
Ammie Akin won the Republican primary for the 7th District while Jenny Carl won the race for the 1st District.
The fight to replace Lindsey Graham isn’t over
Lindsey Graham’s sister, Darline Graham, advanced to a runoff for the Republican Party’s nomination for the South Carolina US Senate seat in November’s election following her brother’s death.
In a race between 10 candidates, Graham received 32.7 percent of the vote and US Representative Ralph Norman trailed behind, with 24.7 percent of the vote, according to AP.
She will face Norman in an August 25 run-off. The eventual Republican nominee is favoured to win in November.
Governor Henry McMaster had appointed Graham to serve the rest of her brother’s Senate term through to early January, following his unexpected death from a heart ailment.
Trump endorsed Darline Graham, who has never held public office, for a full six-year term, calling it a “fabulous tribute” to her brother.
But critics said her bid, based on family name recognition and presidential backing without a political record of her own, had the air of a coronation.
Graham has said that she is “not being handed” the seat and that she realises that she needs to earn votes.

Uncertain future for Dutch bike brands after Accell goes under
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12

17:44:24 KST

Uncertain future for Dutch bike brands after Accell goes under
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
The Netherlands’ largest bicycle manufacturer, Accell, has been declared insolvent, leaving an uncertain future for major brands such as Batavus, Sparta and the British-based bike maker Raleigh.
A court appointed curators last week when Accell applied to suspend payments to its creditors, the last step before insolvency in the Netherlands.
In a statement, the curators said they would explore all options, including a relaunch for Accell’s Dutch operations, based in Amsterdam. The company’s other European branches remain in business.
CEO Jonas Nilsson said: “Every realistic option for the future of the business has been tirelessly explored, and none has resulted in a solution to continue the group in its current form.”
Irish media reported that Quanta Capital, a Dublin-based investment firm founded by former road race cyclist Mel Sutcliffe, was preparing a bid with a number of other investors. Sutcliffe sold Eurotrek Raleigh Ireland to Accell 10 years ago.
Pandemic buyout
Accell was bought by a consortium led by New York-based private equity firm KKR for €1.8 billon in 2022 following a surge in demand for bicycles during the coronavirus pandemic.
But the company struggled to produce bikes fast enough and its costs rose after it ordered too many components in anticipation of a sustained rise in sales that never materialised.
By the time supply chains recovered after lockdown, Accell was left with a mountain of unsold bikes that it had to sell at a discount to limit its losses. Revenues fell 22% in 2024 to just over €1 billion.
Accell closed the Netherlands’ last remaining bike factory, the Batavus plant in Heerenveen, last year, shifting production to Hungary and shedding 160 jobs.
Babboe recall
The company was also hit by the mass recall of 22,000 Babboe cargo bikes after it received hundreds of complaints about the frames breaking on the road, which cost it tens of millions of euros as well as severe reputational damage.
The consumer standards agency NVWA briefly banned Babboe from selling new bikes and launched a criminal investigation amid allegations that the company had tried to cover up the flaws.
The collapse of Accell leaves the Netherlands with only one major bike maker, Gazelle, based in Dieren, as well as a handful of smaller manufacturers such as Kruitbosch (whose brands include Cortina) and Azor.
The consumer protection agency Consumentenbond has advised owners of Accell-made bikes to check the status of their guarantee with the shop or retailer where they bought it. Some replacement parts are still available because they were made by other companies.

Hungary’s parliament elected former Supreme Court chief justice András Baka as the country’s new president on the 11th of August, Reuters reports
It is a symbolic step in Prime Minister Péter Magyar’s efforts to dismantle the strongholds of former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán. Bak was elected to the largely ceremonial post with votes from the center-right Tisza party, while members of the opposition Fidesz party did not participate in the presidential election.
In a speech after taking the oath, Baka criticized the previous government, saying that under Orbán, a single party had taken over the country, the branches of power were not separated and there was no functioning system to hold them accountable for their actions and achievements. He added that building a new future for Hungary requires both justice and selflessness, and said the president’s job is to represent people with different views.
Baka stressed that a new Hungary cannot be built on revenge.
Magyar’s victory in the April election ended Orbán’s 16-year rule, and he promised to restore democratic standards and called on Orbán’s party’s elected or appointed officials to resign.
The removal of former Hungarian President Tamás Sulyok, whom Magyar called an Orbán puppet, was one of the new prime minister’s main goals. Sulyok signed the Tisza party’s constitutional amendments in July that ended his own presidency.
Fidesz deputies abstained from the vote on the new president, having previously said that Tisza had arbitrarily and illegally terminated Sulyok’s presidency. The Magyar party was also accused of tyranny and authoritarian policies, which Tisza denied.

‘Rotting flesh’ Titan Arum to bloom at Basel Botanical Garden
A rare Titan Arum is due to flower at the University of Basel’s Botanical Garden in Switzerland. The tropical plant only flowers for two days, giving off an odour of rotting flesh.
The univerrsity’s Tropical House opens its doors to the public on Wednesday evening until 2am. Furthermore, there is no admission charge for visiting the Botanical Gardens.
This endangered plant is native to the tropical rainforests of Sumatra in Indonesia. It produces the world’s largest flower, which can grow to over three metres in height.
On the first evening, the titan arum gives off an intense smell of rotting meat. This stench specifically attracts pollinators such as carrion flies, beetles and bees.
The specimen at the University of Basel’s Botanical Garden last flowered in July 2023. The flower’s development can also be viewed live via a webcam on the Botanical Garden’s website.

After 78 years, IDF identifies grave of soldier killed fleeing British detention camp
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
08:43:00 UTC
17:43:00 KST

Nearly 78 years after he was killed while trying to escape a detention camp in Cyprus and make his way to the newly established State of Israel, the IDF has identified the grave of fallen soldier Shlomo Haimson.
The IDF said Wednesday that an investigation by its Missing Persons Branch, together with the Defense Ministry, the Military Rabbinate and the Cyprus Detainees Association, determined that Haimson is buried in grave No. 11, row 2, in the Cyprus immigrants section of the Haifa cemetery. Haimson was killed by guards at the Karaolos detention camp on the night of September 29-30, 1948, and was initially buried in the Jewish cemetery in Margo, Cyprus.
In 1970, the remains of those buried at Margo were brought to Israel. Around 120 of the 163 people transferred in what became known as Operation Margo could not be identified and were buried as unknowns in a special section at Kfar Samir cemetery in Haifa. Haimson was among them.
Born in Romania in 1930, Haimson lost his father during World War II. After the war, he decided to immigrate to Mandatory Palestine with his mother, Ita, and his partner, Perla, aboard the immigrant ship Pan York-Kibbutz Galuyot. The ship was intercepted by British Mandate forces and its passengers were deported to Cyprus.
While held in the detention camp, Haimson joined the “Defenders’ Ranks,” which operated under the auspices of the Haganah and trained young men in preparation for military service after their arrival in Israel. After the establishment of the state, his mother and partner were released and immigrated to Israel as part of a group designated to establish Kibbutz Magen in the western Negev.
In September 1948, Haimson learned that his daughter, Miriam, had been born and decided to escape the camp. On the night of September 29-30, he joined eight others in breaking through the fences. Guards spotted them and opened fire. Haimson was killed, while his companions were captured and returned to the camp.
He was buried the following day in Margo’s Jewish cemetery. Because people at the camp did not know him well, the headstone placed on his grave carried no inscription.
The effort to identify him began decades later. In 2010, Amir Rogel, one of the founders of the Cyprus Detainees Association, launched a project to identify those buried anonymously and place their names on their graves. During that effort, researchers discovered that Haimson was recognized as a fallen member of Israel’s armed forces.
In 2023, a special investigative team was established within the IDF’s EITAN Missing Persons Branch. Investigators examined archival documents from around the world, collected testimonies, reconstructed and analyzed historical photographs and conducted archaeological surveys. The findings led the team, together with the Military Rabbinate, to conclude that Haimson had been buried at Margo and that his remains were transferred to Israel in 1970 and interred in grave No. 11, row 2, in Haifa.
The head of the IDF Personnel Directorate accepted the findings and approved the placement of a headstone bearing Haimson’s name.
His family, including his daughter Miriam, grandchildren and great-grandchildren, who now live in Rio de Janeiro, were informed Tuesday night that the investigation had been completed. The news was delivered in the presence of Israel’s military attaché in Brazil, Col. Uri Ron, together with senior IDF and Defense Ministry officials and members of the investigative team.
Chief Human Resources Officer and head of the IDF Casualties Division Brig. Gen. Edna Ilia said the army’s obligation to Haimson and his family had never ended. “Seventy-eight years have passed since Shlomo Haimson fell in the detention camp, and our moral debt to his memory and his family has not ceased for a moment,” she said.
“Last night, when the IDF attaché stood in uniform in the family home in Rio de Janeiro and delivered the news to his daughter and descendants, the past embraced the present. The meeting is living proof that the IDF never abandons its soldiers, even after decades.”
Haimson’s family said the discovery brought profound relief after decades of uncertainty. “We are deeply moved, fulfilled and eternally grateful for the unwavering dedication, meticulous efforts and sensitivity shown by every professional and investigator involved in this noble mission,” the family said.
They added that knowing his story and sacrifice would now culminate in “a final resting place identified with his name” had brought “indescribable peace” to the family in Rio de Janeiro.
Haimson’s descendants are expected to travel to Israel for a state military ceremony in Haifa, where a memorial headstone bearing his name will be added to the grave, closing a circle that remained open for nearly eight decades.

Zelenskyy signed a decree on the establishment of the "Chornyi Lis" National Nature Park
Kyiv • UNN
The President signed a decree establishing a park covering more than 13,700 hectares in Kropyvnytskyi District. The territory includes forest and water fund lands, and the administration will operate under the management of the State Forest Resources Agency.
President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy signed a decree establishing the "Chornyi Lis" National Nature Park in the Kirovohrad region, UNN reports.
Details
Under Decree No. 719/2026, published on the president's official website on August 11, the new nature park will be located in Kropyvnytskyi District.
The park will encompass 13,710.2441 hectares of state- and municipally owned land.
In particular:
-  12,844.5 hectares of state-owned forestry land, which are under the permanent use of the State Specialized Forestry Enterprise "Forests of Ukraine," will be withdrawn from the land user and transferred to the national nature park for permanent use; 
-  865.7441 hectares of municipally owned land (water fund, agricultural, and forestry land) will be included in the park's territory without being withdrawn from the current land users. 
In addition, the decree supports the Cabinet of Ministers' proposal to establish a special administration for the "Chornyi Lis" National Nature Park, which will operate within the sphere of management of the State Agency of Forest Resources of Ukraine.
The government must approve the Regulations on the park within six months.
Also, in 2027–2029, the Cabinet of Ministers must develop a land-management plan for allocating land plots and formalizing property rights to the relevant land plots, as well as develop a land-management plan for organizing and establishing the boundaries of the national nature park's territory.
Separately, it is envisaged that in 2027–2028 a Territorial Organization Plan for the "Chornyi Lis" National Nature Park will be developed, defining issues related to the protection, restoration, and recreational use of natural complexes.
Funding for the operation of the new national park is to be provided for when preparing the draft state budgets for 2027 and subsequent years.
The decree enters into force on the day of its publication.

Landslide kills at least six in Mumbai amid heavy monsoon rains
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
08:40:44 UTC
17:40:44 KST

Heavy monsoon rains triggered a landslide in a densely populated neighbourhood in India’s financial capital, Mumbai, on Wednesday, killing at least six people and injuring four others, authorities said.
The landslide struck before dawn when a section of hillside collapsed onto two or three homes in a tightly packed cluster of houses in Mumbai’s suburb of Ghatkopar, said Tanaji Kambli, a civic official.
Authorities immediately launched a rescue operation involving firefighters, police, the National Disaster Response Force and civic officials but efforts were hampered by narrow access lanes that prevented the use of heavy machinery, officials said.
Rescue teams pulled at least 10 people from the debris and rushed them to a government hospital. Six people, including two children and two teenagers, were declared dead on arrival, Tanaji said. Four others were hospitalised and were receiving treatment.
Ritu Tawde, the mayor of Mumbai, visited the area and announced monetary compensation for the families of the victims.
India’s weather department has forecast more active monsoon conditions across western India. Authorities have urged residents in flood and landslide-prone areas to remain alert.
Mumbai, a city of more than 20 million people, receives some of its heaviest rainfall between June and September. Torrential downpours routinely inundate roads and railway lines, disrupt air and rail traffic. They trigger landslides and building collapses, particularly in crowded hillside settlements where houses are often built on unstable slopes.
Experts have long warned that rapid urbanisation, construction on fragile hillsides and poor drainage have left Mumbai increasingly vulnerable to deadly monsoon-related disasters, with climate crisis adding to those risks, bringing heavier and more unpredictable rainfall.

Report: Iran tracked Trump as missile threat prompted Air Force One decoy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
08:38:48 UTC
17:38:48 KST

The New York Times on Wednesday reported new details about an alleged Iranian plot to assassinate U.S. President Donald Trump that prompted an elaborate security deception last month, with Trump secretly moved off Air Force One, transported across an airport in a catering truck and flown out of Turkey aboard another aircraft after a NATO summit.
The Times report cited two U.S. officials familiar with the threat, who said American intelligence agencies based their assessment on multiple streams of intelligence about the alleged plot.
U.S. officials learned of a specific threat involving a surface-to-air missile targeting the presidential aircraft, according to the report. A person near the NATO summit was also spotted with a shoulder-fired missile, and Iranian operatives were believed to know specifically where Trump was staying in Ankara, including the floor of the building.
The operation to conceal Trump’s location amid fears that Iran could target either the president or his aircraft was first revealed Monday night by The Washington Post.
According to that report, Trump secretly left Turkey for Britain aboard a smaller military aircraft while the plane publicly operating as Air Force One departed without him, effectively serving as a decoy. The president’s actual location was concealed for hours not only from the public and journalists but also from many White House staffers and senior administration officials.
The deception took place July 8 at the conclusion of the NATO summit in Ankara, a day after the United States resumed strikes on Iran at Trump’s direction following the collapse of negotiations aimed at ending the war.
The Post reported that security officials received a credible warning linked to Iran, prompting what was described as a deception operation.
CBS News had reported last month, citing U.S. officials, that intelligence agencies had identified a credible plot to fire a missile at the aircraft carrying Trump and that the Secret Service quickly switched to an alternate plan.
The Wall Street Journal subsequently reported that Trump’s departure from Turkey aboard an older Air Force One aircraft rather than the newer Boeing 747-8 received from Qatar was prompted by intelligence supplied by Israel. U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee confirmed that Israel had provided the intelligence.
Trump boards Air Force One — then secretly leaves
The deception began before Trump’s aircraft ever left the ground.
In full view of cameras, Trump arrived at the familiar blue-and-white Boeing 747 that has served for decades as one of the presidential Air Force One aircraft. He climbed the stairs, waved and entered the plane, giving observers no reason to believe he would travel aboard a different aircraft.
Minutes later, however, Trump and several members of his entourage secretly left through a door on the opposite side of the aircraft.
Security personnel used an airline catering truck, the type normally positioned alongside aircraft to load food and supplies, to conceal the transfer.
The truck’s cargo compartment was raised hydraulically to the level of the aircraft door. Trump and members of his team entered the compartment, which was then lowered to the ground.
The truck transported them to a nearby C-32A, the military version of a Boeing 757 used to carry senior U.S. government officials.
The Washington Post reconstructed parts of the operation using videos recorded at the airport.
One video showed the catering truck leaving Air Force One and traveling toward the smaller aircraft. At one point, it disappeared from view for about 40 seconds, in part behind the C-32A’s engines. The truck’s compartment was subsequently raised again to the height of the aircraft door.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth was also part of the deception.
Hegseth separately boarded the C-32A in public using exterior stairs, apparently making the aircraft look like an ordinary government flight. According to the Post, Hegseth then traveled aboard the aircraft with Trump to Britain.
Meanwhile, White House journalists and other administration personnel began boarding the older Air Force One aircraft without knowing the president was no longer aboard.
White House officials also instructed journalists to close their window shades before takeoff.
According to the report, some of the people who participated in the deception did not themselves know that they were helping carry out such an operation.
Trump’s aircraft disappears from tracking systems
The effort to conceal Trump’s location continued after takeoff.
“Air Force One” is not the name of a particular aircraft. It is the call sign assigned to any U.S. Air Force aircraft while the president is aboard.
Despite carrying Trump, the C-32A flew to Britain under the routine call sign RCH18, or “Reach 18,” a designation typically associated with military flights transporting personnel and equipment.
Systems that would have allowed the aircraft to be easily tracked were switched off, and no public flight-tracking data showing its route was available.
The older Boeing 747 carrying journalists and White House personnel — but not Trump — appeared on flight-tracking systems under the call sign “AF1.”
Flight data showed the aircraft arriving at Royal Air Force Mildenhall in England at about 10:29 p.m.
A contemporaneous report filed by the White House press pool described the flight as uneventful and noted that nobody had visited the journalists’ cabin — an absence whose significance only became clear later.
Three aircraft were involved in the journey that evening.
The newer Boeing 747-8 given to the United States by Qatar departed Turkey first and landed at Mildenhall at 6:26 p.m.
The C-32A carrying Trump arrived at about 10:20 p.m., followed several minutes later by the decoy Air Force One.
It remains unclear how Trump transferred from the C-32A to the presidential aircraft after landing. But by 10:56 p.m., he appeared before cameras descending the stairs of the older Boeing 747, again creating the impression that it was the aircraft on which he had traveled from Turkey.
Five minutes later, Trump boarded the newer aircraft received from Qatar and continued to Washington with his staff and the press corps.
The White House issued a statement that night saying Trump had arrived in Britain aboard the older Air Force One, although the Post’s subsequent reporting found that he had actually made the journey aboard the C-32A.
During the flight back to the United States, Trump spoke with journalists for about 15 minutes and discussed the Iranian threat but did not disclose the deception operation that had unfolded only hours earlier.
Asked why reporters had been required to close their window shades in Turkey, Trump said it was probably because the flight was dangerous given America’s enemies. He added that he regularly faced threats and was a major target for Iran.
Concerns over the aircraft received from Qatar
The threat emerged only days after Trump began using the Boeing 747-8 that the United States received as a gift from Qatar.
Washington spent about $400 million adapting the aircraft for presidential use, but reports and photographs have indicated that it lacks some of the missile-detection and countermeasure systems installed on the two older aircraft traditionally used as Air Force One.
According to CBS News, the older presidential aircraft are equipped with laser technology designed to disrupt incoming missiles, along with other defensive countermeasures.
It has not been publicly disclosed which of those systems, if any, have been installed on the Qatari-provided aircraft.
The White House and U.S. Air Force have maintained that the newer plane is safe and suitable for presidential travel.
The White House later announced that Trump would return to using the older presidential aircraft for about a month while the newer plane underwent “additional upgrades and improvements.”
The potential threat was considered particularly serious because of Turkey’s proximity to Iran.
Turkey shares a border with Iran, and Iran possesses missiles and drones capable of traveling the roughly 1,300 kilometers, or about 800 miles, between Iran and parts of Turkey.
Britain, by contrast, is roughly 4,000 kilometers, or about 2,500 miles, from Iran. According to the Center for Strategic and International Studies, Iran does not currently possess a weapons system capable of effectively striking a target in Britain from that distance.
The older presidential aircraft, known as VC-25As, entered service more than three decades ago and were designed from the outset to transport the U.S. president.
Among other protections, they are hardened against some effects of a nuclear explosion, carry missile countermeasures, include onboard medical facilities capable of functioning as an operating room and can be refueled in flight during an emergency.
Two new aircraft intended to permanently replace them have faced repeated delays and, under the current schedule, are not expected to be delivered until 2028.
The disclosures about potential gaps in the Qatari-provided aircraft’s defenses have already caused controversy in Washington.
The Trump administration last month issued subpoenas to New York Times journalists as part of an effort to identify who had provided information about the aircraft’s capabilities.
The administration said the subpoenas were part of an investigation into a breach of national security, while the Times accused the government of attempting to intimidate journalists and their sources.
The administration later withdrew the subpoenas.

U.S. Air Force seeks new maker for B-1B bomber control panel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
08:38:39 UTC
17:38:39 KST

- The Defense Logistics Agency is seeking manufacturers for 11 electric control panels for the B-1B Lancer bomber, with responses due August 18, 2026.
- The notice is a market research request issued by the 422nd Supply Chain Management Squadron at Tinker Air Force Base and carries no funding or contract commitment.
The Defense Logistics Agency, the Pentagon office responsible for keeping military equipment supplied with everything from fuel to spare parts, published a notice on August 11 seeking manufacturers capable of building a replacement electric control panel for the B-1B Lancer, a swing-wing bomber that has served as a backbone of American long-range strike capability since the mid-1980s.
The notice, issued by the 422nd Supply Chain Management Squadron based at Tinker Air Force Base in Oklahoma, is what the Pentagon calls a Sources Sought Synopsis, a formal way of asking industry who out there can actually build a part before the government commits to a real contract. This is not a purchase order and carries no funding attached to it, meaning no company will get paid based on this notice alone. Instead, it functions as market research, a step the Air Force uses to figure out how many qualified manufacturers exist for a given component and whether the eventual contract should be opened to full competition or reserved specifically for small businesses, a decision that shapes which kinds of companies get the chance to bid once real money is on the table.
The part itself carries the designation Panel, Control, Electric, identified by a National Stock Number, the standardized tracking code the Pentagon uses to catalog literally every piece of equipment across the entire U.S. military supply chain, so that a specific bolt, gasket, or circuit panel can be identified and reordered from anywhere in the world without confusion. The Air Force is seeking an estimated 11 units of this particular panel, a modest quantity that reflects the reality of sustaining an aircraft fleet that has been flying for four decades rather than a mass-production run for a brand-new weapon system.
That aircraft, the B-1B Lancer, entered service with the Air Force in 1986 as a supersonic, variable-sweep-wing bomber designed originally during the Cold War to penetrate Soviet air defenses at high speed and low altitude. Built by what was then Rockwell International, later absorbed into Boeing, the B-1B can carry a larger payload of conventional weapons than either of the Air Force’s other two strategic bombers, the B-2 Spirit and the aging B-52 Stratofortress, though the B-1B lost its ability to carry nuclear weapons in 2011 under the terms of the New START arms control treaty with Russia, leaving it as a conventional-only strike aircraft. The fleet has flown extensively in recent decades over Afghanistan, Iraq, and Syria, where its ability to loiter over a battlefield for extended periods and drop large quantities of precision-guided bombs made it a valuable close air support asset for troops on the ground.
Keeping a fleet of aircraft this old flying reliably depends entirely on exactly the kind of unglamorous parts sourcing this notice represents. As the original manufacturers of specific components either stop producing them or exit the defense industry entirely, a problem the Pentagon refers to as diminishing manufacturing sources, the military has to find new companies willing and able to reverse-engineer or rebuild parts that may not have been manufactured in years. The notice specifically flags that potential suppliers may need to handle nonrecurring engineering costs, the expense of essentially relearning how to build a part from scratch when the original technical drawings or production line no longer exist, a routine but often expensive hurdle for legacy aircraft sustainment programs across the military.
Work under any eventual contract would take place at Tinker Air Force Base, which serves as the Air Force’s primary depot for maintaining and overhauling the B-1B fleet alongside several other aircraft types, making the base a central hub for exactly the kind of parts procurement this notice represents. Companies interested in supplying the panel have until 11:59 p.m. Central time on August 18, 2026, to respond, and the Air Force is explicitly seeking interest from businesses of every size and category, including small businesses, service-disabled veteran-owned businesses, and businesses located in historically underutilized zones, a standard part of how the Pentagon tries to broaden its industrial base beyond a handful of major defense contractors.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan’s Food and Drug Administration has ordered the recall of a batch of Beniel F C Tablets 8 mg, a prescription medication for high blood pressure, after testing raised concerns about its effectiveness.
The affected batch, numbered 2KA31, failed to meet dissolution standards during stability testing. A total of 87,360 tablets have been distributed, according to CTEE.
The FDA was notified by Synmosa Biopharma Corp., the holder of the drug’s marketing authorization. The company has been instructed to complete the recall by Aug. 24 and submit an investigation report and preventive action plan.
Failure to carry out the recall as required could result in a fine of NT$200,000 (US$6,207) to NT$5 million under Article 91 of the Pharmaceutical Affairs Act.
The FDA said there are no concerns about a shortage, as other batches remain available and production will continue. Two other products containing the same active ingredient are also authorized for sale.
The affected tablets contain benidipine hydrochloride, which is primarily used to treat high blood pressure. It works by widening blood vessels, lowering blood pressure and making it easier for the heart to pump blood, according to Synapse.
The FDA advised patients with concerns about their medication to return to their doctors as soon as possible.

Interior ministry faces criticism over scaling back social housing target

2026-08-12
08:36:56 UTC

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Interior Minister Liu Shyh-fang (劉世芳) clarified Wednesday that a 30,000-unit social housing construction target refers to projects jointly undertaken with local governments, after an advocacy group raised concerns that the government had drastically scaled back its goal from 130,000 units.
The Interior Ministry amended its “Assist a Million Renting Households” plan in July, prompting the Organization of Urban Re-s (OURs) and other groups to point out that the social housing construction target for 2025-2032 had been reduced from 130,000 units to 30,000, per PTS. The groups argued that social housing provides better protection for vulnerable people than rental management and rent subsidies, despite its higher upfront cost.
Liu initially said excessive social housing construction could result in more vacant housing units in the future. She noted that more than 600,000 housing units are currently vacant across Taiwan’s six major municipalities.
OURs held a news conference Sunday, saying the reduction in the social housing target would betray voter trust and abandon policies established under former President Tsai Ing-wen (蔡英文), per Liberty Times. The group said about 25,000 of the 30,000 planned units would continue projects initiated under Tsai, while the remaining target could be supplemented with rental subsidies or rental management units.
OURs added the central government planned to remove subsidies for local governments’ social housing projects while lowering the construction target, making it easier for local governments to meet their goals. The group called on the leaders of major municipalities to continue expanding social housing.
The advocacy group said that although social housing construction requires higher upfront costs, it provides longer leases, creates public assets, and offers greater protection for socially vulnerable groups than the alternatives.
Liu clarified that the 30,000-unit figure referred to projects jointly undertaken with local governments, per NOWNews. She said that if President Lai Ching-te (賴清德) remains in office for a second term, the government’s target over his two terms would remain at 130,000 units.
News of the reduced target and Liu’s initial comments drew criticism from opposition parties. Both the KMT and TPP echoed OURs’ concerns, accusing the Lai administration of backing away from its promises.
The New Power Party criticized the government for including rental management units and rent subsidies in its assisted housing goals, per Liberty Times. The party noted that each social housing project is legally required to reserve 40% of its units for disadvantaged groups, while private landlords face no such requirement.
The governments of Taichung, Taipei, New Taipei, and Tainan all said demand for social housing remained high, per UDN. New Taipei said slightly more than 10% of applicants for social housing would ultimately be able to secure a unit.
National Chengchi University Professor Chiang Ying-hui (江穎慧) questioned the government’s claims about the management of social housing units and the lack of available land as reasons for reducing the target, per UDN. She said the reduction from 130,000 to 30,000 units was too drastic to be considered reasonable and criticized the government for failing to provide transparency about the specific reasons behind the reduction.
OURs Secretary-General Peng Yang-kai (彭揚凱) said that when the central government asked local governments how many social housing units they could build over eight years, their assessment was at least 40,000 units. He warned that the outlook for these projects could be affected because the assessment was based on the assumption that local governments would receive subsidies.
Peng suggested that Lai was seeking to scale back his campaign promises before implementing them.

17:36:45 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — TSMC on Tuesday announced that foreign investors registered under Taiwan's overseas-investor regulations will be able to receive cash dividends in US dollars, following recent regulatory changes.
The new option will apply to the distribution of TSMC’s second-quarter dividend. Market observers said companies that have raised money overseas or have a large base of foreign shareholders are expected to be among those most likely to consider paying dividends in foreign currencies, according to CTEE and Sinotrade.
Companies can return part of their profits to shareholders through cash dividends, which may be paid annually, semiannually, or quarterly. Paying dividends directly in US dollars would eliminate the need for foreign investors to convert Taiwan dollars, reducing transaction costs and currency exchange volatility.
Foreign investors held a 69.16% stake in TSMC as of Tuesday, making the chipmaker a major test case for the new payment option. Based on its NT$7-per-share dividend for the second quarter, TSMC is set to distribute about NT$181.5 billion (US$5.6 billion).
Central Bank Foreign Exchange Department Director Tsai Chiung-min (蔡烱民) said TSMC could play an important role in introducing US-dollar dividend payments in the country. He said the move could make local stocks more attractive to foreign investors and help further open up the domestic capital market to international investors.
The Financial Supervisory Commission said it recently issued the directive as the stock market has grown into one of the world’s largest by market capitalization. The change is intended to support market internationalization and provide a more convenient investment environment for foreign investors.
Taiwan Stock Exchange data shows that 49 listed companies in Taiwan, including heavyweights Foxconn and ASE, have issued depositary receipts overseas, which allows investors abroad to hold their shares through financial instruments traded outside Taiwan. Another 84 listed and over-the-counter companies have foreign investors holding more than half of their shares.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Cabinet is considering additional spending on defense, welfare benefits, public-sector allowances, and price stabilization in a supplementary budget, CNA reported Wednesday.
The central government budget for 2026 is still under review in the legislature. The Cabinet said it will finalize the supplementary budget after lawmakers complete the review.
Planned spending includes higher payments for elderly farmers, national pension recipients, and six welfare programs. The government also plans to increase professional and supervisory allowances for military personnel, civil servants, and public school teachers.
Professional and supervisory allowances would each rise by NT$2,000 (US$62.09) per month. The increases would require about NT$11.2 billion in additional spending this year.
The monthly allowance for elderly farmers would increase from NT$8,110 to NT$10,000. Income eligibility rules would also be relaxed, while a new adjustment mechanism would take effect when the consumer price index reaches 3%.
More than 530,000 elderly farmers are expected to benefit from the changes. The government estimates they would require an additional NT$12.9 billion this year.
National pension payments would also increase to NT$5,000, benefiting more than 1.76 million people. The program is expected to cost NT$86 billion annually, including NT$16.98 billion from the 2026 supplementary budget.
Another NT$6.59 billion would be used to increase six categories of welfare payments. Recipients include people with disabilities, low-income households, and disadvantaged children and teenagers, UDN reported.
The Cabinet is also considering additional defense spending, though the amount has not been decided. The legislature recently approved a NT$780 billion special defense program, down from the Cabinet's original NT$1.25 trillion proposal.
The Cabinet has separately proposed a NT$210 billion special budget for domestically developed unmanned vehicles. Together, the two programs total NT$990 billion, NT$260 billion less than the Cabinet's original defense proposal.
CNA reported that other ministries may request additional funding before the supplementary budget is finalized. The final amount will depend on completion of the 2026 budget review and further discussions among government agencies.

Rising flu cases in Taiwan led by Type A
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
08:36:18 UTC
17:36:18 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Influenza cases are gradually intensifying and could peak in mid-September, with flu-like illnesses now accounting for about 10% of emergency room visits, the Centers for Disease Control said Tuesday at a regularly scheduled press conference.
The CDC said Type A (H1N1) was the predominant strain circulating in the community, accounting for 57% of cases and causing respiratory complications. The number of severe influenza complications and deaths has also increased, particularly among people age 65 and older, those with chronic diseases, and those who have not received this season's influenza vaccine, per a press release.
From Aug. 2-8, there were 92,075 outpatient and emergency room visits for influenza-like illnesses, up 2.4% from the previous week. During a similar period, 70 new severe influenza cases were reported, including 64 H1N1 cases, two H3N2 cases, and four unidentified Type A cases.
Twelve influenza-related deaths were also reported, including eight involving H1N1, one H3N2, two unidentified Type A cases, and one Type B case. So far this flu season, Taiwan has recorded 995 severe influenza cases and 188 deaths, according to the CDC.
The agency said publicly funded antiviral medications are available at 4,000 contracted medical institutions nationwide. The medications include Tamiflu, Ictazyl, and Relenza. People experiencing shortness of breath, difficulty breathing, turning blue (cyanosis), coughing up blood, chest pain, altered consciousness, or low blood pressure should seek medical attention immediately.
Influenza antiviral medications are typically not covered by National Health Insurance. Doctors, however, can determine whether publicly funded antiviral medications can be prescribed based on each patient's condition. A rapid influenza test is not required for patients who meet the eligibility criteria, per the press release.
The CDC urged the public to practice good hygiene and respiratory etiquette and to stay home when experiencing a fever, coughing, a runny nose, sore throat, or other respiratory symptoms. Sick people should avoid unnecessary outings and wear masks when going outside. Masks are also recommended when visiting medical facilities or crowded, poorly ventilated places.
The agency urged people with flu-like symptoms to seek medical attention and rest until fully recovered before returning to school or work to prevent further transmission. Information on publicly funded antiviral medications, contracted medical institutions, and influenza prevention is available from the website or by calling the epidemic prevention hotline at 1922 or 0800-001922.

Estonian intimacy coordinator: Always ask if the nudity is necessary
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
08:36:00 UTC
17:36:00 KST

Estonian intimacy coordinator: Always ask if the nudity is necessary
A new Estonian summer production brings intimacy front and center onstage. A professional intimacy coordinator explains how performers can safely handle vulnerable scenes.
"By intimacy, we mean all those moments where you're vulnerable," said Alice Aleksandridi, an intimacy coordinator who trained in the U.S. and France. That can include simulated sex, but also medical or hospital scenes, racism or scenes involving minors.
"Many professions emerge from situations where something went wrong and ask how to make sure it doesn't happen again," she explained, adding that intimacy coordination is one of them.
Aleksandridi works as a choreographer and liaison between performers and productions, helping actors feel safe while ensuring directors can safely achieve the intended scene and message. She said the profession combines her backgrounds in law and choreography.
The point of their work, she continued, is not to impose rules but find a way to stage difficult material safely. If an intimate scene is genuinely necessary, the next question is how to handle it appropriately.
"One of the basic questions an intimacy coordinator asks as a rule when reading a script is, 'Could this be done another way? Do we actually need this nudity to get the message across?'" she explained. "If the answer is yes, we move forward and figure out how to do it."
Intimate onstage
That question is relevant to "Moonlight" ("Kuuvalgel"), a Haapsalu summer production based on Terrence McNally's 1987 play "Frankie and Johnny in the Clair de Lune." Kaia Skoblov and Karl-Markus Pihlakas play the two leads in a story about intimacy, trust and fear of letting another person get close.
Pihlakas said the material immediately appealed to the cast and director Helen Rekkor because of its focus on intimacy and closeness. The production also uses headphones to create an even more intimate experience for the audience.
Skoblov noted she would not have accepted the role if she had been uncomfortable performing intimate scenes.
"I read the material and felt this was a story worth telling, because these themes really spoke to me," she said.
Pihlakas said the production also reflects a broader change in how intimacy is viewed onstage.
"Society has gotten more open about these topics," he said, adding that the increased interest in seeing intimacy onstage and on screen is in some ways a reflection of that. "'We're freer and we want to see that [freedom] onstage too!'"
'You bring it with you on set'
While the two actors confirmed they were able to handle the intimate scenes themselves and did not need an intimacy coordinator for this production, Aleksandridi said the need for such a coordinator can arise even when performers and directors know each other well.
She recalled examples from her training where actors struggled with violent or intimate scenes due to various personal circumstances or experiences.
In one case, two actors had played a couple in several films already, and the male actor denied needing an intimacy coordinator because they had worked together for so long already.
"But he didn't know the female actor had been raped two weeks before filming began," the Estonian intimacy coordinator said.
"At the end of the day, an actor is first and foremost a person," she stressed. "Whatever's going on in your everyday life, you bring it with you on set."

VIENTIANE, Aug. 12 (Xinhua) -- Lao officials and business representatives have gathered for the country's first nationwide investment promotion and management conference, emphasizing investment's role in national development and the need for improved management to attract more investment.
The meeting, held in Lao capital Vientiane from Tuesday to Wednesday, was chaired by Lao Deputy Prime Minister Saleumxay Kommasith and attended by Lao Prime Minister Sonexay Siphandone, ministers and deputy ministers, senior officials, and business representatives, the Vientiane Mai newspaper reported on Wednesday.

During the first seven months of 2026, 34 investment projects, worth a total of 8.5 billion dollars, were approved, an increase of 68 percent year-on-year.
Addressing the conference, Prime Minister Sonexay called for a new approach to investment promotion and management to make the process faster, more timely, transparent, professional, and effective.
He emphasized the need to strengthen monitoring and management of both existing projects and newly approved projects, ensuring strict and consistent compliance with laws and regulations. He also called for stronger action to address irregularities in the investment sector, including stricter enforcement against violations and greater use of modern tools and cooperation across sectors.
The meeting called on relevant sectors to strengthen their roles in promoting private-sector investment to increase private investment in line with the 10th National Socio-Economic Development Plan (2026-2030). ■
