Millions of US tax dollars sent to rightwing European thinktanks. Did any Trump supporters vote for that? | Arwa Mahdawi
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
08:00:23 UTC
17:00:23 KST

“THE CORRUPTION IS AT LEVELS RARELY SEEN BEFORE,” Donald Trump posted on Truth Social in February 2025. He was not referring to his own administration, but to the US Agency for International Development (USAID). “CLOSE IT DOWN!” the president added.
Just a few hours later USAID was in effect closed down, with most of the staff placed on indefinite administration leave. This was framed as part of Trump’s “America first” agenda. USAID, the Trump administration and his sycophants in the rightwing media had argued, was wasting taxpayers’ hard-earned money on ridiculous projects abroad instead of improving life at home. In the lead-up to the shuttering of USAID, for example, one of the most shameless lies about the agency, repeated without any evidence by the likes of Fox News, was that it was spending millions on condoms for Gaza.
Now that humanitarian aid has been slashed in the name of putting America first, is taxpayer money staying in the country? Not quite. A lot is still going abroad. But instead of being used to help the world’s most impoverished people, that money is going to thinktanks across Europe set up by multimillionaires who want to take Trumpism global.
Last month the Guardian reported that the US state department intends to grant $12m to conservative organisations in the UK; a move described by many critics as an attempt to influence foreign politics. Of that, $7m is going to a group called 878, co-founded by the former Conservative minister, now TV host Jacob Rees-Mogg (whose net worth is estimated at more than £100m) that appears to have been incorporated in the UK in March. The website describes it as a “leading British and American thinktank, dedicated to strengthening the civilisational partnership between the United Kingdom and the United States”. If millions in funding going to a new organisation with vague goals sounds a bit weird, it’s because it is. A former US official told the Guardian that normal funding processes are being subverted so that money can go to Trump-aligned causes.
Millions in grants are also being offered for proposals from groups in Europe to develop “civilizational self-confidence in Europe … [and] address national sovereignty, migration, censorship, and lawfare challenges in line with our shared political philosophy, law, and Western heritage”. If all this sounds vague, that’s by design. Zsuzsanna Végh, a researcher in liberal democracy, told the i Paper that “the advertising of the funding calls follows a long period of networking among Maga and like-minded European actors, which have already facilitated the identification of a pool of possible recipients”. In other words, it seems to be a bureaucratic form of meddling. Indeed, the German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, warned Trump’s administration against interfering in German elections following those grants. I imagine Trump has very much taken that to heart.
The US embassy in London is also offering grants of up to $500,000 for “public education” programmes that foster a “national conversation” about “shared civilizational values” between the UK and US. One recently departed US state department official told the Guardian that this seems to be an attempt to “create UK-originated narratives to support Maga propaganda”. Meanwhile Lisa Smart, a Liberal Democrat MP, accused Trump’s Maga money of “meddling in our democracy”.
What does the average Trump voter, who was promised an America-first agenda, think about all this money going to “public education” programmes in the UK instead of all the underfunded public schools at home? The short answer is: they’re not thinking about it at all. I am fairly certain there isn’t a single Fox News devotee who knows about the grants. They’re too busy getting worked up over Anthony Fauci and trans people in sports. There is a reason Trump has put so much energy into dismantling the free press: it’s a lot easier to lie to people and distract them from your broken promises when your billionaire buddies own the media.
Twelve million dollars of US taxpayer money going to projects in the UK may not seem like a lot in the grand scheme of things. It’s a few million less than Pete Hegseth spent on ribeye steak for the Pentagon last September. And it’s certainly chump change compared with the war on Iran, which has cost at least $37.5bn so far. But the money going to the UK and Europe represents a different kind of war effort. These are not isolated initiatives, but instead point to the growing transnationalisation of the hard right and a coordinated effort to make the Maga movement global under the guise of saving western civilisation.
The Trump administration has not been shy about its international intentions. Last December the new US national security strategy claimed Europe faced “civilizational erasure” and stated that US policies must include “cultivating resistance to Europe’s current trajectory within European nations”. In other words: bolstering far-right parties and influencers. It is doing this financially, but also through direct endorsements. Trump’s buddy Elon Musk has amplified rightwing populist movements across Europe. And at the Conservative Political Action Conference (CPAC) conference in Warsaw last year, Kristi Noem, who was then homeland security secretary, broke established norms by calling for Karol Nawrocki, who ran under the Trumpy slogan “Poland first, Poles first”, to be president of Poland. (He narrowly won.)
The fact that Noem was even at a CPAC conference in Poland is also telling. CPAC, one of the most high-profile gatherings of conservatives on the US right, used to be a domestic affair, but has taken on an international focus in the past decade. Its first international conference was held in Tokyo in 2017, followed by conferences everywhere from Australia to Hungary. Last month also saw the inaugural British franchise of CPAC, called CPAC GB, spearheaded by the former Conservative prime minister Liz Truss, who ran the country for just 49 days. “We believe the fight for freedom and conservative values doesn’t stop at America’s borders,” CPAC’s chair, Matt Schlapp, told Axios last year.
All this brazen meddling in foreign affairs is alarming. However, the US hard right may have overreached by trying to take Maga global without actually addressing American problems first. The average person in the US cares less about this crusade to “save” western civilisation than about whether they can afford petrol and groceries. And trying to square America first promises and Trump’s pledge not to start any new wars with rising costs thanks to the Iran war is starting to get tricky. Last month a Politico poll found that just a third of Trump’s Maga base thought the war in Iran was worth the cost, down from half in May. Influential Trump supporters such as the podcaster Joe Rogan have also turned on the president because of Iran.
Trump, for his part, has brushed off cost-of-living concerns, declaring last year: “I don’t want to hear about the affordability.” But the president, who made an estimated $2.2bn last year, should start listening. The average Trump voter may not know anything about all the grants their taxpayer money is funding in Europe. But it’s becoming more obvious to even the most diehard Maga fan that they are being put last.
- 
  Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist

Russia Produces Around 3,000 Geran-4/5 Kamikaze Drones per Month
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
07:59:56 UTC
16:59:56 KST

The Russian defense industry produces about 3,000 Geran-4/5 kamikaze drones per month, Defence Intelligence of Ukraine (DIU) told Militarnyi in response to an inquiry.
The use of this type of drone is becoming increasingly widespread due to improvements in its flight performance, particularly for overcoming Ukraine’s air defenses.
Serial production of the Geran-4/5 has been established at a plant in Yelabuga, within the Alabuga Special Economic Zone in Tatarstan. Other Russian enterprises are also involved in the production process, supplying individual components and forming the corresponding production chain.
Despite the significant monthly production volume, Russia’s defense ministry is seeking to expand the production capacity of the facilities in Alabuga. In early July 2026, satellite imagery captured large-scale construction work at the special economic zone.
Construction of the new production facilities began in May 2026. The exact purpose of the new buildings is currently unknown, but their construction indicates preparations for further expansion of production capacity.
Back in June 2026, the then-Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, Oleksandr Syrskyi, stated that Russia planned to significantly increase its use of jet-powered strike drones during air attacks on Ukraine. According to him, the share of such drones could reach 50%.
New information provided by the Defence Intelligence of Ukraine (DIU) to Militarnyi confirms a trend toward increased Russian production of jet-powered variants of the Geran drone family.
At the same time, according to the agency, Russia has halted production of the Geran-3 jet-powered kamikaze drones.
The Geran-4 and Geran-5 kamikaze drones are among the newest members of Russia’s Geran family. Despite sharing the same designation, they differ significantly in design.
It is known that the Geran-4, based on the concept of the Geran-3 jet-powered UAV, features a fuselage optimized for flight at higher speeds and a more powerful engine.
The drone has a wingspan of about 3 meters and a length of 3.5 meters, matching the dimensions of the previous version. At the same time, its maximum takeoff weight has increased from 350 to 450 kilograms.
The Geran-4 is equipped with a turbojet engine producing 160 kgf of thrust — twice as much as the Chinese Telefly JT80 installed on the previous version. This has increased its cruising speed from 280–330 to 350–500 km/h and its flight range from 600 to 850 kilometers.
The drone can fly at altitudes ranging from 100 to 5,000 meters, with a flight endurance of around 2.5 hours and a minimum warhead weight of 50 kilograms.
The Geran-5 has a fundamentally different design. Its developers abandoned the aerodynamic configuration characteristic of previous models.
In terms of its fuselage shape, the new aircraft resembles a cruise missile more than it does Shahed-type drones with delta wings.
For this reason, it can be classified as a ‘missile-drone’ — a class of weaponry that is already being actively developed, particularly by Ukrainian manufacturers.
The Geran-5 carries a 90-kilogram warhead and has a declared strike range of around 1,000 kilometers. In addition to its main warhead, the aircraft can be fitted with R-73 air-to-air missiles equipped with infrared homing seekers.
The Defence Intelligence of Ukraine also notes that the Geran-5 can be launched from airborne platforms, including Su-25 attack aircraft.

Wildfires, heatwaves pose growing fiscal risk to Greece, PM adviser says
Aug 12 - Wildfires and heatwaves pose a growing medium- and long-term fiscal risk for Greece and the wider region, a senior adviser to Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis said, as the government boosts investment to shore up its tourism-dependent economy.
Michael Arghyrou, the prime minister's chief economic adviser, said Athens was pursuing investments in water and energy infrastructure in tourism hotspots while examining measures to improve insurance coverage against climate-related losses.
• "These events are becoming a more significant and, in many respects, more frequent and severe risk phenomenon," Arghyrou told Reuters. "This is a medium, long-term fiscal risk, not just for Greece, but the whole of the Mediterranean area."
• To address those risks, the government is pursuing an investment strategy aimed at strengthening water and energy infrastructure in tourism hotspots from Mykonos to Santorini, while also seeking to attract private capital, Arghyrou told Reuters.
• The strategy also targets Epirus, the North Aegean islands, Thessaloniki, Crete, Rhodes and the Peloponnese, where the release of Christopher Nolan's film "The Odyssey" has fueled growing tourist interest.
• Hotter summers are extending the tourism season, drawing visitors from as early as April through October and November, a trend Arghyrou said was helping support tourism revenues.
• Arghyrou declined to say how much public funding would be allocated to the strategy, but said additional investment would be financed largely through higher tax revenues generated by a crackdown on Greece's informal economy.
• Greece has no plans to issue catastrophe bonds, which provide funding after major disasters, though Arghyrou said the idea merited consideration.
• The government is exploring incentives to boost insurance coverage among households and businesses while encouraging insurers to offer affordable policies.
• Prime Minister Mitsotakis is expected to unveil tax incentives for businesses, workers and the self-employed next month ahead of a general election next year. Arghyrou said the measures would not come at the expense of fiscal discipline. REUTERS

US military operations killed 153 civilians in Yemen in 2025
US military operations in 2025 killed 153 civilians and wounded 243, all occurring in Yemen, a US official said on Tuesday, citing Pentagon assessments.
This compares with a Pentagon assessment that two civilians were killed and two were injured by US military operations in 2024.
A Pentagon report submitted to the US Congress and published by US media said that all the death and injury tolls against civilians recorded in 2025 were due to three US strikes in Yemen.
The Pentagon report said the US Central Command had assessed that the three strikes in April 2025 in Yemen "more likely than not" resulted in civilian harm.
The Pentagon report also said that as of February 2026, there were 15 other incidents in Yemen that the US Central Command was currently assessing in response to reports received through non-governmental organisations.
The US military says it aims to degrade the capabilities of Iran-backed Houthi militants in Yemen.
The Pentagon report did not include any casualties from US strikes in the Caribbean and Eastern Pacific.
The report said as of 1 February 2026, the US Southern Command assessed that "there were no incidents in which civilian casualties more likely than not resulted from U.S. military operations in the USSOUTHCOM area of responsibility in 2025."
President Donald Trump's administration has struck vessels that it accuses of transporting narcotics in the Eastern Pacific, casting its targets as "narco-terrorists."
The US military's strikes on such vessels have killed more than 200 people since September 2025, according to a tally of death tolls published after each strike.
Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International consider such strikes unlawful extrajudicial killings. The American Civil Liberties Union casts the assertions by the Trump administration against those it targets as "unsubstantiated, fear-mongering claims."

AI inhibits job prospects of young people, says Geneva-based ILO
Artificial intelligence (AI) is making it harder for young people to land their first job, according to the Geneva-based International Labour Organisation (ILO).
Weak economic growth, cautious recruitment policies, geopolitical tensions and rapid technological change are also impacting the job market for young adults, the ILO added.
In particular, the jobs through which many young people have traditionally entered the workforce could change particularly rapidly as a result of automation and generative AI.
The ILO cites commercial and administrative roles, jobs in sales and the service sector, as well as positions in manufacturing and certain technical professions. Whilst some jobs will remain, they will entail new requirements.
More
How artificial intelligence is shaping the Swiss job market
Digital skills, the ability to monitor AI outputs and an understanding of when human judgement remains essential will therefore be in demand. At the same time, demand continues to grow in knowledge-intensive technical professions, such as the natural sciences, engineering, healthcare and information and communication technologies.
The organisation is therefore calling for greater investment in high-quality education, vocational training, lifelong learning and apprenticeships.
+ Read about how the future of work will change
According to the ILO, youth unemployment rose from 12.3% to 12.4% between 2023 and 2025. This corresponds to 67 million people aged between 15 and 24.
The sharpest increases were recorded in North Africa, North America and Europe. In Europe, the rate stood at 15%, according to these figures.

                    MINSK, 12 August (BelTA) – Around Br1 billion is planned to be allocated for the repair of local roads in Brest Oblast in 2026-2030, Deputy Director General of the Brestobldorstroi road construction company Sergei Demko said in a new episode of BelTA’s project The Nation Speaks.

However, according to inspections, only 31% of our roads are currently in need of repair.”
Reviewing the results of 2025, the final year of the previous stage of the Roads of Belarus state program, it was noted that Brestobldorstroi had been set a target to repair 302km of roads. “In fact, works were completed on 425.4km, meaning we exceeded the plan. Just over Br166 million (nearly Br167 million) was allocated and utilized for these purposes,” Sergei Demko said.
He also emphasized that funding for the Roads of Belarus program increases significantly with each subsequent stage. “Funding for local roads in Brest Oblast between 2021 and 2025 was nearly half of what is planned for the 2026–2030 phase. For the new period, around Br1 billion is set to be allocated for the local road network, with a target to repair just over 2,200km,” he said.

Companies embrace IPOs but investors turn more cautious
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
07:56:47 UTC
16:56:47 KST

The enthusiasm of companies seeking alternative financing through initial public offerings (IPOs) continues to grow, with firms awaiting approval from Türkiye’s Capital Markets Board (SPK) gradually making their way onto the stock exchange.
While 18 companies went public in the whole of 2025, 29 firms were listed in the first seven months of this year alone. However, investor response and IPO returns have weakened compared with previous years.
Companies, driven by high borrowing costs, have accelerated their search for alternative sources of financing. In the first seven months of the year, the number of IPOs exceeded the total recorded in 2025. The 18 companies that went public last year raised a combined 45 billion Turkish Liras, while the 29 firms listed through the end of July this year raised 66.7 billion liras. July alone accounted for 61 percent of those IPOs.
Unlike 2024, when nearly every IPO was met with consecutive limit-up gains, the current market has seen a much more mixed performance. While some newly listed shares have posted only modest gains, others are now trading below their offering prices. As a result, IPO performance has lacked a clear direction. Demand for new offerings has also been neither particularly strong nor particularly weak.
Applications for public offerings that built up at the SPK following the pandemic have begun to receive approvals in small batches this year, but whether investor demand and returns have met expectations remains open to debate.
Onur Can Bal, at Gedik Investment, said investor interest in IPOs has not disappeared but is no longer strong. He noted that fresh liquidity entering the stock market has remained limited this year and that investors have often sold existing holdings in order to participate in new offerings, putting pressure on the benchmark BIST 100 index.
“IPO performances have shown a differentiated picture this year. Sharp moves in some stocks have also left investors feeling trapped. The IPO rally seen in 2024 was a frenzy unique to that period,” Bal said.
According to Bal, the outlook for the Turkish stock market during the remainder of the year will depend on geopolitical risks and the timing of interest-rate cuts. He said higher oil prices linked to the Iran conflict have kept inflationary pressures alive and contributed to stagnation in equities.
Bal also said foreign investor inflows have remained limited, while high lira interest rates have curbed domestic investors’ appetite for stocks.
“The main condition for a stock market rally is the start of interest-rate cuts. Depending on developments regarding the Strait of Hormuz, oil prices continue to sustain inflation concerns and keep central banks cautious,” he added.
“For this reason, it is difficult to forecast where the BIST 100 index will stand at year-end. If rate cuts begin, we could see gains in the stock market, but no one can clearly predict when that will happen,” Bal said.

Lebanon's parliament votes to abolish death penalty, Hezbollah votes against bill
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
07:55:24 UTC
16:55:24 KST

Lebanon’s parliament voted Tuesday to abolish the death penalty, a major move welcomed by international bodies and human rights organizations.
Although a majority of the 128 members of parliament voted in favor of the bill, Hezbollah’s parliamentary bloc notably voted against ending capital punishment.
The legislation will now go before Lebanon’s cabinet before being submitted to President Joseph Aoun for approval.
It has been more than 20 years since Lebanon last carried out an execution. In January 2004, Ahmad Ali Mansour, Badi Hamadeh, and Remi Antoan Zaatar were executed in connection with separate murder cases involving multiple victims.
Hamadeh, who was executed by firing squad, was convicted of killing three security officers during a 2002 raid on his fiancée’s home. Mansour, who was hanged, was convicted of murdering eight of his colleagues when he opened fire at a teachers’ pension fund in 2002. Zaatar was also hanged after being convicted of killing three people during an armed robbery.
UN, European Commission officials welcome decision
UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk congratulated Lebanon on becoming the first country in the Middle East to ban the death penalty.
“In a country subject to devastating attacks and experiencing profound loss and suffering, this decision represents a powerful and principled commitment to the right to life,” he said.
Kaja Kallas, vice president of the European Commission, also welcomed parliament’s decision in a statement Tuesday.
“The abolition of the death penalty for all crimes, including through its retroactive application, is an important achievement,” Kallas said. She added that the move builds on Lebanon’s de facto moratorium on executions, maintained since 2004, and demonstrates the country’s commitment to respecting, protecting, and fulfilling the right to life.
“As the first country in the region to abolish the death penalty, Lebanon is setting a powerful example for other countries in the Middle East and beyond, reinforcing the strong global trend towards abolition and the growing international support for ending the death penalty worldwide,” Kallas said.
The movement to ban the death penalty comes only days after Judge Rabih Houssami sentenced Syrian national Bassel Attieh al-Hamdeh for the sexual assault and murder of 26-year-old Rayyah Chidac in 2017.
As of the end of January 2026, 85 people remained on death row, according to the Directorate of Prisons at Lebanon’s Justice Ministry.

How Britain’s mapmakers track climate change
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
07:55:00 UTC
16:55:00 KST

How Britain’s mapmakers track climate change
SOUTHAMPTON, Britain – Once used to defend Britain’s shores against Napoleonic France, the Ordnance Survey’s (OS) detailed maps are now essential for tracking and adapting to climate change.
“I would argue there is no clearer way to see the impact of climate change than looking at a traditional map,” Tom Gray, a utilities and transport expert for Britain’s national mapping agency, told AFP.
He was sitting in front of an aerial photograph of dry land projected onto a big screen at the OS headquarters in the port city of Southampton, southern England.
Here, hundreds of people work to collect location data and maintain the National Geographic Database, which includes more than 600 million features, monitoring “almost anything you can think of” and updated 30,000 times a day, Gray said.
The OS first started mapping Britain 230 years ago and has since documented the changes in the country’s topography.
“There’s a noticeable change in habitats, mainly because of human intervention... but also the direct impacts of climate change, especially around waterways,” said Gray.
On the screen behind him, he cycled through OS maps of the country, highlighting where climate-related subsidence is likely to happen, which homes bordering rural areas are at the highest risk of wildfire, and which parts of the country face flooding – the biggest climate threat to Britain, according to him.
“Twelve per cent of all of the UK’s strategic road network is in the highest risk zone for flooding, and 20 per cent of the rail network is,” Gray said.
“When an emergency service worker needs to attend a flood, they can use our data to determine exactly where the hotspots are for flooding, where it’s most likely to happen, and how they can access that property,” he explained.
Climate emergencies
Many services rely on OS data to react to climate emergencies.
“There was some coastal erosion across on the Isle of Wight (off the coast of southern England) that needed to be updated quickly,” Helen Jones recalled.
She is one of 21 drone pilots for the OS, in charge of collecting footage to track changes on the ground.
“We flew the site with the drone to update the mapping, which allowed other agencies like emergency services and councils to look at that particular area and predict where they might have to cut off gas and water, and potentially evacuate people.”
She spoke to AFP from Winchester, near Southampton, where she was filming a new housing development.
“If that rural land has any issues in terms of fires or flooding, if the estate isn’t mapped, (emergency services) won’t know that people will be in trouble or that there needs to be a certain response,” she said.
The footage she was collecting will be sent to the OS’s headquarters, where specialists add it to maps, capturing all the changes on the ground within 1cm and including everything from buildings to bins and lampposts.
The process of turning her drone footage into maps is so detailed that a single block can take several hours, said specialist Sean Kennedy, armed with 3D glasses to better identify objects.
Such detail is important so that the authorities can see where access points to the housing estate are, useful when planning for climate emergencies such as wildfires.
“It’s quite good when we come out on site because people come and ask what you’re doing and we’re able to explain that actually, because the emergency services use our data, it’s really important that we get their house on the map,” Jones said.
She has been a surveyor for seven years and said she is seeing the impact of the drought in 2026, as England and Wales experienced their driest July on record, according to the Met Office weather agency.
“I think everyone’s going to have to start taking (climate change) seriously,” Jones added.
“I’ve not had a summer where we haven’t had any kind of rain. And we can’t fly in rain so it’s been good in terms of drone footage, but it’s not good for anything else.” AFP

07:54:49 UTC
16:54:49 KST

IDF reservists are growing frustrated with constantly pursuing Israelis who try to cross the Syrian border, particularly from the "HaBashan Pioneers" movement, multiple soldiers told Army Radio in a report published on Wednesday.
"It's absurd that we're stopping our lives for this," one reserve soldier serving in the Syria sector said.
"We're exhausted! I'm putting my life on hold; there are students here, people with families, kids at home, and instead of dealing with the important things, this is what we're doing. It raises questions and doubts: what are we even doing here?" he asked.
The reservists serving in the Syria sector spent Tuesday night in another pursuit that they told Army Radio endangered their own safety and was an unnecessary use of resources.
"We found ourselves for several hours during the night in the Hermon, searching for them; they hid among trees and bushes in steep and dangerous spots. We chased them, climbed boulders; we're putting ourselves at risk of injuries, falls, on very, very steep slopes," one said.
"We're wasting a ton of resources, time, and energy on this stuff. This isn't our mission; the mission is to protect the sector and the settlements," the soldiers told Army Radio.
Police fail to deter repeat offenses
Additionally, reservists describe the lack of support from other agencies. After the Tuesday night pursuit, soldiers were forced to look after the three Israelis at the outpost until they were retrieved.
Eventually, when the police still hadn't shown up, the soldiers called the 100 emergency service hotline.
"We told them: Come get them, and that's what happened. If we hadn't called 100, no one would have come. Just a total game of passing the buck between all the agencies," one reservist said.
Once the police do come, the reservists warn that those who cross the border are often not dealt with effectively and may come back a second or third time.
"The police aren't doing their job properly, because if a guy gets arrested and released the same day, then comes back the next, we haven't accomplished anything here. We tried explaining to them, you're getting in the way of us doing our job. We're dealing with you way too much," the reservist said.
"Three years of reserves, and what am I busy with? Pulling Israeli civilians out of Syria?" they added.

UK’s biggest power supplier issues solar eclipse warning
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
07:54:34 UTC
16:54:34 KST

UK’s biggest power supplier issues solar eclipse warning
Britain’s biggest household power supplier, Octopus Energy, has asked customers to cut electricity use for two hours on Wednesday to cope with a solar eclipse during peak demand.
A total eclipse of the Sun – the first visible from mainland Europe since 1999 – will occur on August 12 from 15:00 to 19:00 GMT (4-8 PM London time). The UK is expected to experience a deep partial eclipse, with around 90% to 96% of the Sun obscured.
The National Energy System Operator (NESO), which runs Britain’s grid, estimates solar generation could fall by up to 1.3 gigawatts – equivalent to the power used by around 1 million homes.
With the eclipse partly coinciding with peak evening demand, Octopus Energy asked its roughly 8 million UK customers on Monday to avoid using appliances and devices such as dishwashers, games consoles, and washing machines from 6-8 PM.
The voluntary scheme offers households that comply one hour of free electricity on August 16. Customers who share photos on social media showing what they did outside instead of using power can also win free solar panels and installation or a £12,000 ($16,200) cash alternative.
Octopus believes that if enough households delay electricity use during the eclipse, it could reduce the need for Britain’s grid operator to fire up additional gas-powered stations to replace lost solar generation.
Solar Energy UK recently reported that solar accounted for 14.4% of UK electricity generation in July, a monthly record, while a single-day record of 19.5% was set in late May. NESO data shows renewables now account for around 40% of Britain’s energy mix, up from 30% five years ago.
Persistent energy woes
The news comes as the UK – a major Western sponsor of the Kiev regime and leading advocate of sanctions on Russia – continues to grapple with high energy costs after largely cutting itself off from cheap Russian energy following the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in 2022.
Direct imports of Russian coal, crude oil, and refined petroleum products fell to zero by mid-2022, forcing British suppliers to accelerate the shift to renewables and secure alternative imports. Growing reliance on costly liquefied natural gas (LNG) has left Britain paying premiums on the global market and more exposed to price volatility.
Greater dependence on wind and solar has brought its own challenges, as output fluctuates with weather and daylight, requiring backup capacity. According to Ofgem, the average household energy bill this year is expected to be around £1,862 – almost 50% higher than in 2021.
The US war against Iran put further pressure on Britain this year. In May, it was forced to delay some sanctions on Russian oil and LNG to help contain soaring prices as the conflict disrupted global supplies.
London issued a trade license allowing imports of jet fuel and diesel refined from Russian crude in third countries, while another waived restrictions on shipping LNG from two Russian terminals. Former Bank of England Deputy Governor Howard Davies recently warned that Britain could be heading toward an energy crisis comparable to the 1970s, when oil prices quadrupled following the 1973 Arab-Israeli War and an embargo by Arab producers on Western nations.
Moscow has warned that sanctions, particularly those targeting energy, are illegal and self-defeating, and will backfire on the countries that impose them. Russia has also signaled that it is prepared to fill oil supply gaps caused by the Middle East conflict and resume deliveries to European countries, but says it has received no response.

Borino launches first plan for coexistence with bears in Bulgaria
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
07:53:04 UTC
16:53:04 KST

Author
Yanitsa Marova
Wednesday 12 August 2026 08:50
Wednesday, 12 August 2026, 08:50
PHOTO wwf.bg
Font size
Borino becomes the first municipality in Bulgaria with a plan for
peaceful coexistence with bears, which will be implemented in stages.
The idea is for it to start operating comprehensively in the autumn and aims
at limiting conflicts through a combination of preventive measures -
electric fences, protected garbage containers, cameras and devices
that drive away bears with light and sound.
The first video cameras are expected to be installed this week. They
will monitor apiaries, flocks of sheep and tourist sites around which
bear visits have already been registered. This will identify the
so-called "hot spots" - the places through which the
animals most often reach human properties and food sources.
At
this stage, about seven to eight potential problem areas have been
identified. However, their number may change depending on new signals
and camera data.
PHOTO wwf.bg
The installation of electric fences and
bear-proof waste containers is also expected to begin in September.
It is planned to initially provide between 20 and 30 electric fences,
as their number can increase if necessary.
The
electric fences will be provided free of charge to farmers, but they
will have to take care of the equipment. According to the experience
of other European countries, similar measures can almost completely
prevent bears from accessing apiaries and food waste containers
PHOTO krib.bg
In some Romanian towns located in an area with many bears, the combination of protected containers, electric fences and the removal of easily accessible food sources has reduced the problems to almost zero, experts say.
In Borino it is also planned to test devices for scaring away bears, which use a sudden flashing light and a variable high-frequency sound. The aim is to prevent bears from getting used to the signal. Similar technology has already been used successfully in Greece and Italy.
The problem of bears entering people’s neighbourhoods is exacerbated in years when there is not enough food in the wild. In 2023 and 2025, for example, a shortage of wild berries led to more cases of bears foraging around human settlements. Warm winters can also change the animals’ behaviour and easy access to food waste attracts them.
PHOTO wwf.bg
Among the most sensitive areas in the Rhodopes are the municipality of Banite and the area around Smilyan. According to experts, the depopulation of mountain villages is also important - old pastures and agricultural territories are gradually turning into dense forest areas and the remaining fruit trees provide additional food for the bears.
Along with the technical measures, educational activities with students are also planned in Borino. They will take place in the autumn, when the bears are particularly active.
Experts say that the goal is not to drive the animals out of the mountains, but to prevent them from becoming accustomed to human food. The bear plays an important role in the ecosystem – it spreads seeds, helps the natural regeneration of vegetation and feeds on dead animals, thus also performing a sanitary function. As a species that needs large territories, it is also a kind of indicator of the state of the mountain ecosystem.
PHOTO wwf.bg
The exact number of brown bears in Bulgaria has not yet been established. Official estimates are for about 400-500 animals, while according to representatives of hunting and forestry circles, their number may exceed 1300. More accurate information is expected to be provided by genetic monitoring, during which about 4000 samples were collected last year. Their analysis should show not only the number of bears, but also their sex, family ties and genetic condition.
In Borino, the goal is clear – to prevent conflicts before they cause damage to the owners or dangerous habituation of the bears to human presence. The project is being implemented with the participation of the environmental organization WWF and the local authorities. Experience has been gained from the USA, Italy, Greece and several settlements in Romania, where similar measures are already yielding results.

Canadian firm wins $212M deal to train British soldiers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
07:50:11 UTC
16:50:11 KST

- Calian UK signed a 15-year agreement worth approximately $212 million to support the British Army's Collective Training Service starting October 2026.
- The deal extends Calian's prior Project NUMIDIAN work as part of the Raytheon UK-led Omnia Training consortium.
The British Army has locked in a 15-year training contract worth roughly $212 million with a Canadian defense company that has become one of the country’s most reliable simulation and training providers overseas.
Calian Group, an Ottawa-based company that builds and delivers training programs, engineering, and other mission-critical services for defense and space clients, announced Tuesday that its UK subsidiary, Calian UK, has signed a long-term agreement with Raytheon UK to support the British Army’s Collective Training Service, known by the acronym ACTS. Raytheon UK is the lead contractor for a consortium called Omnia Training, and Raytheon itself operates as a business unit of the American defense giant RTX.
Collective training refers to exercises that bring soldiers, commanders, and allied forces together in realistic, often high-stress operational environments designed to test how well units coordinate, communicate, and fight together before they ever deploy for real. It differs from individual soldier training, which focuses on a single person’s marksmanship or physical fitness, by instead testing whether an entire company, battalion, or coalition force can function as one system under pressure. Western militaries have leaned harder into this kind of training over the past decade as combat has grown more complex, requiring infantry, armor, artillery, air support, and increasingly drones and electronic warfare units to operate in sync rather than in isolation.
The new agreement takes effect in October 2026, once the current contract, known as Project NUMIDIAN, wraps up. Calian has run NUMIDIAN for years as its support vehicle for delivering collective training services to the British Army, exposing troops to contemporary battlefield threats meant to mirror what they might actually face in a modern conflict. The transition to ACTS extends that relationship rather than replacing it, giving Calian continuity on one of its largest defense training contracts while folding the work into a broader modernization effort the British Army has undertaken alongside industry partners.
Chris Pogue, Calian’s President of Defence and Space, framed the deal as part of a larger philosophy about what actually prepares troops for combat.
“Military readiness begins long before a mission starts; it begins with training that prepares troops to operate with confidence in complex, high-pressure environments,” said Chris Pogue, President, Defence and Space, Calian. “We’re proud to continue supporting the British Army through ACTS alongside Raytheon UK and our Omnia Training partners. This agreement reflects the trust our allies place in Calian’s expertise and strengthens our position as a leading provider of collective training and simulation solutions that respond effectively to real-world conditions.”
James Gray, the Managing Director and Chief Executive of Raytheon UK, described the Omnia Training consortium’s broader ambition for reshaping how the British Army trains.
“Omnia Training brings together world-class organisations with proven expertise in military training and simulation,” said James Gray, Managing Director and Chief Executive, Raytheon UK. “Our UK based team of innovators, engineers and experts will give soldiers and commanders a new level of training realism and set an example for effective collaboration between the Army and industry.”
Under ACTS, Calian will keep delivering specialist collective training services while helping modernize how the British Army trains through what the company describes as advanced digital, synthetic, and integrated training capabilities. Synthetic training refers to simulation environments, often built around virtual reality, computer modeling, or networked simulators, that let soldiers rehearse combat scenarios without the cost, safety risk, or environmental footprint of live-fire exercises using real ammunition and vehicles across open terrain. Militaries around the world have invested heavily in synthetic training over the past decade because it allows far more repetitions of a scenario at a fraction of the cost, and because it can recreate threats, like massed drone attacks or electronic warfare jamming, that would be dangerous or impossible to simulate safely in a live environment.
The deal arrives as Western militaries broadly reassess how they prepare troops for the kind of warfare unfolding in Ukraine, where drones, electronic warfare, and long-range precision strikes have upended assumptions about what makes a unit survivable on a modern battlefield. Britain has repeatedly signaled that it wants its own training programs to reflect those lessons rather than rehearsing for a previous era of conflict, and Calian’s legacy work under Project NUMIDIAN specifically emphasized exposing troops to what the company calls contemporary threats, language that points toward exactly that kind of updated battlefield realism.
For Calian, the agreement reinforces a defense business built over decades around collective training, simulation, systems engineering, and interoperability, the ability of different military units, equipment, and even allied nations to work together smoothly despite using different systems and procedures. The company has positioned itself as a specialist that helps militaries and coalition partners operate effectively across what it calls increasingly complex, multi-domain environments, a term referring to combat that spans land, air, sea, cyber, and space simultaneously rather than unfolding in a single traditional battlespace.

Solar eclipse: What to look forward to
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
07:50:00 UTC
16:50:00 KST

Solar eclipse: What to look forward to
August 12, 2026
On Wednesday, about 980 million people across parts of the Northern Hemisphere will have the chance to observe this upcoming solar eclipse.
They will be joined by hosts of researchers who will be taking advantage of the fleeting minutes when the sun's corona is visible from Earth to test specialized instruments and capture rare images. With them, they hope to gain a deeper appreciation of the material above the sun's surface.
What's going to happen?
During a solar eclipse, the moon orbits between Earth and the sun during the daytime, casting a shadow which temporarily darkens the sky and appears to blot out the sun. At the height of an eclipse, the moon's disk appears to align with the sun, revealing the sun's corona — its outermost atmosphere that flares outward like a crown (hence the name).
As the moon approaches and the sky darkens, you might also notice the temperature dropping, shadows appearing crescent-shaped, the wind beginning to shift and animals behaving unusually.
Solar panels will be able to produce less energy in this time. In Germany, this is expected to lead to a brief surge in electricity prices.
Right before the eclipse reaches its maximum point, known as totality, watch out for Baily's beads. These are the final rays of sun reaching Earth through valleys on the moon's surface. They appear as white specks encircling the moon like a string of pearls.
As night closes in during totality, keep an eye out for the stars that appear. Some might even be able to catch a glimpse of auroras or passing meteors.
Where will the eclipse occur?
If you live in Greenland, Iceland, northern Russia, northern Spain or northeastern Portugal, you're in luck! Viewers in these locations will be able to observe a total solar eclipse.
In most of Western Europe, as well as parts of northern Africa and northern America, astronomy enthusiasts will still be able to watch a partial solar eclipse.
And this is just the first of two eclipses in August. The second will take place on August 27-28, when Earth moves between the sun and the moon to create a lunar eclipse.
The next solar eclipse will happen February 2, 2027, over much of Africa, South America, as well as parts of Antarctica.
While eclipses themselves are fairly frequent occurrences, it's not that often that a total solar eclipse is visible on inhabited parts of the globe. The last solar eclipse visible for most of mainland Europe, for example, was in 1999.
What time is the eclipse happening?
The spectacle will begin at 15:34 GMT, with the moon slowly dimming the sun's light as it creeps into position. About two hours later, at 17:46 GMT, the eclipse will reach totality for about two minutes.
But where on the globe you are watching from will make a difference. While Icelanders will be able to observe the eclipse's totality at 17:48 GMT, viewers in Spain will have to wait until 18:27 for their chance.
Where can I watch the eclipse?
Since the eclipse is happening relatively late in the day, viewers are recommended to watch from high places to catch a good view of the sun as it dips toward the horizon. Most west-facing hills, towers and (safe) rooftops with an unobstructed view should do the trick.
If you're the kind who prefers crisper images, NASA is also offering a livestream.
Can I wear normal sunglasses to watch the eclipse?
In short, no. Looking directly into the sun can cause permanent damage to the retina at the back of your eye. Ordinary sunglasses, even polarized ones, are far too weak to provide enough protection.
Instead, you'll need certified ISO 12312-2 glasses, available at most pharmacies and opticians. Most are sold out already, but there are plenty of directions online for building a pinhole camera to safely watch the eclipse with small children.
You can also use a kitchen colander, or any other tool with small holes, to project tiny crescent-shaped shadows onto a safe surface.
Whether or not you are wearing eclipse glasses, never look at the sun through a camera, telescope or binoculars without a specialized filter, as the concentrated light can cause serious damage to your eyes.
Edited by: Martin Kuebler

Mental health services lose track of 62,500 people, says report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
07:49:33 UTC
16:49:33 KST

Mental health services lose track of 62,500 people, says report
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
A quarter of adults with a severe mental illness in the Netherlands – an estimated 62,500 people – are receiving no or insufficient care and have dropped out of sight of mental health services altogether, according to a report from the sector body de Nederlandse GGZ.
The organisation puts the total number of adults with a severe mental illness at around 250,000. What goes wrong, it says, is rarely the treatment itself but the handover – the point at which someone leaves a clinic, moves house or finishes a prison sentence.
“A discharge from a clinic, a house move or the end of a period in detention must not become the moment at which someone loses their support,” GGZ chair Ruth Peetoom said in a statement on Tuesday. “A psychological vulnerability does not disappear when a care pathway or an assessment comes to an end.”
Nowhere to go
 The housing crisis is one of the biggest obstacles in helping patients through the transition out of care. The report calculates that 3,980 social housing units are needed each year for people leaving sheltered accommodation, but only 1,320 came free in 2023.
Around 33,000 people aged between 18 and 65 were registered as homeless at the start of 2024.
The pattern is similar for people leaving prison. Of the roughly 5,000 people released each year after more than three months inside, 27% are homeless or have no known address immediately afterwards, and almost half reoffend within two years.
Outreach 
 The report calls for assertive outreach – teams that actively go looking for people who are not asking for help – to be made a statutory duty for councils again.
It has not been one since social care was devolved in 2015, and funding is now split between health insurers, councils and central government, on top of the pressure on waiting lists that has already prompted legal action against the state.
Debate about severe mental illness in the Netherlands is dominated by figures on nuisance and public safety, the report says. It puts the number of people who pose a safety risk to others at around 1,500, against 24,000 to 60,000 who are a risk to themselves, through self-neglect, homelessness or avoiding care.
If you are struggling with your mental health, support is available. The MIND Hulplijn offers free, anonymous advice on 0900-1450, on weekdays from 9am to 9pm, or via mindhulplijn.nl. In a crisis, contact your family doctor or call 113.

Ukraine hits grain terminals at Russia’s Novorossiysk port, killing three
Russia’s Novorossiysk ‘endured a horrific night’, with a child killed and dozens of buildings damaged, says local mayor.
Ukraine has pounded Russia’s Black Sea port city of Novorossiysk in a massive overnight drone attack that killed three people and put two major grain terminals out of action, according to local officials, raising fears in global markets of a disruption to supplies.
Veniamin Kondratyev, the governor of Krasnodar region, where Novorossiysk is located, said on Wednesday that a child was among those killed, with 24 people wounded in the attack.

Russia is the world’s largest wheat exporter and most of those exports are shipped via its Black Sea ports. Russia’s main grain lobby group warned last month that Ukrainian attacks could shut down grain exports via the Black Sea in the near future, pushing up prices and causing hunger in Africa and the Middle East.
Al Jazeera’s Yulia Shapovalova, reporting from Moscow, said Ukrainian drones “heavily pounded” the Novorossiysk port, through which “a significant share of [Russia’s] domestic grain exports” pass.

“Novorossiysk endured a horrific night,” Andrei Kravchenko, the mayor of the city, wrote in a post on Telegram.

In Ukraine’s southeastern city of Zaporizhzhia, a Russian attack triggered a blaze at a shopping mall, according to regional governor Ivan Fedorov. He shared pictures and a video of a building on fire.
The attack cut off power for some 1,200 consumers in Zaporizhzhia, Fedorov added.
A separate Russian attack on Odesa, Ukraine’s largest seaport, damaged infrastructure there, said the head of the city’s military administration, Serhiy Lysak.
Russia’s Defence Ministry claimed it hit a fuel depot in the port of Odesa, which it said was used to supply the Ukrainian army. Elsewhere, the ministry said its forces had taken control of the village of Vodiane, in Ukraine’s northeastern Kharkiv region.
Moscow has recently intensified strikes on Ukraine’s food, agriculture and warehouse facilities, in response to Kyiv’s attacks on Russian energy, port and logistics hubs.
Zelenskyy said on Tuesday that Kyiv had handed proposals to US negotiators for a plan to end the war, which started with Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
According to a Financial Times report citing Ukrainian officials, Kyiv has also committed to halting drone strikes on oil tankers using the Novorossiysk port after a request at the end of last month from United States Vice President JD Vance.
Talks to end Russia’s war on Ukraine have largely stalled since the US and Israel launched their war on Iran.
Ukraine has repeatedly called for a ceasefire after years of fighting. Russia says it wants a settlement, but any solution must involve Ukraine fully ceding four regions Moscow claims, as well as resolving the conflict’s “root causes”. Ukraine has rejected those demands.

SBU officers exposed the subversive activities of the enemy agents in advance, documented their crimes and detained all four members. ====================================================================================================

Italy’s ‘Fort Knox of cheese’ feels the heat as climate change drives up costs and risks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
07:42:09 UTC
16:42:09 KST

Italy’s unusual “cheese banks” are being forced to spend significantly more on energy as Europe’s heat wave threatens hundreds of thousands of wheels of Parmigiano Reggiano held as collateral for loans.
Credito Emiliano, which operates two major storage facilities holding cheese valued at about $350 million, has upgraded cooling and heating systems, improved insulation and expanded its use of renewable energy to keep conditions stable. Even so, extreme heat is pushing daily electricity consumption at the facilities up by about 30%, squeezing profitability as the bank works to maintain the precise temperature and humidity required for the cheese to mature safely.
The model, in place since 1953, allows Parmesan producers to receive an advance worth roughly 60% to 80% of a wheel’s value while the cheese is still young. The wheels then age for between 12 and 36 months in bank-controlled warehouses in Reggio Emilia and Modena before reaching full market value.
Around 500,000 wheels are held in such “cheese banks,” out of total annual Italian production of roughly 4 million wheels. One vault alone contains cheese worth more than 300 million euros. A bank spokesman described the facility as the “Fort Knox of cheese,” noting that high outdoor temperatures require increasingly large amounts of energy to preserve the stable environment the product needs.
The heat is also affecting the industry before the cheese even reaches storage. Cows eat less and become less active during periods of extreme heat, reducing milk output by as much as 10% and affecting both the quantity and quality of milk available for production.
That vulnerability is increasingly becoming part of lenders’ credit-risk calculations. If climate conditions reduce production or damage aging cheese, the value of the collateral underpinning the loans can also be affected.
The broader Parmesan economy is estimated at about $4.7 billion, making climate-related disruption a concern not only for farmers and cheesemakers but also for lenders whose financing model depends on the future value of the product.
The same heat is disrupting other key parts of Italy’s food and beverage industry.
In Lombardy, the 2026 wine harvest began on July 30, the earliest start on record, while producers in Sicily stretched harvesting across nearly 100 days in an effort to cope with repeated heat waves.
Italian agricultural organization Coldiretti estimated additional costs of about 250 euros per hectare for energy, fertilizer and other inputs, while export values fell 7% during the first four months of 2026.
Olive oil production has also been affected. National output this year is estimated at around 270,000 to 300,000 tons, compared with a historical average of more than 350,000 tons.
Economists warn that the headline losses may understate the longer-term damage because heat shocks can ripple through supply chains. Lower output at one stage can create shortages and higher costs elsewhere months later, magnifying the financial impact.
At the same time, Italy has pushed back the planned closure of its coal-fired power plants to 2038 amid cost pressures, highlighting the tension between climate-related disruption and the pace of Europe’s transition to renewable energy.
For Italy’s cheese banks, that tension is already tangible. The hotter the climate becomes, the more expensive it is to preserve the cold, controlled conditions on which both Parmesan production and a decades-old lending model depend.

The repatriation of three Latvian climbers who died in Alaska from the United States to Latvia has been completed, the Latvian Ministry of Foreign Affairs told the LETA news agency.
The repatriation process was organised by Latvian insurers in cooperation with partner companies in the United States. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs stressed that the repatriation was carried out in accordance with US rules and procedures.
As previously reported, three Latvian climbers – Inese Pučeka, Vija Olte and Renārs Kunigs-Salaks – died in late May after falling on a steep slope of Denali, the highest mountain in North America. Another member of the expedition, Mārtiņš Bilzēns, was taken to a hospital in Anchorage in serious condition.
Meanwhile, three other members of the expedition – Puriņš, Edgars Madžulis and Guntis Svariņš – were evacuated from the mountain with the assistance of rescuers. Two of them were diagnosed with frostbite.
According to information provided by the Latvian Embassy in the United States,
ALL THREE DECEASED CLIMBERS WERE BROUGHT DOWN FROM DENALI DURING THE NIGHT LEADING INTO the 4th of June,
Latvian time.
According to the US National Park Service, the accident occurred on the climbing route between the mountain’s upper camp, known as High Camp, and Denali Pass, beginning near Denali Pass at an altitude of approximately 18,200 feet, or 5,545 metres.
Information published on the National Park Service website on the 28th of May indicated that, in the first incident, two climbers were evacuated from the mountain at around 11 p.m. local time. The service later clarified that this was a separate incident.
Around midnight, National Park Service rangers received a second report stating that four climbers from a seven-member team had fallen in the Denali Pass area. Three climbers returned to High Camp after assisting their fallen teammates.
The expedition team previously told LETA that
the Latvian climbers’ high-altitude expedition had been scheduled to take place from the 10th of May to the 11th of June.
Its objective was to reach the summit of Denali, North America’s highest peak at 6,190 metres.
Denali is one of the world’s highest mountains situated closest to the Arctic Circle. The climbers had previously stressed that the expedition was not so much about altitude as it was about extreme cold. They expected temperatures of minus 30°C, storms and more than three weeks of living in tents on snow, while carrying 25-kilogram backpacks and, at the beginning of the expedition, pulling sledges weighing another 25 kilograms.
The climbers had previously said that Puriņš, Madžulis and the late Pučeka had participated in two previous expeditions organised by clubs affiliated with the Latvian Mountaineering Association. They had reached the summits of Avicenna Peak at 7,134 metres, Ozodi Peak at 7,105 metres and Ismoil Somoni Peak at 7,495 metres, as well as completing a first ascent of a nearly 6,000-metre peak in the Mindžāras Valley in the Pamir Mountains, gaining extensive high-altitude experience.
It was also stated that the other members of expedition – the late Olte and Kunigs-Salaks, as well as Bilzēns, Zeimulis and Svariņš – had the necessary high-altitude mountaineering experience.
Denali’s summit lies only around 390 kilometres from the Arctic Circle.
The route begins at an altitude of 2,200 metres on the Kahiltna Glacier, which can only be reached by aircraft landing directly on the ice.
The climbers previously explained that after snowstorms, everyone at Base Camp helps pack down the snow so aircraft can land and take off safely. During the expedition, climbers must gain almost 4,000 metres in elevation and cover approximately 100 kilometres in total. Nearly every section of the route has to be travelled several times while transporting equipment and enough food for 25 days.

Continuing education becomes easier for children who've studied abroad
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
07:41:00 UTC
16:41:00 KST

Continuing education becomes easier for children who've studied abroad
The Ministry of Education and Research plans to change general upper secondary school admission requirements to ensure fair opportunities for students who have studied abroad or followed an international curriculum.
Admission to upper secondary school requires completion of basic education and the results of basic school final exams are often also an important criterion. However, this makes it difficult for young people who have studied abroad to continue their education in Estonia as the lack of final exam results often means they are directed to international schools, which does not support their integration or return to Estonian society.
Ülle Matsin, head of the Ministry of Education and Research's general and vocational secondary education department, said that every year, around 200 to 300 upper secondary school-age students who completed their basic education abroad want to continue their education in Estonia. Matsin added that children of compulsory school age living in Estonia are required to attend school in any case, which is why she does not consider it fair for children who have studied abroad to be denied admission to schools because they do not have exam results.
"A school has the right and also the obligation to assess and take into account the education acquired abroad. Students do not have to also take final exams in Estonia and schools must therefore describe in their admissions procedures how they will determine whether applications from students returning from abroad meet the requirements. This must be transparent and based on clearly defined criteria, just as it is for all other students."
Urmo Uiboleht, chair of the board of the Estonian Association of School Leaders and head of Tartu Private School, believes the change is important for both schools and students coming to Estonia. He said families arriving from abroad currently do not feel welcome in Estonia because it is difficult to find school places for their children. Equal opportunities would make the country more welcoming and attractive. At the same time, Uiboleht said the new regulation would increase schools' workload by giving them a new area of responsibility.
Matsin, however, said the change would not increase schools' workload because graduates from abroad already come to Estonia to study every year. She added that the change only clarifies admission requirements and does not create a new situation. Schools will, however, need to take into account that students who have studied abroad may have varying levels of Estonian proficiency.
"Schools now have the right to adapt their teaching. These students can, for example, be given an individual curriculum, which may include differences in course content and the amount of time spent studying, to help them bring their Estonian up to the required level."
Matsin said schools would not be left to handle the changes alone and that the Ministry of Education and Research is prepared to provide support in developing admission requirements.
"For example, in connection with the transition to Estonian-language education, we also have a wide range of teaching materials to support Estonian-language learning that schools can use."
In addition to creating fair admission requirements, the changes will also affect admission dates and give schools a clearer legal basis for requesting data from students' graduation certificates and transcripts.

====================================================================================================

Eclipse craze grips Spain, Iceland as millions get set for 'event of the century'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
07:39:58 UTC
16:39:58 KST

Europe looks to the skies as solar eclipse cast its shadow
BURGOS, Spain - Millions of people will turn their gaze towards the heavens on Aug 12 to witness one of nature’s greatest spectacles – a rare total solar eclipse – as it sweeps towards mainland Europe to briefly turn day into night.
The Moon is first expected to blot out the Sun from 5pm GMT (1am on Aug 13, Singapore time) in Russia’s remote Arctic north, leaving only the shimmering glow of its outer corona, before parts of Greenland and Iceland are enveloped in the arc of its eerie shadow.
Excitement was highest in Spain, where tourists thronged the streets of normally quiet villages to experience the dramatic natural phenomenon as the eclipse’s narrow path cuts across the Iberian Peninsula from the northern Atlantic coast to the Mediterranean Sea in the south.
Mainland Europe has not experienced a total solar eclipse for 20 years while Spain has not witnessed one in more than a century.
Iceland’s capital, Reykjavik, however, has not seen a total solar eclipse since 1433.
“It’s the first time and it’s the last time, the only time I’m going to see an eclipse,” Yenny Guevera, a 50-year-old Peruvian living in France, told AFP excitedly in Burgos, northwest Spain.
“I like painting and I really like light,” said Mercedes Bua, a 51-year-old engineer awaiting the eclipse’s passage in a park in Colmenar Viejo, some 30 kilometres north of Madrid.
“So I find it interesting to see how it’s going to look.”
Supplies of special viewing glasses were in high demand as a partial eclipse will be visible for millions more in most of Europe, Canada, the northern United States and north-west Africa.
Fleeting
Throughout human history, eclipses have stirred amazement, fear and reverence, as they appear to momentarily halt the normal course of nature.
The shadow or “umbra” cast by the alignment of Sun and Moon creates a strange twilight during which temperatures drop, shadows appear at strange angles and some animals go to sleep.
But the phenomenon is fleeting: in parts of Russia and Greenland, the total eclipse will last under two-and-a-half minutes.
In Spain, it will last less than two minutes just before sunset.
The partial eclipse – which occurs as the Moon starts and finishes crossing the Sun’s path, dimming its light – will last around one hour and 45 minutes.
Lucie Green, a British solar physicist who has travelled the world to witness eclipses, called it “a moving experience”. She will watch from a boat off the island of Mallorca.
The event, to be livestreamed by both NASA and the European Space Agency, presents scientists with a rare opportunity to study the Sun’s atmosphere and its outermost layer, as they seek to uncover secrets about solar winds and our star’s magnetic field.
Weather
Rain could spoil the occasion in the Westfjords region of north-west Iceland.
Scientist and astronomer Saevar Helgi Bragason told AFP in Reykjavik that he felt “both excitement and heartbreak” because of the unfavourable weather forecast.
But he said he hoped the skies would clear just long enough so he could see “the shortest, most sudden, most beautiful, most unique and, hopefully, most memorable and beautiful nighttime of our life” from his home.
No such problems are expected in Spain, however, with clear skies forecast, although there are concerns due to high temperatures and the continued risk of wildfires.
Eclipse fever has gripped Spain, with government predictions that nearly 450,000 extra tourists could bring a €347 million (S$511 million) boost to the economy.
Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska said nearly 25,000 police officers had been mobilised to ensure the event goes off without a hitch.
“The path of totality is very narrow. It’s only a couple of hundred kilometres wide,” British astrophysicist and science communicator Graham Jones told AFP on Aug 11 from Fontanil de los Oteros in northern Spain.
“That’s what’s so special about Spain. The path of totality really goes across the Spanish peninsula.”
Another total eclipse will cross southern Spain and northern Africa in August 2027, while an annular eclipse – when the Moon is not big enough to completely blot out the Sun, creating a so-called “ring of fire” – is due to visit the Iberian Peninsula in 2028. AFP

On August 11, no volumes of liquefied gas for shipment from the loading point in Tobolsk were offered for sale on the St. Petersburg International Mercantile Exchange (SPIMEX). Approximately 4,000 metric tons of technical propane-butane mixture (PBG) were regularly sold from this point per day.
According to sources, "ZapSibNeftekhim" in Tobolsk produces about 6 million tons of feedstock per year, which accounts for approximately 40% of Russia's total production of technical butane-propane mixture.

Russia's war drifted into Romania's Black Sea waters again, and this time the country's military blew the intruders up, acting Defense Minister Radu Miruță said. A vessel near an offshore gas field spotted two floating Russian drones, and army bomb-disposal divers destroyed them. Ukraine confirmed the aircraft were not its own.
A ship raised the alarm
Miruță announced the operation on Facebook, sharing a video. Crews working near the gas platform first noticed the drones in the water. Miruță identified both as Gerberas. A coast guard vessel carrying Romanian army sappers then sailed to the scene. The divers found two uncrewed aircraft adrift, along with several other fragments.
The drones lay in Romania's exclusive economic zone, roughly 90 nautical miles (about 167 km) east of Constanța, Militarnyi reported. Miruță said Romania's Defense Ministry then contacted Kyiv:
"The Ministry of National Defense contacted the Ukrainian partners, who confirmed the systems do not belong to them."
To protect the shipping route and the work around the platform, the military destroyed the drones in a controlled blast, Suspilne relayed.
Russia designed the Gerbera as a decoy. The cheap foam aircraft forces Ukrainian air defenses to waste time and interceptors, and helps Russian crews locate those defenses. Later, Russia fitted some Gerberas with warheads, turning the decoy into a strike drone. The same model can also carry smaller attack drones or gather intelligence.
Custom Code
The attack on Ukraine
Ukraine's Air Force reported that last night Russia hit Ukraine with an Iskander-M ballistic missile, a Kh-31P anti-radar missile, and Kh-35 guided missiles, plus 138 Shahed-type strike drones — among them jet-powered ones, Gerberas, and Parodiya decoys — fired from several sites inside Russia and from occupied territory.
The main targets were Sumy Oblast in the northeast and Odesa Oblast, Ukraine's Black Sea coastal region that lies northeast of Romania's shore. By morning, air defenses had downed or suppressed 112 of the drones, though strikes hit 16 locations.
Adrift far from any front
The drones surfaced far from any battlefield. Russian uncrewed aircraft have repeatedly drifted into neighboring states during Moscow's attacks on Ukraine. Romania itself has shifted from escorting stray drones to shooting them down.
Neptun Deep is Romania's largest offshore gas project, due to start production in 2027. Bucharest is counting on the field to cut its reliance on outside supply and to feed neighbors that still lean on Russia. The two drones drifted into the waters around it.

Renowned Chinese singer Guo Lanying dies at 97
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
15:38:12 CST
16:38:12 KST

This file photo taken on Oct. 28, 1989 shows Guo Lanying performing at the Capital Indoor Stadium in Beijing, capital of China. Guo Lanying, one of China's most celebrated opera singers hailed as a "People's Artist," died at the age of 97 on Tuesday, the China National Opera and Dance Drama Theater said in an obituary on Wednesday. (Xinhua/Cheng Zhishan)
BEIJING, Aug. 12 (Xinhua) -- Guo Lanying, one of China's most celebrated opera singers hailed as a "People's Artist," died at the age of 97 on Tuesday, the China National Opera and Dance Drama Theater said in an obituary on Wednesday.
Guo, whose powerful yet lyrical voice made her a household name in China and one of the most recognizable figures in Chinese performing arts, left behind a body of work that includes some of the country's most enduring songs, many of which remain popular decades after they were first performed.
Among her most famous works was the song "My Motherland," which she sang for a 1950s film set against the backdrop of the battle at Shangganling, one of the most fiercely contested engagements during the War to Resist U.S. Aggression and Aid Korea (1950-1953). With its stirring melody and heartfelt lyrics expressing deep affection for the homeland, the song became a lasting part of the collective memory of generations of Chinese people over the following 70 years and continues to be widely sung today in China.
Guo also won widespread acclaim for her portrayal of the heroine Xi'er in the revolutionary-themed opera "The White-Haired Girl," a landmark work in modern Chinese opera.
In 2019, Guo was awarded the national honorary title of "People's Artist," one of China's highest national honors. The award citation praised her for her "pioneering contributions to the establishment of China's national opera performance system and the development of Chinese vocal art." ■
