16:26:45 KST

Nigel Farage has been standing in British elections since 1994, when he narrowly beat Screaming Lord Sutch of the Monster Raving Loony party into fourth place in a Commons byelection. He was elected five times to the European parliament before achieving his goal of abolishing his seat.
Finally, after 30 years of trying, he was elected to the Commons as member for Clacton in 2024. He resigned that hard-won seat in July after a parliamentary inquiry was launched into a £5m gift he accepted from a Thailand-based businessman shortly before the general election, but is standing again in the resulting byelection on Thursday. The other major parties are not putting up candidates, so the chief contenders, according to the limited polling, are Farage and Count Binface.
These charts show the respective electoral histories of the two main runners.
Count Binface, or rather, his earthling avatar the comedian and writer Jon Harvey, has had a shorter and, so far, less successful electoral career, although he has stood against four prime ministers. On Thursday, he will face Farage at the ballot box for the first time, alongside his longstanding electoral adversary Laurence Fox, standing for Reclaim.
Over the years, Nigel Farage has stood against dozens of British politicians, including in 2006 a young Labour candidate by the name of Rachel Reeves.
In her capacity as chancellor a few weeks ago, it fell to Reeves to accept Farage’s resignation as MP for Clacton. There was some speculation at the time that she was not obliged to do it, but she accepted the resignation on the basis that “if he [Farage] wants to spend summer arguing with a bin, I won’t stop him.”
Thursday’s contest will, of course, not be the first time that either Farage or Binface has faced a novelty opponent. Riding high in the polls in 2015, Farage was so confident of winning Thanet South in that year’s general election that he pledged to resign as leader of Ukip if he did not take the seat.
This led Al Murray, a comedian whose main persona is the Pub Landlord, a straight-talking conservative patriot, to stand against Farage. Even without the resulting split in the straight-talking conservative patriot vote, Farage would have lost the seat. Ever a man of his word, Farage resigned, and then unresigned three days later.
Harvey’s first electoral foray was not as Count Binface at all, but rather as the similarly behatted persona of Lord Buckethead. He was moved to adopt the Binface persona when a man got in touch claiming to hold copyright in the Buckethead character. In 2019, having failed to prorogue parliament, the then prime minister, Boris Johnson, called an early general election. A roster of novelty candidates – and Boris Johnson – ran in Uxbridge and South Ruislip, among them for the first and only time, both Count Binface and a copyright-approved Lord Buckethead.
Voters in Clacton on Thursday can, of course, choose to vote for neither Binface nor Farage. In fact, there are 34 candidates in all, including three from the Monster Raving Loony party.

Coffee exports from Colombia have been largely halted after a powerful earthquake
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
10:25:45 EEST

Coffee exports from Colombia have been largely halted after a powerful earthquake
Kyiv • UNN
The earthquake disrupted operations at the port of Buenaventura and blocked key roads, suspending coffee exports. The head of Asoexport reported that operations had been halted and that there was uncertainty about the timeline for their resumption.
Coffee exports from Colombia have largely been put on hold after a devastating earthquake disrupted operations at the country's main port and caused road closures on key highways, the head of a coffee exporters' group said, UNN reports, citing Bloomberg.
Details
Buenaventura, Colombia's main coffee export port, is effectively inaccessible because of several blocked roads, especially around tunnels along the Cali-Buenaventura highway, a key route to the country's Pacific coast, Gustavo Gómez, head of Asoexport, said in an interview.
"Coffee operations are currently suspended. Some individual operations may be possible, but at this point coffee export operations are halted," Gómez said. "At this point, there is no specific official information on when the road will be fully reopened," he added.
Port terminal operators are assessing the damage and have suspended or limited coffee-receiving operations. Other ports in Cartagena and Santa Marta on Colombia's Caribbean coast have not reported serious disruptions, but redirecting coffee north has been complicated by a severe shortage of trucks.
The disruptions are being exacerbated by the concentration of transport companies and processing facilities in the country's coffee-growing region near the area affected by the earthquake, where operations have also been disrupted.
Arabica coffee futures in New York fell sharply from multi-week highs to slight losses as traders assessed the potential impact on supplies and logistics of the earthquake that struck the world's second-largest producer of premium beans. Colombia's coffee production reached 13.4 million 60-kilogram bags in 2025.
Although Colombia produces coffee across much of the country, the timing of the disruptions is particularly problematic because the harvest is currently concentrated in the southern regions, including Cauca, Nariño, Valle del Cauca, and Huila. Much of this coffee is normally exported through Buenaventura.
"Processing facilities are still assessing the damage. So far, there have been no reports of serious structural damage to coffee mills, but operations are being affected by power outages, communications problems, and the personal consequences for workers, including people who have lost their homes," Gómez said.
Even after roads and facilities resume operations, exports may face further delays as accumulated coffee begins moving again, potentially creating congestion and bottlenecks at ports. Colombia exports around 1 million 60-kilogram bags of coffee per month, meaning that each day of disruption could delay significant volumes of shipments.
"This will ultimately lead to delivery delays and also put pressure on the supply chain once everything begins to recover and operations resume," Gómez said.

Source: the latest IBRiS poll for Polish newspaper Rzeczpospolita
Details: The poll found that 67.2% of respondents support the deportation of Ukrainian men without legal employment, while 23.4% oppose it.

But the heatwave is not the only cause for concern. The lack of rainfall (source in French) is worsening the drought. Soils remain extremely dry and small rivers are in a particularly worrying state. Nearly 1,400 waterways are thought to have run dry, according to the OFB, the French Office for Biodiversity. (source in French) Restrictions on water use now affect a very large majority of the population in mainland France and in Corsica.

MELITOPOL, August 12. /TASS/. Three people, including two Zaporozhye Nuclear Power Plant (ZNPP) employees, were injured in an August 11 Ukrainian attack on Energodar's industrial zone, the nuclear facility reported.
"Yesterday, on August 11, three people were injured in the industrial zone of Energodar as a result of a Ukrainian drone attack. Two of them are employees of the electrical shop at the ZNPP, which is part of Rosatom. Their colleagues were heading to the site to restore power to facilities in the industrial zone that had been damaged by previous Ukrainian attacks," the ZNPP said in a statement on its Telegram channel.
One of the injured is in serious condition, the nuclear facility added.
The Zaporozhye NPP emphasized that its electrical shop employees restore power to Energodar and facilities in the industrial zone daily following Ukrainian strikes. The Ukrainian armed forces deliberately targeted them, the statement noted.

India, 5 southern African nations agree to open trade talks
India and the five countries that make up the Southern African Customs Union (SACU) have agreed to begin negotiations on a preferential trade agreemen (PTA).
South Africa, Botswana, Namibia, Lesotho and Eswatini are members of SACU.
SACU and India held five rounds of trade talks between 2002 and 2010, but negotiations stalled.
The move comes as India looks to secure lower tariffs on its exports, including vehicles, pharmaceuticals and industrial machinery, the Reuters news agency reported Wednesday.
Under President Donald Trump, the US has imposed a range of tariffs on many of its trading partners, including India. Washington and New Delhi are currently negotiating a bilateral trade agreement.
After the US Supreme Court struck down Trump's emergency tariffs in July, the Trump administration turned to another law in a bid to make the tariffs stick.
Cockroach founder hints at new wave of protests
Abhijeet Dipke, the founder of the youth-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) , has suggested that a new wave of protests could be imminent.
The movement led weeks of protests and hunger strikes calling for education reform, which culminated in the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan on July 25.
Thousands of protesters camped out at the Jantar Mantar observatory in central Delhi.
"Many people were commenting on Instagram when Season 2 of 'Jantar-Mantar' will begin. I want to tell them that Season 2 of 'Jantar-Mantar' is going to start very soon," Dipke said Wednesday.
It was not clear when or where the next phase of protests would begin.
Similar demonstrations and rallies have since spread to other parts of the country.
The movement has emerged as one of the most serious challenges to Prime Minister Narendra Modi's 12 years in power.
Tata Sons' chairman will not seek reappointment at end of term
Indian conglomerate Tata Sons' Chairman N Chandrasekaran said on Wednesday he would not seek reappointment when his term ends in February.
The 63-year-old, who has led Tata Sons since 2017, cited a lack of board support amid tensions with the charity arm, Tata Trusts, which controls 66% of the conglomerate's holding company.
Chandrasekaran said uncertainty over the leadership situation had remained unresolved for six months and that a decision was important for employees, investors and other stakeholders.
Tata Trusts Chairman Noel Tata opposed Chandrasekaran's reappointment at a February board meeting, Reuters reported.
Seven killed, more feared trapped after landslide in Mumbai
At least seven people were killed and several injured after a landslide hit Mumbai's Kurla area early Wednesday following heavy rain, the Hindustan Times reported.
According to the report, the landslide occurred around 3 a.m. local time, with more people feared trapped, Deputy Commissioner of Police Ganesh Shinde said.
Rescue operations are underway, with teams from various emergency agencies deployed.
Mumbai has experienced heavy monsoon rain in recent weeks, causing waterlogging and disruptions to air and road traffic.
Two people killed in Mumbai fire
Two people, including a two-and-a-half-year-old, were killed and eight others injured after a fire broke out in two apartments on the 11th floor of a residential building in Mumbai late Tuesday, officials said.
The fire broke out around 10 pm in Vile Parle West area and was brought under control shortly after midnight on Wednesday.
Supreme Court urges faster adjudication of West Bengal SIR appeals
India's Supreme Court on Tuesday urged tribunals handling appeals against voter deletions in West Bengal to speed up their work, saying the process could not drag on indefinitely, a report in the Times of India said.
Nearly 3.4 million appeals are pending before tribunals set up to hear challenges to deletions from electoral rolls during a Special Intensive Revision (SIR), according to the court.
"The process cannot be so slow that the next assembly elections would be due by the time the appeals are decided," Chief Justice of India Surya Kant said, according to the report.
India's election commission conducted the SIR of electoral rolls in several states and territories ahead of state election, including West Bengal, where Prime Minister Narendra Modi's party recently won state elections.
The commission said the "intensive revision" was needed to remove the names of deceased individuals, those who have permanently moved and duplicate entries — as well as avoiding the "inclusion of the names of foreign illegal immigrants."
Critics of the SIR say it is skewed against marginalized and minority communities.
IN DEPTH: Disrupted monsoons force India to face climate threat
For generations, India has lived by the rhythm of the southwest monsoon. But with the country hit by dry spells, cloudbursts and deadly floods, climate swings now expose the costs of building for yesterday's weather.
Food safety, hygiene issues plague India's quick commerce firms
India's quick commerce sector, especially grocery delivery services, is in the doldrums as authorities flag serious food safety and hygiene violations.
Authorities in the southern Karnataka and western Maharashtra states sealed a Zepto warehouse on Tuesday and suspended the license of a Blinkit facility after inspections found serious violations, reports said.
In Karnataka, a Zepto warehouse near Bengaluru was sealed by the food safety department after finding unhygienic food handling and storage conditions, improper labelling and misbranding.
Zepto said in a statement that it had cooperated with officials and was taking steps to address their observations, the Hindustan Times reported, adding that it remained committed to food safety and hygiene standards.
In Mumbai, authorities suspended the license of a Blinkit facility after finding a large-scale cockroach infestation, improperly stored food and expired or tampered products.
Food was also found on rusted racks, while cold-storage areas lacked adequate cleanliness.
The facility has been barred from selling or distributing food or conducting any food business during the license suspension, authorities said.
Air India pilot tests positive in drug test
The captain of an Air India flight from Phuket to Delhi that suddenly lost altitude last week tested positive for marijuana in a confirmatory drug test.
The Airbus A320neo, carrying 137 passengers and eight crew, lost about 300 feet of over Odisha before landing safely in Delhi.
The plane stabilized and landed safely. India's Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau has classified the incident as serious.
The incident had left 13 passengers and four crew members injured, and led to India's aviation ministry summoning Air India CEO Campbell Wilson on Tuesday.
Emergency at Chennai airport after IndiGo plane suffers engine failure
Late on Tuesday night, Chennai airport declared a full emergency after an IndiGo flight suffered an engine failure, media reports said.
This came only a few hours after reports emerged that the captain of an Air India flight that suddenly lost altitude last week, injuring crew and passengers, tested positive in a drug test, further plunging India's aviation into turmoil.
On Tuesday, the pilot of an IndiGo plane, flying from Kolkata to Chennai with 224 people on board, noticed that the left engine had failed while the plane prepared to land, reports said Airports Authority of India (AAI) officials.
Airport authorities activated emergency response measures, which remained in place till the plane landed safely. The declaration of full emergency was withdrawn soon after.

Romania Blows Up Two Gerbera Drones Drifting Near Black Sea Gas Platform
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
07:19:48 UTC
16:19:48 KST

Romanian military forces destroyed two Gerbera-type drones on Tuesday that were drifting within the country’s exclusive economic zone in the Black Sea, near a gas platform operated as part of the Neptun Deep project.
Romania’s acting Defence Minister, Radu Miruță, reported the incident on August 11.
The drones were detected by one of the vessels carrying out work in the area of the gas platform. A Romanian Coast Guard vessel carrying bomb-disposal specialists was dispatched to the scene.
The drones were located approximately 90 nautical miles east of Constanța. Several other pieces of debris were also found alongside them.
Romania’s Ministry of National Defence contacted the Ukrainian side, which confirmed that the drones did not belong to Ukraine.
“Two drifting drones and several other pieces of debris were found. Romania’s Ministry of National Defence contacted Ukrainian officials, who confirmed that the drones did not belong to Ukraine,” Miruță added.
To ensure the safety of ships and workers operating near the platform, the Romanian military decided to safely destroy the drones by detonating them in a controlled explosion.
The Gerbera UAV was primarily designed for use as a decoy target. These drones force air-defense forces to spend time and resources detecting and intercepting them, while also helping Russian forces identify the positions of Ukrainian air-defense systems.
Later, Russian forces began equipping Gerbera drones with warheads, turning them into strike UAVs. The drone can also be used for reconnaissance and intelligence gathering.

'Will take notes &amp; respond': Amit Shah 'ready to debate' in Parliament; Rahul says 'minister has no courage'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
07:18:20 UTC
16:18:20 KST

Amit Shah 'ready to answer any question'; Rahul Gandhi says 'not interested in him giving us lecture'
TOI News Desk / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Updated: Aug 12, 2026, 18:01 IST
Comments
Share
AA
Text Size
Small
Medium
Large
Amit Shah says 'ready to sit through, take notes and respond to anything' in Parliament.
NEW DELHI: Union home minister Amit Shah on Wednesday offered to sit in Parliament from "3pm today till 3pm the next day" to hear the opposition's concerns and respond to every point, amid protests over his "absence" from the Houses. Leader of opposition in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi, however, rejected the offer saying they "seek answers, not lectures."Shah's offer came amid opposition protests demanding that he make a statement in Parliament on the police action against students during their July 20 march over the NEET paper leak issue.Speaking to reporters, Shah rejected opposition allegations that he had been absent from Parliament and said the government was ready for a detailed discussion on the issue."First of all, terms like 'laapata', 'bhaag gaye' are the kind of language increasingly being heard in India's public and parliamentary life. I have been coming to Parliament regularly since the session began; I sit in my chamber, but since the opposition is not allowing Parliament to function—in either House—what is one supposed to do?" Shah said.He said Parliamentary affairs minister Kiren Rijiju had already made it clear that the government was ready for a full discussion on the student protests.
"We asked for a time to be fixed and for the Opposition to be ready. That was their initial demand, and we agreed to it. I, too, have stated that I am ready to answer any question in Parliament, yet they simply do not want the discussion to take place," Shah said."Now, let the public decide who is running away. Let them submit a letter to the Speaker by 3:00 pm today. We are ready for a discussion on all aspects from 3:00 pm today until 3:00 pm tomorrow. I will sit in the House; I will listen to everyone and respond to every point. The government has nothing to hide," he added.Shah said he was even willing to discuss why the opposition had not allowed the debate to take place. "The NDA government—under Modi ji's leadership is ready to discuss anything; they just need to let Parliament function," he said.Elaborating on his offer, Shah said, "I want to tell the opposition: submit a letter to the Speaker by 2.00 pm, we will start the discussion at 3.00pm, and I will provide answers to everything by 3:00 PM tomorrow.""There are established rules and procedures for parliamentary discussions. Yet, some ask me to simply make a statement. Such a serious issue cannot be discussed in that manner. That may be your method, but it is not the parliamentary way. In Parliament, discussions are held at length," he said."In Parliament, discussions are held at length. I am ready for the debate to continue from 3:00 PM today, sitting late into the night and continuing until 3:00 PM tomorrow; I am even prepared to suspend the Question Hour if the Speaker grants permission," Shah said."I am ready for the discussion to go on until 3:00 PM tomorrow. I will sit through it myself, take notes on everything, and respond to every point so that the entire matter becomes clear to the people of the country—so that the truth is fully revealed. Now, the Opposition must decide whether they want to engage in a discussion or create an uproar," he added.
Rahul Gandhi hits backCongress leader Rahul Gandhi rejected Shah's offer, saying the opposition was seeking answers on the alleged police action against students rather than a lecture from the home minister."The opposition has clearly said that we are not interested in Amit Shah giving us a lecture. When I say 'we', I mean the younger generation of this country. Who shot the students? Who gave the order to beat up the students with lathis with nails? Did Amit Shah give this order to shoot our children? If he did, then he should resign. For the last 20 days, Amit Shah has been missing. The Home Minister of India has no courage; he cannot come to the House," Rahul said."Did home minister Shah give orders to shoot our children or not; if he did, he is culpable and if he did not, he is incompetent," he added.
The leader of opposition also took to X, sharing a video of his remark saying "When a man lacks the courage to speak the truth, his silence speaks for him. Amit Shah’s silence is his confession."Centre vs oppositionThe opposition has been demanding Shah's presence in Parliament and a statement on the "police action" against students during the Jantar Mantar protest.Earlier in the day, opposition MPs, including Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge and party general secretary Priyanka Gandhi Vadra, staged a protest in the Parliament House Complex over the alleged theft of donations at the Ram temple in Ayodhya and the alleged police excesses against student protesters.Priyanka also questioned the government over the alleged use of force against students.The INDIA bloc has been protesting for more than three weeks, demanding Shah's presence in the House and a statement from him.Earlier on Monday, Kiren Rijiju said the government was ready for a detailed discussion on the student protests and urged the opposition not to disrupt proceedings when Shah responds."The offer made by the government is very clear that it is ready to have a full and detailed discussion on students' movement and activities related to it," Rijiju said.
"My only point made to the opposition is that while the discussion and a reply are being made, the opposition should not create disturbances to prevent the statement of the home minister," he said, adding that, "They must listen to the reply of the home minister and the government. Once discussion begins, we must have a threadbare discussion."Rijiju's remarks came after Rahul criticised the Centre over the alleged police action during the July 20 student protests at Jantar Mantar and demanded a court-monitored probe. Parliament proceedings have repeatedly been disrupted during the Monsoon Session, with several Bills passed by the Lok Sabha amid the continuing deadlock.

Germany moves to give spy agencies sweeping new covert powers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
07:15:47 UTC
16:15:47 KST

The German government plans to put forward a major overhaul of the country's intelligence agencies on Wednesday, to give them broad new powers to conduct covert operations and take action against foreign threats.
The reforms, under discussion for several months, would loosen strict rules that have largely limited Germany's secret services to gathering intelligence and passing on reports.
Chancellor Friedrich Merz's coalition has argued that more powerful intelligence agencies are needed to counter the threats posed by hostile foreign powers as well as terrorist groups and cybercriminals.
German officials accuse Moscow of waging a "hybrid" campaign of sabotage, espionage and disinformation against the country, which is among Ukraine's biggest military supporters in the war with Russia.
"We are in the thick of a hybrid conflict not only with Russia but also with other actors," Marc Henrichmann, chairman of the parliament's intelligence oversight committee, told AFP. "And so our intelligence services must also keep pace with the times and stay one step ahead of the curve."
He argued Germany's cautious approach has left it "behind the curve" and unable to properly contribute to European security.
Henrichmann pointed to a string of recent incidents, including an explosive-laden drone discovered at Leipzig airport last week, to underscore the importance of the changes.
"We face adversaries who play without any rules at all," he said. "They have no regard for law and order. Their goal is not merely to put the West, the EU and Germany under pressure, but ideally to bring them to their knees."
No lethal operations
For decades, Germany has placed its BND foreign intelligence agency and the BfV domestic spy service under tight restrictions that largely rule out cloak-and-dagger operations as practised by the CIA or Mossad.
Those rules were imposed in part because of the gruesome abuses carried out by the Nazi dictatorship and communist East Germany, as well as a strong German sense of privacy rights.
"The German intelligence services were essentially, until recently, information collection services," Peter Neumann, a professor of security studies at King's College London, told AFP.
"They have some powers to collect information and give policymakers a better picture, but they are very restricted in what they were allowed to do with that information."
Germany has invested record sums in rebuilding its military in the wake of the Russia-Ukraine war, and Henrichmann and others argue that an expansion of the spy services is likewise needed.
The proposal would potentially allow the spy agencies to carry out cyberattacks of their own, such as disabling foreign IT systems being used by hostile actors or blocking flows of payments.
Powers to collect and analyse data are also being expanded for both the BND and the BfV, including permission to use artificial intelligence to scan vast datasets and retain certain data for longer periods.
The legislative package, spanning over 700 pages, also regulates powers for controversial measures such as online surveillance and tracking.
In rare situations, the BND spy agency could also receive permission to carry out foreign sabotage missions, though assassinations and other lethal operations would remain strictly forbidden under German law.
'Genuine secret services'
"We are turning our intelligence agencies into genuine secret services," Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt told the Bild daily.
"We are providing a new response to the hybrid threat landscape and attempts at destabilisation through sabotage, espionage, cyberattacks, and covert actions by foreign powers," Dobrindt told the newspaper, adding that the reform would put Germany "on an equal footing with our partner agencies around the world".
Neumann said that the spy services in many of Germany's European allies, such as Britain, France or the Netherlands, already have "significantly more powers".
Germany's tight limits on covert action have sometimes made cooperation with allied intelligence agencies difficult and joint operations rare, Neumann said.
"It is about time for German intelligence services to have similar powers to other European democracies," he told AFP.
Greens MP Konstantin von Notz, vice-chairman of the intelligence oversight committee, said that "new and robust powers are fundamentally appropriate given the challenging current security climate".
But von Notz argued the current draft legislation goes "too far" in failing to strengthen independent oversight of the agencies, and risks violating a ban in Germany's constitution on a secret service holding any kind of police power.
The Society for Civil Rights has also argued that the new digital surveillance powers would "deeply infringe upon fundamental rights".
Henrichmann, however, defended the expanded powers in light of current threats, and contended that Germany's legal protections and oversight mean that "we have the most heavily scrutinised intelligence agencies in the world".

HSL wants to increase penalty fines to 130 euros, fare increases also in pipeline
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
10:15:10 EEST
16:15:10 KST

The Helsinki Regional Transport Authority (acronymed as HSL in Finnish) has proposed raising the fine imposed on passengers travelling without a valid ticket from 100 to 130 euros.
Helsinki city councillor Mirita Saxberg (NCP), who also chairs the HSL board, told Yle she is in favour of the proposal.
"Travelling without a ticket is a problem for HSL's finances and ticket revenue. In the name of fairness, it should be understood that if I don't pay, someone else pays," Saxberg said.
The proposed increase is part of a package of operational and budgetary plans currently under consideration by the authority, which also include a rise in ticket prices of between 3 and 6 percent.
HSL introduced a ticket price hike of 3.1 percent at the beginning of this year, when a 6 percent increase was also on the table.
Saxberg noted that the HSL board opted for the smaller increase at the time because there was political agreement on gradual price development for the period 2026–2029 — and that a similar level of increase would be made annually.
HSL decision later this year
There has been a mixed reaction to the proposals among HSL's member municipalities.
The Helsinki city council seems broadly in favour of the increase in penalty fines, but Vantaa's council has counter-proposed that HSL improve its inspection operations rather than handing out more severe penalties.
By contrast, Helsinki would prefer to see a smaller rise in ticket prices, up to a maximum of 3.1 percent, while Vantaa's transport committee has deemed an increase of 4-5 percent to be justified.
According to Saxberg, the decision on raising fines and fares will rest on finding the right balance between ticket prices, good service levels, and municipal funding.
"These cannot be resolved as separate issues. If we want to keep price increases moderate while increasing public transport use, we must also ensure that costs are kept under control and municipal contributions are on a sustainable basis," she said.
The decisions regarding the proposed increases will be made at a HSL board meeting later in the autumn, but an exact date is not currently known.

Millions of Europeans will contemplate the sky in awe on Wednesday as a rare total solar eclipse crosses part of the continent and plunges a swath of Spain into eerie daytime darkness.
The shadow cast when the Moon blots out the Sun will begin in Russia's remote Arctic north at around 1700 GMT and continue in an arc over Greenland and Iceland.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
In Spain, where the total eclipse will be best viewed, the shadow will cross the country diagonally from the northern Atlantic coast to the Mediterranean Sea, where it will vanish at around 1830 GMT.
Far more observers will see a partial eclipse, visible in most of Europe, Canada, the northern United States and northwest Africa.
This will be mainland Europe's first total eclipse since 2006.
Read moreFrom Solar corona to human emotions: What can we learn from eclipses?
Throughout human history eclipses have stirred amazement, fear and reverence, as they appear to momentarily halt the normal course of nature.
The shadow cast by the alignment of Sun and Moon creates a strange twilight during which temperatures drop, shadows appear at strange angles and some animals go to sleep.
But the phenomenon is fleeting: for observers in Spain, the total eclipse will last less than two minutes just before sunset.
It will last slightly longer in parts of Russia and Greenland, though still under two-and-a-half minutes.
The partial eclipse -- which occurs as the Moon starts and finishes crossing the Sun's path – will last around one hour and 45 minutes.
The phenomenon will present scientists with a rare opportunity to study the Sun's atmosphere and its outermost layer, as they seek to uncover secrets about solar winds and our star's magnetic field.
Eclipse fever
Eclipse chasers will rush to secure a vantage point with an unimpeded sight of the setting Sun and pray for the dissipation of any clouds, dust or smoke.
Read moreEclipse chasers: When chasing totality becomes a way of life
Rain and clouds were forecast to spoil the occasion in the Westfjords region of northwestern Iceland, while Reykjavik, the capital, was set to experience its first total eclipse since 1433.
Further south, the Madrid-based AEMET weather agency has predicted clear skies for most of Spain, with a few exceptions in northern and eastern areas.
Eclipse fever is gripping the country, with the type of glasses certified to safely view the Sun hard to find in some places.
The country is banking on eclipse-driven tourism for an economic boost, especially in rural, northern regions that have suffered decades of population decline.
The net contribution to the economy is forecast to be €347 million ($400 million), with more than 446,000 extra tourists visiting the key areas affected by the eclipse, according to the economy ministry.
Sleepy villages that would normally never feature in a typical tourist itinerary have suddenly found themselves inundated with eclipse hunters from around the world.
In Benavente, a small northwestern town that is expected to offer excellent views of the total eclipse, accommodation options have run out.
"We're getting 50 calls a day to ask about where to stay, where to see it, where to park," Benavente tourism office worker Laura del Teso told AFP.
Benavente had "never" had so many foreign tourists, including visitors from Belgium, Britain, Australia, New Zealand, the Netherlands and Germany, she added.
Hazards on horizon
The expected rush has caused trepidation for the authorities, who are pleading for caution amid fears that the heavenly phenomenon will unleash hell on the ground.
Temperatures are expected to exceed 35C Wednesday in most of mainland Spain and could climb above 40C in parts of the northeast, posing health risks for those spending hours outdoors.
AEMET also forecasts a "very high" or "extreme" wildfire risk for much of the country – with the risk amplified by thousands of people occupying parched countryside and clogging small rural roads with their cars.
Officials expect there to be as many as 1.5 million extra road journeys towards the band of totality.
Municipalities have set up dedicated observation points and beefed up security, emergency and transport resources in the hope of managing the mayhem during mainland Spain's first total eclipse in more than a century.
Another total eclipse will cross southern Spain and northern Africa in August 2027, while an annular eclipse – when the Moon is not big enough to completely blot out the Sun, creating a so-called "ring of fire" – is due to visit the Iberian Peninsula in 2028.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

A heated confrontation between an Israeli family and a tuk-tuk driver in Phuket has sparked controversy on Thai social media and in local media, after the driver posted a video showing an argument in which one of the Israelis repeatedly curses him in English and tells him in Hebrew, “You’re trash.”
The driver also alleged that members of the family threatened him and attempted to attack him, though his account has not been independently corroborated.
According to Thai news site The Thaiger, citing the driver and a report by Phuket Times, the incident began when members of the family approached the driver and asked about the price of a ride. The two sides failed to agree, and the driver remained at the location waiting for other passengers.
A short time later, an Australian couple arrived and booked a ride to the Bangla area, one of Phuket’s main nightlife districts. After the couple entered the tuk-tuk, the Israeli family returned and, according to the driver, asked to join the trip. He refused and directed them to another tuk-tuk parked nearby.
The disagreement then escalated.
The driver claimed that members of the family attempted to prevent the Australian couple from leaving with him and that he intervened to protect his passengers.
In the video he later published, five people identified in local reports as members of the Israeli family can be seen standing beside the tuk-tuk. One of them repeatedly curses the driver in English, tells him in Hebrew, “You’re trash,” and appears to spit on the road.
The driver responds that he does not want to transport passengers who behave that way and then leaves the scene.
According to his account, threats were also directed at him during the confrontation. He further claimed that at one point one of the family members tried to lift a concrete slab from the side of the road in order to attack him.
The Thaiger reported that the man was unable to lift the slab because it was too heavy and that no physical assault ultimately took place.
The driver said he decided to publish the video because he objected to the family’s behavior and believed conduct of that kind was inappropriate at tourist destinations in Thailand. The footage was subsequently shared by Phuket Times and other Thai media outlets.
As of now, no response from the family to the allegations has been published, and there has been no report that the driver filed a police complaint or contacted Thai tourism authorities.
Israeli embassy previously urged tourists to respect local culture
The incident comes after a series of confrontations involving Israeli tourists in Thailand last year that fueled tensions with residents and local authorities.
In February 2025, the Israeli embassy in Thailand issued special guidance to Israeli travelers, urging them to respect local residents and avoid behavior that could damage the image of Israeli tourists.
Later, Israeli Ambassador to Thailand Orna Sagiv traveled to the northern town of Pai together with senior Thai officials in an effort to calm tensions following several incidents involving Israelis.
The visit took place amid reports that some local businesses had refused to serve Israeli tourists, highlighting broader concern over the conduct of a minority of visitors and its impact on relations between Israelis and local communities.

Ukrainian intelligence identifies AI module in new Russian missile – photos
Defence Intelligence of Ukraine (DIU) has identified an NVIDIA Jetson Orin computer module in the S-71 Monochrome, a new Russian cruise missile.
Source: Defence Intelligence of Ukraine
Quote: "The use of this component may indicate that artificial intelligence technologies are being implemented in the missile."
Details: DIU has released data on 35 electronic components identified in samples of Russian weaponry in the Foreign components in weapons section of its War&Sanctions portal.
Among them are components of a passive radar seeker that the Russians have begun installing on Shahed-type loitering munitions. According to DIU, it is designed to detect and strike air defence missile systems and radar stations operated by Ukraine's defence forces.
DIU also identified a Chinese-made Honpho TS130C-01 camera in the Shahed-4 jet-powered drone and components of the active seeker used in the Kh-47M2 Kinzhal aeroballistic missile.
Ukrainian intelligence noted that together with Ukrainian research institutions, it is continuing to examine Russian weaponry and establish the origin of its electronic component base.
The intelligence agency estimates that Russia has still been unable to fully replace foreign high-tech components with domestically produced equivalents. Releasing information about the components is intended to help Ukraine and its partners identify foreign technologies critical to Russian weapons and strengthen efforts to block their supply to the Kremlin.
According to the manufacturer's data, the NVIDIA Jetson Orin is a compact computing module designed for use with artificial intelligence systems, computer vision, robotics and autonomous machines.
Background: Earlier, DIU released a detailed breakdown of the new Russian Shahed-4 jet-powered attack drone on War&Sanctions: an interactive 3D model, information on its components and foreign-made parts, and key technical specifications.

British spy plane probes Russian territory
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
08:12:41 BST
16:12:41 KST

A Royal Air Force RC-135W Rivet Joint electronic surveillance aircraft has conducted a patrol around the Russian territory of Kaliningrad.
The aircraft, ZZ664, operated under the callsign RRR7207 and returned to RAF Waddington in Lincolnshire on Friday 7 August after routing out across the North Sea and into the Baltic.
These flights form part of regular allied intelligence-gathering missions along NATO’s eastern frontier. The UK has carried out such patrols for years, maintaining a persistent watch on Russian military activity well before the 2022 invasion of Ukraine.
Rivet Joint missions are designed to be overt and their tracks are visible on civilian flight monitoring platforms, providing transparency about the aircraft’s presence and allowing observers to verify the frequency of operations in the area. Although British surveillance activity over the Baltic Sea was always routine, the tempo of such flights has increased noticeably amid the continuing conflict in Ukraine. U.S. reconnaissance aircraft are also active in the region as part of coordinated NATO intelligence and deterrence efforts.
Kaliningrad remains one of the most closely watched pieces of territory in Europe. The exclave sits between Poland and Lithuania with no land connection to the rest of Russia, hosts the headquarters of the Baltic Fleet at Baltiysk, and carries air defence and missile systems that reach well into NATO airspace. It also sits alongside the Suwalki gap, the stretch of Polish and Lithuanian border that separates it from Belarus and forms the only land route between the Baltic states and the rest of the alliance.
What does the RC-135W do?
According to the Royal Air Force website, the RC-135W Rivet Joint is a dedicated electronic surveillance aircraft that can be employed in all theatres on strategic and tactical missions. Its sensors soak up electronic emissions from communications, radar and other systems.
“RC-135W Rivet Joint employs multidiscipline Weapons System Officer (WSO) and Weapons System Operator (WSOp) specialists whose mission is to survey elements of the electromagnetic spectrum in order to derive intelligence for commanders.”
The Royal Air Force say that Rivet Joint has been deployed extensively for Operation Shader and on other operational taskings. It had been formally named Airseeker, but is almost universally known in service as the RC-135W Rivet Joint. The UK operates three of these aircraft.
All three were converted from KC-135 tanker airframes under a co-operative programme with the United States Air Force, which operates a larger fleet of the type from Offutt Air Force Base in Nebraska. ZZ664 was built in 1964 and is now 61 years old, an airframe age that is unremarkable for the type given the extent of the rebuild each aircraft receives during conversion.

Factions in Iran openly fight over war’s direction amid Khamenei’s absence
Hardliners opposing talks with the US demand President Pezeshkian’s resignation, deepening political tensions over how to end the war
When Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian told state television last week that he found it “very difficult” to reach the country’s supreme leader, it sparked fresh speculation about the whereabouts of Mojtaba Khamenei who has not been seen in public since taking over as the country’s ultimate authority in March.
By Monday, Pezeshkian told the official broadcaster that the two had in fact recently held a meeting lasting “seven or eight hours”.
“It was a very good meeting,” Pezeshkian told a reporter on the sidelines of a summit of the heads of political factions and politicians in Tehran, adding that the two discussed how to tackle worsening living standards in Iran as well as sharing that Khamenei’s most pressing concern was “unity and cohesion” in the country.
The statement came after weeks of bitter public infighting in Tehran over the conduct of the war, with calls from hardliners for Pezeshkian to resign over his support for Iran’s beleaguered peace deal with the US, and days after the under-pressure president said in a lengthy television interview that he was not going to budge.
Khamenei was hurt in the same Israeli air strike on February 28 that killed his father and predecessor, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei. It was the opening salvo in the US-Israel war on Iran.
The extent of his injuries is unknown. Pezeshkian said on Monday that the supreme leader was in “perfect health”. But Khamenei’s absence from public life has left a vacuum in which disputes between political factions – a mainstay of Iranian life – have become more pronounced and seeped into the open.

But mutual deep distrust and an unwillingness by either party to make large concessions mean a lasting deal is unlikely to be reached and maintained anytime soon.

Happy eclipse day to all who celebrate*! (* though customers are being asked to turn off their lights and fans to support the grid)
As my colleague Jillian Ambrose reported earlier this week, Great Britain’s biggest household energy supplier, Octopus Energy, has been urging customers to use less electricity during what is meant to be the deepest solar eclipse in almost 30 years.
The eclipse, due to hit its peak around 7pm local time, is expected to knock out the last of Great Britain’s solar power generation for the day, at the same time as the country’s fifth heatwave of the year is likely to increase demand for electricity to run air conditioning, fans and refrigeration systems.
Now, Britain’s national energy system operator (Neso) is forecasts a shortfall of nearly 1.2 gigawatts of energy on Wednesday, between 6pm-8pm BST , according to a market notice published early this morning.
The notice is effectively a call for any energy producers to offer any spare capacity to shore up the country’s power supplies.
Neso’s notices are a rarity for summer months, with these notices usually taking place during winter. However, consecutive heatwaves in recent months have put pressure on UK power supplies, as households turn to fans and air conditioning to keep cool.
Shares in German-listed Tui Group are down 3.1% as the company revealed the ongoing fallout from the Iran war.
Cautious travellers have hit booking levels, while geopolitical tensions kept fuel prices high, weighing on operating profits which fell nearly 27% in Q3 to €234.6m.
Profits at Tui’s hotels and resorts division fell 6.2% to €122.7m, while occupancy fell 5% due to 77% following a drop in demand across the eastern Mediterranean, Mexico and the Caribbean.
Meanwhile, its cruises business saw profits tumble 7.2% to €132.4m after taking a €20m hit from the war in Iran.
It comes months after Tui cut its profit forecast and suspended its revenue guidance in March, amid spiralling jet fuel costs and the uncertainty surrounding the Iran war.
Tui CEO Sebastian Ebel in a statement said that while 2026 “is no ordinary year” Tui had “held its own well in a difficult global environment.”
Our business model is proving to be resilient.
Travel remains highly relevant to people’s lives, but the timing of travel decisions has shifted.
Rivals including Lufthansa, and Air France-KLM, and British Airways owner IAG have also said they were either cutting, or maintaining capacity, in the coming months in order to help offset a broader fallout on their bottom line.
Introduction: Oil prices climb as Iran talks hit impasse

The US and Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis have said they endured separate attackson ships in the strait of Hormuz and the Bab al-Mandeb strait on Tuesday, while Iran’s top security official, Mohsen Rezaei, said the strait would stay closed unless the US accepted Iran’s conditions to end the war, including the release of its frozen assets and an end to other regional conflicts.

Yesterday, the rally in US crude paused for a minute after Pakistan’s Defence Minister said that they were getting “close to some sort of arrangement”, but the relief remained short-lived after Iran added that the Strait of Hormuz would remain closed until the conditions it demands from the US are met.
And the conditions that both parties demand from each other suggest that the problems won’t be solved by tomorrow.

DMK backs Tamil Nadu’s delimitation resolution
NEW DELHI: DMK on Wednesday supported the Tamil Nadu government’s resolution opposing the Centre’s proposed delimitation exercise, with Leader of Opposition Udhayanidhi Stalin saying the state’s representation in the Lok Sabha should not be reduced.He said the number of Members of Parliament from Tamil Nadu should not be reduced in the name of delimitation and called for the exercise to be deferred for 25 years.
"In the name of constituency delimitation, the number of Members of Parliament should not be reduced. Our stand is that constituency delimitation should not be carried out for the next 25 years. We welcome the resolution on the 33% reservation for women. Our firm stand is that Tamil Nadu should not be affected by constituency delimitation. The movement that first told India what the impact of delimitation would be is the DMK," Udhayanidhi added.The development comes after Tamil Nadu assembly on Wednesday passed a resolution in the state Assembly opposing the Union government’s proposed delimitation exercise.Speaking in the assembly, CM Vijay also called for the implementation of 33 per cent reservation for women in the 2029 Lok Sabha elections based on the existing 543 constituencies.
"The 33% reservation for women should be implemented in the 2029 Lok Sabha elections itself, based on the existing 543 constituencies. The 33% reservation for women should not be delayed any further. In Tamil Nadu, more women have voted than men. Providing reservation for women is not a concession; it is a matter of social justice. The 33% reservation for women must be implemented without any further delay," he said.The resolution seeks to safeguard the political representation of southern states, particularly Tamil Nadu, arguing that their success in controlling population growth should not result in reduced representation in Parliament."All the states including Tamil Nadu and the people / elected representatives of the union territories have not had their population counted for more than 50 years. The next census to count the population was supposed to be held in 2026. Therefore, since the delimitation of constituencies has not been carried out for the last 50 years, based on the 2011 population census, the constituencies should be delimited and the number of Lok Sabha and Assembly members should be increased from 550 to 850 by bringing in a constitutional amendment Bill," the resolution stated.
The Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill, 2026, was introduced in the Lok Sabha on April 16, proposing to increase the strength of the Lower House to 850 seats and expedite the implementation of the Women's Reservation Bill passed in 2023. However, the Bill failed to secure the constitutionally required two-thirds majority of members present and voting and was not passed.While the Congress and other opposition parties have supported the Women's Reservation Bill, they have opposed the proposed delimitation exercise and called for an increase in the number of Lok Sabha seats. The Opposition has also demanded that women's reservation be delinked from delimitation.

Lithuanian Church withholds priest's name as he faces charges involving 11 minors
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
07:11:00 UTC
16:11:00 KST

Fresh allegations of child sexual abuse against a priest is shaking Lithuania’s Catholic Church. The decision by the prosecutors and church authorities to withhold the name of the suspect is adding fuel to the fire.
A priest who worked in the Archdiocese of Vilnius has been charged with committing sexual offenses against minors over a 23-year period, including rape, sexual abuse and providing alcohol to children, prosecutors said.
Eleven minors have been recognised as victims in the case, which has been referred to the Vilnius Regional Court. Prosecutors have filed 34 charges against the priest, including two counts of rape of a minor and one count involving the rape of a young child.
The alleged offenses took place between 2002 and 2025, when the victims were between 12 and 18 years old, according to prosecutors.
Further reading
Justas Laucius, chief prosecutor at the Vilnius Regional Prosecutor’s Office, said the charges include four incidents involving the sexual abuse of people younger than 16 and three incidents in which the priest allegedly paid for sexual acts involving a minor.
The priest is also accused of 13 incidents involving providing alcohol to children and nine incidents involving the exploitation of children for pornography, prosecutors have said.
The case came to light during an investigation involving another Catholic priest, who has been charged with possessing child pornography.
“The case concerns pornographic material depicting a child or a person presented as a child,” Laucius said.
Neither prosecutors nor the church have publicly identified the two priests. However, Lithuanian news outlet Delfi has reported that the priest accused of sexual offenses is 56-year-old Tadas Švedavičius, while the second priest, 51-year-old Ryšardas Pečiūnas, is accused of possessing child pornography.
Both priests have been removed from their duties and previously worked within the Archdiocese of Vilnius. Prosecutors said the alleged offenses in the first case occurred in six locations in Lithuania, but neither the church nor prosecutors have identified the parishes involved.
The church said one of the priests had admitted guilt.
“One of the priests admitted his guilt, regretted what he had done and cooperated with investigators,” said Mykolas Sotničenka, a representative of the Archdiocese of Vilnius. “Which one? I cannot answer that question.”
Sotničenka said the archdiocese learned about the alleged crimes from prosecutors and has launched an investigation under canon law.
He said the church intends to provide assistance to victims. One person who has been recognised as a victim has contacted the archbishop and received an offer of assistance, he said. He declined to provide details about any potential compensation.
The decision not to identify the priests has prompted debate. Juozas Ruzgys, head of the Bernardinai.lt news outlet, said publishing their names could help people who may have been victims but have not come forward.
“At the very least, the names should be made public so that those who have been affected and are afraid to come forward can contact the authorities,” Ruzgys said.
But he also said he feared that publicly naming the suspects could lead to vigilante justice.
Prosecutors said the alleged crimes took years to surface in part because victims did not report them.
“There is a high level of latency – nobody complained,” Laucius said.
The archdiocese said it had received no previous reports or warnings concerning either priest.
“We received no signals, no reports, no suspicions about either priest,” Sotničenka said.
The church said it has been conducting safe-environment training for clergy for about 18 months. One of the accused priests participated in the training, Sotničenka said, acknowledging that “the training did not work” in that case.
Both priests have been ordered not to leave Lithuania while the proceedings continue.

Estonians at Euro athletics champs: Mülla makes pole vault final, Sai out in 100m heats

Estonians at Euro athletics champs: Mülla makes pole vault final, Sai out in 100m heats
Estonia's athletes saw mixed fortunes again at day two of the European Athletics Championships in Birmingham, England.
Pole vaulter Marleen Mülla comfortably reached Thursday's final at the Alexander Stadium on Tuesday, with 4.40 her best attempt. She came close to clearing 4.50 on her third, but the height proved too much. However, while the automatic qualifying benchmark was 4.55, the top 12, including Mülla, who placed eighth, had already been determined at the 4.50 attempt.
Allika Inkeri Moser, who competed at the World U20 Championships in Eugene, Oregon last week and only arrived in the U.K. on Monday, cleared the opening height of 4.10 on her first attempt but was unable to clear 4.25, so she did not go through.
The women's pole vault final begins at 9.50 p.m. Estonian time on Thursday and can be followed via the ERR sports portal.
Making his senior championship debut at the European Athletics Championships was sprinter Henri Sai, who placed 19th in the 100m heats Tuesday, not quite enough to go through.
"I was definitely ready, my reaction was very good, but I stumbled a little on the third step. I managed to recover and the first 40 meters were very decent, but I have some problems in the middle section, where the others just shoot straight past me," Sai told ERR. "But overall I can be satisfied, because the 100m wasn't what I came here for. I still wanted to run well, but that 3.0 headwind was a bit like running into a wall."
"With a 3.0 headwind and 10.66, that run is actually around my personal-best level, so there's nothing wrong in that. The time may look poor, but it was more of a good tune-up for the 200m," he added. "The feedback I got was that I'm actually in good shape and my legs are moving well. I'm the kind of person who just doesn't know how to run into a headwind and can't put together a good race in those conditions. But today I beat a couple of people who have better personal bests than me. The goal was still to beat some of those stronger guys."
Sai got off to a good start and finished sixth in his heat in 10.66 seconds, compared with a PB of 10.32 set earlier this year. The 12 fastest athletes by heat times advanced to the semifinals, with 10.57 the final qualifying time, meaning Sai did not progress.
He is next in action in Birmingham Thursday in the 200m heats.

Narva Tsar's Route initiators willing to change the name to keep plan alive
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
07:07:00 UTC
16:07:00 KST

Narva Tsar's Route initiators willing to change the name to keep plan alive
Narva City Council Chair Urbo Vaarmann is defending the idea of the Tsar's Route but is prepared to change the name of the planned tourism route to help ensure its success.
The tourism route called the Tsar's Route is intended to connect Narva and Tartu, following the example of the Postal Road (Postitee) and the Onion Route (Sibulatee) and mark the route once traveled by Russian rulers.
The Tsar's Route does not even exist yet, but it has already been described in the media as an attempt at Russification and as promoting the history of the Russian Empire — an entirely inappropriate undertaking given the current security situation. Narva City Council Chair Urbo Vaarmann, who initiated the tourism route, said the Tsar's Route is a clear and understandable name for foreign tourists, but that the idea is more important than the name.
"We are creating a major tourism product that connects the rest of the world with Narva and has to be equally understandable to everyone. After all, we're talking about manor houses and crowned heads who traveled along this route. The historical period we're dealing with here is very, very broad. And to link it to the war — come on, don't take it to the point of absurdity."
Vaarmann acknowledges that tsars also traveled between Narva and Tallinn, but said the route toward Tartu has been somewhat neglected from Narva's perspective and that a new tourism route would bring visitors to Narva from both Latvia and Lithuania.
"There are around 70 sites between Narva and Tartu that can be visited. It's like a never-ending story that can be developed not just for years, but for decades. I like to use the American example of U.S. Route 66 where even at the individual stops you pass through, you make sure to take a picture."
To help ensure the idea's success, Vaarmann is even willing to change the route's name.
"It doesn't have to be the Tsar's Route. Help come up with a name and I promise I'll put whoever can find a name that resonates with everyone on the committee."
Ida-Viru tourism developers do not want to criticize the Tsar's Route because, they say, the issue has already become too political. However, the route also has supporters, including avastaEESTI.ee guide Marko Kaldur.
"I'm not going to shy away from or be afraid of the fact that the word 'tsar' might rub someone the wrong way. All these issues that politicians, for the most part, complain about can be presented from very different perspectives — a neutral one if necessary — and all the historical aspects can be explained if needed. Calling all of this bad or inappropriate is simply some kind of hang-up among a small group of people, or a need to prove themselves somehow and hypocritically portray themselves as the ones standing up for the Estonian state."
Vaarmann believes it will take several years to get the Tsar's Route up and running as a tourism product. Kaldur will begin offering Tsar's Route tours this fall.
Former mayor: Tsar's Route inappropriate in the modern world
Katri Raik, who was removed as mayor of Narva in late July, said the historical Tsar's Route focusing on Russian tsars is ill-suited to the present day and, in her view, does not entirely align with historical facts either.
Raik acknowledged that more than 10 years ago she herself proposed the idea of promoting a route taken by tsars in Narva and onward to Tallinn, but said the new city government's idea differs from what she proposed at the time. Historians, she said, understand the Tsar's Route to mean the former Tallinn-Narva-St. Petersburg postal road, which connected St. Petersburg, the capital of the Russian Empire, with Western Europe.
"There is certainly a connection between the Russian tsars and Narva. But as a rule, rulers traveled from here onward to Tallinn and from there by ship to Europe, or back to St. Petersburg. Their route did not take them to Torma and Tartu County, home turf of Narva's new city leaders. A Russian Tsar's Route is not appropriate today, nor is it consistent with historical facts," Raik wrote on social media. She added that before the arrival of the railroad, the postal road was an important transportation link for Russia, with Narva located along the route.
Historian Pärtel Piirimäe wrote in the thread under Raik's social media post that the importance of the St. Petersburg-Narva-Torma-Tartu-Riga postal road should not be underestimated, however.
"Russian emperors also used it when traveling to Tartu and Riga. I haven't researched it specifically, but Catherine II and Alexander I, for example, definitely traveled that way to Livonia. Calling the old postal road the Tsar's Route is, of course, silly, and at this particular moment simply provocative," the historian said.

A Ukrainian drone attack killed a child and injured eight people in the Russian Black Sea port city of Novorossiysk, damaging four businesses and more than two dozen residential buildings, local officials said on Wednesday.
Novorossiysk Mayor Andrei Kravchenko said the overnight attack killed a child and damaged four enterprises and more than 20 residential buildings.
Krasnodar Governor Veniamin Kondratyev said another person was killed and several others were wounded elsewhere in the southern region, where Novorossiysk is located.
Novorossiysk is a major oil and grain export hub. Unverified videos circulated on Telegram purporting to show flames and smoke rising over the city.
In Russian-occupied Crimea, more than 30 drones were downed over Sevastopol, according to city Governor Mikhail Razvozhayev. Several houses were damaged, but no injuries were reported.
Russian strikes hit Ukraine
In Ukraine, a Russian attack sparked a fire at a shopping centre in the southeastern city of Zaporizhzhia, regional Governor Ivan Fedorov said.
The attack also cut power to about 1,200 consumers, he said.
A separate Russian attack damaged infrastructure in Ukraine's largest seaport Odessa, according to Serhiy Lysak, head of the city's military administration.
Russia's Defence Ministry said it had intercepted and destroyed 502 Ukrainian drones overnight across several Russian regions.
Black Sea strikes and oil exports
The attacks come as Ukraine has intensified strikes on Russian energy infrastructure and other sites, saying the campaign aims to deprive Moscow of resources used to fund its military.
Ukraine has paused drone attacks on oil tankers using Novorossiysk's Black Sea port following a request from US Vice President JD Vance, the Financial Times reported on Wednesday, citing Ukrainian officials.
The report said Washington was concerned that the attacks were disrupting oil markets and affecting US companies by targeting tankers carrying crude from Kazakhstan to a Caspian Pipeline Consortium (CPC) terminal at Novorossiysk.
According to the report, Ukraine agreed not to target CPC infrastructure or non-Russian vessels provided they were not under Ukrainian sanctions and were not carrying Russian oil or cargo.
War spills into regional energy markets
Black Sea drone attacks disrupted as much as one-fifth of CPC oil loadings in July, according to four sources familiar with the data, affecting crude exports from Kazakhstan and operations by Western oil companies including Chevron and Exxon Mobil.
Kazakhstan, which relies heavily on the CPC route to export crude, recorded a 14 percent drop in oil production in July compared with June, according to the sources.
The escalation comes as Kiev pursues diplomatic efforts to end the war. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Tuesday that Ukraine had handed US negotiators proposals for a peace plan.

Europe scrambles for eclipse glasses as solar power output set to dip
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
07:05:32 UTC
16:05:32 KST

The eclipse will be the first total solar eclipse visible from Europe since 2006. The path of totality will cross northern Spain, Portugal, Iceland, Greenland and northern Russia. London is expected to see around 90 per cent of the Sun obscured, while shoppers in Paris queued for more than two hours outside a specialist store on Rue de Rivoli.
In Spain, where several areas lie within the path of totality, many distribution points have already sold out. Pharmacies in central Madrid have been selling certified glasses for between €3 and €4 a pair, while prices in France range from €1.50 to €5.95.
In London, one shopkeeper was limiting customers to a single pair as stocks fell to around 100. In Brussels, optician Fouad Mehdaoui was taking orders by phone and adding customers to a waiting list after securing a last-minute restock.
The eclipse is also expected to cause a temporary drop in solar power generation across Europe. Grid operator association ENTSO-E estimates that output could fall by up to 9.7 gigawatts between 19:15 and 21:30 CET, with the largest reductions expected in Spain and Germany.
Solar power currently accounts for around 13 per cent of Europe’s electricity generation. Grid operators have prepared control rooms, arranged back-up generation and postponed planned maintenance to manage the temporary fall in output.
France’s grid operator RTE expects solar generation to drop by around 1.8 gigawatts, while German operators are preparing for a reduction of roughly 2 gigawatts. Despite the scale of the change, transmission system operators say they do not expect the eclipse to threaten the security of Europe’s electricity supply.

A passenger ferry caught fire off the coast of Bali; 106 people have been rescued, while another 25 remain on board
Kyiv • UNN
The Putri Yasmin ferry caught fire off the coast of Bali during a storm, and 106 people were rescued. Another 25 passengers and crew members remain on board, and the rescue operation is ongoing.
The Putri Yasmin ferry caught fire off the coast of Bali, Indonesia, during a severe storm: rescuers managed to evacuate 106 people, while another 25 passengers and crew members remain on board. Rescuers and vessels passing nearby managed to save 106 people. At the same time, they were attempting to evacuate another 25 people from the burning vessel, authorities said. Associated Press reports this, writes UNN.
Details
"Our top priority is the safety of all passengers and crew members," said Muhammad Hariyadi, who heads the Mataram Search and Rescue Office.
According to him, difficult weather conditions, including waves up to 4 meters high, complicated the rescue operation.
The fire started at approximately 4:15 a.m. as the Putri Yasmin ferry was sailing from Padang Bai Port in Bali to Lembar Port on the neighboring island of Lombok in the province of West Nusa Tenggara, the search and rescue office in Mataram, the province's administrative center, reported.
About half an hour later, the agency received an emergency report and immediately dispatched personnel and rescue vessels to the scene.
Hariyadi said that Indonesian Navy ships, patrol and rescue boats, as well as a helicopter conducting an aerial survey of the area, took part in the rescue operation.
According to Hariyadi, the ferry was carrying 114 passengers and 17 crew members, according to the passenger manifest released by the Padang Bai Port administration. There were also 44 cars and 53 motorcycles on board.
Background
Indonesia is an archipelago consisting of more than 17,000 islands, where ferries are a common means of transportation. Disasters occur regularly, and insufficient oversight of compliance with safety regulations is often cited as the cause.

A drone targeted a power station in Libya’s western city of Zawiya on Wednesday, sparking a fire at the facility, local media reported.

The attack follows a series of drone strikes on key infrastructure in Zawiya, around 40 kilometres west of Tripoli.
Libya’s General Electricity Company said the South Zawiya transformation station was targeted, causing it to burn completely and go out of service, cutting electricity to wide areas.

All work has halted at the plant and teams have been evacuated until safe working conditions are restored, the company said.
The company warned that continued attacks on electricity infrastructure could threaten the stability of the national grid and lead to wider disruptions, including partial or general blackouts.
No group has claimed responsibility.
Series of attacks
On Tuesday, Libya’s National Oil Corporation (NOC) said the Zawiya Oil Refinery had been targeted for the fifth time since Sunday.
The state-run company said an explosive-laden drone struck the roof of a diesel tank, piercing it and triggering a fire that emergency teams later brought under control.
Another drone had targeted a separate diesel tank at the refinery on Tuesday, also causing a fire. No casualties were reported in either attack.
The corporation said refinery operations had resumed following the earlier strikes and that fuel supplies and reserves remained unaffected.
Last week, clashes between armed groups in Zawiya spread to the nearby city of Surman, leaving people dead and injured and resulting in a prison break.
Libya remains divided between the internationally regonised Tripoli-based Government of National Unity led by Abdul Hamid Dbeibeh and a rival administration appointed by the House of Representatives and headed by Osama Hammad in Benghazi.
The UN Support Mission in Libya (UNSMIL) has sought to resolve political disputes that have delayed long-awaited national elections, which Libyans hope will help end years of political division and armed conflict following the 2011 overthrow of longtime ruler Moammar Gadhafi.

====================================================================================================

Northrop reveals 50mm gun built to beat drone swarms
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
08:02:36 BST
16:02:36 KST

Northrop Grumman has given a name to the 50mm gun-based air defence system it has been developing to shoot down cruise missiles and drone swarms, calling it Raid Hunter, and says testing through the rest of this year will support accelerated fielding.
The system pairs the company’s Chain Gun with precision-guided 50mm ammunition and a networked system controller. Its purpose is to handle raids large enough to saturate conventional defences, which is a problem missiles alone cannot solve because a magazine of interceptors runs out faster than an attacker runs out of drones.
That economic point is the one the company keeps returning to. A high rate of fire, deep magazines and fast reloads are what it offers against massed threats, in place of expending an interceptor worth several hundred thousand pounds on a target worth a few thousand.
Kenn Todorov, vice president and general manager for command and control and weapons integration, said: “Raid Hunter addresses a critical short-range defense gap by delivering rapid, high-capacity protection against complex, mass aerial threats like cruise missiles and drone swarms. It provides warfighters with a cost-effective, flexible tool to decisively defeat evolving threats now and in the future, strengthening the security of vital bases and infrastructure.”
He said: “War has evolved. Air Defenders need the ability to defend against large, complex raids designed to overwhelm traditional defense solutions. Raid Hunter addresses this critical need by delivering a cost effective and deep magazine solution which can be rapidly delivered to the warfighter at scale.”
The system is built on a modular palletised form factor sized for transport aboard a C-130, with vehicle-mounted and container-based variants planned. Northrop Grumman has not said when those variants will appear, nor which customers it is working with beyond a reference to government and allied partners.
Guns had largely been written off for air defence by the 1990s, displaced by missiles that were more accurate at greater range. What has brought them back is the arithmetic of the drone war. Russian and Ukrainian forces launch small uncrewed aircraft in numbers that make missile defence unaffordable, and the same problem has appeared in the Red Sea, where Western warships have fired multi-million pound rounds at Houthi drones costing a fraction of that.
Guided ammunition is what makes the return viable as unguided cannon fire against a small manoeuvring target requires a large volume of rounds and a very good fire control solution, whereas a course-correcting projectile allows hits at longer range with fewer shots, while keeping the cost per engagement far below that of a missile.
Raid Hunter sits within what the company calls Raid Defense Solutions, its portfolio of layered kinetic counter-drone and air defence products, which combines fielded programmes with command and control software and sensor fusion.
Similar thinking is visible across the industry and among European governments. Rheinmetall has continued to develop its Skyranger turret in 30mm and 35mm forms, several armies have brought older self-propelled anti-aircraft guns back into service, and Britain has pursued the problem through directed energy work on DragonFire alongside a series of counter-drone trials.
The 50mm chain gun itself is not a new weapon. Northrop Grumman developed the XM913 in that calibre for the US Army’s optionally manned fighting vehicle programme, work that produced a gun capable of firing airburst and guided rounds from a mechanically driven, externally powered action of the kind the company has built since the Bushmaster series entered service in the 1970s.

Between January and July, Chinese carmakers delivered a total of 5.67 million EVs to domestic customers, down 12.5 per cent from a year earlier, according to the CPCA.

Water-smart by 2030: the EU's plan to boost water efficiency by 10%
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
07:00:05 UTC
16:00:05 KST

Europe is losing 38 percent of its soil to droughts. The EU's Water Resilience Strategy wants to restore water ecosystems, cut waste, and digitalise water management to increase water resilience across the bloc. Watch the video.
Record temperatures are sweeping across Spain and into Finland. This summer, droughts have spread across Europe, prompting urgent water rationing measures and temporary bans on non-essential water uses.
The World Weather Attribution links current droughts to months of below-average rainfall and record heat between April and June. In 2026 alone, soil moisture deficits are 5 to 11 times more likely. France's maize harvest is at a 50-year low, and Romania is losing over a million hectares. Reduced water levels in rivers and lakes are affecting tourism and transportation, including on the Danube, which is at its lowest since 1996.
Extreme dryness is also fuelling wildfires. The EU reports that, so far, 500,852 hectares have been burned across the bloc, up from 381,444 hectares in the same period in 2025.
The EU struggles to combat current droughts because decades of overuse, pollution, and poor water management have depleted water resources.
Its Water Resilience Strategy (2025) secures Europe’s long-term water supply. It aims to make the EU water-resilient to climate change by improving its water efficiency by at least 10 percent by 2030. The roadmap includes over 50 actions, 30 of which are crucial. To date, 3 actions are complete.
The roadmap is based on three pillars: restoring and protecting water quality and quantity by reducing pollution and over-extraction; building a water-smart economy through digitalisation to monitor and manage use and cut waste; and ensuring access to clean, affordable water while encouraging water-saving habits and water-efficient products.
