Tarte tatin, spicy pork chops and crumble: Ravinder Bhogal’s gooseberry recipes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
05:00:19 UTC
14:00:19 KST

In the summer glut of saccharine fruits such as strawberries and peaches, gooseberries may not be the ones you reach for first. But behind their strange burr of fine fuzz, these translucent, marble-like fruits offer a complex, defiant flavour. They are juicy, fragrant, a little sweet (especially the red ones that come along later in the season), but, overall, they are raspishly sour. Like rhubarb, they need sweetening if you’re using them in compotes or desserts, but their natural tartness offers a wonderful contrast and cuts through cheese, fatty meat such as pork or oily fish such as mackerel.
Spiced pork chops with fennel, tarragon and gooseberry salad (pictured top)
The addition of tart fruit in the salad helps to cut through the fattiness of the meat.
Prep 15 min
Marinate 20 min
Pickle 10 min
 Cook 30 min
 Serves 4
2 tsp sea salt
  2 tsp fennel seeds
2 tbsp coriander seeds
  1 tsp black peppercorns
  1 tsp caster sugar
  ½ tsp paprika
  1 tsp dried oregano
  4 pork chops
  2 tbsp olive oil
  25g butter
  4 garlic cloves, unpeeled and bashed flat
For the salad
3 tbsp white-wine vinegar
  1 tbsp caster sugar, or honey
  Sea salt and black pepper
  1 tsp coriander seeds, toasted and very lightly crushed
2 fennel bulbs, trimmed and very finely sliced from top to base (preferably with a mandoline)
1 cucumber, peeled and sliced into long ribbons with a vegetable peeler or mandoline
1 banana shallot, peeled and very finely sliced
200g gooseberries
25g tarragon, leaves picked
25g mint, leaves picked and finely chopped
3 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil
Put the salt, fennel seeds, coriander seeds, pepper and sugar in a mortar and grind to a fine powder. Add the paprika and oregano, and grind again. Pat the chops dry with kitchen paper, then press the spice mix all over the meat. Leave to marinate at room temperature for 20 minutes.
Heat the oven to 200C (180C fan)/350F/gas 6. Heat the oil and butter in an ovenproof frying pan and add the garlic. Using tongs, hold the chops skin-side down in the pan for five minutes to crisp up and render the fat. Once the fat is a lovely amber colour, fry the chops for three minutes on each side, basting as you go, then transfer to the oven for six minutes, or until cooked all the way through. Rest the meat for five minutes.
Meanwhile, make the salad. Mix the vinegar and caster sugar in a mixing bowl until the sugar has dissolved, then season well with salt and pepper. Add the coriander seeds, fennel, cucumber and shallot, and set aside to lightly pickle for 10 minutes. Finally, add the gooseberries and herbs and drizzle over the olive oil. Toss well and serve with the pork chops.
Gooseberry tarte tatin with goat’s cheese
A savoury take on the classic apple tarte tatin. This version features a wonderful partnership between tart gooseberries and funky goat’s cheese. Serve with some dressed salad leaves and toasted hazelnuts for crunch.
Prep 10 min
 Cook 55 min
 Serves 6
40g butter
A few sprigs of thyme
2½ tbsp runny honey
3 tbsp apple cider vinegar
Sea salt and black pepper
  750g gooseberries, topped and tailed
Plain flour, for dusting
500g block puff pastry
  150g soft goat’s cheese
 Heat the oven to 200C (180C fan)/425F/gas 6. Put a 20cm ovenproof frying pan on a medium heat and melt the butter. Once the butter has completely melted, add the thyme and fry briefly for 30 seconds, then stir in the honey and vinegar and season well.
Once the glaze has thickened and caramelised, remove the pan from the heat and leave to cool for eight to 10 minutes. Add the gooseberries and stir to coat.
On a floured work surface, roll out the pastry to 3mm thick, then cut out a circle slightly larger than the pan. Cover the gooseberries with the pastry, using your fingers to carefully tuck it in at the edges. Bake for 30-35 minutes, or until crisp and golden on top.
Remove from the oven and leave to cool for at least five minutes before carefully inverting on to a serving plate. Serve hot or cold, scattered with crumbled goat’s cheese and more black pepper.
Gooseberry crumble custard cake
The sour fruit offers a welcome respite in this nursery-sweet cake layered with custard. Raspberries would also work well here.
Prep 5 min
 Cook 1 hr 20 min, plus cooling
 Chill 4 hr
 Serves 12
300g unsalted butter, plus extra to grease tin
300g golden caster sugar
  5 medium eggs
  300g plain flour
  2 tsp baking powder
  150ml milk
  400g gooseberries
  500ml fresh vanilla custard
For the crumble
200g plain flour
  125g chilled butter 
  125g golden caster sugar
  A fat pinch of sea salt
  70g flaked almonds
  Finely grated zest of 1 lemon
Heat the oven to 160C (140C fan)/325F/gas 3. For the crumble topping, rub the flour and butter between your fingertips to a breadcrumb-like consistency, then mix in the sugar, salt, almonds, and lemon zest. Chill until needed.
Grease a 20cm x 30cm rectangular cake tin with butter, then line it with baking paper.
In a stand mixer or with an electric whisk, beat the butter and caster sugar until light and fluffy. Add the eggs one at a time, beating each one in thoroughly, then sift in the flour and baking powder. Pour in the milk, gently fold in, then add half the gooseberries.
Spread half the gooseberry batter evenly into the lined tin, then pour the custard on top. Carefully spread the rest of the batter on top, then dot with the remaining gooseberries.
Sprinkle with the crumble mixture, then bake for about an hour, until golden but still a bit wobbly in the centre. Leave to cool in the tin, then chill for at least four hours, and ideally overnight. Cut into 12 rectangles and serve.

China’s quant funds have an edge on foreign rivals, even as Beijing curbs trading speed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
05:00:07 UTC
14:00:07 KST

China’s quant funds have an edge on foreign rivals, even as Beijing curbs trading speed
Top US quant teams unable to beat native competitors in mainland China unlike in Japan or India, despite regulatory clampdown on trading
“If a top US quant team goes to Japan or India, they can beat virtually all the native quants,” Xia Chun, founder and chief economist at Chinese financial research firm Wiselink Group and former finance professor at the University of Hong Kong, told the South China Morning Post this week.
The reason, Xia said, lies in China’s unique valuation logic for state-owned enterprises, whose state-backed financing advantages create pricing dynamics that traditional foreign models fail to capture.
Frequent administrative policy interventions such as initial public offering suspensions and policy-driven trading halts become trading signals that outside models struggle to replicate, he added.
The comments from Xia, who has also advised the China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC), came as Beijing tightens its grip on the quant trading industry. On the night of July 31, stock exchanges in Shanghai and Shenzhen cut the dedicated local-network queues that let quant funds’ co-located servers receive price feeds tens to hundreds of microseconds ahead of other participants.

Winding trails and coastal treks: Three of Europe’s best autumn hikes, according to Lonely Planet
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
05:00:03 UTC
14:00:03 KST

In its new guide book, Lonely Planet has picked out some of the best hikes around the world. Here we take a look at three of the top European options for hiking this autumn.
With the arrival of autumn comes a spectacular transformation of scenery and the opportunity to lace up your walking boots and to be at one with nature.
Hiking has become one of the most popular outdoor activities and in Europe we’re spoiled for choice when it comes to trails and routes to tackle.
In its new guide book – "Where to Go When: Hiking" – Lonely Planet has showcased more than 90 of the world's best hikes and the months to explore them in, from "micro walks and multi-day treks to pilgrimage routes and mountainous rambles".
Here we take a look at three of the featured hikes in Europe to do during the cooler autumn months, plus other popular options further afield.
Three of Europe’s best autumn hikes
Premužić Trail, Croatia (challenging)
Winding through Croatia's Northern Velebit National Park, the Premužić Trail is “one of Europe's finest examples of dry-stone engineering”, said Lonely Planet. Crafted pathways weave through rugged landscapes, passing wildflower meadows and shepherds' huts with views across the Adriatic Sea. September offers pleasant temperatures, snow-free trails and warm coastal waters, making it the “perfect time to discover this dramatic corner of Croatia”.
Coast to Coast Path, England (moderate/challenging)
Follow in the footsteps of fell-walking legend Alfred Wainwright with this west-to-east walk across England, which starts from the Cumbrian village of St Bees to Robin Hood’s Bay in Yorkshire. Going through three National Parks, this iconic route has recently been awarded National Trail status and now has clearer signage, better accessibility and is managed to a higher environmental standard. Lonely Planet recommends doing the English Coast to Coast Path in October.
Via Francigena, Swiss Alps and Northern Italy (moderate)
The Via Francigena is a pilgrimage from Bourg-Saint-Pierre in the Swiss Alps, through Italy’s Aosta Valley all the way to Rome. Hike in “historic, holy footsteps” and savour stunning panoramic mountain views, flower filled meadows and the cultural and culinary delights of Italy’s diverse regions.
Three of the best international autumn hikes
Choquequirao – Southern Peru (challenging)
For travellers seeking an alternative to the busy Inca Trail, Choquequirao is a 15th-century Inca site that’s sometimes described as “Machu Picchu's lesser-known sister”, with a fraction of the visitors. The demanding route descends deep into the flower-filled Apurímac Canyon before climbing steeply back towards the ruins, “rewarding hikers with ceremonial platforms, temples, ritual baths and intricate llama carvings etched into its ancient terraces”. September is one of the best times to visit, with warm, clear days arriving after the peak tourist season.
Quilotoa Loop, Ecuador (easy)
Explore Ecuador's Andean highlands on a gentle and rewarding journey through traditional villages and rolling mountain landscapes before reaching the "breathtaking" Laguna Quilotoa. Nestled within the crater of an extinct volcano, the emerald-green lake is celebrated for its Indigenous culture and striking scenery. As well as crisp blue-sky mornings and lush green hillsides, November offers quieter trails and plenty of time to explore local artisan stores.
Langtang and Helambu Trek, Northern Nepal (challenging)
Journey through one of Nepal's most spectacular Himalayan regions, where dense forests, sacred lakes and centuries-old Buddhist monasteries can be found beneath snow-capped peaks. Rich in Tibetan culture, the Langtang and Helambu valleys also “tell a story of resilience”, with tourism continuing to support communities rebuilding after the 2015 earthquake. November is among the best months to trek here, bringing dry, clear days, comfortable temperatures and unbeatable mountain views.

Lithuania is getting ready for EU Council presidency
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
05:00:00 UTC
14:00:00 KST

Lithuania is in the final stretch of preparations to take over the rotating presidency of the Council of the European Union in the first half of next year – a six-month stint that will bring hundreds of meetings, and thousands of visiting officials, to Vilnius. But even as workers scramble to renovate parliament and repave city streets, the capital is about to become slightly harder to reach by air.
A parliament under repair
Workers, not lawmakers, have become the regular fixture at Lithuania's parliament, the Seimas, this summer.
Corridors are being refurbished, the historic Hall of March 11 – where Lithuania's 1990 declaration of independence was signed – is being restored, and previously unused spaces are being converted, all at a cost of around €1.2 million.
Visiting delegations are set to arrive through the courtyard, which is also being tidied up, though parliament received only a single bid when it put the courtyard work out to tender. Contractors, it turns out, aren't queuing up for jobs that must be squeezed into the narrow gaps between sessions.
The fact that the Hall of March 11 is a listed heritage space doesn't help either, as renovators' hands are largely tied.
"Everything here counts as cultural heritage – absolutely everything, the tables, the plasterwork, all of it," said parliamentary Chancellor Algirdas Stončaitis.
"This is the first refurbishment the hall has had since it was originally built," he added. Walls, benches, carpeting, lighting and ventilation have all been redone.
Other spaces are getting attention for the first time since the Soviet era, including the main cloakroom and a set of public toilets nearby – "five in total," Stončaitis noted, "but let's be clear, they won't be gold-plated."
Some stairwells will be repainted and the press centre lightly refreshed, though he added a wry aside that the building's appearance is getting more attention than the substance behind it.
Speaker Juozas Olekas, watching the work from his office window, framed it as ordinary housekeeping ahead of company: "Everyone tidies their house before guests come – that's essentially what's happening here too."
He pointed to accessibility improvements for people with disabilities as one substantive change amid the cosmetic ones, and said he expects everything to be ready by the autumn session.
The city has learned from experience, too. When Vilnius hosted a NATO leaders' summit three years ago, authorities faced criticism for cosmetic fixes – old trolleybuses hidden from view, street lamps given a quick coat of paint.
This time, Mayor Valdas Benkunskas says the approach will be different: "We're not repainting the lamp posts, we're replacing them with new ones."
The cost of preparation is already running over budget. More than €140 million was earmarked for the presidency, but Finance Minister Taurimas Valys says that won't be enough.
"More costs keep surfacing – there are procedures in some areas that were previously overlooked," he said.
Around 300 events are planned over the six-month presidency, with the largest – just like during the NATO summit – held at the Litexpo exhibition centre.
Heads of state, government and ministers from across the EU are expected to pass through the capital.
What Lithuania wants to prioritise
Valys says tackling inflation will be one focus, though he's candid about the limits of what a rotating presidency can actually achieve.
"We're second-from-last in the bloc on inflation, but we're not alone in this, and we can't fight it alone," he said before acknowledging that interest rates, not EU presidency initiatives, remain the primary lever in the long run.
The minister will also be involved in the early stages of negotiations over the EU's next seven-year budget, a process that requires balancing competing national interests.
"Naturally, we can't publicly play up any one position," he said.
The social security and labour minister, Inga Ruginienė, has named demographics – code, in an EU context increasingly worried about ageing populations, for boosting birth rates – as a priority.
Asked whether that might extend to matchmaking events for young people (a previous minister had floated the idea of a singles disco), Ruginienė laughed it off: "I do like to dance. If you join in, we'll dance together."
She says more substantive proposals on parental leave are coming this autumn, though she declined to give details, saying only that they'll go beyond "cosmetic adjustments."
The interior minister, Martynas Katelynas, has flagged migration as a priority. He suggested that the EU's new Migration and Asylum Pact, which took effect in June and introduces tighter border checks and a burden-sharing mechanism for asylum seekers among member states, already has shortcomings.
"The pact shouldn't come at the expense of states' security, and I think going forward we'll need to take account of the realities on the ground, in the world and in Europe, without trying to be holier than the Pope," he said.
The opposition isn't attacking the government's agenda outright, framing the preparations instead as the product of continuity in the civil service rather than the current governing coalition.
"Regardless of the change of political teams in government, the state apparatus is preparing the substance well," said Radvilė Morkūnaitė-Mikulėnienė, a member of the parliament's European affairs committee.
Getting there may be harder
Despite the preparations, reaching Vilnius during the presidency could get trickier. Latvia's airBaltic, which has been under financial strain, is cutting its winter routes from Vilnius to Berlin and Dubai, and reducing flights to Tallinn as well.

‘Shortcuts will cut you short’: PM Modi’s message for youngsters at former President Kovind’s autobiography launch

Former President Ram Nath Kovind with PM Narendra Modi at book launch
NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Wednesday urged youngsters to avoid taking shortcuts in life, warning that “a shortcut will cut you short.”He made the remarks while releasing the autobiography of former President Ram Nath Kovind in the national capital."I would particularly like to urge the younger generation—we live in the age of 'Reels' and social media influencers. Even in this era of shortcuts, let us remember something often written at railway stations: A shortcut will cut you short," PM Modi said.He also encouraged youngsters to read the autobiographies of personalities they admire, saying such accounts offer a unique perspective on the historic events of their time.
“The period covered in a biography brings one very close to history itself. That is why I sincerely hope that the hard work put in by Kovind ji proves beneficial to future generations and especially to the youth,” PM Modi added.PM Modi further praised Kovind’s "guidance" and recalled the former president's “special affection and warmth” for him.“Today, we have the opportunity to witness the launch of Ramnath Kovind ji's autobiography.
I have known Kovind ji for a very long time and have had the opportunity to know him closely. His guidance during his tenure as President, along with his special affection and warmth towards me, has been a truly valuable asset for me,” he said.
Expressing confidence in the book’s significance, the prime minister described Kovind’s autobiography as a potential “cherished legacy” for Indian democracy and society.“... Based on my understanding of his life and my knowledge of his capabilities, I can say with full confidence that Ramnath Kovind ji's autobiography will become a cherished legacy for Indian democracy and society. There is so much I could speak about at length--regarding Kovind ji's life journey and his contributions to society and the nation. However, a book launch event should only serve as a 'curtain-raiser'; it is best if you all derive the full benefit of the book by reading it yourselves,” he added.Meanwhile, Kovind described the launch as an emotional moment and expressed gratitude to those who attended the event.“It is an emotional moment for me to address you all from this platform today. I have addressed you on several occasions, but today's occasion is different. I am grateful to all of you for joining this programme to mark the launch of my autobiography. I was wondering what I should say today. I have already written everything in my autobiography, and readers will read it,” the former president remarked.

Israeli raids, arrests continue as UN warns West Bank at ‘breaking point’
Israeli forces arrest 23 Palestinians and demolish the home of a man killed in a confrontation with Israeli settlers in July.
Israeli forces have continued their crackdown in the occupied West Bank, arresting at least 23 Palestinians and demolishing several homes, as the United Nations warned that the situation in the territory was at a “breaking point”.
The arrests and demolitions on Tuesday came as dozens of Israeli settlers continued attacks and raids on Palestinian villages, including one in Khirbet ar-Ras al-Ahmar, where parts of a water pipeline was destroyed.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Concerns mount over integrity of Israel’s upcoming October elections
- list 2 of 4Israel is ‘trying to make Palestine disappear’: The Elders
- list 3 of 4Israel demolishes home of Palestinian killed during settler attack

According to the Palestinian Wafa news agency, those detained on Tuesday included two children, one of whom had a disability, as well as a man who was taken while he was grazing his livestock in al-Hadidiyah in the northern Jordan Valley.
At least 11 others were arrested in the Jenin governorate, while five were detained in the Bethlehem area.
In the village of Tal, southwest of Nablus, Israeli forces demolished the family home of Farouq Ramadan, one of four Palestinians killed during a confrontation with Israeli settlers on July 24. Two Israelis were also killed in the incident.
Israel maintains a policy of demolishing the homes belonging to relatives of Palestinians involved in attacks against Israelis in an approach human rights groups have condemned as collective punishment.
Israeli forces also demolished another home near Yatta in the Hebron governorate and filled in a water well there, displacing nine Palestinians, according to Wafa. Twelve commercial warehouses in the village of Anza and an agricultural facility in the village of Yarza were also bulldozed, while in Masafer Yatta, south of Hebron, Israeli forces issued demolition notices for the Khallat al-Dabaa school, as well as several homes and agricultural structures.
According to UN figures, Israel has demolished an average of 122 Palestinian buildings every month this year.
Settler attacks
Separately, dozens of settlers attacked a group of Palestinians ploughing their lands in Al-Mughayyir, wounding six people, including three children and two women.
Al Jazeera’s Nour Odeh, reporting from Al-Mughayyir, said the settlers also burned part of the valley and attacked nearby homes.
“Upwards of 60 percent of Al-Mughayyir’s land has been confiscated by the Israeli army, while Israeli settlers have set up at least 11 illegal outposts in the village, barring the farmers from their land,” she said.
“Some 119 Palestinian communities in the occupied West Bank have been uprooted by this very dynamic in the past three years. Palestinians are treated as trespassers in their own land, while Israeli settlers slash, burn, and steal the land with impunity,” she added.
In Khirbet Ras al-Ahmar, settlers also destroyed parts of the main water pipeline, cutting off supplies to 30 Palestinian herding families and to nearby farms, according to Wafa.
In Burqa, northwest of Nablus, six Palestinians, including two children, were wounded after Israeli forces assaulted residents during a raid, according to the Palestinian Red Crescent. Settlers also raided the Nablus-area villages of Awarta, Osarin and Sarra.
The attacks form part of a sharp escalation in violence by Israeli forces and settlers across the occupied West Bank as Israel gears up for a parliamentary election in October.
UN warns of ‘de facto annexation’
Addressing the UN Security Council on Tuesday, Deputy Special Coordinator for the Middle East Peace Process Ramiz Alakbarov said the West Bank was at “breaking point”.
He said Israeli forces and settlers have killed 76 Palestinians, including 18 children, in the occupied territory so far this year, while about 3,800 Palestinians – nearly half of them children – have been displaced by settler violence, demolitions and evictions.
The UN has documented more than 1,430 settler attacks resulting in casualties or property damage across roughly 260 Palestinian communities in 2026, he said, with many carried out in the presence of Israeli forces. Since January 2023, 127 Palestinian communities have been fully or partially displaced, including 47 completely uprooted, affecting more than 6,390 people.
Alakbarov said settler attacks, once concentrated mainly in Area C, where Israel holds full civil and security control, are increasingly spreading into Areas A and B.
Israeli authorities have also advanced or approved roughly 12,360 settlement housing units across the West Bank this year, including 5,160 in occupied East Jerusalem, he said.
“These are interconnected steps, not isolated developments,” Alakbarov said, warning that they were reshaping the occupied West Bank, weakening Palestinian governance and advancing “de facto annexation”.

Traveling Through Poland to Ukraine: Observations of a Norwegian
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
04:50:55 UTC
13:50:55 KST

On Sunday I crossed the Polish border at Przemyśl to board a train for Kyiv.
I stood two and a half hours in line before embarkation. Many waited up to four. The train left 90 minutes late because only three border guards checked the documents of some 500–600 travelers – and they opened late.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The passengers, mostly Ukrainians, stood exposed to the weather, sharing two mobile toilets meant for public events. At one point, there was real distress and unrest as people feared they would not reach the train in time.
Ukrainian railways do not leave their citizens behind. Hence the delay.
The process is a disgrace, and an example of how many Poles relate to Ukrainians. Their well-being is not a priority. Four and a half years into the war, with no end on the horizon, temporary solutions are no longer acceptable. Nor is xenophobia.
I do not understand Poland – and I am not sure it does either.
Perhaps “strategically ambivalent” is the better description. It wants to be European, yet fiercely sovereign from Brussels. It is one of Ukraine’s strongest supporters, yet increasingly willing to challenge Kyiv over trade, history, and refugees.
It acknowledges that Ukraine is protecting Poland yet is willing to undermine its economy and make its EU and NATO membership politically conditional.
It is arguably America’s strongest European ally, while building European defense capabilities as Washington becomes unreliable.
Russian Drone Hits 5-Story Residential Building in Odesa
It elects a pro-European Prime Minister, then turns around and elects an anti-EU president.
It wants Germany stronger against Russia, while wary of German dominance.
It wants to lead the region yet quarrels with the very partners it needs. It is restrictive on migration while heavily dependent on Ukrainian labor.
It is also divided against itself: east, rural, older, more Catholic and right-leaning against west, urban, younger, more secular, and liberal – each convinced it is the real Poland.
These contradictions are more than opportunism. Poland is trying to escape dependence on any major power—Russia, Germany, France, Brussels, or even the US. It wants the security that comes from alliances and integration while keeping the freedom of action of full sovereignty. For a medium-sized power, those ambitions collide.
They also breed nationalism and xenophobia. Polish society is becoming more polarized over Ukraine, and anti-Ukrainian hostility has genuinely increased. Polish police recorded 180 suspected hate crimes against Ukrainians in the first half of 2026, about 30% more than in the same period of 2025. And yet –the contradiction again – Poles march against the very hostility their politics feeds.
Having many Polish friends and welcoming Polish leadership, I am genuinely distressed by what I see and experience. Anti-Ukrainian hostility reflects badly on Poland while most of Europe looks to Ukraine with admiration and respect.

Ukraine’s first domestically built CBRN scout vehicle just replaced Soviet jeep with no armor at all
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
04:45:08 UTC
13:45:08 KST

Ukraine is retiring a Soviet chemical-scout vehicle in favor of one it built itself. Ukraine's National Guard has received the first Ukrainian radiation and chemical reconnaissance vehicles on the armored Tisa chassis, replacing the outdated Soviet UAZ-469RKh, National Guard commander Oleksandr Pivnenko announced.
The vehicle is a step in Ukraine's shift from Soviet legacy equipment to its own modern designs. Developed to National Guard specifications for current battlefield conditions, the armored scout allows crews to survey and monitor contaminated zones without leaving the protected vehicle.
What the vehicle does
The vehicle carries radiation and chemical reconnaissance instruments, an automated system for collecting and processing information, a weather station, modern communications, and satellite navigation, all of which enable real-time data collection and transmission to assess a situation and make decisions faster.
The mission is early warning of invisible threats. The task of chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear (CBRN) units is to detect radiation, chemical, and biological threats in time, determine the extent of contamination, and quickly pass the information to command.
"The safety of soldiers, the completion of combat tasks, and the protection of the civilian population depend on the speed and accuracy of this work," Pivnenko said.
The armored base is the upgrade
The Tisa chassis is what sets the new vehicle apart from its Soviet predecessor. The light-armored Tisa is built on the Toyota Land Cruiser 79 platform and meets the NATO STANAG 4569 protection standard, providing ballistic and mine protection that the open-topped UAZ never offered.
The vehicle is equipped for hard conditions. It carries night-vision systems and air ventilation and filtration systems, letting the crew work in contaminated or dangerous environments while staying protected. The filtration matters especially for a CBRN vehicle: it lets the crew operate inside a sealed, over-pressured cabin in exactly the toxic zones the vehicle is sent to scout.

Russia turns to India for petrol as Ukraine pummels refineries
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
04:45:00 UTC
13:45:00 KST

Russia turns to India for petrol as Ukraine pummels refineries
MOSCOW – Russia has started importing petrol from as far away as India, as Ukrainian attacks on its refineries trigger severe local shortages.
It is the first time Moscow has imported the motor fuel from the South Asian nation, according to Kpler data, with the lengthy journey required an indication of how dire the crunch is becoming.
The first shipment was received on Aug 5, and more may be on the way. According to Kpler. Indian processor Nayara Energy – backed by Rosneft, Russia’s top oil producer – has emerged as a source of the fuel, which is being moved on a chain of Russian-linked tankers via transfers off Egypt.
“The emergence of Indian barrels is particularly notable,” said Sumit Ritolia, lead analyst at Kpler.
The cargoes, which complement continued imports from Belarus and other neighbouring markets, highlight “the severity of the current domestic petrol imbalance, and the extent to which lower refinery runs are reshaping Russia’s traditional product trade flows”, he said.
The global energy market is coping with the fallout from two major conflicts, as Kyiv presses on with its assault on Russia’s refineries, while the US and Iran continue to face off in the Middle East.
The combined disruptions have acted to tighten fuel markets, with Moscow – traditionally a supplier of fuels overseas – banning both petrol and diesel exports to prioritise local users.
Following a wave of attacks, EA Analytics estimated that Russia’s crude-processing rates were running at 3.6 million barrels a day in July, about a third below the seasonal norm.
Since then, Kyiv has intensified strikes, hitting five processors last week and at least two more this week.
Russia’s Energy Ministry, India’s Oil Ministry, and Nayara’s communications team did not respond to Bloomberg requests for comment.
Since getting sanctioned by the European Union in July 2025, Nayara has been relying on so-called dark-fleet tankers and trans-shipment operations to receive its crude, and export fuels.
Its 400,000 barrel-a-day refinery at Vadinar on India’s west coast also needs to widen its export market, after a key buyer, Hindustan Petroleum, recently started producing more of its own fuel in the region.
For the inaugural shipment, Russian-flagged products tanker Cyclone (formerly Agni) loaded a 42,000 tonne petrol cargo from Vadinar on June 18, ship-tracking data compiled by Bloomberg shows.
The fuel was then transferred to the Oman-flagged Garnet at Damietta Port, off Egypt’s Mediterranean coast, on July 6. That vessel then reached Russia in early August.
More petrol may follow. The products tanker Varg loaded nearly 40,000 tonnes of the fuel at Vadinar on July 6 and likely conducted a ship-to-ship transfer at Damietta in late July, based on changes in its draft, according to Kpler.
Ship-to-ship transfers, or STS, typically take place so that individual vessels can cut travel times.
No receiving vessel has been confirmed, though Kpler identified Beast as a possibility.
The vessel was at Damietta and recorded an increase in draft on July 30 and 31.
Beast had signalled Morocco’s Tangier as a destination, but has since gone beyond that port and is now sailing north in the Atlantic Ocean, with its cargo intact, the data shows.
Another products tanker, Cameroon-flagged Photon, also left Vadinar on July 13 before transferring its petrol cargo at Damietta to the Russia-flagged Talisman on July 28 and 29, the data shows.
These ships were classed on the Russian register, with the exception of Garnet.
All of them have been sanctioned by the European Union, with Garnet and Talisman also being targeted by the US.
“The final destination of Talisman and Beast remain unconfirmed but, the emerging trading pattern suggests Damietta STS hub continues to facilitate the movement of Indian-origin petrol toward Russian import channels,” Kpler said. BLOOMBERG

U.S. ICE to spend up to $20 million on electroshock gloves for its agents
Kyiv • UNN
U.S. ICE plans to purchase thousands of Glove electroshock gloves worth up to $20 million. Human rights advocates have expressed concern about possible abuses.
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) plans to spend up to $20 million on purchasing thousands of gloves capable of delivering painful electric shocks. The Guardian reports this, citing documents from the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, writes UNN.
Details
The devices, called Glove (Generated Low Output Voltage Emitter), are manufactured by Kentucky-based Compliant Technologies LLC. ICE plans to receive the gloves by March.
According to the manufacturer, the device functions as an ordinary patrol glove until an officer activates the electrical mode. To apply the effect, the glove must be placed directly against the skin.
The discomfort associated with the stimulation is usually effective in bringing people into a state of compliance in less than three seconds and does not leave burns, marks, or scars
Human rights advocates fear abuse
Such gloves were previously used, among other places, in U.S. prisons. John Peters, president of the Institute for the Prevention of Deaths in Custody, who studied the device's use, described its effect as sharp and instantaneous.
It is an instantaneous and sharp effect that will divert your attention. I call it a bee sting
Human rights advocates opposed the purchase, citing concerns about the use of force by ICE officers during immigration operations. The ACLU said that access to such a device could make it easier to use electric shocks, which are more difficult to detect during arrests.
At the same time, the manufacturer warns against using the gloves as punishment for verbal disobedience and against using them on children, pregnant women, elderly people, or people with disabilities. The company declined to comment on ICE's purchase.

Mass evacuations in Beijing as Typhoon Dolphin brings more torrential rain to China
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
04:43:19 UTC
13:43:19 KST

Thousands of people have been evacuated from areas at risk of flooding and landslides in Beijing, as the remnants of Typhoon Dolphin continue to bring torrential rain to northern and central China.
Forecasters warned on Tuesday that the Chinese capital could receive more than 150mm of rain over the following 24 hours, with some districts forecast to exceed 200mm – more than one-third of Beijing’s average annual rainfall of 528mm.
Beijing remained under an orange rainstorm warning, the second-highest level, on Wednesday, with the heaviest rainfall expected across the morning.
Authorities closed hundreds of tourist attractions and campsites on Wednesday, with more than 1,300 tourists evacuated or turned away. Meanwhile, over 5,000 elderly people were moved from care facilities and about 1,800 people living around construction projects in mountainous or riverside areas were relocated.
The rain also disrupted Wednesday morning’s commute. Official local media reported that 250 bus routes had been suspended and trains were running at reduced speeds on 10 metro lines.
Dolphin, the strongest typhoon to hit China so far this year, has weakened after making landfall in the eastern province of Zhejiang on Sunday, but its remnants have continued to draw large amounts of tropical moisture deep inland and drench central and northern parts of the country.
The neighbouring Hebei province was also on alert for mountain floods, landslides and other geological hazards. Authorities said they had dispatched 623 teams to mountainous areas and equipped more than 2,100 at-risk villages with satellite phones or satellite messaging terminals to maintain communications during emergencies, according to state media.
In the central province of Henan, authorities raised the warning for torrential rain to the highest-level red alert on Wednesday morning, as downpours continue to batter large swathes of the province. More heavy rain was forecast through Thursday morning, with 24-hour rainfall totals of up to 350mm expected in some areas.
Classes, business operations and non-essential outdoor activities have been suspended in the affected areas of Henan. Residents were told to avoid deep flood waters and evacuate immediately if vehicles stall in water, state media reports.
China, the world’s second-largest economy, is increasingly exposed to destructive weather events that scientists link to climate change. This year is proving particularly tough due to the emergence of the El Niño weather pattern that is driving up temperatures and fuelling more frequent and intense typhoons.
Rainfall records have also been broken elsewhere in central China. Wugang in Henan received 209.5mm in a day and Xiangyang in neighbouring Hubei recorded 169.1mm, both the highest single-day rainfall totals for August, according to state media.
Reuters contributed to this report

'Big Tobacco' moment?: Meta faces $1.4 trillion lawsuit over harm to children
Jury selection begins Wednesday in a lawsuit filed by the US states of California, Colorado, Kentucky and New Jersey alleging that Meta uses technology to make Facebook and Instagram addictive for children. With billions of users around the world, Meta will defend itself against allegations of harming children in a new trial in the United States this week which experts are describing as social media's big tobacco moment.
After a coalition of states sued Meta in 2023 for allegedly designing addictive features for kids in its apps, four states were selected to represent their claims: California, Colorado, Kentucky and New Jersey.
Top prosecutors of those states now aim to prove in federal court that Meta deliberately made Facebook and Instagram addictive for children.
Read moreFacebook and Instagram must stop ‘addictive’ features like infinite scroll, EU tells Meta
Meta "strongly disagrees with these allegations" and is "confident the evidence will show our longstanding commitment to supporting young people", a spokesperson told AFP, adding that the company has "listened to parents, worked with experts and law enforcement".
Although it's not the first lawsuit that seeks to hold a social media company accountable for its impact on mental health and safety, it could become one of the most consequential.
"It really feels like tobacco in the 1990s," Vincent Joralemon, a director at Berkeley's Life Sciences Law and Policy Center, told AFP.
While these cases about social media harms revolve around the intersection of technology and addiction, the legal argument in this case against Meta centers on its business practices, just like when the federal government sued tobacco companies around three decades ago, Joralemon said.
By the early 1990s, decades of research showed that tobacco use caused health problems such as cancer, and eventually additional investigations revealed how the industry deliberately downplayed, and even concealed, the harmful impacts of its products.

'Protecting teens'
Dozens of US states sued four major tobacco companies, and by 1998, won a landmark settlement agreement which included financial penalties and changes to how products were marketed, particularly to children whom the industry targeted with advertisements featuring cartoon characters, the most famous of which was known as "Joe Camel".
Jury selection begins today in Oakland, a short drive from San Francisco and opening statements are expected to begin August 18.
Meta was convicted on similar grounds in separate trials held in Los Angeles and New Mexico, with combined damages that approach $1 billion.
Read moreSocial media giant Meta ordered to pay $567 million in New Mexico child safety ruling
In Oakland, the states are demanding a long list of changes to Meta's apps, in addition to financial penalties as high as $1.4 trillion – close to Meta's entire market value, which hovers around $1.5 trillion.
Despite the eye-popping number, money isn't Meta's biggest problem, if it were to lose the case.
"The huge issue here is reputational harm" and being forced to make major changes, Joralemon said.
"Putting a CEO on the witness stand can be quite damning," as well, he said.
Meta founder and chief Mark Zuckerberg is among the star witnesses expected to testify.
The case could be "the beginning of a broader reckoning" for Meta, Nora Freeman Engstrom told AFP via email. She is a law professor and associate dean at Stanford.
It will be important to see the "gap" between what Meta knew privately and what it disclosed publicly, Engstrom said.
Meta is "confident in our record of protecting teens online and will continue to defend ourselves against claims that misrepresent the facts," Meta told AFP last week.

With so many plaintiffs suing Meta and other social media companies, these lawsuits could potentially "go on for decades", Joralemon said.
In May, Snap, TikTok, YouTube and Meta settled with a school district in Kentucky for $27 million to avoid another trial that was expected to set a precedent for around 1,200 similar lawsuits.
On Monday, a federal appeals court ruled that more than 3,000 additional lawsuits filed against Meta, YouTube-parent Google, Snap and TikTok can proceed.

NDA MPs participate in 'Tiranga Yatra' rally in Delhi
NEW DELHI: Vice President CP Radhakrishnan on Wednesday flagged off a “Har Ghar Tiranga” bike rally in the national capital ahead of Independence Day celebrations on August 15.The rally, organised as part of the ongoing “Har Ghar Tiranga” campaign, saw participation from MPs of the ruling National Democratic Alliance (NDA) and a large number of supporters carrying the national flag. The rally is scheduled to cover the stretch from Bharat Mandapam to Major Dhyan Chand National Stadium.
Addressing participants, Radhakrishnan noted that the various activities organised under the campaign may differ in form but carry the same sentiment of national belonging.
“In Tiranga Yatra, bike rallies, cultural programmes, the activities are different but the sentiment they carry is the same, that is the collective sense of belonging... I urge each one of you to actively engage in this campaign and inspire every citizen to hoist the Tricolour with pride,” ANI quoted him as saying.The vice president also emphasised the unity of the country, declaring, “Bharat is one, and it will be one forever.”He paid tribute to Pingali Venkayya, who designed the national flag, and recalled Hansa Mehta, who led a group of 72 women who presented the first National Flag of independent India to Dr Rajendra Prasad, the country’s first president.
Several NDA MPs attended the rally. BJP MP Tarun Chugh highlighted the enthusiasm of young people and their resolve to contribute towards the goal of a developed India.“Under the leadership of PM Modi, the youth have come out today with the resolution of ‘Viksit Bharat’. Tiranga is the pride of India. Under PM Modi, India will realise the resolve to become a developed India,” Chugh said.Union minister of state for Home Nityanand Rai highlighted the significance of the national flag, describing the Tricolour as a sentiment deeply connected with the country and its people.“The Tiranga is our pride, and it is more precious to us than our life,” Rai said.BJP MP Ramvir Singh Bidhuri pointed to the participation of a large number of MPs in response to Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s call for the Tiranga Yatra.“In response to PM Modi's call, a large number of MPs are joining this Tiranga Yatra today, and the Vice President will inaugurate this Tiranga Yatra. The journey will go from Bharat Mandapam to the Major Dhyan Chand National Stadium, and a spectacular celebration is visible here,” Bidhuri said.
The “Har Ghar Tiranga” campaign is being held across the country ahead of Independence Day, encouraging citizens, public representatives and organisations to display the national flag.The Delhi rally is part of a series of programmes being organised in the capital to mark Independence Day, with the Tricolour at the centre of celebrations aimed at strengthening the sense of unity and national pride.

Tamil Nadu assembly backs 543 Lok Sabha seat freeze
NEW DELHI: Tamil Nadu assembly on Wednesday passed a special resolution in the urging the Centre to permanently retain the Lok Sabha’s strength at 543 seats.Days after convening a meeting of parties supporting his government, including the Congress and the Left parties that extend support from outside, CM Vijay moved the resolution in the assembly urging the Centre to maintain the Lok Sabha-Rajya Sabha seat ratio at 2.2:1.The government-sponsored resolution urged the Centre to implement 33 per cent reservation for women in the 2029 Lok Sabha elections without delay, based on the existing strength of 543 seats.
"The 33% reservation for women should be implemented in the 2029 Lok Sabha elections itself, based on the existing 543 constituencies. The 33% reservation for women should not be delayed any further. In Tamil Nadu, more women have voted than men. Providing reservation for women is not a concession; it is a matter of social justice. The 33% reservation for women must be implemented without any further delay," Vijay said in the assembly.The resolution noted that the population of states, including Tamil Nadu, and the Union Territories has not been counted for more than five decades, with the next census scheduled for 2026."All the states including Tamil Nadu and the people / elected representatives of the union territories have not had their population counted for more than 50 years.
The next census to count the population was supposed to be held in 2026. Therefore, since the delimitation of constituencies has not been carried out for the last 50 years, based on the 2011 population census, the constituencies should be delimited and the number of Lok Sabha and Assembly members should be increased from 550 to 850 by bringing in a constitutional amendment Bill," the resolution stated.Last week, a meeting convened by Vijay with Tamil Nadu MPs from alliance and friendly parties decided to oppose the Union government’s proposed delimitation exercise in its entirety.The meeting was boycotted by the main opposition DMK and the AIADMK, with the former calling the deliberations a “farce” and the latter describing them as a “hurriedly staged drama”.The MPs had demanded that the ratio of seats between the Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha be maintained at 2.2:1. They also unanimously agreed to adopt a resolution in the state Assembly to permanently safeguard the interests of Tamil Nadu and other southern states in the delimitation process.Meanwhile, the AIADMK called the meeting a “hurriedly staged drama”, pointing out that no fresh delimitation Bill had been introduced in Parliament and that there had been no official announcement on the exercise.While the Congress and other opposition parties have supported the Women's Reservation Bill, they have opposed linking its implementation to the delimitation exercise and have demanded that the two be delinked.
The Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam, 2023, was passed by both Houses of Parliament. However, its implementation has not moved forward after the Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill fell in the Lok Sabha on April 17, failing to secure the constitutionally required two-thirds majority of members present and voting.

More than 16,000 civilians detained by Russia in its invasion of Ukraine are still held, UN says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
04:31:23 UTC
13:31:23 KST

The UN also reported more than 95% of the Ukrainian prisoners of war and 85% of the civilian detainees are being tortured or ill-treated, often repeatedly.
Over 16,000 civilians captured by Russia following its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in early 2022 remain "deprived of their liberty," with many being held in violation of international law, an informal UN Security Council meeting has been told.
According to UN Assistant Secretary-General for Human Rights Claudia Fuentes Julio, Russia has persisted in widespread, systematic torture and ill-treatment of both Ukrainian civilian detainees and prisoners of war, including cases of sexual violence.
Julio gave the estimates at the informal meeting of the UNSC — which includes Russia as a permanent member — called by Latvia and the UK on Monday to spotlight the condition of civilians and soldiers taken during the war that Russia launched in 2022.
Julio presented results of interviews UN human rights personnel conducted with 910 Ukrainian prisoners of war and 403 civilian detainees following their release.
More than 95% of the Ukrainian prisoners of war and 85% of the civilian detainees reported being tortured or ill-treated, often repeatedly, the UN official said.
They also reported being subjected to sexual abuse and food deprivation while being held in inhumane conditions and not being provided adequate medical services.
The Geneva-based human rights office “has documented the execution of 129 Ukrainian prisoners of war at the beginning of their captivity and the deaths of 48 Ukrainian prisoners of war in custody, resulting from torture, denial of medical care, or other inhumane conditions of detention,” Julio said.
The UN has not been permitted to visit Russian detention facilities, and its estimate of the number of people detained does not include a breakdown of adults and children.
Former detainees shared their ordeal
The Security Council also heard emotionally wrenching accounts from some former detainees who shared their ordeal.
Crimean Tatar human rights activist Leniie Umerova, who was Russia's political prisoner for almost two years, and Khuan Leyva Garsiya, a Ukrainian soldier who was among the hundreds who held out for months at the Azovstal steel plant in the besieged city of Mariupol before Russian troops took control in May 2022, shared their stories.
Garsiya, who was born in Mariupol to a Ukrainian mother and Cuban father, spent 1,183 days as a prisoner of war. He said he weighed 55 kilograms when he was freed, showing a picture of his emaciated body to the council.
Garsiya said he was tortured, heavily beaten and humiliated more than other prisoners because the Russians suspected that he was a foreign mercenary due to his Cuban ancestry or an American spy because he went to college in the US.
“Russians were outraged that someone with a connection to Cuba, whom they consider an ally, would fight against their occupation army,” said Garsiya, who is still part of the Ukrainian military.
UN human rights experts also interviewed 816 Russians and 57 third-country national prisoners of war from over 45 countries who were members of the Russian armed forces in Ukraine, said Julio.
About half reported ill-treatment, primarily during the initial stages of captivity and interrogation by Ukrainians, she said.
UN monitors however reported that once they arrived in Ukrainian detention facilities, “the conditions generally comply with international humanitarian law and have improved since 2022.”
Responding to the findings, Russia’s deputy UN Ambassador Maria Zabolotskaya told the council the Russian armed forces are complying with international humanitarian law, which includes the treatment of prisoners.
Volodymyr Pavlichenko, Kyiv's deputy UN ambassador, expressed his displeasure that Russia was not prepared to talk about the return of prisoners of war, "including their POWs," and all civilian detainees, including kidnapped children.

Country diary: One flower here is thriving, defying the drought | Derek Niemann
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
04:30:18 UTC
13:30:18 KST

At first light, the scent of ’76 hangs in the air, a reminder of that endless summer burning itself into autumn, just like this one. I first caught a sniff of it walking home one sweltering evening in the June heatwave and said: “Too soon, too soon.”
Now the toasted aroma of spent grass is everywhere – on crispy playing fields, straw village greens, and these scorched tawny meadows of the combe. Scattered groups of cattle have their heads down here. For them I think eating the grass must be like consuming a Pot Noodle before the water is poured in.
And then I find the outflow of one of the hillside’s springs. Though it registers nothing more than a seep, it is nevertheless a pocket oasis of comparative lushness, a blessing to a heifer’s eyes.
These cows know a thing or two; against the fiercest sun in that hottest spell, they fashioned themselves a long awning on the riverbank, chomping the trees, twigs and all, up to a browse line, then sheltered under the canopy. Clearly barely palatable, the alders survived this first onslaught, but even they were stripped out by mid-July. Cow licks tugged out the grass from below, hooves pounded the ground to bare earth. The adjoining path still wears a dried cowpat crust.
Beyond the gate, beyond the cows, one plant in particular defies the drought, striking for its sprinkling of vivid colour against the skeletons of umbellifers and wilting greens. Tansy grows in such localised profusion that it gives the immediate impression of great sprays of primary yellow buttons. Close observation confirms a dual identity in appearance. From the neck down, it displays fern-like leaves. But the aster family is there in its little bunched-together disc florets, each about a centimetre across, bobbled like compound eyes.
Richard Mabey’s magisterial Flora Britannica attests to tansy’s medieval lineage as an all-purpose, largely medicinal herb, ranging from the mildly toxic and purgative to its inclusion as bitter flavouring for an omelette. Another source claims tansy leaves were garlanded into an embalming wreath for the coffined first president of Harvard University. I think I might leave them for other mouths to sample.

Beijing’s tree die-off reveals hidden risks of rapid underground water recovery
Thousands of trees die in Jinzhandian Park, a lush flood-storage wetland, amid exceptionally wet and rainy summer
At a time of year when Beijing’s vegetation should be at its greenest, thousands of trees of various species in a park in the city’s Chaoyang district have withered and died because they were too wet.
Beijing Daily, the Chinese capital’s official newspaper, said on Monday that rising groundwater levels might be to blame.
Jinzhandian Park, a lush flood-storage wetland park nicknamed Beijing’s “Little Lake Baikal” for its lake and extensive woodlands, has drawn large numbers of visitors since opening in September last year.
However, according to the report, thousands of trees – including locust, poplar, willow, ginkgo and pine – have died across just four wooded areas near the water. Most were newly planted, but some were about 20 years old and had previously been thriving.
A staff member from the park’s administrative town told Beijing Daily that the large-scale die-off along the shore was “most likely due to prolonged waterlogging”.
An official at the Chaoyang district water bureau – the body responsible for planting and maintaining the saplings in the park – said the damage was likely to have been caused by rising groundwater levels. “When the groundwater table rises, it can have an impact on tree growth,” the official said.
The official added that the bureau was still assessing the number of dead trees and deciding how to address the issue. For trees showing signs they might survive, the bureau was stepping up maintenance measures, including the use of growth-promoting treatments and drainage.

MyPillow Founder Mike Lindell is refusing to to concede in Minnesota's Republican gubernatorial primary, despite Speaker of the House Lisa Demuth's win on Tuesday.
The Associated Press called the race just before midnight as Demuth was leading with more than 43% of the vote to Mike Lindell’s less than 33% of the ballots counted. However, the Trump-backed candidate alleges irregularity in voting totals.
“There’s 265,000 votes left to count. I’m down by 18,000 now,” he said on his live streaming network, LindellTV. “I’m not going to give up this race until the votes are counted. That’s nonsense.”
Lindell garnered national attention in the aftermath of the 2020 election as a prominent election denier.
The state Republican Party, meanwhile, opted to endorse Kendall Qualls, a businessman and Army veteran, at a state convention in May.
Despite earning neither endorsement, Demuth remained competitive in the race—and ultimately pulled out the win.
She now heads to the general election in November, where she is expected to face an uphill battle against Democratic Sen. Amy Klobuchar.
How Trump shaped Mike Lindell’s campaign for Minnesota governor
Trump has never won Minnesota in any of his three presidential runs, but Lindell, who appeared to open a lead in the polls in recent weeks, touted the President’s endorsement days before the election.
"I have an advantage over everyone up here,” Lindell said at an event on Sunday. “I can call up and work with the President of the United States.”
The former CEO, like Trump, has vocally denied the results of the 2020 presidential election, which Trump lost to Joe Biden. Lindell has faced defamation suits over comments he made related voting machines, some of which are ongoing. Last June, he was ordered to pay $2.3 million to a Dominion Voting Systems executive after a jury found that he spread false and damaging claims related to the 2020 election.
Prior to that election, Lindell had also become known for his MyPillow advertisements and his self-published memoir What Are the Odds? From Crack Addict to CEO, in which he chronicled his experience overcoming substance abuse and gambling. He stepped down as CEO of the pillow company earlier this month to focus on his campaign.
Lindell aligns largely with Trump’s approach to many issues, including slashing government spending. Among his campaign proposals was a “Minnesota DOGE,” a reference to the Trump Administration’s now-shuttered Department of Government Efficiency.
Although he later secured the President’s public support, Lindell was beat out by both Qualls and Demuth in the contentious voting process for the state GOP endorsement, being eliminated after finishing third in the fourth round of voting. After 10 ballots, Qualls just surpassed the 60% vote needed to formally secure the endorsement.
Qualls, the first Black candidate to win a major party endorsement for governor in Minnesota, called for unity in the party following his win.
“Now is the time to remind everyone what our first Republican President said on the field of Gettysburg: That a house divided cannot stand,” Qualls said. “If we’re going to win, we got to win as a united Republican Party.”
Can Republicans flip the Minnesota governor’s mansion?
Minnesota hasn’t elected a Republican governor since 2006, while the last Republican senator was elected in 2002. In presidential elections, it holds the current record among the 50 states for the longest streak of voting for the Democratic candidate; it last went for a Republican in 1972, when it gave its electoral votes to Richard Nixon.
However, Qualls and Demuth aimed to make headway.
Qualls has never previously held public office, but he was not a new face on the campaign trail in Minnesota. This year’s primary marked Qualls’ third campaign for a major seat. He mounted an unsuccessful bid in the race to represent Minnesota’s third congressional district in the U.S. House in 2020 and previously ran for governor, also unsuccessfully, in 2022.
In his bid this year, Qualls called for a “radical transformation” to the state’s tax policy and education system. “We can do a lot more with less,” he said to ABC affiliate 5 EYEWITNESS NEWS.
Demuth largely aligned on policy with Qualls, but sought to distinguish herself on the campaign trail by emphasizing her government experience as the first Black woman and Republican woman to serve as House Speaker.
“I am the best candidate who is able to look forward to November and beating Amy Klobuchar and I’ll say the Democrat machine,” Demuth said in an interview with KSTP in June. “And the reason I know I’m best-positioned to do that is when you look at my work as Speaker of the House I can draw people together.”
Demuth, who leads a state House with an even split between the two parties, touted her ability to broker deals and communicate within a thinly divided government.
“I have solid, conservative values that really do cross party lines,” she said at a news conference. “It’s not just Republican values. They’re conservative values that are supported by many Minnesotans.”
Tim Walz, who has been the governor since 2019, launched a bid for a third term but dropped out in early January amid investigations into state welfare agencies and government-affiliated programs that were widely targeted by fraud.
The Cook Political Report rates the Minnesota governor’s mansion as Solid Democrat, among those it deems least likely to flip in this election cycle.

July inflation report to provide crucial signs of where prices are headed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
04:23:02 UTC
13:23:02 KST

Inflation slows but prices remain elevated as Iran war and spending on AI push up prices
WASHINGTON (AP) — U.S. inflation declined slightly last month as the cost of gas and groceries slipped, though prices are still rising more quickly than before the Iran war, posing challenges for the White House as the midterm elections near.
Consumer prices increased 3.4% in July from a year ago, down slightly from 3.5% in June, the Labor Department said Wednesday. Inflation had fallen to 2.4% before the Iran war. On a monthly basis, prices rose just 0.1% from June to July.
The mild decrease is the second straight decline after sharply higher gas prices pushed inflation to 4.2% in May, a three-year high. Yet even with the pause, prices are still rising more quickly than average wages, underscoring the struggle many Americans have had paying for groceries, gas, and healthcare. And many costs grew last month, including airfares, computers, and used cars.
Excluding the volatile food and energy categories, core inflation slipped to 2.5% in July from a year ago, down from 2.6% in June. July’s figure matches a post-pandemic low reached in January and February, before the Iran war.
Core prices rose 0.2% from June to July. Monthly increases at about 0.2% would be low enough over time to bring inflation closer to the Fed’s 2% goal.
“America still has an inflation problem, but there are encouraging signs that price pressures outside of the gas pump are easing,” Heather Long, chief economist at Navy Federal Credit Union, said.
Inflation report could make Fed rate hike less likely
Cooler inflation could also ease pressure on the Federal Reserve to raise their key interest rate to combat rising costs. Fed officials are sharply split over their next steps. Roughly half the members of the central bank’s rate-setting committee support raising borrowing costs this year, while another half think rates are already high enough to slowly push inflation back to their 2% target.
“We’re clearly not out of the woods, however it makes the Fed’s decision a little bit easier, because now you see that inflation is creeping down,” said Dan North, senior economist at Allianz Trade North America.
Still, oil prices remain elevated and gas prices rose in late July and August, suggesting overall inflation could accelerate next month. On Wednesday, gas averaged $4.04 a gallon nationwide, 16 cents higher than a month ago, according to the motor club AAA.
Inflation has been pushed higher by a series of shocks to the economy, including President Donald Trump’s tariffs imposed last spring, higher gas prices stemming from the U.S attack on Iran, and a surge in investment in artificial intelligence infrastructure that has boosted computer chip prices. The key question for the inflation-fighters at the Federal Reserve — not to mention for consumers struggling with high gas and grocery prices — is how quickly those one-time effects will fade or whether they will lead to persistently rising prices.
Some companies, however, are still struggling with higher costs from Trump’s tariffs.
Julie Robbins, CEO of Earthquaker Devices, an Akron, Ohio-based maker of pedals used to create effects for guitars, said her company has paid $200,000 in tariffs this year and has had to raise prices twice to offset the costs.
Only a small amount of those tariffs have been refunded after the Supreme Court struck down Trump’s emergency duties. Robbins is worried they will have to raise prices again as the White House has sought to impose new tariffs to replace the ones that lost due to the Supreme Court decision.
Her company’s electric bills have also risen in recent months and the rising costs of fuel have pushed up her shipping costs.
“I am just seeing more and more costs going up all the time,” Robbins said. “The money we paid on tariffs, that easily could have paid for two or three more employees.”
Gas, grocery prices fell, while computers, airfares rose
Wednesday’s report showed that gasoline prices fell 2.9% from June to July, and even grocery prices declined slightly, falling by 0.1%. Yet gas prices are 25% higher than a year ago. And groceries are 2.7% more expensive than a year earlier.
Hotel room prices dropped 2.8% from June to July, likely reflecting the end of the World Cup tournament. Clothing costs rose just 0.1%, though they are up 3.9% in the past year.
Other things are growing more expensive: Computer prices jumped 3.5% from June to July, reflecting a decision by Apple to sharply raise prices for its computers and tablets as AI spending pushes up the cost of semiconductors. Smartphone prices rose 1.1%.
Airline fares rose 2.2% from June to July as jet fuel prices spiral higher along with oil.
Price increases have stayed above the Fed’s 2% target for more than five years, suggesting there is more than temporary factors at play.
The cost of services such as healthcare, restaurant meals, and car maintenance rose 3% in July from a year earlier, and they aren’t particularly sensitive to gas prices or AI investment. Rising costs for services often reflect higher wages, as companies charge more to offset the cost of higher pay. But incomes aren’t growing fast enough to sustain inflation, economists note.
It’s a confounding situation that has left many economists — and Fed officials — seeking more information to determine where inflation is headed.
“You’ve got all these things that are just not the way the economy used to behave,” Diane Swonk, chief economist at KPMG, said.
For many consumers, years of sharply rising grocery prices have led them to adopt a wide range of coping strategies, from comparison shopping, to couponing, to cutting back on favorite foods.
Retailers, including Walmart, have responded by rolling back food prices, a trend that could have lowered July’s inflation figures. Yet many other businesses are still passing on higher costs.
Paint company Sherwin-Williams is planning an 8% price increase in September to offset higher raw material costs, CEO Heidi Petz said late last month.
“We are seeing the impact of higher oil and related cost pressures, and we expect continued volatility throughout the balance of the year,” she said.
___
AP Writer Anne D’Innocenzio contributed to this report from New York.

Rescuers evacuate more than 200 from a ferry fire that left at least 1 dead near Bali
JAKARTA, Indonesia (AP) — Crews rescued 211 people and recovered the body of a passenger from a ferry that caught fire in rough seas Wednesday near the Indonesian tourist island of Bali, authorities said.
The Putri Yasmin ferry was traveling from Bali to the neighboring island of Lombok in West Nusa Tenggara province when the fire broke out at about 4:15 a.m. The ferry was also transporting 44 vehicles and 53 motorcycles.
The Search and Rescue Office in Mataram, the capital of West Nusa Tenggara province, received an emergency report almost half an hour later and immediately deployed personnel and rescue vessels.
“Our top priority is the safety of all passengers and crew members,” said Muhammad Hariyadi, who heads the Mataram Search and Rescue Office.
Videos released by the National Search and Rescue Agency showed people wearing life jackets crowding an inflatable life raft in choppy waters during a rescue operation at sea, as thick black smoke billows from the ferry.
The rescue agency said that as of Wednesday afternoon, rescuers evacuated 211 people from the burned vessel, including 2 Australian tourists, and recovered the body of a 19-year-old Indonesian woman.
Initial reports had said the ferry was carrying 131 people, including 17 crew members, based on the ship’s manifest.
However, hours after the incident, officials said more people were aboard than listed. It is common in Indonesia for the number of passengers on a boat or ferry to differ from the manifest.
Authorities have not yet explained why the number of people evacuated exceeded the total listed on the initial passenger manifest. Transportation Minister Dudy Purwagandhi said officials will look into the discrepancy.
“The findings will be thoroughly reviewed as part of the ministry’s evaluation,” Purwagandhi said. “This is a serious issue that will be thoroughly investigated.”
He said investigators were determining the cause of the fire.
Syamsurizal, head of the Lembar Port Authority in Lombok, said that survivors told authorities the blaze appeared to have started in a cargo truck before quickly spreading through the ferry. The heat forced some passengers to jump into the sea, he said.
“The response operation is ongoing, and authorities are continuing to account for all victims,” said Syamsurizal, who like many Indonesians uses a single name. He said at least two injured passengers were rushed to a nearby hospital.
Hariyadi said the rescue effort was supported by six vessels, a helicopter, two inflatable boats and two private yachts. He said rough seas with waves reported as high as 4 meters (13 feet) complicated rescue efforts.
Wednesday’s incident happened less than two weeks after another Indonesian ferry, the Mutiara Sentosa 2, caught fire in waters off the main island of Java, leaving at least five people dead.
Indonesia is an archipelago of more than 17,000 islands where ferries are a common method of travel. Disasters occur regularly, with weak safety enforcement often blamed.

Earthquake response strains Colombia’s new government and rescuers as they race against the clock

Unknown Publisher

Earthquake response strains Colombia’s new government and rescuers as they race against the clock
PEREIRA, Colombia (AP) — The search for survivors in the rubble of Colombia’s powerful earthquake grew more desperate on Wednesday, two days after the quake brought down buildings, buckled roads and crushed cars.
The devastation has tested Colombia’s new President Abelardo de la Espriella and his government as it scrambles to respond to the natural disaster and civil society as it pushes to provide aid to the vulnerable communities most affected by the quake.
By Tuesday, de la Espriella said the 7.4 magnitude earthquake had killed at least 181 people and left 2,595 more injured in the west of the country. He said at least 195 remained missing, but civilian-run databases put that number at more than 4,000 Wednesday morning.
Teams continued to pick through the rubble overnight in the hardest-hit cities of Cali, Pereira, Manizales and Quibdo, as time ticked away for victims to be found — and rescued — alive.
Aid agencies consider the first 48 to 72 hours crucial for retrieving survivors, though that threshold can be extended if those trapped have access to food and water.
Survival takes many forms in hard-hit areas
There have been fleeting moments of hope amid the devastation.
In hard-hit Pereira, rescuers pulled Daniela Largo alive from the rubble late Tuesday, capping a complex 12-hour rescue in which crews carved a small opening through the debris to free her pinned arm and a doctor administered IV fluids to stabilize her. Wrapped in a blue blanket, the young woman was carried to a waiting ambulance as firefighters embraced and onlookers erupted in cheers.
Across the coffee-growing region, among the areas worst affected by the quake, authorities have converted sports arenas, schools and other public buildings into temporary shelters for thousands of displaced Colombians. In Pereira and Cali, families have been sleeping in parks — some fearing aftershocks or the collapse of their damaged homes, others without homes to return to.
“We have the most important things: a roof over our heads, food, water and, in my case, medical care,” said Edith Penagos, 48, who was staying with her teenage son in one of the white tents set up in a Pereira park after the earthquake forced them from their apartment.
Colombia’s geological service has documented 130 aftershocks since the quake.
Rodrigo León Loya, a seismologist and professor in the Department of Geosciences at the University of the Andes, said the probability of an earthquake of a similar magnitude occurring in the same area has fallen because “the accumulated energy” has been released. But he would not rule out more seismic activity.
“Let’s remember that Colombia is full of active fault lines,” he said. “The question isn’t whether it can happen again. The question is rather when an earthquake of similar magnitude will occur at another of Colombia’s seismic sources.”
Regional partners promise help and aid groups already on the ground dig in
In many areas, the official response to the disaster has been complicated by the ongoing crises of deep poverty and civil warfare that has created waves of forced displacement for decades.
“This earthquake compounds an already severe humanitarian situation, and there is a need for increased support for the humanitarian response,” said Giovanni Rizzo, Colombia director for the Norwegian Refugee Council.
Many aid organizations were already on the ground at the epicenter of the quake in Colombia, supporting a 2016 peace accord between the government and leftist rebels, and responding to violence involving other armed groups that has persisted since then, particularly in Choco.
That presence allowed humanitarian workers to quickly pivot to disaster relief, said María José Torres, the U.N. resident coordinator in Colombia.
“We have a presence on the ground. Therefore, our ability to be there, present with the people, I think, has increased exponentially,” Torres said in a statement Tuesday.
At the same time, aid from other countries and nonprofits abroad continued to roll in.
On Wednesday, the State Department said it would send two search and rescue teams to Colombia that helped with rescue efforts in Venezuela just weeks before. The U.S. has also offered over $15 million in aid.
Mexico’s president has said she is prepared to send hundreds of search and health workers, tons of health supplies and other equipment.
On Tuesday afternoon, Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele said his country would send two planes loaded with 100 tons of aid.
“Our prayers are with the families of the victims, the wounded and all the Colombian people,” Bukele wrote on X.
___
Suarez reported from Bogota, Colombia, and Janetsky reported from Mexico City. Associated Press writers Edith M. Lederer at the United Nations, Isabel DeBre in Buenos Aires, Argentina and Gabriela Aoun in San Diego contributed.
