Trump says Air Force One ruse was Secret Service, military call
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
02:05:47 UTC
11:05:47 KST

Trump says Air Force One ruse was Secret Service, military call
President Donald Trump deflected criticisms about a decision to secretly fly him out of Turkey on a different aircraft while the White House indicated he was aboard Air Force One, saying the Secret Service and military demanded it in response to unspecified safety threats.
“They wanted me to go on a different flight, a different plane, equal safety, but they wanted me to do it, so I do it. I do what they say,” Trump told reporters on Aug 11 after deplaning Air Force One at Joint Base Andrews outside Washington while returning from Ohio.
The elaborate manoeuvre, first reported by the Washington Post, was prompted by an Iranian assassination threat against Trump.
The deception was carried out as journalists, White House staff members and other government officials aboard Air Force One were given the impression Trump was flying with them back to the US from a NATO summit in Ankara.
Asked why, the President replied: “I guess there was a threat out there, I didn’t really ask too much about it. I get a lot of threats.”
Trump confirmed he covertly switched planes upon his departure from Turkey. But he declined to elaborate on the nature of the threat, nor did he explain why the military thought it was safe for others to fly on the regular presidential aircraft, but not him.
“I don’t know, I think actually the plane that I flew on was at greater risk,” hesaid.
The incident showed the lengths the US government is willing to go to protect the president from Iranian attempts on his life, as the US war against Iran stretches into its sixth month.
It also marked an extraordinary breach in protocol, as the White House misled the public about the president’s whereabouts.
The Post cited materials it reviewed as well as a US official and another person familiar with the matter who it said spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to reveal the scheme.
Bloomberg has not confirmed the details of the Post report.
Trump flew to the summit in the Qatari-gifted, Boeing luxury jumbo jet that is serving as a temporary presidential aircraft.
But upon departing Turkey, Trump said he would travel to a refuelling stop aboard the old Air Force One plane so that troops based in England could view the new one.
That never happened. In view of television cameras in Ankara, Trump boarded the old Air Force One jet. But according to the Post, after entering the aircraft, Trump disembarked on the other side of the aircraft and was taken by an airport catering truck to a smaller Air Force C-32A. He then flew to England on that plane instead.
The White House earlier declined to confirm details when asked about the Post report.
“The new Air Force One is a state-of-the-art aircraft that has been fitted with high-level security protocols that ensure the safety of the President and his staff. As the President has said recently, there are many enemies of America who have their sights on him, and we use every tool at our disposal to address those threats,” White House communications director Steven Cheung said late on Aug 10 in a statement.
While Trump was in Turkey, the US carried out strikes against Iran after Iranian forces attacked shipping around the Strait of Hormuz.
The New York Times reported in July that security officials raised concerns about a possible attack against the president, which triggered the move from the new plane to the old one for the return flight to the US.
That change prompted questions about whether the Qatari-gifted plane has the proper security features to protect the president. The Trump administration issued subpoenas to Times reporters in an effort to find who revealed that information, but eventually withdrew them.
The president has said the plane would undergo more upgrades.
The US Air Force said in a statement that the new Air Force One “is safe, secure and equipped with the most advanced technologies necessary to meet the requirements of the presidential mission” and that “no risk was taken in security, safety or mission communications, but the collective team made trades on some of the less commonly used mission sets that Boeing must deliver to support the next 40 years”.
The Post report raised questions about the nature of the threat against the president, and why officials thought it appropriate to effectively use the older Air Force One jet as a decoy with people on board.
For decades, the White House press pool has travelled with the president. It is a rotating group of journalists that report on the president’s movements and whereabouts on behalf of the entire press corps.
The set-up is designed to ensure the public has an independent account of the president’s activities, and to be nearby in moments of crisis.
In 2000, then president Bill Clinton clandestinely flew on an unmarked plane from India and Pakistan due to security risks, while others travelled on the traditional Air Force One.
But unlike Trump’s gambit, a small group of White House reporters at the time were briefed ahead of time on the operation, the Post reported.
“I have a lot of threats,” Trump said late on Aug 11. “I have a lot of threats that you don’t know about.” BLOOMBERG

Passenger jet billed as China’s answer to Boeing and Airbus prepares to make first international flight
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
02:02:04 UTC
11:02:04 KST

China hopes to break into the world of commercial aviation with the first international flight of a Chinese-made passenger jet scheduled for Wednesday.
The Comac C919 will take off from Beijing capital international airport at 3pm, landing in Ulaanbaatar, the capital of Mongolia, just over two hours later.
It has been billed as China’s alternative to the Boeing-Airbus duopoly that dominates global aviation, particularly in Asia, but analysts say it could take generations before a Chinese aircraft could meaningfully challenge their global dominance.
The C919 is made by the Chinese state-owned aircraft manufacturer Commercial Aircraft Corporation of China (Comac) and is similar in size to the Boeing 737.
The C919 has been flying on domestic routes operated by Chinese airlines since 2023. But Wednesday’s Air China flight to Ulaanbaatar will be the first time that the narrow-body jet is used on a commercial international route.
“This is essentially a public relations move,” said Scott Kennedy, a senior adviser at the Centre for Strategic and International Studies. “Ulaanbaatar was likely chosen because of how close it is to Beijing. It doesn’t change the fact that the plane was years overdue, is composed of western components, and is less efficient than its Boeing and Airbus cousins.”
China has long dreamed of building its own jet. When the C919 was unveiled in 2015, Li Jiaxiang, the head of China’s civil aviation authority, said: “A great nation must have its own large commercial aircraft.”
But progress has been slow, even while China has whizzed ahead in other hi-tech fields, such as robotics and electric vehicles (EVs).
That is because aviation requires the integration of many different types of advanced science and engineering, as well as parts sourced from overseas. An analysis by the Centre for Strategic and International Studies in 2020 found that more than half of the C919’s suppliers were in the US.
“Large passenger aircraft and jet engines are extremely complex and challenging to manufacture. They require precision components, complex electro-mechanical control systems, and the ability to coordinate a vast global supply chain,” said Kyle Chan, a fellow at Brookings focused on China’s industrial policy.
“There’s a reason there are basically only two major commercial aircraft makers in the world. Building large passenger jets that are safe and reliable is an order of magnitude more difficult than making EVs,” Chan said.
Last year Comac reportedly delivered only 15 units of the C919 to customers, well short of its target of 75.
Comac did not respond to a request for comment.
Comac primarily serves Chinese domestic airlines. In 2023, the Brunei-based airline GallopAir signed a $2bn deal to purchase 30 planes from Comac, including 15 of the C919, but the airline is not operating commercially yet. The C919 has not been approved by European or American regulators.
Last year the US reportedly suspended the export of some products to Comac for use in the C919 jet amid the tit-for-tat restrictions that Beijing and Washington used against each other during the US-China trade war.
The two countries later agreed a trade war truce that is set to expire in November.
When US president Donald Trump visited Beijing in May for a state visit, one of the few takeaways from the trip was an agreement from China to buy 200 jets from Boeing.
In return, the US provided supply guarantees for aircraft engine parts and components for its own manufacturing.
China sees being able to build its own commercial aircraft as a national security priority.
In a recent interview with Chinese state media, Zhang Yanzhong, an academic of the Chinese Academy of Engineering and a leading aviation expert who worked on the C919, said reliance on other countries for large aircraft technology would “threaten national strategic security”.
However, there was still “a long way to go before achieving commercial success”, Zhang said.
Experts have pointed out that Comac’s dependence on foreign suppliers goes beyond the supply of individual components. International suppliers have also provided guidance about how to integrate complex components and software together into sky-worthy commercial aircraft.
Kennedy argued it was misleading to describe the C919 as a Chinese plane because so many of its parts were imported. He said it was “very unlikely” for Comac to become a serious challenger to Boeing and Airbus, “even a generation from now”.
Chan said Comac could still face “a long road to gaining trust among airlines and passengers”.
Zhang called on China’s young engineers to contribute their talents to China’s aviation ambitions, saying: “Though the journey may be fraught with difficulties, a fledgling eagle can soar faster than its parent.”

Why does SK Hynix want to sell its chip facility in southwest China?

Why does SK Hynix want to sell its chip facility in southwest China?
The South Korean chipmaker wants to pivot towards the high-margin AI memory sector, but analysts warn any sale would face valuation hurdles
South Korean chipmaker SK Hynix’s potential deal to offload a packaging plant in southwest China is part of a strategic pivot towards higher-margin artificial intelligence memory products, according to analysts.
But they cautioned a sale might not be straightforward, as the memory chip giant would need to navigate valuation hurdles and a volatile chip cycle.
SK Hynix said on Monday it was “looking into various solutions to enhance the competitiveness of its packaging business”, after reports emerged last week it was weighing options for its facility in Chongqing, a megacity in China’s southwest.
Those options include bringing in an investor for a stake sale that could value the plant at around US$3 billion, Bloomberg reported. SK Hynix said in a statement that no final decisions had been made.
The Chongqing plant functions as a back-end hub focused on downstream packaging and testing for SK Hynix’s NAND flash memory products. The company also operates two front-end wafer fabrication plants in China for dynamic random access memory (DRAM) and NAND – one in the eastern city of Wuxi and another in Dalian, a busy port in the country’s northeast.
Industry watchers said they considered the potential sale a move to recycle capital away from lower-margin legacy products. Profit growth in high-bandwidth memory (HBM) is far clearer than in standard NAND flash, according to Diana Wang, an analyst at Chinese semiconductor research firm ICWise.
Zhang Guobin, founder of Chinese semiconductor news platform eetrend.com, described SK Hynix’s decision as a strategic shift from low-value back-end assembly to high-margin front-end manufacturing.

Showdown in Indonesia’s Solo pits Widodo’s dynasty against Megawati’s machine
Analysts say the 2029 parliamentary bid will test whether Widodo can convert his personal popularity into lasting family influence
Kaesang Pangarep plans to seek a parliamentary seat in Central Java V in 2029. The constituency has been represented since 2009 by House Speaker Puan Maharani – one of the Indonesian Democratic Party of Struggle’s (PDI-P) most prominent figures and the offspring of the woman whose party carried Widodo from Solo’s city hall to the presidency.
Kaesang, who chairs the upstart Indonesian Solidarity Party (PSI), announced the plan at a party meeting in Solo on July 25. Central Java V covers Solo, Boyolali, Klaten and Sukoharjo, combining Widodo’s home base with one of PDI-P’s long-standing strongholds.
That makes the race a prospective proxy contest between two political families at very different stages of dynastic power. Analysts see it as part of Widodo’s broader challenge to Megawati and PDI-P – an effort to turn his family’s recent rise and PSI into a durable political machine capable of competing with a party rooted in the legacy of Megawati’s father, Indonesia’s first president Sukarno.
Marcus Mietzner, a professor of political and social change at the Australian National University and author of Ruling Indonesia, a recent study of Widodo’s decade in office, described Kaesang’s candidacy as “the boldest expression of this challenge so far”.
It is not necessarily a winner-takes-all duel – Indonesia’s proportional electoral system could allow both Kaesang and Puan to secure seats.

Merz’s deal with the Taliban alarms Afghan dissidents in Germany
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

Zarmina Paryani and her four sisters fear they may soon have to again face the persecutors they fled from in Afghanistan — and this time inside Germany.
Paryani and her sisters were imprisoned twice in Kabul for protesting against the Taliban after the Afghan militants retook the capital in 2021, the 27-year-old said. After going into hiding for several months, the family eventually made their way to Germany in search of safe haven.
But now, Berlin has struck a Faustian bargain that allows the Taliban to deepen its diplomatic foothold in Germany in return for cooperation on deporting Afghan migrants back to Afghanistan. For Paryani and other Afghan activists who resisted the Taliban at home, the arrangement is giving their former persecutors new leverage over their lives in exile.
Advertisement
“It’s hard to accept that my fate and my affairs are being discussed with the very same representatives whose oppression, prisons, whippings and violence I fled from,” Paryani, who worked as a midwife in Kabul and now lives in western Germany, told POLITICO.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s government first struck a deal with the Afghan government announced last October that gives Taliban officials control of diplomatic missions in Berlin and Bonn in exchange for permission to return Afghan migrants directly to Afghanistan. That cooperation was deepened early this summer with a deal that allows more Taliban officials to work in Germany in return for cooperation on additional deportation flights — now up to three per month.
Under the new deal, Germany has expanded deportations to include not only Afghan men convicted of crimes, but also, more broadly, Afghan men with no protected status or legal right to remain in Germany.
The agreement with the Taliban makes Germany an outlier in Europe, making it the first EU country to allow Taliban-appointed officials to work in diplomatic missions inside the country. Before the agreement, Western-oriented Afghan officials representing the former government in Afghanistan had remained in charge.
The arrangement comes as Merz’s government grapples with rock-bottom approval ratings and the rise of the anti-immigrant Alternative for Germany (AfD) party, now the country’s most popular political force, according to polls. The AfD’s surge comes ahead of two elections in the former East Germany, where the far-right party is ahead in polls by wide margins. In one of those states, Saxony-Anhalt, the party may take real governing power for the first time since it was founded in 2013, a result that would serve as a great humiliation for the conservative Merz, who was elected chancellor last year partly on a promise to crack down on migration.
Advertisement
The AfD’s rise is piling pressure on the chancellor to deliver on his election pledge to deport more migrants — even as he insists that working with the Taliban does not legitimize a regime notorious for its human rights abuses. Overall, Afghans are the third-largest group of refugees or people who have fled war to come to Germany, behind Ukrainians and Syrians.
“We are not extending a hand to this Taliban regime,” Merz said in the German parliament in June. “Rather, we are seeking cooperation at the necessary technical level, which is in our country’s national interest.”
‘Nightmares’ and ‘psychological distress’
For Afghan rights activists in Germany, one of the worst consequences of Berlin’s deal with the Taliban is that it may particularly put at risk some 35,000 Afghans who came to Germany under special humanitarian programs for people deemed especially vulnerable to the Taliban. They include Paryani and her sisters in addition to thousands of human rights activists and Afghans who worked with the German military during its nearly two-decade presence in the country.
Paryani and others fear they will have to face the Taliban when attempting to renew their Afghan passports — which they need to extend their humanitarian visas — at Afghan diplomatic missions. Another 321,000 Afghans live in Germany as refugees or with other forms of protected status. They do not necessarily need Afghan passports, unless they want to apply for a permanent residence status.
More generally, activists and refugees also fear the Taliban, with their growing presence in Germany, could gain access to personal information held in databases in German missions, including details about their families, making them susceptible to blackmail and extortion.
“Given my personal history and my stance on extremism, I am concerned for my safety and that of my family,” one former teacher from Afghanistan granted anonymity due to his fear of retribution from the Taliban told POLITICO.
The former teacher, who lives in Germany with a humanitarian visa, said German immigration officials have asked him to renew his expired Afghan passport, a request that he fears will force him to deal directly with his persecutors.
“This situation continues to cause me significant psychological distress,” he said. “Sometimes I wake up at night because of nightmares related to the Taliban and this situation.”
‘Vulnerable to blackmail’
With its handling of the Taliban, Merz’s government is setting a precedent that will be closely watched by other EU countries. Government officials in Austria and Belgium have said they’re watching Germany’s cooperation with the Taliban closely. Taliban officials also held talks focused on deportations with the EU Commission in June in Brussels.
But Hamid Nangialay Kabiri, the former head of the Afghan consulate in Bonn, who quit last September in protest over the initial deal allowing Taliban officials to serve in diplomatic missions in Germany, warned that the German government’s decision to cooperate with the Afghan regime would come back to haunt it — and that the Taliban would use their new leverage over Germany to advance their interests in Europe, including by building networks that intimidate dissidents.
“They are destroying my country, and now they are coming here,” he said. “They are not thinking of diplomacy. They have a lot of plans in their mind.”
Advertisement
It’s a sentiment politicians inside the left-leaning opposition also share.
“The German government has made itself vulnerable to blackmail,” Schahina Gambir, a lawmaker for the Greens who was born in Kabul, told POLITICO. “We’re seeing recognition through the back door. The Taliban are being granted access to embassies, they’re being granted immunity, they’re given channels for dialogue — and at the same time, the situation for women and girls in Afghanistan is getting worse and worse.”
There are already signs that the Taliban are exercising their newfound leverage.
Last May, Kabul unexpectedly halted a deportation flight at the last minute, seemingly seeking to extract additional concessions from the German government. A couple of weeks later, Berlin announced the terms of the latest agreement allowing additional Taliban-appointed officials to work at diplomatic missions in Germany.
Officials in Berlin depicted the new deal as a victory and a practical necessity, allowing for more deportations.
Advertisement
“To increase the number of repatriations, more passports must be issued, more identities must be verified, and so on,” Martin Giese, a spokesperson for Germany’s foreign ministry, said at the time. “To this end, it will also be necessary for more consular officials to be involved.”
But Paryani, the Afghan midwife who fled to Germany with her four sisters, said the Taliban would use their new power to torment them in the country they had sought safety in.
“A Taliban member once wrote to me: ‘Just wait until our embassy in Germany reopens. Then we’ll find you there,'” she said of a comment that had surfaced under one of her social media posts about two years ago. She then deemed it irrelevant because it seemed so unrealistic.
“Today, I feel as though that threat has become a reality,” she said.

Farage vs. Binface: Inside the Clacton by-election circus
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

Then-London mayoral candidate Count Binface posing for a photo in London in 2024, left, and Reform UK Leader Nigel Farage speaking in southeast London on July 17, 2026. | Henry Nicholls/AFP via Getty Images
CLACTON-ON-SEA — Voters seeking to re-elect Nigel Farage Thursday will have to scan past an array of comedy characters and oddballs on the longest ballot paper in British history.
The man who hopes to be the U.K.’s next prime minister is all but certain to retain his seaside fiefdom of Clacton — but his self-styled “people versus the establishment” electoral gambit is sowing some seeds of discontent even among loyal supporters.
Fear of Clacton becoming a “laughing stock” is a common refrain during a pair of focus groups POLITICO attended in the run-up to this week’s election.
Advertisement
The feeling that the town has been made to look daft was apparent even among those preparing to vote once again to return the Reform UK leader to parliament. And it’s not the rival candidate wearing a trash can on his head that they’re holding responsible for the “farce.”
Thursday may not be the end of the matter, either. A parliamentary investigation into Farage’s alleged failure to declare millions of pounds of donations in the run-up to his 2024 election could mean yet another by-election — and a tougher battle for the right-wing populist next time around.
Bid for absolution
This self-inflicted campaign is taking place because of Farage’s decision to resign his parliamentary seat and put his fate in the hands of Clacton’s residents.
Ordinary punters, he argued, should be the ones to have their say as he faced mounting questions over undeclared donations. The gamble was that such a vote would absolve him of wrongdoing in the eyes of the public, regardless of the findings in two parliamentary probes — one over a £5 million donation from a crypto-entrepreneur, and the other into support from a convicted fraudster. Farage has denied wrongdoing in both instances, arguing that help was given in a personal capacity.
Farage speaks during a press conference on a plan to deport foreign prisoners, in London on Aug. 10, 2026. | Dan Kitwood/Getty Images
But Britain’s main political parties took one look at this ploy and opted out. That’s how Count Binface, one of the most enthusiastic inheritors of a rich British tradition of standing as a satirical candidate in elections, ended up as Farage’s most high-profile rival.
Others risking their £500 deposit to get their names on the 90-cm-long ballot paper include rival jokesters with names ranging from Howling Laud Hope, Nick the Incredible Flying Brick and Baron Von Thunderclap. Broadcast rules mean the 34-strong candidate list needs to be read in full at every mention of Farage’s by-election on TV.
Advertisement
A seaside town back on the map — in ways unwanted
The first focus group arranged by the More in Common think tank that POLITICO observed was made up of nine constituents who all voted for Farage in the 2024 general election, and are minded to do so again in the by-election. (Their names were withheld so they could speak candidly).
It was a retiree who was first to volunteer regret at Farage’s decision, blaming him for provoking an “influx of idiots” into the constituency. “Unfortunately, the action of causing a by-election has,” the former shopkeeper offered, “really made Clacton, in my opinion, a bit of a laughing stock.”
Two others repeated that same phrase, with one dog groomer-by-trade adding: “I think it was all a bit of a farce. I think he should have admitted that he was given this £5 million.”
“I guess it makes it very hard to trust him,” a delivery driver chimed in. “Most of my friends have gone towards Count Binface as opposed to Farage.”
Count Binface speaks to the media in Wigan, England on June 19, 2026. | Ryan Jenkinson/Getty Images
Farage has since given varying explanations for some of the money he’s received, including as a “reward” for Brexit, or to cover lifelong security in the perilous world of modern politics. The veteran campaigner has been tetchy about the “unconditional gift” during media appearances, telling a radio interviewer he could spend it on Ferraris or bet on the horses, adding: “What’s it got to do with you?”
The dog groomer was among those lamenting the cost of running the by-election too. Reform had offered to pay for it, but in reality there is no mechanism to do this. The sheer number of candidates running has some extraordinary consequences.
Advertisement
Tendring Council, which is presiding over the vote, said even the cost of printing the ballot papers is four times that of a typical election because of their sheer length. Additional planning has had to go into every stage, from how the ballot is printed, folded and actually cast at polling stations — and counting will go on through the night and possibly past breakfast.
Then there are the Reform voters who have now been forced to choose whether to cast a vote for a comedy candidate or for Farage.
“From what I can tell about Binface, he seems like an okay guy from the research I’ve done,” said one local businessman. “And I do think there would be some tourism involved because of the absurdity of having that candidate as the MP of Clacton.”
This self-inflicted campaign is taking place because of Farage’s decision to resign his parliamentary seat and put his fate in the hands of Clacton’s residents. | Dan Kitwood/Getty Images
That influx could already be observed, to some extent, on Tuesday this week. Even though it’s a school holiday, the pier and the amusement arcades in town weren’t exactly heaving with holiday-makers.
But there was a steady stream of journalists — so many that they even tried to vox pop each other at times. Then there was an obscure mobile phone network that set up an ice cream van selling “99s for 99p” — in a publicity stunt echoing one of Binface’s manifesto pledges. A vintage Jaguar painted all over with the Union Jack (and used in the Austin Powers franchise) is touring the streets all day in support of Binface.
Farage’s social media has done a good job of showing how much support he still commands from the diehards — at times at messiah-like levels. And it’s not hard to find his “I’m with Nigel” placards outside homes, a picture of the candidate ringed with a halo-like ferris wheel.
Advertisement
But supporters in the first focus group suggested that the sheen could be coming off a man who has, just this year, been enough of a campaigning force to send the governing Labour Party searching for a new leader.
Old-school Tories’ views harden
The second focus group, held in a community garden overlooking the town, featured right-wing voters, and comprised largely of former Conservative supporters who, though discontented with their old party, aren’t eager to back Farage any time soon.
They roundly agreed with the “farce” analysis of the by-election. “People see this by-election as a total joke. If you talk to anyone, then that is their view,” said a retired printer.
They all lamented having no proper choice, though they generally backed the decision by Farage’s mainstream rivals not to contest the vote.
A poster that reads “Clacton Fear” is seen in Clacton-on-Sea, England on Aug. 06, 2026. | Dan Kitwood/Getty Images
One bridge player with a firm grasp on politics described playing “eeny, meeny, miny, moe” with her postal vote to randomly pick a candidate who wasn’t Farage. Another spoke of spoiling her postal ballot and writing that the whole affair is a waste of time and money.
These were all the kind of right-wingers who Farage would want to win over to elevate himself from an insurgent outsider to true contender for high office — but their stances only seemed to have hardened in response to the by-election.
Advertisement
Anything but a crushing Farage victory would be a major upset. Constituency polling has him on course to win 73 percent of the vote to Binface’s 20 percent. Turnout in this bizarre by-election will also be closely looked at, as will spoiled ballots.
Reform aides have already been planning a victory speech to take place after the votes have finally been counted on Friday. But first their candidate will have to undergo that British ritual of standing next to an array of comedy characters on a stage in a leisure center to hear the results.
Should Farage make it back to parliament as expected, then the standards commissioner’s investigation into the donations resumes. That means yet more scrutiny at a time when Labour is riding a polling bounce after Andy Burnham took over as prime minister.
For the first time since March last year, Labour has topped POLITICO’s poll of polls ahead of Reform. The government’s apparent rehabilitation — combined with Reform being squeezed on the right by the splinter Restore Britain party — is adding to a worsening picture for Farage.
If the Reform UK leader is found to have committed wrongdoing and ends up being suspended from parliament, the next by-election — should he choose to fight it — could pose a far greater challenge. Not only would he come up against real opposition, but voters will have read yet more headlines about mega-bucks donations as they’re forced to the polls once again.
“It’ll be bad for us and it’ll make us look even more stupid,” said a Reform-minded instrument salesman when asked about the prospect of another by-election. “But then he [Farage] was the one that called it.”

Zelenskyy’s Balkan fumble
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

PRISTINA — Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s weekend trip to Serbia triggered reverberations in the Balkans long after the Ukrainian president jetted back to Kyiv.
Zelenskyy visited Serbian President Aleksandar Vučić — who has refused to join the EU’s sanctions regime against Russia and maintains a cozy relationship with the Kremlin — for the first time on Saturday. He then waded into the thorniest regional dispute by declaring Ukraine would continue not to recognize the independence of Kosovo, a former province of Serbia.
Kosovo’s response was swift. A building-sized blue-and-yellow “Free Ukraine” banner that has been up on Pristina’s main thoroughfare since 2022 came down immediately, with Mayor Përparim Rama declaring that while his sympathies remain with “peoples facing war, violence and persecution … respect must be mutual.”
Advertisement
Since Zelenskyy’s visit, Vučić threatened to physically redirect the Iber River that runs from Serbia to Kosovo in retaliation for Kosovo demolishing Serb-owned houses along the reservoir’s shore. Such a move would drain the reservoir supplying much of Kosovo’s water and crucial cooling capacity to its largest power plant.
In addition, Serbian Foreign Minister Marko Djurić and Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama exchanged barbs on X, with the latter accusing Serbia of being in “a political bubble” and being in denial over the fact that “Serbia lost Kosova” long ago.
Kosovo was an Albanian-majority southern province of Serbia for most of the 20th century. Its people held broad political rights under socialist Yugoslavia until a decade-long Serb crackdown on dissent led to the armed conflict of 1998-99. A three-month NATO bombing campaign drove Serbian forces out and made the province a U.N. protectorate.
Kosovo declared independence in 2008 and, to date, it is recognized by over 100 nations, including the U.S., U.K. and 22 of the 27 EU member countries. It is also a potential EU candidate country, submitting its application in December 2022.
The country’s status has long been a favorite talking point for Russian President Vladimir Putin, who has used it to justify invading Georgia in 2008 and annexing Crimea in 2014. Kosovo’s Foreign Minister Glauk Konjufca said he took note of Zelenskyy’s views “with regret” and that such rhetoric echoes “Russia’s attempts to invoke Kosova as a precedent.”
As for why Ukraine’s leader would wade into the intractable Balkan issue at all, it likely comes down to weaponry.
Advertisement
Serbia still produces considerable quantities of ammunition in the Soviet-standard calibers which would be impossible to acquire from Kyiv’s Western allies, who use the NATO standard instead. Ukraine retains Soviet-era heavy howitzers and tanks that remain key to the fight in the Donbas and beyond. And despite his pro-Russian stance, Vučić is happy to provide them to Kyiv quietly.
“Ukraine is in a position where it cannot care about things beyond the more immediate needs for Ukraine, and Vučić matters to him more,” explained Florian Bieber, who directs the Centre for Southeast European Studies at the University of Graz.
Vučić’s overtures toward Zelenskyy could be in part an effort to placate criticism from Brussels. EU leaders have condemned the “explosion of violence” during the ongoing anti-government protest movement and the “collapse in democratic standards” in Serbia.
“He’s hoping that he will get less critical remarks in the coming months because of his close, at least symbolically closer, ties with Zelenskyy. Vučić is doing this for leverage with the EU ahead of possible elections in the country,” Bieber continued.
Kosovo’s supporters have long cast its independence as a one-off, not a template. But the circumstances of its journey away from Serbia remains divisive, particularly for EU members like Spain and Cyprus, who have their own separatist headaches and still refuse to recognize Kosovo’s independence.
“Depending on which side of this argument you’re coming down on, you will have a different view over what Kosovo’s independence means for other conflicts and other territorial disputes around the world,” said Bieber.
Advertisement
Oleksandr Lytvynenko, Ukraine’s ambassador to Serbia, said in an emailed statement that Zelenskyy’s trip to Belgrade included the reaching of practical agreements on mutual support for EU integration, as both countries are EU candidates. “The integration of the Western Balkans into the European Union remains the most reliable way to address long-term security threats and resolve outstanding regional disputes,” he said.
He added: “This visit was not about ammunition. It was about Europe. The greater Ukraine’s engagement in the Western Balkans, the greater the prospects for stability and peace.”
This article was updated with comments from the Ukrainian ambassador to Serbia.

Breakfast looks a lot more expensive under new EU pesticide plans
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

Adding further uncertainty for growers, the European Commission has yet to specify which banned pesticides would be covered by the measure. | Stéphane Rouillard/Hans Lucas/AFP via Getty Images
Fancy a morning coffee, orange juice or blueberry pancakes for your Sunday brunch? Prepare to fork out more for those items if Brussels' plan to get foreign growers to align with the bloc's pesticide rules holds.
An analysis by the European Commission's in-house researchers confirms what non-EU farmers have been saying for months: A plan to prohibit any trace of some of the "most hazardous" pesticides banned in the EU for health and environmental reasons would lead to fewer and more expensive products.
Under a worst-case, hypothetical scenario — in which the non-EU producers don't adjust to the rules — you'd have to pay 332 percent more for coffee and 82 percent more for citrus fruit, the Joint Research Centre said in an analysis published on Tuesday. The EU's agricultural imports would decline by 41 percent and livestock farmers would also be hit with higher feed costs.
Advertisement
Even under more plausible scenarios envisioned by the researchers, in which external growers get on board to varying degrees, consumer prices would rise and EU agricultural imports decline. Though that would in turn boost domestic production, with exact numbers depending on producers' willingness to adapt.
The findings lay out an unpalatable political choice for Brussels: Keep angry farmers' tractors off the streets, or hit consumers' wallets as they fulfill basic needs at the grocery store.
The proposed residue ban, which is part of the food and feed safetysimplification package, is popular with European farmers seeking a level playing field with foreign growers — after all, it was partly designed to appease their ire over the EU's trade deal with the Mercosur bloc of Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay, and Uruguay. In order to avoid leaving any residue on fruits and vegetables, producers would essentially have to stop using the substance in question.
However, critics say it clashes with global trade rules, as it essentially imposes EU rules on foreign producers, which is known as a mirror clause.
A wide range of international producer groups argue that the proposed ban goes beyond existing health protections in order to push a one-size-fits-all approach, ignoring the reality that growers around the world face different pests, climates and farming conditions.
“The choice is between berries that are available all year round — healthy, safe and at a fair price — or limited production at a high price,” said Amine Bennani, president of the Moroccan Association of Red Fruit Producers.
Advertisement
What Brussels calls an “alignment of standards,” he said in an emailed statement, amounts in practice to “a trade barrier.” Bennani also complained that the association has never been consulted, even though the legislation will affect 250,000 Moroccans working in the sector.
The concerns are not unique to Moroccan berry growers. South African fruit farmer association Hortgro and the South African Table Grape Industry argued that country's grape exports are critical to livelihoods of thousands of people working in the sector.
The Commission said its aim is to prevent the most hazardous substances — banned for use in the bloc — from re-entering the EU through imports altogether by lowering their residue limits to a technical zero.
Both the Commission and the global producers agree on one point: Residue limits are already set to ensure safe levels of consumption for human health. Critics argue, though, that the EU executive wants to go well beyond existing safeguards for human health as it looks to block traces of substances banned for broader health and environmental threats.
Europe’s “very high standards” for safety “need to be adequately controlled,” said Elisabeth Werner, director-general of DG AGRI, at the POLITICO Sustainable Futures Summit just ahead of the proposal's debut last year.
Advertisement
Adding further uncertainty for growers, the Commission has yet to specify which banned pesticides would be covered by the measure. The JRC study identified 18 active substances that could be subject to the residue ban, affecting 235 commodities and 86 countries.
The EU will make those decisions case-by-case, using impact assessments, said Commission spokesperson Eva Hrnčířová.
In an emailed statement, Hrnčířová did not directly address concerns about higher prices or reduced availability. Yet she stressed that any action "would take into account the importance of preserving the EU’s food security and possible international implications."
The EU has reason to be concerned about international implications. Several countries, including Australia, Canada, Paraguay and the U.S., have challenged the measure at the World Trade Organization level, while the International Fresh Produce Association argues that existing global food safety standards already protect consumers while facilitating trade.
Some EU countries support mirror clauses as a way to be more fair to European farmers, who fear free trade deals like Mercosur allow competition from abroad that isn't subject to the same restrictions. Paris has been especially vocal, already imposing national-level bans earlier this year on products with residual levels of some pesticides whose use is forbidden in the EU — restricting some potatoes and avocados from entering the country. So much for avocado toast.

Ukraine pounds grain terminals at Russia's Black Sea Novorossiysk port
Aug 12 - Ukraine hammered Russia's Black Sea port city of Novorossiysk in a massive overnight drone attack that put two major grain terminals out of action, according to Russian industry sources, raising fears in global markets of a disruption to supplies.
Russia is the world's largest wheat exporter and most of those exports are shipped via its Black Sea ports like Novorossiysk. Russia's main grain lobby group warned last month that Ukrainian attacks could shut down grain exports via the Black Sea in the near future, pushing up prices and causing hunger in Africa and the Middle East.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said on Telegram that Ukraine had hit Russia's Novorossiysk naval base with drones, missiles and unmanned boats. Russia moved some of its Black Sea Fleet vessels to Novorossiysk after Kyiv's forces attacked them repeatedly in Crimea, which Moscow seized and annexed from Ukraine in 2014.
Veniamin Kondratyev, the governor of Krasnodar region, where Novorossiysk is located, said a "massive" wave of Ukrainian attacks had targeted the area and killed at least two people, including an 8-year-old child.
Andrei Kravchenko, the mayor of Novorossiysk, said the Black Sea port's water supply had been suspended and an emergency situation had been declared following the attack, which damaged four unspecified enterprises, more than two dozen residential buildings and some educational facilities.
Unverified video on social media showed images of a tower of flames and smoke rising from somewhere in Novorossiysk.
Amid fears of disruptions to wheat supplies on global markets, Chicago wheat futures rose around 3% on Wednesday following reports of the Novorossiysk attack.
Russian strikes on ships in the Black Sea have drastically reduced grain shipments from Ukraine, which is also a major grain exporter. Shipments tumbled 76% in the first two weeks of August, versus the same period last year, Ukraine's agriculture ministry said.
REPORT OF DEAL ON OIL SHIPMENTS
Novorossiysk also hosts oil export infrastructure, including for the Caspian Pipeline Consortium (CPC), which is owned partly by U.S. oil majors Chevron and Exxon Mobil and carries Kazakh oil exports to market.
The Financial Times reported on Wednesday that, following a request from U.S. Vice President JD Vance in late July, Ukraine had agreed not to target CPC infrastructure and non-Russian vessels, as long as they were not under Ukrainian sanctions or carrying Russian oil or other cargo.
Ukraine's presidency did not respond to a request for comment on the story.
There was no indication that the CPC or tankers collecting oil from the pipeline had been struck during the overnight attacks.
In Sevastopol in Crimea, more than three dozen drones were downed, the city's Russian-installed governor, Mikhail Razvozhayev, said on Telegram.
Separately, a Russian attack caused a fire at a shopping mall in the southeastern Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia, regional Governor Ivan Fedorov said on Telegram, posting pictures of a building ablaze.
A Russian attack on Odesa, Ukraine's largest seaport, damaged infrastructure there, Serhiy Lysak, head of the city's military administration, said on Telegram, without giving details.
Moscow has intensified its strikes on Ukraine's logistics and warehouse facilities in response to Kyiv's attacks on Russian energy, port and logistic hubs.
Zelenskiy said on Tuesday that Kyiv had handed proposals to U.S. negotiators for a plan to end the conflict, which started when Russia launched its full-scale war on Ukraine in February 2022.
Ukraine has repeatedly called for a ceasefire after nearly 4-1/2 years of fighting. Russia says it wants a settlement, but any solution must involve Ukraine fully ceding four regions Moscow claims as well as resolving the conflict's "root causes." REUTERS

Major US supplier recalls jalapenos amid Salmonella outbreak

Major US supplier recalls jalapenos amid Salmonella outbreak
A major US produce supplier has recalled jalapeno products sold through major grocery store and restaurant chains amid a Salmonella outbreak, according to the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA). Taylor Farms has also been linked to a separate multistate outbreak of another foodborne illness.
The recalled products contained jalapenos grown in the Mexican state of Sinaloa and distributed by Coast Citrus Distributors, according to the FDA. 
A number of retailers, including Hannaford, Kroger, Stop & Shop, Target, Trader Joe’s, Walmart, and Whole Foods, received recalled products across 26 states. An investigation into the outbreak is still underway.
At least 345 people have contracted Salmonella since mid-June, according to health authorities, with dozens of hospitalizations reported.
People usually contract Salmonella infections after consuming food contaminated with the bacteria. Symptoms commonly include diarrhea, fever, and abdominal cramps. Young children, older adults, and people with weakened immune systems are at greater risk of developing serious complications.
Last month, Taylor Farms de Mexico also removed shredded iceberg lettuce sourced from central Mexico from the US market after health authorities identified the produce as the source of a cyclosporiasis outbreak, a parasite-borne intestinal illness. Investigators linked illnesses to people who had eaten at Taco Bell restaurants in multiple states.
The outbreak, which began in May, has sickened at least 6,358 people across 15 states, according to the CDC. In total, 278 people have been hospitalized and two deaths reported. Health officials have warned that the true number of infections is likely higher, as some people recover without medical care and are never tested for Cyclospora.
Cyclosporiasis can cause prolonged diarrhea, as well as bloating, gas, stomach cramps, nausea, fatigue, and other gastrointestinal symptoms.
Taylor Farms was also the supplier of yellow onions implicated in a 2024 E. coli outbreak linked to McDonald’s Quarter Pounders.

China childhood staple ‘White Rabbit’ candy gains global praise for classic wrapper design
Brand’s pure milk flavour and iconic wrapper ensure it remains a beloved icon in consumer memories, says expert
The time-honoured Chinese creamy candy brand White Rabbit recently went viral for its iconic wrapper design, but the brand, having pursued an active rebranding strategy and collaborations, offers much more than its traditional legacy.
A netizen on X, under the handle @weeabob, shared a post featuring the candy’s classic blue, red, and white wrapper, praising it as an “absolute masterstroke of graphic design.”
This post garnered 260,000 likes and 600 comments, with many users reminiscing about the candy, as well as the brand’s innovative new products and collaborations.
Introduced in 1959 to commemorate the 10th anniversary of the People’s Republic of China, White Rabbit is widely recognised as China’s national creamy candy.
Its lesser-known precursor, the “ABC Mickey Mouse Candy,” was developed in 1943 by the Shanghai ABC Candy Factory, inspired by British creamy sweets. As its name suggests, this candy’s wrapper featured Mickey Mouse.
In 1954, the ABC Candy Factory rebranded to the Aimin (Love People) Candy and Biscuit Factory, abandoning the Mickey Mouse design due to concerns over copyright and the designation of rats as one of the “four pests.” The candy was subsequently rebranded as White Rabbit creamy candy.
During times of extreme resource scarcity, White Rabbit candy was regarded as a premium source of nourishment, famously said to be “equivalent to a glass of milk” for every seven pieces consumed.

Anti-Muslim hate against Michigan Senate candidate surged 20-fold after primary win, watchdog finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
01:37:18 UTC
10:37:18 KST

Washington, DC — Within hours of Abdul El-Sayed’s victory in Michigan's Democratic Senate primary, the volume of anti-Muslim posts naming El-Sayed exploded.
New research from the Centre for the Study of Organised Hate (CSOH) shows posts targeting El-Sayed with Islamophobic abuse averaged 3,099 a day in the week after his win, up from a daily average of 155 in the two months before it, an increase of 1,895 percent.
On August 5, the day his rival conceded, the volume of anti-Muslim posts about him peaked at nearly 7,000 in a single day.
That single week produced more Islamophobic content about El-Sayed than the previous seven months combined.
It accounts for 56.7 percent of all 38,280 such posts recorded about him since January.
El-Sayed, a former Michigan public health official running for the US Senate seat vacated by Gary Peters, is Muslim. That has become central to the abuse directed at him. 
CSOH's analysis, which drew on posts across X, Facebook, Instagram, YouTube, Reddit and Bluesky, found the content clustered around a handful of recurring conspiracy tropes rather than genuine political critique.
The largest single theme linked him to Hamas, Hezbollah and the Muslim Brotherhood, with widely shared posts branding him "a jihadist."
Others baselessly accused him of planning to impose Sharia law, while a significant share of posts went further still, calling for "remigration” of Muslims from Western countries, as the only response.
Not an isolated spike
El-Sayed surge was not confined to posts about him.
Across X alone, CSOH tracked 409,640 posts promoting anti-Muslim bigotry and conspiracy theories in the US between June 1 and August 10.
Overall Islamophobic posting on the platform hit its highest single-day total of the summer on August 5, the day El-Sayed's win was declared, with nearly 12,000 posts. That was more than double the previous 30-day average and the first day in that period to cross 10,000 posts.
Six days on, researchers said, the surge had not subsided.
General anti-Muslim posting volume remained 59 percent above its pre-primary baseline, while abuse aimed specifically at El-Sayed stayed roughly ten times higher than its levels earlier in the summer.
Rising number of Muslim candidates
CSOH linked the online surge to a wider, organised effort.
That campaign, researchers said, has built its narrative around ideas drawn from the Great Replacement theory, escalating around events such as the war in the Middle East and the rising number of Muslim candidates for office.
El-Sayed's win in Michigan was one of several closely watched results in this month's round of US primary contests, part of the run-up to next year's midterm elections. But what followed it, researchers say, now looks less like a reaction to one candidate than a script that runs whenever a Muslim politician wins or gains ground.
CSOH said it expects anti-Muslim bigotry to intensify further as campaigning for the 2026 midterms builds.

ICE plans $20M purchase of electric shock gloves to gain compliance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
01:33:17 UTC
10:33:17 KST

US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers have prepared to outfit agents with gloves that deliver electric shocks intended to gain compliance from combative individuals, according to official notices.
ICE plans to spend up to $20 million to purchase thousands of "conductive distraction and de-escalation devices" for officers and agents by March, according to a notice published on Monday by the US Department of Homeland Security.
The devices are known as the G.L.O.V.E., which stands for Generated Low Output Voltage Emitter, and are manufactured by Compliant Technologies LLC of Lexington, Kentucky.
They have been used in recent years by some jails and police departments.
Civil rights concerns
Civil rights advocates expressed alarm at the plan, saying ICE officers already face criticism for their use of force with little oversight.
Compliant Technologies says the devices function as a normal pair of patrol gloves until officers press a switch to activate their electrical mode.
The gloves must be applied directly to someone's skin to deliver a pain stimulus that typically helps an officer gain compliance within seconds, according to the company.
"It's immediate and sharp, and it will distract you. I call it like a bee sting," said John Peters, president of the Institute for the Prevention of In-Custody Deaths, who is studying how the device has been used.
"If the officer is getting any type of resistance from the person, this is certainly an effective tool."
Peters said he believed ICE's planned purchase would likely be the largest from the company to date.
He said he could envision ICE officers using the gloves to help remove uncooperative subjects from cars and houses and in and out of detention facilities.
Accountability debate
The manufacturer warns the device should not be misused.
Jenn Rolnick Borchetta, deputy project director on policing at the American Civil Liberties Union, said the public should have no confidence that ICE officers will use the devices appropriately.
She questioned why the devices would be necessary for civil immigration enforcement and noted those getting shocked might have no advance warning.
"Introducing gloves that can so easily be used to deliver terrible pain in encounters is a recipe for harm to the public."

Hong Kong is no longer a Western playground – and it’s not looking back
Stephen Roach and his like-minded critics should let go of their fantasy of a bygone era. The city has already moved on
When it comes to bad prognostication, no one can beat Fortune, which came up with the mother of all “Hong Kong is doomed” narratives. In June 1995, the magazine ran its infamous “The Death of Hong Kong” cover story, predicting its demise following the 1997 handover to China.
Who can argue with that? You and I are very different from our younger selves. We all have to change and adapt. Not changing with the times in this day and age is positively suicidal, at least with your career.
As it is with people, so it is with cities. As mainland China emerges as a superpower, how can Hong Kong not change with the rest of the nation, and for the better?
Do you know what next-door Shenzhen was like in the mid-1960s when I was born? Well, it didn’t exist as an economic entity, and certainly did not register anywhere in the then global economy.

Lindsey Graham's sister Darline Graham advances to runoff in South Carolina Republican Senate primary
Aug 11 - Lindsey Graham's sister Darline Graham on Tuesday advanced to a run-off to be the Republican Party's nominee for the South Carolina U.S. Senate seat in November's election following her brother's death, according to media projections.
She will face U.S. Representative Ralph Norman in the August 25 run-off. The eventual Republican nominee is favored to win in November.
Governor Henry McMaster had appointed Darline Graham to serve the rest of the senator's term through early January, after his unexpected death from a heart ailment.
President Donald Trump endorsed Darline Graham, who has never held public office, for a full six-year term, calling it a "fabulous tribute" to her brother.
But critics said her bid, based on family name recognition and presidential backing without a political record of her own, had the air of an attempted coronation.
Graham has said that she is "not being handed" the seat and that she realizes that she need to earn votes.
Ten candidates stood for the Republican nomination in Tuesday's election. With none of them gaining more than 50% of the vote, the top two finishers will head to the run-off later this month.
The winner will face Democrat Annie Andrews, a pediatrician who had more than $3 million in her campaign war chest at the start of July.
Other candidates in Tuesday's race included U.S. Representative Russell Fry, former Governor Mark Sanford and self-funded Greenville businessman Mark Lynch.
With 80% of the vote counted, the Associated Press placed Graham in first position so far with 32.6% of the vote and Norman second with just over 24%.
ALABAMA VOTE IN REDRAWN SEAT
In Alabama, Republicans in the state's 2nd Congressional District for the U.S. House were projected by media to have chosen state representative Rhett Marques to be their candidate in a seat that they hope to flip from the Democrats with help from a redrawn map.
The race is potentially crucial to their bid to hold the House, which they narrowly control.
The Republican majorities in Congress are essential to Trump's ability to power ahead with his agenda, but he faces a tough challenge ahead in the November midterm election, given a low approval rating that has eroded further as the Iran war drags on and gasoline prices remain high.
Republican-led states in the U.S. South rushed through a round of congressional redistricting earlier this year, to take advantage of an April Supreme Court decision that severely weakened the Voting Rights Act, a 1965 law intended to prevent discrimination in voting.
Earlier this year, the court cleared the way for Alabama to use a congressional map that favors Republicans by eliminating one of two districts where Black voters make up a majority or near-majority.
Marques will face incumbent Democrat Shomari Figures, who is Black and is hoping for a second term.
TIME FOR CHANGE IN SOUTH CAROLINA?
Lindsey Graham won his June 9 primary in South Carolina by almost 28 percentage points, as he sought his fifth Senate term. Lynch, who placed second with nearly 29% of the vote, is the only candidate in the special primary from the original primary field.
Lynch received more than 130,000 votes in that primary, suggesting some Republican primary voters had an appetite for change before Lindsey Graham's death.
"People are furious" about "the coronation of Darline Graham," Lynch said in an interview. "It's OK that they picked her to be the interim senator until January but not to run for office."
Skeptics have questioned Graham's credentials and the president's decision to endorse her over other candidates who have run in previous campaigns. Her rivals expect voters who do not choose her on Tuesday to back her opponent in a runoff.
Trump won South Carolina in 2024 by nearly 18 percentage points.
In interviews, Republicans questioned the potency of Trump's endorsement in South Carolina, where he backed a pair of runoff candidates for governor after polls showed his first pick, Lieutenant Governor Pamela Evette, was poised to lose against Attorney General Alan Wilson.
U.S. Representative Nancy Mace, who ran unsuccessfully for governor, predicted Graham would lose her Senate bid just as Trump's original choice for governor lost.
The president's endorsement "gets you into a runoff," she told Reuters. "But ... it's not enough to win a race anymore." REUTERS

“Ghosts of Bakhmut: Memoirs of Sniper” by legendary unit commander to be published in Ukraine

Unknown Publisher

“Ghosts of Bakhmut: Memoirs of Sniper” by legendary unit commander to be published in Ukraine
This is the personal story of a man fighting for Ukraine who recounts the war not through the language of official reports or heroic legends, but through his own experience, according to Ukrinform.
As the publishers note, this book is neither a documentary reconstruction of battles nor a chronology of military operations. The author does not seek to create a heroic image of the war or his own unit. Instead, he offers the reader an honest, personal account—of the people who voluntarily took up arms, of fatigue, fear, responsibility, brotherhood, and a memory that does not end after the last battle.
“The Ghosts of Bakhmut” begins with the words: "This book is not about the kind of war shown on the news. There are no grand words or clichés here.” This principle defines the entire text. The author recounts not only the snipers’ combat operations but also the inner experience of war: life between missions, the loss of comrades, moments of despair, and the strength that comes from powerful mutual support.
The book consists of 46 chapters, which can be read as separate short stories and cover the unit’s journey from its formation to its withdrawal from Bakhmut. Alongside the combat scenes, these stories feature specific individuals—comrades, medics, mechanics, and commanders—both those who died and those who survived. They are the true protagonists of the story, for, as the author notes, it is not about heroes, but about people who learned to fight, survive, and remain human.
Memory is a separate theme of the book. The book is dedicated to the author’s fallen comrades—Vadym, whose call sign was “Father Taras,” and Oleh, whose call sign was “Cunning.” At the end of the book, the author admits that he wrote it not to prove anything, but to preserve the memory unvarnished, just as it is. That is precisely why “The Ghosts of Bakhmut” becomes not only a collection of personal memories but also a way to preserve the voices of those who can no longer be heard.
“The Ghosts of Bakhmut” is not just a book about snipers and war. It is the story of people whom the war forced to change, taught to see death up close, and at the same time to cherish life more than ever. We went through Bakhmut, changed along with the war, and continued on our path. This book is about those who remained, those who are no longer with us, and the price Ukraine is paying for its future. I want people, after reading this book, to understand not only how we fought, but also what we stood for and continue to stand for,” notes “The Ghost.”
Read also: Presentation of Oleksandra Shutko’s book on Ukrainian women’s influence on Ottoman Empire to be held
In addition to the text, the book contains QR codes that link to photos, videos, and additional materials about the unit’s activities. They allow readers to see the people and places mentioned in the story and expand the documentary dimension of the publication.
“The Ghosts of Bakhmut: Memoirs of a Sniper” is now available for pre-order.

Widow of Oct. 7 victim denied entry to Israel: 'Callousness and lack of sensitivity'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
01:28:22 UTC
10:28:22 KST

Her husband was murdered on October 7 at Kibbutz Be'eri. She was nine months pregnant, hiding in a safe room at Kibbutz Or Haner, and survived. Now, the State of Israel is not allowing her to attend the wedding of people with whom she formed a profound bond, or to exercise the rights she is entitled to as a widow.
Her name is Jovel Santiago Castellvi, a caregiver from the Philippines. Her husband, Paul Vincent Castellvi, 42, also a caregiver, was murdered by Hamas terrorists in Be'eri, where he remained alongside his patient, Eviatar Kipnis, 65.
"We don't really know what happened in Eviatar and Lilach's final moments," Nadav Kipnis and Sharon Lavon told ynet and Yedioth Ahronoth. "But one of the things that comforts us is that Paul was there. We wish fate had been different, but I'm glad he was by his side and I'm certain he tried to protect them in every way he could."
Nadav lost both of his parents, Eviatar and Lilach, while other members of his family were abducted to Gaza and later released in hostage deals. His partner, Sharon, became pregnant after the massacre and the couple decided to name their son Oliver, an acronym in Hebrew for the phrase "Eviatar and Lilach also left joy in our hearts."
A special bond developed between them and Jovel.
"A few days after October 7, she called me when Paul's body had been identified," Sharon said.
"She was nine months pregnant and gave birth to their son on Nov. 3. She gave birth without an epidural and told me that she had already experienced the greatest pain of her life — losing her husband, Paul. All the baby equipment was on the upper floor in Be'eri and everything burned. Nothing was left — no crib, no stroller. Everything was gone. And after October 7, on the day our loved ones died together, our fate, our story, became even more closely intertwined."
'We were in turmoil'
Israel recognized Jovel as the widow of a victim of hostile acts, and she later left Israel with her infant son, Jaysen Paul.
Nadav and Sharon have now decided to marry after six and a half years together and having a child. They sent invitations to family and friends, including, of course, Jovel. But to her surprise, she discovered that Israel was refusing to allow her to attend the wedding, which is expected to take place in September.
"We were supposed to get married a few years ago, and then October 7 happened," Sharon said. "We were in turmoil. Nadav's parents were murdered and there were other hostages from the family. We were constantly traveling and taking part in delegations, and life stopped. Only recently, after all the hostages returned, did we feel we had the ability to celebrate ourselves. Only now are we processing what we went through and focusing on what is good, and that is the thought that we have the privilege of celebrating a wedding."
But the celebration cannot feel complete without the woman who has become an inseparable part of their family.
The Population and Immigration Authority initially refused to allow Jovel to return to Israel because of her request to relocate to the country, despite the fact that she had purchased a round-trip ticket. It later barred her from coming to Israel with her young son, Jaysen Paul, to attend the wedding and asked her to deposit 100,000 shekels before authorities would consider allowing her to enter.
"After she flew to the Philippines with Jaysen, she returned to Israel in order to maintain her work visa," Sharon said. "She left Jaysen with family, but we saw how difficult it was for her to be without her son, especially after everything she had been through.
"She realized she couldn't be here without him. In June, she returned to the Philippines to be with her son, and last November she submitted an application for residency in Israel and for recognition as a victim of hostile acts. Many of the rights she is entitled to can only be exercised in Israel. The problem is that she has to be physically in Israel to submit those applications. Every attempt to help her has been rejected. In the Philippines, they don't understand what she went through. Here in Israel, people understand her. It's different."
For now, the couple simply wants her to be present on their wedding day.
"We speak with her on the phone every few days," they said. "Our son Oliver talks with Jaysen. But they refuse to approve her coming here."
The couple, both teachers, generally stay out of the public eye.
"We hope that once her story is published, they will correct this," they said. "We hope it's only bureaucracy. Time after time, they make things more difficult for us and put us through more and more obstacles. We're tired and exhausted and feel that something here is unfair."
Attorney Michal Pomeranz, who represents Jovel through the Justice Ministry's Legal Aid Department, said: "We hope the Population Authority does not intend to reject Jovel's request — either to enter Israel for a visit or to receive status here. Preventing entry to Israel for a widow who was forced to give birth to her son alone after her husband was murdered alongside his Israeli patient, and who has been unable to recover in the Philippines, denies her the possibility of rebuilding her life in the country where she lost her husband.
"In our view, this is the least the State of Israel can do for her. Rejecting her request, and the request of the Lavon-Kipnis family, for her and her son to come to Israel to attend Nadav and Sharon's wedding, after the families' fates became so tragically intertwined, demonstrates callousness and a lack of sensitivity to the situation."
'My second family'
Jovel told ynet and Yedioth Ahronoth that attending Nadav and Sharon's wedding was deeply important to her.
"It is important for us to attend Nadav and Sharon's wedding," she said. "On October 7, they became my second family. After Paul was murdered, I had people to lean on. In Israel, I only had Paul, and in Israel I met so many people. The wonderful Kipnis family helped me at the hospital after I gave birth. Because of them, I met wonderful people, people who can understand what I went through.
"It still hurts. And even though Nadav lost his parents, he supported me 100%. I can't explain how important that is. We bought round-trip tickets. I am so disappointed."
Explaining her desire to eventually settle in Israel, she said: "I wanted so much to return to Israel, which supports me and my son. Now I don't know what will happen. Maybe my chapter in Israel is over. I am still traumatized by October 7. Paul and I had so many plans for the future. Now I don't know what the future will be."
The Population and Immigration Authority said in response: "A review of the case found that the late Mr. Castellvi was buried in the couple's country of origin, the Philippines, and that the applicant subsequently chose to leave Israel together with her son and return to her country of origin, where members of her family reside.
"The applicant is now seeking to enter Israel together with her son for the purpose of settling in Israel under the relevant procedure. The procedure is intended to allow foreign nationals who are staying in Israel to apply for a temporary residence permit for a short and defined period in order to exercise their rights vis-a-vis the National Insurance Institute.
"The applicant's request to come to Israel now, two years later, together with her son for the purpose of settling in the country does not meet the requirements of the procedure. This was explained to her attorney in full detail. However, an appeal has been submitted and is currently being carefully reviewed."

Count Binface, the 'joke' UK candidate challenging far-right Farage
Britain's Count Binface, a man wearing a metallic rubbish bin over his head, challenges far-right politician Nigel Farage on Thursday in the Clacton by-election sparked by the Reform UK leader's shock resignation from his post in July. None of the UK's mainstream political parties are fielding candidates, so the outlandish Binface is stealing the show.

British politics has a long-cherished reputation for attracting the weird and wonderful.
But in a pantheon of colourful characters, Count Binface, a man wearing a rubbish bin over his head, is stealing the show.
The self-described "intergalactic space warrior" from the fictional planet Sigma IX takes on hardline anti-immigrant politician Nigel Farage on Thursday in the Clacton by-election, triggered when the Reform UK leader resigned in a shock move.
Read moreBritain's Farage resigns as MP to stand for re-election amid furore over gift worth millions
With Farage running again for his seat, none of the UK's mainstream political parties is fielding candidates, having dismissed the move as a stunt designed to stall a parliamentary inquiry into his finances.
That has left the door open to Count Binface and a host of other independent and parody candidates.
While polls give Farage a clear victory with more than 70 percent of the vote, Binface, the alter ego of comedian and comedy writer Jon Harvey, is grabbing all the attention and could win as much as 20 percent.
During almost a decade as the joke candidate in UK politics, Binface has fully embraced the absurd.
He arrives at election counts wearing a metallic dustbin-shaped helmet, a silver cape and silver-and-black armour and brandishing his razor-sharp, deadpan sense of humour.
His manifestos mix smart political satire with comedic promises to cap croissant prices, improve WiFi on UK trains and conscript people using speakerphones on public transport.
"In the UK anybody, literally anybody, is free to stand in an election, no matter how idiotic the get-up", he told AFP ahead of the 2024 London mayoral elections.

The British political system "fosters the eccentricity, the wonderment and the humour of politics", he added.
Democracy matters
Harvey, 46, is a University of Oxford Classics graduate who has written for popular satirical television programmes including "The Thick of It" and "Have I Got News for You".
In a recent appearance on the "The Rest is Politics" podcast, he quoted from Homer's "Odyssey" in fluent Homeric Greek.
He first attracted attention in 2017 as Lord Buckethead, when he challenged then-prime minister Theresa May in the general election.
A copyright dispute later prompted a rebranding, leading to the birth of Count Binface in 2018.
Since then, Binface has contested elections against former prime ministers Boris Johnson and Rishi Sunak as well as London mayor Sadiq Khan, consistently drawing thousands of votes and extensive media coverage.
In the 2021 London mayoral race, he won 24,775 first-preference ballots – one percent of the vote – and netted a similar tally at the next vote in 2024, easily beating the far-right Britain First party.
Khan, who won re-election in the 2024 election, paid tribute to Binface for standing, joking the count had made him "work hard for it".
Unlike some novelty candidates, Harvey insists there is a serious point to his activism.
His policy platform often lampoons mainstream politics while drawing on genuine public anger and frustration and advocating in support of democracy.
"Behind every one of these campaigns is a simple argument ... that a ballot is worth casting even when you know how the night ends," he writes on his website.
'Unity candidate'
On Monday, he posted an "interplanetary address" on X which played on a screen attached to a balloon floating at an altitude of 100,000 feet (30,500 metres) above Earth thanks to a specialist company.
"Join me. Let's take out the trash and make 13th of August bin day!" he says.
Other manifesto pledges have included forcing water company bosses to swim in polluted rivers and banning loud snacks in cinemas.
"I pledge to build at least one affordable house," Binface joked in his Clacton manifesto.
He skewers Farage, vowing not to take £5 million gifts from crypto billionaires, and spend more time in Clacton than Washington. He also presents himself as a "unity candidate".
The looming battle between Farage and a candidate with a tongue-in-cheek slogan "Make Earth great again" has triggered huge international media interest.
And as Britain's political landscape fragments, Binface has become more than a comic sideshow.
For Farage, "while it's embarrassing for him to win against a dustbin, and not the mainstream parties, he will return as MP", said Catherine Barnard, a political expert at Cambridge University.
But she added there "are some indications that Nigel Farage is worried that he will not win as comprehensively as he wants to".
Even former prime minister Keir Starmer had one last dig at Farage in parliament, saying: "My advice to everyone is put your vote in the bin".
