Russia releases former US Marine reported in poor health
- Published
President Donald Trump said a former US Marine held in a Russian prison, whose health was reportedly in extremely poor condition, has been released.
"After my discussions with President Vladimir Putin, Russia has agreed to release him, very much on a Humanitarian Basis," Trump wrote on Truth Social, adding that no prisoner swap took place.
Robert Gilman, who is from Massachusetts, was arrested in 2022 for allegedly kicking a police officer while aboard a train. He had recently been moved from prison to a civilian hospital in Russia after going into a catatonic-like state.
Gilman was on a flight back to the US accompanied by his mother, doctors, and members of the administration.
The BBC understands Gilman is expected to arrive early on Wednesday morning at a US military hospital in Texas where he will be assessed and treated.
Trump said he spoke to Gilman on the phone, "and he had one request — A GREAT cheeseburger when he lands. I will take care of that!"
"During my Administration, we have prioritised bringing home Americans detained abroad, and have done so at a level never seen before," Trump added.
Gilman's health was in "life-threatening condition" after he was subjected to "harsh and abusive treatment", his family said in a statement.
"The Russians treated my brother so badly. They hurt him for no reason, other than that he was both and American and a Marine," his sister, Lexi Hudson, said.
"I am so grateful to President Trump for saving my brother's life," she added.
Massachusetts Senator Ed Markey also helped secure her brother's release, she said.
In a statement, Markey said: "Approximately 50 days ago, Robert was diagnosed with a dissociative stupor - a condition where he is non-responsive and unable to interact or eat. "
Kieran Ramsey, chief investigative officer for Global Reach, the advocacy group representing the former Marine, told Reuters that Gilman was released because the Russian government realised "they're not losing any geopolitical power position by releasing him. This is a humanitarian release".
Gilman served in the US Marines for a year until August 2020.
He was arrested for allegedly kicking a police officer while drunk aboard a train to Moscow in January 2022 and was initially given a sentence of three and a half years.
He was later found guilty of assaulting prison guards, after he allegedly attacked a prison inspector during a cell check. His sentence was increased to 10 years.
In Russian confinement, Gilman was subjected to repeated harassment, including forced exercise training sessions that lasted up to 16 hours and the administration of psychotropic drugs, Eric Lebson of Global Reach told CBS, the BBC's US media partner.
The abuse was so severe that at one point Gilman had required a feeding tube in his nose, according to Lebson.
He said five other Americans remain in Russia, each contending with medical issues. Their names are Aleksandr Antonov, David Barnes, Olga Jezler, Andre Khachatoorian and Chuck Zimmerman.
"While we appreciate this positive step, we are still seeking the immediate return of all other unjustly detained Americans," Secretary of State Marco Rubio wrote on X.
"The President will not stop until all unjustly detained Americans are home," he continued.

NEW DELHI: Supreme Court on Tuesday asked the Union ministries of home affairs and electronics and information technology to take urgent steps to create a URL-specific and judicially supervised emergency mechanism to protect citizens from grave unlawful digital content.While disposing of a PIL by advocate N K Goswami, a bench headed by CJI Surya Kant said the petitioner in public interest had highlighted the danger from digital threats of violence, doxxing, exposure of minor children’s private details, non-consensual intimate/deepfake content and identity-manipulating digital impersonation.
The SC bench, also comprising Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana, said such cyber crimes severely impacted an individual’s right to freedom of speech, the right to dignity, privacy and the right to life.It said the petitioner had highlighted protections against such threats using internet, digital mediums and Artificial Intelligence existing in other countries and suggested to the govt to consider problems highlighted in PIL for urgent remedial measures.Goswami said given the misuse of AI and proliferation of social media and its reach, it was urgently required to create “a constitutionally compliant emergency mechanism against grave unlawful digital harms, namely specific threats, doxxing, unauthorised exposure of children’s private details, non-consensual intimate or Al-generated morphed content, and deepfake/digitally manipulated impersonation causing immediate grave harm”.He said he neither sought a blanket ban on any speech nor suppression of political speech, criticism, satire, parody, journalism, academic comment, public-interest reporting, or legal commentary.

Romanian military divers destroyed two Gerbera-type drones found drifting near the strategic Neptun Deep offshore gas project in the Black Sea on Tuesday, Aug. 11, weeks after the NATO country began shooting down Russian drones violating its airspace.
The drones were discovered in Romania’s exclusive economic zone about 90 nautical miles – roughly 167 kilometers – east of the Black Sea port city of Constanța, acting Defense Minister Radu Miruță reported.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
A civilian vessel working in the area of the Neptun Deep project first spotted the objects and alerted Romanian authorities. A coast guard vessel carrying Romanian military explosive ordnance disposal specialists was then dispatched to the site.
Romanian personnel found two drifting UAVs along with several additional pieces of wreckage.
Bucharest contacted Ukraine to determine whether the drones could have originated from Ukrainian forces.
“The Ministry of National Defense contacted our Ukrainian partners, who confirmed that these systems did not belong to them,” Miruță reported.
Romanian authorities ordered the drones destroyed in controlled explosions because of the potential danger they posed to vessels and operations around the offshore energy project.
The precise origin of the drones has not yet been established. They were identified as Gerbera-type UAVs, a Russian-produced platform extensively used by Moscow during attacks against Ukraine, including as a decoy, reconnaissance platform and, in some configurations, an attack drone.
Austria Uncovers Sanctions-Evasion Scheme Supplying Russian Military Industry
Drones found beside strategic European gas project
Their discovery near Neptun Deep adds an energy-security dimension to a growing series of drone incidents around NATO’s Black Sea flank.
Neptun Deep, jointly owned by OMV Petrom and Romanian state-controlled gas producer Romgaz, is one of the European Union’s most important new offshore energy projects.
Production is expected to begin in 2027 and could help make Romania the EU’s largest natural gas producer.
Romania, Bulgaria and Turkey already operate a joint Black Sea task force that has cleared more than 150 drifting mines since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. In July, the three countries agreed to expand cooperation to protecting critical maritime infrastructure.
Romania increasingly confronting Russian drones
Tuesday’s operation follows a sharp escalation in Romania’s response to drones.
On July 24, a Romanian F-16 shot down a drone that breached the country’s airspace – the first time Romania had used a fighter jet to destroy such a target since Russia launched its full-scale invasion. Investigators subsequently identified that drone as Russian.
Romania downed another drone the following day and a third on July 26, when an F-16 intercepted a UAV over the Black Sea near Sulina. President Nicușor Dan condemned the repeated incursions as “inadmissible and intolerable.”
Romanian authorities said Russian drones had violated the country’s airspace more than 30 times since Moscow began repeatedly attacking Ukrainian Danube ports across the border.

Benchmark hospital room cost against 3-star hotel tariff: Panel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
23:27:14 UTC
08:27:14 KST

Hospital administrators, however, questioned the comparison.
NEW DELHI: A patient’s hospital room in a private hospital could soon cost no more than a room in a nearby three-star hotel if a key recommendation of the parliamentary standing committee on health and family welfare is accepted. In an effort to rein in soaring medical bills, the panel has proposed linking room rents in private hospitals in major metropolitan cities to the average tariff charged by three-star hotels nearby.The recommendation is part of the committee’s report on the affordability and accessibility of healthcare facilities in public and private sector, which says the absence of a transparent mechanism for fixing room charges has led to wide variations in bills. It recommended benchmarking room rents to nearby three-star hotels, while allowing hospitals to levy separate charges for resident doctors, nursing care, consumables, meals and laundry.
Beyond room rents, the panel, headed by SP MP Ram Gopal Yadav, proposed standardised package rates for common medical and surgical procedures.
Citing the 80th National Sample Survey (Jan-Dec 2025), the panel said average cost of hospitalisation was Rs 6,631 in govt hospitals compared with Rs 50,508 in private hospitals. For childbirth alone, the average out-of-pocket expenditure was Rs 37,630 in private hospitals against Rs 2,299 in govt facilities.
Hospital administrators, however, questioned the comparison. “Hotel room tariffs should not be the yardstick for hospital room rents because medical infra, staffing and support services are different,” said Dr Vinoy Kumar Upadhyay, CMD of Hope Hospital in Greater Noida.
Noting the sharp difference in treatment costs, the panel said reducing out-of-pocket expenditure should be a key priority. It called for a legal mechanism to standardise and cap charges for essential treatments and routine procedures in private hospitals, mandatory disclosure of treatment costs before admission, and a fast-track grievance redressal mechanism for complaints related to billing.Beyond room rents, the panel, headed by SP MP Ram Gopal Yadav, proposed standardised package rates for common medical and surgical procedures. It also recommended advance cost estimates for complex treatments, financial navigators to guide patients on treatment costs and insurance, and ‘Continuum of Care’ packages covering screening, treatment and palliative care under a single capped payment. It urged the Centre to raise public health spending to 2.5% of GDP, strengthen govt hospitals, expand affordable medicines, and ensure stricter implementation of the Clinical Establishments Act.
Anuja Jaiswal is a Senior Assistant Editor at The Times of India, with an impressive 18-year career in narrative journalism. She specializes in health and heritage reporting, expertly simplifying complex health information to make it engaging and understandable for readers. Her deep dives into heritage topics are well-researched, resulting in captivating narratives that resonate with her audience. Britain plans to restore direct dialogue with Russia's military leadership
Kyiv • UNN
The United Kingdom seeks to restore direct lines of communication with the Russian command to prevent incidents that could escalate into confrontations. The last high-level contact took place in 2022.
The United Kingdom seeks to restore direct lines of communication between its military and the Russian command in order to prevent incidents that could escalate into a direct confrontation. The Times reports, as UNN writes.
Details
The idea of restoring contacts emerged after an incident in June in the English Channel, when the Russian frigate "Admiral Grigorovich" opened fire after a British yacht approached it at a dangerous distance.
British officials fear that, in the absence of a direct line of communication, similar situations could quickly escalate. A representative of the British government confirmed to The Times that London is interested in restoring military contacts with Moscow.
The direct line of communication has been inactive for almost four years
According to her, the British Embassy in Russia should ensure the possibility of directly conveying London's position to the Kremlin, which helps protect British interests and prevent escalation.
Direct communication between the militaries of the two countries effectively ceased almost four years ago. The last time Russia's Chief of the General Staff Valery Gerasimov and then-British Chief of the General Staff Admiral Tony Radakin spoke was in September 2022.
In October of the same year, Russian Defense Minister Sergei Shoigu called his British counterpart Ben Wallace over Moscow's claims about Ukraine possibly using a "dirty bomb." After that, contacts at the senior military level practically ceased.
In 2024, tensions intensified after Britain expelled the Russian military attaché. Moscow responded with a similar step.

He was arrested July 23 after he was stopped while driving south on Interstate 43 in Wisconsin. According to the Milwaukee County Sheriff’s Office, Romo performed poorly on field sobriety tests before getting arrested, booked and released.
He has a court date set for Sept. 21.
Romo went to high school about 35 miles southwest of Milwaukee in Burlington, Wisconsin.

NEW YORK (AP) — Sir Rod Stewart will be unable to continue his “One Last Time” farewell tour following a coronary stent procedure and after postponing and canceling a few performances, a representative for the singer has confirmed.

====================================================================================================

Europe awaits celestial spectacle as total solar eclipse turns daylight to darkness
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
23:16:57 UTC
08:16:57 KST

Washington, DC — A total solar eclipse will sweep across parts of the Northern Hemisphere, briefly turning day into night along a narrow path stretching from the Arctic through Iceland and into northern Spain.
The Moon will pass directly between Earth and the Sun, completely blocking the Sun's bright face for observers inside the path of totality.
Outside that band, a partial eclipse will be visible across much of Europe, northwestern Africa and portions of North America.
When and where?
The greatest eclipse will occur at about 17:46 UTC, with maximum totality lasting 2 minutes and 18 seconds near 65 degrees north latitude in the North Atlantic, west of Iceland, according to NASA.
The path of totality, roughly 294 kilometres wide at its broadest, crosses remote areas of northern Russia and the Arctic, eastern Greenland, western and northern Iceland, the Atlantic Ocean, northern Spain and a sliver of northeastern Portugal.
Cities expected to experience totality include Reykjavik, Leon, Zaragoza, Bilbao, Valencia and parts of the Balearic Islands.
In Spain, the event occurs low on the western horizon shortly before sunset.
Nearly 1 billion people live in areas where at least part of the eclipse could be visible, including about 15 million within the narrow path of totality.
Coverage reaches more than 90 percent across much of western Europe and approaches 99 percent near Madrid and Barcelona, which lie just outside the total path.
Partial views extend to parts of Alaska, northern and eastern Canada, and the northeastern US.
This marks the first total solar eclipse visible from mainland Europe since 1999 and the first over the Iberian Peninsula in more than a century.
It is the only total eclipse Iceland will experience this century.
Why it matters
Total eclipses briefly expose the Sun's outer atmosphere, or corona, which is normally invisible against the Sun's glare.
Scientists use the rare alignment to study solar activity that shapes space weather on Earth.
NASA-funded teams plan to track the Moon's shadow using a high-altitude research jet and scientific balloons launched from Iceland to study how the sudden darkness affects the atmosphere.
"From our unique perspective on Earth during a total solar eclipse, scientists can study the Sun's corona in a way we can't from anywhere else in the solar system," Kelly Korreck, eclipse programme manager at NASA headquarters, said in a statement.
"The Sun impacts our daily life, satellites, and astronauts in space, and we can take advantage of this moment to advance our understanding of that influence."
Amir Caspi, a researcher involved in NASA's eclipse studies, said each eclipse offers new data.
"The Sun is always changing," Caspi said.
"Every eclipse is different. So we could see things we didn't see before."
How to watch and photograph safely
Experts stress that it is never safe to look directly at the Sun without certified eclipse glasses, except during the brief seconds of full totality.
Regular sunglasses do not offer adequate protection.
NASA recommends eclipse glasses that meet the ISO 12312-2 international safety standard, or an indirect method such as a pinhole projector.
Can you photograph the eclipse safely with your phone? Yes, but precautions are required.
Pointing a smartphone directly at the Sun during partial phases without protection can damage the camera sensor, just as concentrated sunlight harms human eyes.
Holding a spare ISO-certified solar filter or eclipse lens over the phone camera lens is necessary during all partial phases.
Only during the brief window of 100 percent totality — when the Sun is completely covered — can eye protection and camera filters safely come off to capture the glowing corona.
Cameras, telescopes and binoculars require their own professional solar filters to avoid permanent equipment damage.
Annual Perseid meteor shower
Iceland has leaned heavily into the rare event.
In Hellissandur, on the Snaefellsnes Peninsula, organisers are hosting the Iceland Eclipse festival with live music and talks from scientists and astronauts timed around totality.
Cruise operators have scheduled voyages along the Iceland-Spain corridor, and tourism authorities have published viewing guides as hotels and rental cars near the path have filled up in recent months.
The eclipse also coincides with the annual Perseid meteor shower, giving skywatchers a secondary celestial event overnight.

Forgot to do the census? There's still time to complete it before you get fined
Have you completed the census yet?
Technically, census night was last night, but that doesn't mean you've missed the boat.
What happens if you don't do the census?
Don't worry, you can still complete the census.
"There is still time to complete your form after census night," an Australian Bureau of Statistics spokesperson said.
Get to it as soon as you can and you shouldn't have a problem.
When is the census due?
As soon as possible.
Census night was on August 11, but this doesn't mean people had to complete the census on that exact date.
It just means you have to answer questions about where you were on the night of August 11.
More than 5 million Australian households completed their forms early this year and the ABS expected quite a few households to submit their forms after census night.
A report about the 2021 census said the online census form was open for about 10 weeks.
And paper forms were accepted "for as long as practicable", with the last paper form included in the census received in December 2021.
That was months after the 2021 census night in early August.
Do I have to do the census?
Yes, participating in the census is compulsory under the Census and Statistics Act 1905.
But you may not have to fill out a form yourself if someone in your household includes you and your information on the household form.
Almost everyone who is in Australia on census night must be included on a census form, including international students, visitors, visa holders and babies.
However, foreign diplomats and their families living in Australia are not included.
Is there a fine for not doing the census?
Yes, but that doesn't mean you'll be fined for being a few days late.
The ABS will contact you to encourage you to complete and submit your form first.
"We aim to get everyone to participate in the census voluntarily," an ABS spokesperson said.
If you don't respond to this gentle nudge, the ABS may serve you with a written direction to complete the census.
This is a formal legal instruction and if you fail to comply, you could be prosecuted and fined.
What is the fine for not doing the census?
If you're prosecuted for failing to comply with the legal instruction to complete the census, you could be fined up to $364 a day.
But remember, it doesn't have to come to that.
While we're on the topic of fines, it's also an offence to knowingly provide false or misleading statements or information in the census.
If you're prosecuted for this, you could face a fine of up to $3,640.
What is the point of the census?
The data gathered from the census is really important.
It helps the government plan for the future.
Information collected via the census helps the government make decisions about things like health care, transport, schools and infrastructure.
How often is the census?
Every five years.
The last one was in 2021.
Worried about what happens to your answers?
The personal information you give on your census form is confidential and protected by law.
It is not shared with anyone else outside the ABS.
This means government agencies like the Department of Home Affairs, the Australian Taxation Office and Centrelink cannot see what you have written on your census form.
The data is handled by the Australian Bureau of Statistics, which is an independent statutory authority and an official organisation trusted by 90 per cent of the general community, according to an ABS survey last year.
"We have a range of processes and protections that make sure information on census forms stays confidential," an ABS spokesperson said.
"For example, we use the strongest encryption technology available to make sure information from the online census form is secure.
"People should be reassured that organisations [other government departments and marketing companies] can't access any personal information you include on your census form."
The legislation around the census also imposes strict secrecy obligations on all ABS employees.
What if I don't want my household to see my answers?
You are allowed to fill out your own form, separate to your household.
All you need to do is call the Census Contact Centre on 1800 181 227 and someone will either provide you with a census number to complete your census online or send you your own paper form.
The ABS keeps the form with the most complete information about the person, so answer as many questions as you can in your separate form.
"To ensure your separate form is counted, we ask that you use the same name, date of birth and sex recorded at birth details as those recorded on the household form where possible," an ABS spokesperson said.
"You can then respond to other questions on the census form in the way that best reflects you."
Can I do the census online?
Yes.
You can either fill out a paper form or complete it on the ABS census website.

You will need your census number to complete the form online.

Your home should have received an envelope from the ABS that looks like this:
Inside, there should be a letter containing a census number and a temporary password.
But if you don't have a census number, you can go to this website, where you'll be prompted to enter your mobile phone number so the ABS can text you a one-time PIN and your census number.
For help over the phone, you can call the Census Contact Centre on 1800 181 227.

What is celebrated on August 12 in Ukraine and around the world
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
02:10:16 EEST
08:10:16 KST

What is celebrated on August 12 in Ukraine and around the world
Kyiv • UNN
On August 12, International Youth Day, World Elephant Day, and Vinyl Record Day are observed. According to the new calendar, the martyrs Photius and Anicetus are commemorated; according to the old calendar — John the Warrior.
On August 12, the world observes International Youth Day and celebrates the global holiday of a beloved beverage — World Elephant Day and Vinyl Record Day. According to the new church calendar, Orthodox believers commemorate Saints Martyrs Photius and Anicetus, while according to the old style, they commemorate Saint Martyr John the Warrior, reports UNN.
International Youth Day
A holiday proclaimed by the UN General Assembly in December 1999. Its purpose is to draw attention to the problems, rights, and potentials of the younger generation, as well as to emphasize their role in the development and transformation of global society.
World Elephant Day
An environmental campaign launched in 2012 to protect African and Asian elephants from poaching, the destruction of their natural habitats, and the illegal trade in their tusks.
National Mother's Day in Thailand (Birthday of Queen Mother Sirikit): An official public holiday commemorating the birthday of the revered Queen Mother Sirikit Kitiyakara, observed in Thailand as a symbol of maternal love and respect.
Vinyl Record Day
A popular holiday among music lovers, collectors, and audiophiles, dedicated to the analog sound of vinyl, which is experiencing a new wave of global popularity.
World Domination Day (Middle Child's Day / or humorous observances)
An unofficial date when one can dream of great achievements or treat oneself to a day of pleasant, ambitious plans.
Day of Commemoration of Saints Martyrs Photius and Anicetus
According to the new calendar, August 12 commemorates the uncle and nephew who suffered for the Christian faith in the 4th century during the persecutions of Emperor Diocletian. In popular tradition, this day was called "Photius and Anicetus" or "Photius Day." It was believed that this day should be devoted to cleaning the house and barn, preparing the household for the autumn season.
For those who follow the old calendar: August 12 commemorates Saint Martyr John the Warrior. In popular tradition, this day was called "Ivan the Warrior" or "Silvanus and Silas." Peasants believed that Saint John helped find stolen items and protected against thieves. Traditionally, the sowing of winter crops was also completed on this day.

Gaza rescuers begin recovering bodies from rubble of home destroyed in early days of war

Hosni Nedim, Tarek Chouiref
12 August 2026•Update: 12 August 2026
Civil Defense crews in the Gaza Strip began recovering the bodies of 13 Palestinians on Tuesday from beneath the rubble of a multi-story home destroyed by an Israeli strike during the early days of the war.
The operation is being carried out in coordination with the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) at the home of the Gharbiya family in the Al-Katiba area west of Gaza City.
Civil Defense spokesman Mahmoud Basal told Anadolu that a large number of Palestinians were killed in the strike. Some bodies were recovered at the time, while 13 remain beneath the rubble.
The victims include women, children and the elderly, he said.
Basal warned that severe shortages of heavy machinery, equipment, fuel and protective gear continue to hamper efforts to recover thousands of Palestinians believed to remain beneath destroyed buildings across Gaza.
“If we remain in this situation, we are talking about many years” to complete the recovery operations, he said, adding that adequate equipment and resources could reduce the process to a matter of months.
Basal said Civil Defense crews are working with extremely limited resources and at times “with their bare hands,” without adequate protective equipment while handling bodies, human remains and debris.
He said crews continue their work without salaries, bonuses or compensation and called on the international community, international organizations and human rights groups to provide the heavy machinery and logistical support needed to continue recovery operations.
Tuesday’s operation is part of the second phase of a Civil Defense project launched on July 19 to recover Palestinians buried beneath buildings destroyed during the Israeli war.
The 800-hour phase covers 147 destroyed homes across Gaza City and the northern and central Gaza Strip, where 1,072 bodies are believed to remain beneath the rubble, according to Basal.
During the first phase, launched in November 2025, crews recovered 333 bodies and human remains from 54 destroyed homes and buildings. Limited resources prevented them from reaching around 226 others.
Gaza’s Government Media Office said in October 2025 that around 9,500 Palestinians had been reported missing since the start of the Israeli war, including those believed to remain beneath the rubble and others whose fate remains unknown.
The Israeli army continues to target Palestinians in several areas of the Gaza Strip despite an Israel-Hamas ceasefire that went into effect on Oct. 10, 2025, killing at least 1,258 Palestinians and injuring 4,139 others, according to Gaza’s Health Ministry.
Israel has killed more than 73,000 Palestinians and injured over 174,000 in a genocidal war since October 2023. The war has also caused widespread destruction, affecting 90% of the enclave’s infrastructure.

Why Trump’s Secret Flight Was Extraordinary by Presidential Standards
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
23:08:16 UTC
08:08:16 KST

The “secret flight” that President Donald Trump took out of Turkey last month following an Iranian assassination threat, newly revealed by the Washington Post this week, marked a rare occasion for a commander-in-chief: traveling without the White House press pool.
Multiple outlets have reported, citing unnamed sources, that when Trump left Turkey after the NATO Summit last month, he secretly departed the country on an alternate plane because of an assassination threat made against him from Iran.
Publicly, the Administration said that Trump would fly out of Turkey on July 8 on an older Air Force One aircraft, and the President did board that plane in the sight of cameras and reporters on that day. But the Post reported that Trump then got into a catering truck, which transported him to another plane—all unbeknownst to the journalists who were on the former Air Force One and were under the impression that they were on the same aircraft as the President.
The clandestine operation meant that, for several hours, the President’s real whereabouts were unknown to—and concealed from—both the White House press pool and the American public.
In response to the Post’s questions about the operation, White House communications director Steven Cheung shared a statement defending the plane Trump traveled on to get to Turkey, a Qatar-gifted aircraft that drew controversy.
“The new Air Force One is a state-of-the-art aircraft that has been fitted with high-level security protocols that ensure the safety of the President and his staff,” Cheung said in the statement. “As the President has said recently, there are many enemies of America who have their sights on him, and we use every tool at our disposal to address those threats.”
Historically, the journalists who make up the White House press pool travel with—or alongside—the sitting President nearly everywhere he goes. Here’s what to know about the pool, and previous instances when a commander-in-chief has made the extraordinary move of traveling without those journalists.
What is the White House press pool?
The White House press pool is a small group of journalists from various news outlets who follow the President around to various events, such as bill signings and trips. Because there is limited space to attend these events or travel with the President, the system allows news outlets to “pool” their resources; the print reporter on “pool duty” each day shares “pool reports,” which contain notes and quotes they took down as they followed the President, with the entire White House press corps. The specific journalists who are part of the press pool rotate.
“For nearly a century, the story of the American presidency has been written through the eyes of the ‘press pool,’ the small team of writers, photographers and technicians assigned each day to cover the commander-in-chief on behalf of the broader corps of correspondents,” the White House Correspondents’ Association (WHCA), which works to coordinate and ensure access for journalists covering the White House, said on its website. The WHCA went on to say that the accounts documented by the pool “provide a daily record of the presidency that forever lives in the archives of news organizations.”
“Pool duty is an essential element of the work of White House correspondents because one never knows when the world will need good information about precisely where the president of the United States is and what he is doing at any moment,” the association continued.
Members of the White House press pool have been with Presidents during a slew of historic and high-stakes moments. They were, for instance, in the motorcade when former President John F. Kennedy was assassinated in Dallas in 1963. The press pool was also present when an assassination attempt was made on former President Ronald Reagan’s life in Washington, D.C. in 1981. On Sept. 11, 2001, amid the chaos and fear that followed the 9/11 terrorist attacks on the World Trade Center and the Pentagon, Bush traveled with a smaller press pool to a military facility and then back to the nation’s capital. Journalists have also followed Presidents—including Trump—into dangerous war zones.
When Presidents have traveled without the press pool in the past
While it is rare for the sitting President to travel without the press pool, it has happened on occasion in the past.
In 2010, former President Barack Obama left the White House without the press pool and went to one of his daughter’s soccer games, a decision that generated controversy. The Associated Press wrote at the time that Obama had “quietly breached years of protocol” by doing so.
Soon after Trump first won the presidency in 2016, but before he was sworn into the White House, he went out to dinner without notifying the reporters who were covering him. The move prompted press organizations to release an open letter to Trump, in which they emphasized the importance of the press pool.
“As the new leader of the free world, we expect that you will preserve longstanding traditions that ensure coverage of the Trump presidency,” the organizations said in their 2016 letter. “The idea of a press pool that covers all of the president’s movements is one that dates back to the Franklin Delano Roosevelt administration. Every president of both parties has treated this important tradition with respect. The role of the press pool is critically important to our country, whose citizens depend on and deserve to know what the president is doing.”
Neither of those instances were a result of threats made against Obama or Trump. The operation last month, in contrast, stemmed from a threat against the President’s life that Administration officials deemed credible enough to warrant the secrecy, the Post reported.
Air Force One has been used as a “decoy” for a President’s protection in the past: former President Bill Clinton, for instance, traveled to Pakistan in a white aircraft that followed Air Force One in 2000. But he got off the unmarked plane in Islamabad in view of cameras and journalists, revealing the covert operation. And, before takeoff, Clinton Administration officials told at least one member of the White House pool about the operation.
When Trump boarded the alternate plane in secret last month, the poolers who were assigned to travel with him were not informed that he had switched to a different aircraft—nor were they notified about the adjudged credibility of the threat on the one they were on, an official told the Post.
CNN anchor Jake Tapper emphasized on Tuesday the extraordinary circumstances of the clandestine operation in Turkey.
“Obviously the life of the president is paramount, and previous White Houses have used deception to protect the president’s life,” he said in a post on X. “But no officials I’ve spoken to have ever before heard of using an [Air Force One] full of [White House] staff and journalists as a decoy during an imminent threat.”
Ronald L. Rowe Jr., a former acting director of the Secret Service, told the Post that, if the President’s location is kept secret, it is for a reason.
“We need to keep the ‘secret’ in Secret Service,” Rowe told the news outlet. “The public should know what the president is doing on a daily basis, but when it comes to the methods by which the Secret Service keeps the president safe, that should remain out of public view.”
Robert McDonald, who worked with the Secret Service for more than two decades, told TIME that the operation in Turkey appears to be a result of real-time improvisation by the President’s security team. He also cast doubt on the idea that the journalists who were on the former Air Force One were left at risk.
“I would find it incredibly hard to believe that those two planes weren’t escorted or with other assets from allies or the U.S. Air Force in the area,” he said.
McDonald went on to say that restricting the number of people who are informed of such an operation is standard practice, and stressed that the outcome of the mission was that everyone arrived home safe.
“Everybody that I’m aware of got home from that trip to Turkey,” he said. “The bottom line is everybody got home safe. That’s the main function of the Secret Service.”

Male redback's bizarre death somersault during sex is in its genes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
23:08:04 UTC
08:08:04 KST

Male redback spider's dramatic death somersault during sex coded in its DNA
In short:
Researchers have spotted a genetic source for the bizarre sexual cannibalism behaviour of the redback spider.
Male spiders, which somersault onto their partners' mouths to be eaten while mating, appear to inherit this trait via sex chromosomes.
What's next?
Genetic data and courtship information could help to conserve a related threatened New Zealand spider, the katipō.
Male redback spiders live fast and die young, ending their lives in a gory ritual of sexual cannibalism.
Female spiders eat their male partners while they mate, and males appear to encourage this behaviour, with their final act being a dramatic somersault onto the female's jaws.
A new study, published in Biology Letters, has pointed to a genetic source for this behaviour.
The researchers compared the activity of the Australian redback to its close, but non-cannibalistic cousin, New Zealand's katipō.
By breeding the two species together, the researchers, who are based at the University of Hamburg in Germany, learned more about the DNA behind the self-sacrificing somersault.
"Our interest in these spiders was sparked by the fact that two closely related sister species show very different mating systems," lead researcher Kardelen Uludağ said.
"This is very uncommon in animals. 
"Due to their close relatedness, the two species can be crossed and this provides the perfect opportunity to study the genetic inheritance of male sacrificial behaviour."
Bruno Alves Buzatto, a behavioural ecologist at Flinders University who wasn't involved in the research, said the findings were "very striking".
"It supports the idea that being killed during copulation and cannibalised can actually lead to the male's advantage,"
The self-sacrificial redback backflip
Loading...
Redback spiders (Latrodectus hasselti) are "monogynous": meaning male spiders mate with only one female over their lifetime.
This mating ritual is quite intricate, featuring a "somersault" so that the males' large abdomens are right next to the females' fangs for ease of biting.
Then, the male redbacks constrict their abdomens, which makes them look like they're being squeezed, so they can cheat death for long as possible.
The secret sex lives of redback spiders have been documented for decades, including research by scientists at the University of Toronto seen in the video from ABC TV's Catalyst program in 2010:
Loading...
Dr Buzatto said the self-sacrificing death dance gave males an evolutionary advantage: it improved their chances of offspring.
"The process of being cannibalised increases the time that they mate with the female. Being able to transfer more sperm to the female's spermatheca, which is the organ that the females use to store sperm, provides an advantage."
Female redbacks can store sperm and use it to lay eggs for up to two years after mating.
The katipō (Latrodectus katipo), a venomous spider native to New Zealand, is very closely related to the redback.
But katipō spiders don't engage in this cannibalistic mating ritual. Instead, males and females tend to mate with each other multiple times.
Cor Vink, an entomologist at Lincoln University in New Zealand who assisted with the study, said katipō evolved from redback spiders about 100,000–200,000 years ago: a blink of an eye in evolutionary terms.
"In that small amount of time, that whole behaviour is lost," Dr Vink said.
"It's really interesting when behaviours like that can be lost. We don't know enough about how behaviours are coded in the DNA of invertebrates."
Cross-breeding spiders to test genetics
The researchers bred male redbacks and female katipō together to see how mating behaviours were displayed in their offspring.
Dr Vink collected both species of spider from different sites in New Zealand, where the redback spider is an invasive species.
"We collected adult redbacks and then fed them up, took them back, grabbed their egg sacks and then they got sent to Germany. We did the same thing with the katipō as well," he said.
Both redbacks and katipō bites can require antivenom, but there haven’t been any recorded deaths in decades (for redbacks) or centuries (for katipō).
Dr Vink said both spider species were "shy and retiring", but he and his fellow collectors wore gloves as an extra precaution.
"When they bite you, you won't die, you'll just feel like you're going to,"
"It's a pretty horrible experience from what I've been told and I'm not willing to find out what it's like."
Once the spider eggs had made it to Germany, the researchers bred male redbacks and female katipō together and reared male hybrids to maturity.
Then, they added the hybrids to webs built by, and housing, female katipō, filming their behaviour with infrared cameras.
They analysed the footage from 104 mating rituals, looking for signs of both the somersault trick and the abdominal constriction.
Roughly half the hybrids performed the life-ending somersault while mating.
Because of the way they'd bred male redbacks with female katipō, this 50/50 split allowed the researchers to conclude the somersault trait was inherited on a spider sex chromosome.
But the other behaviour — the abdominal wiggle — wasn't displayed as clearly, suggesting the genetics for this trait were more complicated.
This surprised the researchers, who were expecting both traits to have a common genetic source.
Michael Kasumovic, an evolutionary biologist at the University of New South Wales who wasn't involved in the research, said this was a neat finding.
"Given how important both traits are to survival, we would guess that they should be strongly linked together. But they aren't, and that suggests they evolved independently. And that's really cool," he said.
"This study highlights that maybe we need to think about how different species interact and how that can lead to new traits evolving and new species appearing."
Dr Buzatto said he wasn't surprised by the study's findings.
"We know that a lot of very complex behaviours can be encoded by some fairly simple genetic basis."
But he said spider sex chromosomes were very complicated, and differed from species to species, meaning there was still much to learn.
"I feel like the more we look, the more weird and surprising things we'll find with spiders," Dr Buzatto said.
"We've probably only described and documented a quarter of the spiders that exist, maybe a third, we're not too sure … That really opens people's minds to why we find all these crazy, unusual, surprising behaviours and life histories in these animals."
Genetic research to conserve NZ's spiders
Dr Vink said this genetic research could help to protect the katipō, which is in decline in New Zealand — in part because of the redback spider.
In New Zealand, redback spiders are predating on and threatening several native species like skinks and beetles.
But the biggest threat to the rare katipō is that the two spiders can interbreed and create hybrids.
"In New Zealand, we have a very real danger of losing a species through hybridisation,"
In his own research, Dr Vink is studying redback spider pheromones to see if they can be used to control populations.
"The idea is that if we can attract enough males using the pheromone, we can reduce the male population, which will crash the overall population because males can only mate once," he said.
Research into courtship and genetics can help with this conservation technique, alongside giving researchers more data to track katipō and redback populations.

08:01:12 KST

Households living near new power pylons will have £250 a year taken off their energy bills as the UK government prepares to push ahead with more than 40 grid upgrade projects across the country.
The government has promised hundreds of thousands of homes living within 500 metres of new grid infrastructure a saving of up to £2,500 on their energy bills over 10 years in return for “hosting vital infrastructure” which will help the UK transition away from fossil fuels.
One of the biggest grid upgrade drives since the 1960s will mean communities in over 40 locations across the country will be eligible for the payments as the government hopes to prevent a backlash against increased the building of pylons and substations.
Michael Shanks, the energy minister, said the multibillion-pound upgrades, which will be paid for through household energy bills, were “a vital part of how we deliver secure, homegrown energy and unlock economic growth across the country”.
“It is a moment of national renewal – upgrading what was built largely in the 1960s for the modern age and is our route to bringing down electricity bills for households across the country,” he said.
“It’s vital we build again as a country and we are determined those communities which host pylons should benefit which is why we’re bringing down the energy bills of those hosting this vital national infrastructure,” Shanks added.
Grid companies are expected to spend up to £77bn over five years to build the new networks and power lines needed to carry renewable electricity, often generated offshore or in more remote parts of the country, to urban areas with high electricity demand.
The government confirmed the sweetener for local communities near these projects after ruling out proposals to run the new cables underground.
It said that research, commissioned by the department for energy and net zero (DESNZ), found that “building pylons remains the most cost-effective way of upgrading Britain’s outdated electricity networks” and would provide “the best value for bill-payers”.
The eligible households can expect to receive their energy bill discountsautomatically every six months via their energy supplier. The discounts will begin next year.
The government has also called on grid companies including National Grid, SSE and Scottish Power to plough millions into a fund which will be used to support projects which benefit the local communities.
Some of the biggest beneficiaries will be those living close to National Grid’s Bramford-to-Twinstead grid reinforcement project which will receive more than £4m in payments to fund community projects.
In Scotland, communities near Scottish Power’s Chirmorie overhead line project would be eligible for about £2.4m of community benefit funding.
At present, constraints in the country’s ageing grid network mean that wind and solar farms are paid to stop generating electricity if there is not enough demand in the local area to absorb the power.
The electricity system operator also pays gas plants to fire up to meet demand, and buys electricity imported from the continent via high-voltage power cables. These payments are expected to total £3bn by 2030.

Male redback spiders invite cannibalism through a ‘self-sacrificial somersault’ during sex – but why?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
23:01:12 UTC
08:01:12 KST

If you think you’ve had a bad one-night stand, spare a thought for the male redback spider, whose sole reproductive partner eats him after sex.
Male redbacks appear to invite this cannibalism through a “self-sacrificial somersault”, with new research shedding light on the genetic basis of the behaviour.
The redback, also known as the Australian black widow, is one of two monogynous widow spider species – meaning that males typically only mate with a single female.
During copulation, a male redback uses his pedipalps – two arm-like appendages – to transfer sperm to the larger female’s two sperm storage organs. He also somersaults into the jaws of the female.
“He’s pumping sperm, he flips his abdomen right over into her mouthparts and then he constricts his abdomen … to make it hard for the female to get a purchase on his abdomen. That lets him survive the first mating,” said Cor Vink, an associate professor and spider expert at Lincoln University in New Zealand.
The self-sacrificial flip is thought to help maximise reproductive success, but the males risk being eaten before they are able to transfer sperm to the female’s second storage organ.
“Ideally, males should mate with the same female two times because females have two separate sperm storage organs,” said Kardelen Özgün Uludag of the University of Hamburg, the study’s first author.
“A male needs to inseminate and plug both of them, so that he can sire all of the offspring she produces.
“If a male dies after the first mating, another male can mate with the same female and then half of the female’s offspring would be from the second male.”
To avoid becoming a post-coital meal, previous research has found that some males have developed the survival tactic of mating with immature females not yet experienced in eating their partners.
The venomous redback spider is widespread throughout Australia and has been unintentionally introduced to other countries including New Zealand, Japan and the United Arab Emirates.
Redbacks are closely related to the New Zealand katipō, which do not engage in sexual cannibalism. “In the katipō, the male inseminates the female and runs off the web – that’s the same for most widow spiders,” Vink said. “The term widow is actually a misnomer.”
Of the 31 species of widow spider, male sacrificial behaviour is only usually observed in redbacks and brown widows.
In a study published in Biology Letters on Wednesday, German researchers investigated the genetic basis for why redback males perform a “self-sacrificial somersault” during mating, but katipō males do not.
To do so, they bred female katipō with male redbacks to determine how many offspring inherited the somersaulting behaviour. Close to half of their third-generation offspring also somersaulted, leading the scientists to conclude that the behaviour was linked to a specific location on the spider’s X chromosome.
“It is quite remarkable that a highly complex phenotype such as somersaulting, which may lead to partial reproductive isolation, can have such a simple genetic basis,” the researchers noted.
“Our work shows that this highly complex cannibalistic behaviour can evolve rapidly, with very few genetic changes,” Uludag said.
In New Zealand, Vink has found evidence that interbreeding between native katipō and invasive redbacks occurs in the wild. “This is a concern because we could lose our endemic protected species just through hybridisation,” he said.
Vink, who sourced the katipō spiders for the study but was not otherwise involved in the research, described the work as an “elegant paper” that shed light on the redback’s “weird mating behaviour”.
Katipō are thought to have diverged genetically from redbacks about 100,000 years ago. “It’s really neat that they’ve lost this behaviour in 100,000 to 200,000 years,” Vink said.
“The more we know about the interbreeding, the more we know about what we can do to combat redbacks and katipō interbreeding in New Zealand,” he added.

Milwaukee County executive David Crowley stunned Democratic socialist Francesca Hong in Wisconsin's Democratic gubernatorial primary, surging to victory after polls had him down by double digits.
The Associated Press called the race early Wednesday morning, with Crowley ahead of Hong by less than a percentage point. The result is likely to take some wind out of a progressive surge that has threatened to upend Democratic politics on the economy.
Progressives, however, did score a win in Minnesota on Tuesday with Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan defeating centrist Rep. Angie Craig, D-Minn, in an open Democratic Senate primary. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt. and Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass.
Flanagan was ahead of Craig by roughly 20 percentage points with 99% of ballots counted, according to the AP.
The results come as Democrats try to recraft their identity ahead of the November midterms after crushing losses to the GOP in 2024, when Republicans led by President Donald Trump secured the White House and all of Congress. Progressive candidates across the country have been capitalizing on economic anger to win Democratic primaries — promising to tax the wealthy at a higher rate, crack down on corporate power and secure universal healthcare.
Tuesday's results present a mixed bag for Democrats. Voters in Minnesota went with a progressive, though not Democratic Socialists of America-endorsed, candidate, while Wisconsin rejected a DSA-endorsed candidate.
The outcome could signal that Democrats may temper some of their furthest-left economic policies if they take back power in November, while still pushing for progressive policies on healthcare and foreign policy that helped propel Flanagan to victory.

Sen. Darline Graham, R-S.C., will advance to a runoff election for the nomination, according to the Associated Press. Graham was appointed to the Senate to fill her brother's seat for the remainder of his term, which ends in January, and was endorsed by President Donald Trump for a full term.
Rep. Ralph Norman, R-S.C., will also advance to the runoff, setting up a showdown with Graham for the nomination later this year.
In Minnesota and Wisconsin, polls closed at 9 p.m. ET. In both states, progressive Democrats are facing off with more moderate Democratic candidates — a crucial test as the party's left flank surges across the country.

In Connecticut, former Hartford mayor Luke Bronin beat longtime incumbent Rep. John Larson for the Democratic nomination in the state's 1st Congressional district, according to the AP.

Building CBRN Crisis Ready Supply for Protection and Sustainment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
23:00:00 UTC
08:00:00 KST

Building CBRN Crisis Ready Supply for Protection and Sustainment
The next CBRN crisis will be shaped as much by supply chains, industrial resilience and public trust as by sensors and detection technologies.
When Detection Does Not Deliver Protection
Across the UK, Chemical, Biological, Radiological and Nuclear (CBRN) readiness is frequently framed as a technological problem: sensors, data platforms and modelling tools that promise earlier warning and higher‑resolution situational awareness. Yet early warning alone has never been enough to protect the public. In every major CBRN‑relevant crisis, from pandemics to contamination events, lives were shaped not only by what was detected, but by how quickly essential supplies could be moved from warehouses to people. When personal protective equipment (PPE), diagnostics and medical countermeasures are not available at speed and at scale, detection becomes a hollow milestone rather than a trigger for effective action. This structural gap remains the most significant constraint on the UK’s ability to manage a large‑scale CBRN emergency. The US’ national approach to public‑health supply chains underscores this logic.
Resilience depends on diversified sources, warm-base manufacturing capacity, the maintenance of sovereign or trusted industrial capability at a level sufficient to enable rapid surge production during crises, and continuous visibility across suppliers. Together, these levers allow systems to absorb shocks, adapt to disruption and maintain function under conditions of extreme demand. By preserving production infrastructure, skilled workforces and critical supply networks before an emergency occurs, warm-base manufacturing reduces reliance on overseas suppliers and shortens the period between warning and effective response. Britain's own assessments reach a similar conclusion. Recent parliamentary scrutiny has highlighted serious weaknesses in civil preparedness and CBRN-relevant logistics, warning that these gaps risk undermining the country's ability to operationalise early warning during crisis.
At its core, this is a crisis‑management challenge. CBRN incidents demand the rapid translation of weak or ambiguous early signals into coordinated nationwide action across procurement, logistics and public communication. Without tightly connected sensing and supply, detection offers awareness but not protection. As the UK considers how to rebuild readiness in the face of rising strategic competition and more complex hazard environments, the central question becomes clear: how do we transform sensors into supply, and signals into sustained societal and industrial resilience?
Lessons From Recent Crises: Supply and Information Failures
The COVID‑19 pandemic revealed structural weaknesses that extend far beyond infectious disease response. Across the world, shortages of PPE, diagnostics, reagents and ingredients for vaccine production amplified the impact of the outbreak, not because these products were technologically difficult to make, but because supply chains had become brittle after decades of lean procurement and extensive offshoring. The most effective corrective actions came from countries that invested in on‑shoring or near‑shoring essential manufacturing, expanded domestic capacity and created smarter, better‑managed stockpiles designed for rapid rotation and prepositioning. Britain’s evaluation of its own pandemic response reached similar conclusions.
The supply chain is always responding not only to crisis conditions but also to crisis narratives.
Yet the supply challenge was not the only systemic failure. Modern CBRN incidents unfold within a contested information environment that influences public behaviour, trust and operational decision‑making. Analyses of Fukushima wastewater narratives, Salisbury incident counternarratives and the East Palestine derailment demonstrate that mis‑ and disinformation can distort risk perception, weaken compliance with protective measures and complicate crisis communication. Policymakers and crisis managers increasingly recognise that reactive ‘debunking’ is too slow. Instead, proactive ‘pre‑bunking’, anticipating predictable falsehoods and issuing clear, uncertainty‑aware guidance in advance, has emerged as a more effective strategy.
A recurring lesson across these crises is that information without context is noise. Large, unstructured releases of technical data, such as environmental readings or dispersion models, often increase public confusion rather than improve understanding. Without translation and narrative framing, data overwhelms rather than informs. For CBRN preparedness, this information dimension is inseparable from supply: misinformation‑driven behaviours directly shape demand for medical countermeasures, public willingness to adopt protective actions and the overall tempo of emergency response. The supply chain is always responding not only to crisis conditions but also to crisis narratives.
A Dual‑Lens Model for CBRN Resilience
To protect both society and the industrial ecosystem that sustains protection, the UK must adopt a dual‑lens model that brings together:
- Fused detection and decision‑support systems on the incident side.
- Protected procurement and resilient capacity on the industrial side.
This dual‑lens approach reflects a shift in thinking: from seeing detection and distribution as separate domains to treating them as interlocking components of a single system. Only when these functions are integrated – technically, contractually and operationally – can early warning drive the necessary logistics actions in time.
Incident Side: From Detection to Orchestration
The first requirement is to fuse sensing with logistics. This means building a national Sensing‑to‑Supply Orchestrator capable of receiving detection inputs, concentration levels, deposition patterns and epidemiological indicators, and triggering three categories of response: targeted stockpile releases, demand modulation based on hazard conditions and surge manufacturing at pre‑contracted warm‑base sites. Many of the underlying mechanisms already exist in international practice, particularly in the US, where supply‑chain mapping, bill‑of‑materials transparency at the raw‑material level and demand‑linked analytics provide the basis for real‑time orchestration. Britain can adapt these principles to its own context.
A second requirement is to institutionalise pre‑bunking and embed it directly within command‑and‑control structures. During a CBRN incident, risk communication is not a parallel process but a core operational function. A dedicated Narrative Management and Risk Communication cell should issue templated updates, what is known, what is unknown and what actions the public should take, linked directly to shifts in system state. Co‑locating communication specialists with plume‑modelling and epidemiological analysts ensures alignment between technical assessments and public messaging. This approach reduces confusion, increases compliance and supports the logistics system by stabilising demand.
By combining orchestrated logistics with integrated risk communication, Britain can begin to close the gap between detection and distribution, turning early warning into timely action.
Industrial Side: Protected Procurement and Resilient Capacity
On the industrial side, the UK must treat protected procurement as a national security function rather than a commercial one. Guidance from the National Protective Security Authority (NPSA) outlines a lifecycle for high‑risk procurement, decision to outsource, supplier selection, contracting, oversight and termination, that maps directly onto the supply chains for PPE, diagnostics, reagents and other critical CBRN‑related components. Applying this lifecycle to the CBRN domain requires policies that address several distinct threat vectors.
The first is geographical and legal exposure. Offshoring data, intellectual property or component manufacturing can expose British capabilities to foreign legal regimes and involuntary state access. Contracts must enforce UK or EU data residency, restrict cross‑border transfers of sensitive IP and include mandatory notification clauses if changes in ownership or jurisdiction occur.
The second is hostile ownership, control or influence. Foreign direct investment can create vulnerabilities if suppliers fall under incompatible legal systems or coercive state power. Due‑diligence processes must examine ownership chains, board structures and ultimate beneficial owners. Contracts should enforce change‑of‑control notification rights and allow early termination if unacceptable risks emerge.
A third vector is insider, cyber and technology risk. This includes compromised personnel, privileged system access by third parties and insecure digital infrastructure that provides pathways into operational technology. Procurement frameworks should require elevated personnel screening, strict access controls and provenance assurance for operational equipment. They should also mandate hardened industrial‑control systems for suppliers involved in critical manufacturing or cold‑chain logistics.
Finally, physical security remains essential. Suppliers must meet baseline standards for storage, transport and site protection. Cold‑chain and contract manufacturing organisations, especially those providing vaccines or antidotes, must be stress‑tested to ensure they can operate under disrupted conditions.
Together, these controls form a protected procurement architecture that reduces vulnerabilities, increases industrial resilience and strengthens the UK’s ability to supply critical capabilities during crisis.
Aligning UK Policy with European and NATO Instruments
Alongside domestic reforms, Britain must integrate its CBRN supply‑chain strategy with wider European and NATO priorities and frameworks, such as the NATO Support and Procurement Agency. Parliamentary assessments have identified urgent UK capability gaps in civil preparedness, air and missile defence, space resilience, and logistics, warning that the window to address them is rapidly narrowing.
These findings emphasise the need to connect national CBRN capabilities with broader European industrial instruments such as SAFE (Strategic European Funding for Defence) and the European Union Permanent Structured Cooperation’s Military Mobility initiative. These mechanisms support standardisation, improve cross‑border movement of materials and provide joint procurement opportunities that are essential for scaling production during surges in demand.
For the UK, alignment means several things. Distributed sensing networks must meet European interoperability requirements. British suppliers should have access to joint procurement frameworks that allow rapid expansion during crises. And logistics corridors linking detection, stockpiles, warm‑base manufacturing and distribution must align with cross‑border mobility standards. By embedding CBRN supply chains within these frameworks, Britain can strengthen readiness while maintaining a NATO‑first posture.
The Resilience Triad: Turning Principles into Practice
Operationalising resilience requires a practical model. The Resilience Triad, Robustness, Agility and Visibility, offers a simple but effective framework.
Robustness demands diversified sourcing and geographic redundancy for raw materials and finished goods. Ethical and sustainable production standards strengthen long‑term resilience, and investment in automation can make domestic PPE lines more competitive against subsidised imports.
Agility depends on maintaining warm‑base manufacturing for PPE, diagnostics and key components; designing interchangeable devices to simplify supply; rotating stockpiles with partners to avoid expiry; and applying demand‑management methods that guide conservation during high‑stress periods.
Visibility requires continuous supply‑chain mapping, analytics and forecasting. Publishing a national resilience ‘scorecard’ creates accountability and helps target investment in weak areas.
Embedding these components within a strengthened governance structure, one that links epidemiological triggers to allocation, rotation, surge and risk communication, turns resilience from a slogan into a system.
Case Vignette 1: Fukushima – When Lack of Context Undermines Trust
The Fukushima incident illustrates how inconsistent or poorly contextualised data releases can undermine public confidence even when technical systems function.
If Britain can make its supply chains as instrumented, agile and responsive as its sensors, the next CBRN alert need not be a sign of impending failure.
Early reluctance to release predictive fallout data and later mass distributions of unfiltered information created confusion that, in some cases, directed evacuees towards higher‑risk areas. Years later, outdated images and misinterpreted graphics fuelled misinformation about wastewater discharge. The core lesson is the importance of visibility and context: without clear narrative framing, data alone cannot support public decision‑making.
Case Vignette 2: Salisbury – Narrative Competition in a Domestic Incident
The Salisbury incident demonstrated how quickly state‑linked influence campaigns can exploit an information vacuum. While the UK eventually developed a more adaptive communications posture, initial inconsistencies allowed alternative narratives to proliferate. A surge in automated bot activity complicated the information environment and shaped public perception. The episode illustrates the need for early, consistent messaging with auditable communication chains, especially during CBRN events where public behaviour directly affects operational priorities.
Recommendations: Five Near‑Term Actions
- Mandate Bill of Materials Transparency
Require full material‑level reporting for all licensed CBRN‑relevant products. This enables proactive identification of supply constraints and earlier surge triggers.
- Establish a National Sensing to Supply Orchestrator
A single, joint unit across government, health services and industry should manage stockpile allocation, warm‑base manufacturing and demand modulation. This provides the connective tissue between detection and distribution.
- Institutionalise Pre‑Bunking Within Command & Control (C2)
Integrate risk‑communication specialists into operational structures to provide consistent, uncertainty‑aware public updates. Align these messages with technical assessments and hazard thresholds.
- Implement Protected Procurement Minimums
Enforce data‑residency requirements, ownership‑change notifications, personnel‑security baselines, provenance controls and cold‑chain stress tests across all CBRN‑related contracts.
- Adopt Targeted, Rotational Stockpiling
Create vendor‑managed and virtual stockpiles in high‑risk regions and publish an annual resilience scorecard aligned with civil‑preparedness standards.
Conclusion: Protection Through Distribution
The UK must reframe CBRN resilience as a discipline centred on protection through distribution. Early detection matters, but the decisive capability is the ability to move supplies at speed, under pressure and in the face of contested narratives. A resilient system integrates sensors with supply chains, risk communication with analytics and industrial capacity with protected procurement. Aligning these elements with European and NATO frameworks enhances readiness and ensures interoperability across borders.
If Britain can make its supply chains as instrumented, agile and responsive as its sensors, the next CBRN alert need not be a sign of impending failure. Instead, it can become the moment when a well‑rehearsed, well‑coordinated and well‑supplied system moves into action—protecting people and preserving the industrial foundations on which national resilience depends.

Episode 126: Energy on the Frontline of European Security

Episode 126: Energy on the Frontline of European Security
Energy is no longer the preserve of the business pages and is central to questions of European Security.
Disruption to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz has left European gas prices far above where they sat at the start of 2026 and reserves are lower than where they need to be for winter.
Jet and diesel markets are tighter than at any point since 2022.
And, across the North Sea, unexplained drones and loitering vessels have become a routine feature of offshore operations.
In this episode, Andrew Gee, Director, International Security at RUSI, is joined by Amund Vik, senior advisor at Eurasia Group and former head of strategy and policy for the Norwegian Labour Party, and Petras Katinas, a research fellow in climate, energy and defence at RUSI Europe.
They discuss the following core questions:
- How exposed will the United Kingdom and Europe energy markets be this winter and is more North Sea energy production any kind of solution?
- Who does Europe now depend on for its energy? Is that reliance a partnership or a vulnerability?
- If energy infrastructure is now a target, what does defending it require? Would a turn to civil nuclear power change the picture?

Romania tested the Sahara cruise missile for the first time, aiming to make it the &quot;smartest in the world&quot;
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-12
01:59:07 EEST
07:59:07 KST

Romania tested the Sahara cruise missile for the first time, aiming to make it the "smartest in the world"
Kyiv • UNN
Romanian company Oves Enterprise conducted the first tests of the Sahara cruise missile, which they plan to make the "smartest in the world." The missile weighs 55 kg, has a 10 kg warhead and a range of up to 200 km, and is also equipped with the Nemesis AI artificial intelligence system.
The Romanian private company Oves Enterprise reported the first successful tests of the Sahara cruise missile, which is being developed as a long-range weapon. Defense Express reports this, according to UNN.
Details
The company stated that its goal is "to create the smartest cruise missile in the world." At the same time, no video of the actual test was released, and the report was accompanied by artistic depictions of the missile's flight and a tank being hit.
According to preliminary data, the Sahara weighs approximately 55 kg, has a 10-kg warhead, and a range of up to 200 km. It is planned for use against tanks, air defense systems, ammunition depots, command posts, and communications systems.
The Romanian missile has received artificial intelligence
The developers are also working on longer-range versions of the Sahara. They are expected to have ranges of 500-600 km and 900-1,100 km, respectively, and may also receive more powerful warheads.
One of the missile's features is reportedly the Nemesis AI artificial intelligence system. It is intended to ensure rapid adaptation to the flight mission and increase the satellite navigation system's resistance to interference.
At the same time, Defense Express notes that the use of artificial intelligence in modern missiles is already becoming common practice. Therefore, the claim that this is the "smartest" missile in the world should currently be viewed primarily as the company's marketing statement.
The Sahara project became known in the autumn of 2025. The development is a private initiative of Oves Enterprise: by that time, €1 million had already been invested in the project, while another €2 million was planned for testing and further development of the missile.

Iran to become member of BRICS Bank, increasing economic cooperation, trade - report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-11
22:57:35 UTC
07:57:35 KST

Iran is going to become a member of the BRICS Bank, Governor of the Central Bank of Iran Abdolnaser Hemmati said, state media reported on Tuesday evening.
BRICS is an organization made up of eleven countries: Brazil, China, Egypt, Ethiopia, India, Indonesia, Iran, Russia, Saudi Arabia, South Africa and the United Arab Emirates. It is an economic and geopolitical bloc that focuses on trade and development.
The New Development Bank (BRICS Bank) is a "multilateral development bank established by BRICS with the purpose of mobilizing resources for infrastructure and sustainable development projects in emerging markets and developing countries," its website explains.
Hemmati announced that Iran was set to join the BRICS Bank in the near future, Iran's semi-official Tasnim News Agency reported.
Iran expects the BRICS Bank to provide economic benefits
"Productive cooperation has commenced between our country and India in the areas of monetary affairs, banking, and the digital economy," Hemmati said.
The next BRICS Summit will take place in September. The governor said, "The BRICS summit offers a prime opportunity to meet with officials from member nations with whom our country maintains its most extensive monetary and banking exchanges and interactions," Tasnim reported.
"We believe that BRICS member nations can conduct trade using their national currencies, and we are pursuing bilateral and trilateral monetary cooperation with these members."
Iran's economy in crisis after war with US
Iran’s wartime economic crisis has triggered mass layoffs across multiple industries, with Iranian officials estimating that some two million people have lost work “directly or indirectly” due to the conflict and a prolonged nationwide internet blackout, according to a report by The New York Times.
Businesses across Iran have begun laying off workers as the country’s economy struggles under the combined pressure of war-related disruptions, sanctions, infrastructure damage, and the government-imposed internet blackout.
Iranian Deputy Labor Minister Gholamhossein Mohammadi said the conflict had already resulted in the loss of more than one million jobs and left another two million people “directly or indirectly unemployed,” according to statements given to Tasnim.
Asher Smith contributed to this report.

In the central cities of the Brazilian Amazon, mainly Manaus and Belém, local restaurants observe a century-old custom of serving a festive brunch every Sunday. The special menu includes dishes representing the diverse communities that make up Amazonian society. Alongside local dishes and others that arrived from Japan or England, two surprising additions appear: couscous and dafina, a traditional Jewish-Moroccan stew for Shabbat. They only offer a hint of the remarkable story of the Jewish community of the Brazilian Amazon.

Japan slams North Korea’s ballistic missile firing ahead of US-Seoul drills
Japan’s Defence Minister Shinjiro Koizumi called the launch a ‘threat to peace and security in our region’
2-MIN READ2-MIN
 Listen
North Korea fired a ballistic missile off its east coast towards Japan early on Wednesday, Seoul’s military said, days before the planned start of massive US-South Korea joint drills.
The 11-day exercises due to begin on Monday are a regular fixture of the summer calendar, designed to steel the United States and South Korea for defence against the nuclear-armed North.
Pyongyang calls them rehearsals for an invasion and has staged missile launches before and after them in the past.
“Our military detected at around 6am (local time) a ballistic missile launched by North Korea from the Wonsan area towards the East Sea,” Seoul’s Joint Chiefs of Staff said in a message to reporters.
The missile flew more than 700km (435 miles) over the body of water – also known as the Sea of Japan – it said, adding that Seoul and Washington were analysing its specifications.
Japan’s defence ministry also described the object as a suspected ballistic missile, adding that it was thought to have “already fallen”, without providing further details.
